Counter: age is not importance, and a stale-first ranking would put genuinely deferred ideas above newly urgent ones.

(G) RANK BY ATTENTION RATHER THAN BY CONSEQUENCE — `dec:idea-what-gets-searched-repeatedly-is-becoming-important`, recorded separately the same day. A node the user keeps circling back to may be ripening whether or not it blocks anything. NOT A SUBSTITUTE: a decision can draw attention and block nothing, or block everything and never be searched. Whether the two compose into one ranking, or are two lists, is open in both nodes and settled in neither.

WHAT IS NOT AN OPTION: deciding things to shorten the list. Anthony said the deferral is often deliberate — *"sometimes this is on purpose"* — so a mechanism whose success is measured by the pile shrinking would be optimising against how he actually works. The bound makes this concrete: a top-5 that never changes because he keeps not deciding is working correctly, not failing.

ONE THING TO SETTLE BEFORE ANY OF THESE, because "risk to the goal" needs a goal: the Project's objective is one sentence, "keep a design coherent from concept through operations", and nothing decomposes it. Risk is currently measurable only against EPOCHS, which are the nearest thing to a target the graph holds. Whether the goal itself should be modelled is a separate question this node does not open.
properties.name: OPEN — can unmade decisions be ranked as risk to the goal, bounded to what a person can actually decide in a day, when 61 of 83 of them govern nothing and so have no path?
properties.rationale:
Anthony's idea, recorded as an open question because the measurement changed what the question is. He asked for a critical path; the graph says three quarters of the undecided pile has no successor to path through, so the prior question is whether that disconnection is true or merely unrecorded.

REVISED the same session it was created, to fold in the top-5 bound he added minutes later, rather than minting a second node. The bound is a constraint on the answer to THIS question, not a new question — and given that the complaint driving all of it is a pile of 83 open decisions, answering "how do I triage the pile" by adding another node to the pile would be a poor demonstration. Recorded without a snapshot because the node had not yet been exported or committed and both versions are this session's own capture; a fold after the record ships would need `revise-design` proper.

Kept as one node rather than several because all seven options answer the same question — how to triage undecided work — and splitting them would create a set that can only be half-answered. Options are not registered as alternatives, so `undecided_decision_point` stays quiet and the loop says nothing while this is still thinking.

No approver edge, deliberately, per the brainstorm discipline: this is thinking out loud, and attaching an approver would make `loop_status` start reporting it as owed. If it becomes a real fork — most likely between (A) and (E), which are both buildable now and compose naturally under a bound — `register_alternative` is what promotes it.

Recorded WITHOUT wiring it to `req:what-next` or `cap:what-next`. Those are cited in the text and the relationship is real, but drawing edges from a musing to accepted intent would assert that this idea shapes them, which nobody has decided. That restraint is also the subject of option (B), which makes it worth stating rather than doing silently.

properties.decision: UNSETTLED, and it must be settled as ONE question rather than two. Two dev_storyflow reports a day apart ask for different fields on the same node for the same underlying reason — a Verification's qualifications have nowhere to live except its name. (A) 2026-08-07: structured RESULT fields — `exit_code`, `command`, `observed`/`expected` — so the graph can flag `status: passing` beside a non-zero exit as incoherent, and a re-run can be compared mechanically. (B) 2026-08-08: a `bounds`/`caveats` field and ideally a `grade`, plus a `findings`/`report` field, so `name` can go back to being a name and the qualifications become data the loop can reason about. Also on the table, and cheaper than either: truncate `name` in loop_status's rollup, or return `name` + `detail` separately, which fixes the READ cost without touching the schema. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT DESERVES AIRING: reflow2 already has cap:evidence-scope (what a check pinned and swept, on the VERIFIES edge per dec:evidence-scope-on-the-verifies-edge) and reconcile_verification for feeding real outcomes back, so the machinery for "evidence is structured, not prose" is PARTLY BUILT — and the honest question may be whether these are extensions of it or a second, competing home for the same information.
properties.name: OPEN — does a Verification gain structured fields for its BOUNDS and its FINDINGS, and is that the same decision as giving it structured RESULT fields?
properties.rationale: Recorded as one decision because settling either half alone would put two structured homes for a check's qualifications into the same node type, which is how a schema acquires an overlap nobody can later explain. The urgency is not theoretical: the missing field has already become fleet DOCTRINE at dev_storyflow ("carry the grading and all bounds in the node NAME"), it has made graph_report.top_gaps titles ~2,000-character essays, and reflow2's OWN loop_status digest reads the same way for the same reason. Evidence: fact:defect-a-finding-has-no-bounds-so-grading-goes-in-the-name and fact:defect-verification-evidence-is-prose-so-passing-can-contradict-itself.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-14, in the same breath as settling the page and explicitly flagged as thinking out loud: *"might even be fun to create/generate a small video explaining what reflow2 is for somebody new to it /brainstorm"*.

Nothing here is intent. It is his idea and it is recorded so it is not lost, not so it is claimed.

DISTINCT FROM the page decision on purpose: that one is SETTLED and covers what the page renders. This is an unsettled question about a different artefact, in a different medium, with a different failure mode. Folding it in would have made a decided node read as half-decided.

═══ ⭐ WHY IT IS BETTER THAN "A NICE EXTRA", AND WORTH KEEPING EVEN IF DECLINED ═══

It plausibly answers the cost he accepted one sentence earlier. `dec:idea-what-is-on-reflow2s-public-page` rules that the page carries ONLY renderings, which means **it cannot carry a hand-written "here is what reflow2 is"** — so a newcomer meets a systems-engineering view before knowing what they are looking at. **An explainer is the orientation the ruling removed.** That is not why he suggested it, and the connection is recorded as an observation rather than attributed to him.

═══ ⚠️ THE TENSION, RECORDED BESIDE THE IDEA RATHER THAN AGAINST IT ═══

**A video is the least renderable artefact there is.** The page's whole claim is that its contents come out of the graph and are periodically refreshed. A video is hand-made, expensive to remake, and therefore **the one thing on that page guaranteed to go stale** — and it would sit there asserting, by adjacency, the same provenance as the renderings around it. That is the exact failure `dec:idea-outward-docs-are-rendered-from-the-graph` was opened about, in the medium where it is hardest to fix.

⇒ Not an argument against it. An argument that **if it ships, it must be visibly a different KIND of thing from the renderings** — or the renderings' credibility pays for it.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN.
(a) **A HAND-MADE VIDEO.** Best quality, highest staleness cost, remade by hand every time reflow2 moves.
(b) **A GENERATED WALKTHROUGH DRIVEN BY THE GRAPH** — a scripted tour whose narration and visuals are projected from the same source as the views, so it re-renders with them. Closest to the page's own doctrine; unclear that the tooling exists.
(c) **NOT A VIDEO — AN ANIMATED OR INTERACTIVE RENDERING.** The loop, drawn from the graph and stepped through. `docs/loop-dag.html` already exists as a rendered page and is the nearest thing to a starting point. Keeps the only-renderings rule intact.
(d) **NOTHING, AND LET THE CONFESSIONS DO THE TALKING.** The page's honesty is the pitch; a newcomer who does not get it was not the audience. Cheapest, and consistent — at the cost of the orientation gap being real.

📌 NOT ASSESSED: whether anything in reach can actually generate (b). Nothing in reflow2 renders video, and no attempt was made to find out — recording the idea is not the same as scoping it.

⇒ SEQUENCED AFTER THE RELEASE, like the page. Nothing here is started.
properties.name: OPEN — a short generated video explaining reflow2 to someone new, and the tension that it is the one thing on the page that cannot be rendered from the graph
properties.rationale:
Recorded under the brainstorm skill because he marked it as one. The skill's rule is followed exactly: the idea is not argued down, and the objection — that a video is the one artefact on that page which cannot be re-rendered — is recorded BESIDE it as an option-shaping constraint rather than used to dismiss it. An idea killed in conversation loses its reasoning; recorded with its objection, it keeps both.

Split from the page decision rather than appended to it, per the skill's rule that several unrelated questions mean several Decisions — and because that one is now settled, so anything unsettled living inside it would make a ruling look tentative.

The connection to the orientation gap is the one thing here he did not say. It is attributed as an observation, not to him, so a later reader can tell his idea from the reason it might matter.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — Anthony thinking out loud, 2026-08-09, about using reflow2 behind a web app. Nothing here is intent and nothing has been chosen. DISTINCT FROM dec:live-tier, and the distinction is the whole point: that decision is about MANY WRITERS ON ONE DESIGN (the state-funeral case — thousands replanning one echeloned plan, which needs consensus and would mean replacing single-writer RocksDB). This is the opposite shape: N TENANTS, EACH WITH THEIR OWN graph_id AND ONE WRITER. No write contention, no consensus, no shared-store rewrite. The two cases share a tier and share almost none of their difficulty. THE SCALE STEPS ARE NOT EVENLY SPACED. 1k is a deployment problem and the design already points at it: cap:graph-registry (planned) specifies a bounded, evict-when-idle map from graph key to open design, and cap:select-graph-by-id (unrealized) lets a session name what it wants. Hold a few hundred designs hot, evict the rest. THE STEP CHANGE IS 1k TO 100k, and it is forced by one measured number: reflow2's OWN design is 1,828 nodes = a 3.8 MB export and a 33 MB store on disk — roughly 9x inflation, being RocksDB plus the tantivy index. At 100k tenants that is ~3.3 TB if all were resident, so the hot set is necessarily ~1% or less, which INVERTS the problem: cold open stops being an edge case and becomes the steady state. shared.rs budgets 30 SECONDS for a cold open today. The engineering question changes from 'hold many designs' (which the registry answers) to 'make opening a design cheap' (which it does not address at all). 100k TO 1M IS THEN HORIZONTAL: ~4 TB of cold blobs is unremarkable for object storage and the hot set grows with concurrency, not with registrations. A FIFTH ROAD, alongside dec:live-tier's four, and it fits what reflow2 already believes: OBJECT STORAGE HOLDS THE EXPORT AS THE SOURCE OF TRUTH, a node HYDRATES a RocksDB+tantivy cache on demand, and eviction is free because the cache is derived. This dissolves placement (any node can serve any tenant), dissolves durability (the object store's problem), and makes an idle tenant cost a ~3.8 MB cold blob instead of a 33 MB live store. reflow2 already has the primitive: the export is deterministic, sorted, content-hashed and self-contained — that IS a per-tenant blob, and the store is already derived rather than authoritative. WHAT IS ACTUALLY MISSING TODAY, recorded as unbuilt rather than merely absent: cap:graph-registry is planned and nothing builds it; cap:select-graph-by-id is unrealized and unverified; ver:a-session-cannot-name-another-design is PLANNED, and dec:one-process-many-stores was accepted CONDITIONAL on it, so that condition is half met; and dec:live-tier names 'no identity or authorization', which at this scale is not a gap but the product. THE FOUR WAYS TO FORECLOSE, all cheap to avoid now: (1) PROCESS-GLOBALS THAT ARE REALLY PER-DESIGN — cap:graph-registry's own text already lists graph_path, content_path, identity and write_gen as things that must become per-graph; every new static that is secretly per-design is a future migration. (2) PATH AS IDENTITY — cap:select-graph-by-id frames it correctly as 'the server maps id to path', id primary and path derived; sidecar files beside the store (.id.json, .sync.json) want to become object metadata resolved by a resolver. (3) A WHOLE-DOCUMENT WRITE ON A HOT PATH — the export being whole-document is correct for an archival action and fatal on a per-change path, which also makes BL-198 (stop serializing defaults) a SCALING decision rather than tidiness, since blob size is hydrate time. (4) BUILDING MULTI-TENANCY BEFORE PROVING ISOLATION — at this scale that is a security boundary, and retrofitting one into a running multi-tenant system is the sequencing mistake that cannot be walked back. WHAT IS NOT A PROBLEM, worth stating because it is counter-intuitive: the scaling axis is the NUMBER OF TENANTS, not the size of one design. A tenant's graph is small, so full scans, Leiden, modularity and every detector remain cheap per tenant. Single-writer-per-design is a FEATURE here rather than a limit — it is what makes N tenants embarrassingly parallel — so the box would be removing it, not keeping it. THE ONE MEASUREMENT WORTH TAKING NOW, while nothing depends on the answer: hydrate-and-index time as a function of design size (200 / 2k / 20k nodes, import to first query). Under a second for a typical tenant and the cache model is routine engineering; seconds and a read model in front becomes necessary — and that is better known before designing around the opposite assumption.
properties.name: OPEN — what does reflow2 look like at 1k / 100k / 1M tenants each holding their OWN design, and what must not be foreclosed now?
properties.rationale: Recorded under the brainstorm skill so the thinking survives without being claimed as intent. Kept SEPARATE from dec:live-tier rather than appended to it, because one node holding two questions can only ever be half-answered and these two differ in their hardest part: many-writers-one-design needs consensus, many-single-writer-tenants needs cheap hydration. Worth keeping even if none of it is built, for three reasons: the 9x store-to-export ratio is a measured anchor that decides the architecture and was not previously written down anywhere; the fifth road follows from a primitive reflow2 already has rather than from new invention; and the four foreclosures are cheap now and expensive later, which is exactly the class of thing a design graph exists to hold. Anthony's framing was explicitly about not painting into a corner rather than about building this, and the record should keep that distinction.

properties.decision: ACCEPTED on Anthony's word, 2026-08-08 — shape (a), and he named why it is the right one: it is the only option where the question STOPS EXISTING rather than being answered. No plan ever holds a number it can lose, so neither slipping nor inserting is a problem. THE RULE: a planned increment's identity names its CONTENT (`epoch:planned-read-half`, `epoch:planned-status-accounting`). The version number is not part of the plan at all. At cut time the number is derived from what actually shipped, by the CHANGELOG's own bucket table — patch for fixes, minor for a change to the shape of the tool surface or the schema. WHAT IT DISSOLVES: (1) The id churn. An id cannot be renamed, so a version-named plan guarantees either a lying id or a node replacement that breaks the snapshot trail `dec:arrival-delta` reads plan movement from. A content-named plan never needs renaming, because content is what the plan IS. (2) The slip-versus-insert question entirely. `dec:an-unplanned-cut-slips-every-later-increment-by-one` (accepted an hour earlier) and `dec:idea-an-unplanned-cut-takes-an-in-between-number` were competing answers to "what happens to the planned numbers when unplanned work takes one" — and under this rule there are no planned numbers to disturb. The slip rule is not WRONG; its subject ceases to exist. Recorded with an OBSOLETES edge rather than by un-accepting it, per dec:reopen-supersedes: an accepted Decision is never un-accepted. (3) The pressure to mislabel. With numbering decided at the cut from shipped content, semver stays honest by construction — nobody is tempted to call a shape change a patch to protect a planned number, which is the concrete harm the in-between-number idea carried (the CHANGELOG's own table says patch means the consumer updates blindly). THE OBSERVATION UNDERNEATH, which generalises past versioning: a version number is assigned LAST, at the cut, and a planned increment exists LONG before that. Baking it into the identity records a GUESS as a NAME. That is the same shape as `ver:plan-increments`' finding that a plan's content lived in an epoch's NAME as prose rather than as structure — both are a plan carrying, in its identity or its label, something that belongs elsewhere. COMPOSES WITH THE HYBRID rather than competing: content-named plans plus semver-honest numbering at cut time is the same destination reached from two directions, which is why `dec:idea-an-unplanned-cut-takes-an-in-between-number` stays recorded rather than rejected — its numbering instinct survives, only its premise (that plans own numbers) is gone. NOT CHOSEN: (b) a `version` property on DesignEpoch — smaller, but it leaves the misleading ids in place; (c) redefining the pre-1.0 buckets — cheapest to write, most expensive to be wrong about, since it weakens the one signal consumers act on blindly; (d) keeping version-named ids and reading them as birth numbers — makes every id a small trap for a future reader.
properties.name: A planned increment is identified by what it DELIVERS; the version number is assigned at the cut, from what actually shipped
properties.rationale: Raised immediately after applying the slip, because the cost was concrete rather than theoretical: four planned epochs needed renaming and none could have its id corrected, so the graph now holds ids whose numbers are one behind their content. Recorded rather than fixed — changing how the plan is ADDRESSED is a bigger act than the slip Anthony asked for, and picking (a) would re-point every future reference.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-12.

HIS WORDS: "I think the 'immutability' of satisfied requirements should be a big safety measure of reflow2 projects (including itself, which is a reflow2 project). I mean it shouldn't be impossible to change a satisfied requirement or capability, but there should be safety checks in place that make it hard to change without specific confirmation. maybe once a requirement is satisfied, particularly if it had been tested and demonstrated, should basically become a python tuple."

⭐ THE FIELD EVIDENCE IS A SECOND USER, WHICH IS WHAT MAKES THIS WORTH RECORDING. His brother Alex, evaluating reflow2 for his own work: "Yes potentially. As long as it doesn't mess with the core functionality." Anthony's read of the concern: "he really likes using reflow2 and he's concerned that we'll somehow change reflow2 away from what it currently is and what he likes." That is `rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party` arriving on its own terms — the worry is not deletion, it is DRIFT.

⚠️ WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, AND WHY THIS IS NOT IT. `req:inviolable-intent` is ACCEPTED and covers the same family: "intent that no downstream decision may trade away — a key performance parameter... COMPUTE a violation rather than rely on anyone remembering... A KPP that nothing checks is a comment." But a KPP is DECLARED — opt-in, stated up front, about a THRESHOLD VALUE. Anthony is describing something EARNED — a requirement acquires protection by having been satisfied and demonstrated, retrospectively and automatically, and it is about the requirement's TEXT and STATE rather than a numeric threshold. The KPP protects what you said mattered; this would protect what you have already built and proven. Alex's concern is the second one, and it has no mechanism.

═══ WHAT PROTECTION ACTUALLY EXISTS, MEASURED 2026-08-12 ═══

  accepted requirements                              110
    with a satisfier carrying a PASSING check    102  (92%)
  unproven_capabilities (built, no passing check)     0
  unexamined_claims                                   0

STRONG, AND REAL: delivery is COMPUTED from the golden thread rather than asserted (`req:completion-computed`), so breaking the code reds a check and removing the capability fires `unsatisfied_requirement`. And `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` means no agent can move a requirement off `accepted` — which is the guarantee that matters most while reflow2 is built by agents.

🛑 BUT THE HOLE IS EXACTLY WHERE ANTHONY IS POINTING, and it was measured rather than supposed. In this session an agent appended **+4,770 characters** to `req:recursive-black-box-decomposition` — more than doubling its statement — and afterwards:

  ChangeEvents pointing at it .... 0
  Snapshots of it ............... 0
  status ........................ still `accepted` throughout

⇒ **STATUS IS GUARDED AND CONTENT IS NOT.** A satisfied requirement can be reworded, narrowed, hedged or quietly scoped down while continuing to read as satisfied, and nothing signals it. That is precisely the drift Alex fears, and "immutable" is not currently the right word for it.

📌 A SECOND, WEAKER-THAN-IT-LOOKS SIGNAL: 37 of 139 verifications have NEVER RUN. reflow2's own tripwire says why that matters — "a status is a property any hand can set to `passing` in a single call, and a failing test is not." So freezing on `verified` would sometimes freeze on a claim rather than a result, and "tested and demonstrated" needs to mean the run, not the field.

═══ THE OPTIONS, none taken ═══

A — REFUSE AND NAME, on revising a requirement that is accepted + satisfied + carrying a passing check. The two-sided accept shape already used by `set_artifact_checksum` and by the search-first guard: the write is refused, the refusal names what it protects and the deliberate route through. CHEAP, and it reuses a pattern this project has shipped twice. EXPENSIVE, and the lesson is recent and hard-won: search-first's own record says "a check that refused often would be routed around, and a rule people route around is worse than no rule." Legitimate sharpening happened SIX times in this session alone; a wall would have blocked all of it.

B — SNAPSHOT-FIRST, ENFORCED. Do not block the change; require that it leave a trace — a Snapshot and a ChangeEvent — so a reworded requirement is visible and attributable. `revise-design` already prescribes exactly this and nothing enforces it, and `req:a-discipline-is-delivered-at-the-tool-not-in-a-catalogue` already establishes that a revision with no snapshot is COMPUTABLE FROM GRAPH STATE ALONE. So the machinery exists and is simply not wired to requirement text. CHEAPEST HONEST OPTION, and it answers Alex's actual worry ("will I be able to SEE it") rather than the stronger one nobody asked for.

C — A STORED MUTABILITY CLASS, literally the tuple: a property marking a requirement frozen. Explicit and readable. EXPENSIVE: it is stored state that can disagree with reality, which `dec:certainty-derived` argues against — and it would need setting, which is one more thing to forget.

D — DERIVE THE CLASS, never store it: "protected" IS accepted + satisfied + verified-by-a-check-that-has-actually-RUN. Automatic, no new vocabulary, no opt-in, and it degrades honestly — a requirement whose check never ran is simply not protected yet, which is true. Fits `dec:certainty-derived` exactly. EXPENSIVE: it makes protection a moving target, so the same edit is refused today and allowed tomorrow depending on a check's last run.

⇒ B AND D COMPOSE, and are probably the shape: derive the class (D), and let it govern how loudly a change must announce itself (B) rather than whether it is allowed at all.

═══ THE HONEST COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside the idea ═══

REFLOW2 DEVELOPS ITSELF, AND SHARPENING SATISFIED REQUIREMENTS IS NORMAL, VALUABLE WORK. Six requirements were legitimately extended in this session — with measurements, field evidence and cross-references that made them better. Any mechanism that treats "the text changed" as suspicious will fire constantly on exactly the work that improves the design, and the project's own history says such a rule gets routed around. The distinction that has to be drawn, and it is not obvious: SHARPENING (adding evidence, narrowing ambiguity, recording what was learned) versus WEAKENING (removing a clause, lowering a bar, scoping out something that was promised). Nothing in the graph can currently tell those apart, and an agent asserting which one it just did is exactly the self-report this project distrusts everywhere else.

NOT DECIDED. The narrow question worth answering first is much smaller than the framing: **should a revision to a satisfied requirement be required to leave a trace?** That is option B alone, it needs no new vocabulary, and it turns "nothing can break it silently" from a claim into a checkable property.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SHARPENED SAME DAY — THE UNIT IS THE THREAD, AND THE TRIGGER IS OPERATIONAL
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony corrected the framing above, and the correction is the substance:

"when I'm describing a immutable satisfied requirement, I'm discussing the whole 'chain' as a thread becomes immutable. say I brainstorm an idea, then it leads to an accepted proposal which leads to a requirement which leads to a design to meet that requirement which leads to implementation which leads to test which leads to fielded implementation. basically the whole thread should be immutable or heavily guarded against any changes to it because the thread has been confirmed as 'operational'."

⭐⭐ TWO THINGS CHANGE, AND BOTH MAKE IT A BETTER IDEA THAN THE ONE ABOVE.

(1) THE UNIT IS THE THREAD, NOT THE NODE. Not "this requirement is frozen" but "this Decision → Requirement → Capability → Artifact → Verification → fielded deployment is frozen, as one thing". That is the golden thread reflow2 already computes, extended at the far end into `cmp:fielded` / DEPLOYED_TO / Environment. It is ALREADY TRAVERSABLE: `propagate_change` walks exactly this structure to compute a blast radius, so "what is in this thread" needs no new machinery — only a state.

(2) THE TRIGGER IS OPERATIONAL, NOT SATISFIED. And this ANSWERS THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT recorded above rather than dodging it. The objection was that sharpening satisfied requirements is normal, valuable work — six were extended in this session alone. But almost all of that sharpening happens on intent that has NOT been fielded: recording what was measured, narrowing an ambiguity, cross-referencing. Once something is running in front of users, the calculus genuinely inverts, and the friction stops being a cost and starts being the point.

⭐ THIS IS BASELINING, AND IT IS ANTHONY'S OWN DISCIPLINE. In acquisition terms a fielded thread is a configuration item under a product baseline: changes stop being edits and become change requests. reflow2 ALREADY HAS BASELINE VOCABULARY and it stops short of this exact thing —
  `epoch_type: baseline` on DesignEpoch, and "an Anchor is a checksummed baseline epoch";
  `as_checksum`, "frozen at cut time, so later baseline moves do not rewrite what a past release contained";
  `Artifact.checksum`, the baseline drift detection compares against.
So reflow2 baselines EPOCHS, ARTIFACT CONTENT and RELEASE MANIFESTS — three things — and has no notion of a baselined THREAD OF INTENT. That is the gap this names, and it is the SE-native framing of it.

═══ THE MEASUREMENT THAT SIZES IT, taken 2026-08-12 on reflow2's own design ═══

  accepted requirements                                110
    thread complete AND shipped in a deployed release   67   <- would be frozen
    thread complete but not in a deployed release        4
    incomplete thread                                   39
  deployed releases 1 (v0.28.0) · artifacts shipped 228

🛑 SO THIS IS NOT A CHEAP RULE. **61% of accepted intent would come under configuration control immediately**, not the handful I assumed when I speculated it would cost almost nothing. That cuts both ways and both are worth stating: the safety net would cover the majority of the design from day one, which is what makes it worth having — AND the friction is real, immediate and unavoidable rather than something that arrives gradually as the design matures.

📌 AND THE FRIENDLY READING OF THAT NUMBER: it is high because reflow2 SHIPS. A design that never released would have zero frozen threads and would feel unconstrained — which is correct, because it has promised nobody anything yet. The rule's cost scales with how much you have actually fielded, which is the right shape for a safety measure.

═══ WHAT THIS STILL DOES NOT ANSWER ═══

- WHAT COUNTS AS OPERATIONAL. Above, "shipped in a release whose status is `deployed`" was used as a proxy. Whether that is the right bar, or whether it needs an Environment of a particular kind (`env:production` versus `env:dev`), is undecided — and reflow2's own design lists `env:dev`, `env:ci` and `env:container`, so the proxy would freeze threads that only ever ran on a laptop.
- WHAT A CHANGE TO A FROZEN THREAD ACTUALLY COSTS. Refusal with a named override, a required Snapshot and ChangeEvent, a second approver, or simply a loud finding. The four options above still apply, now scoped to the thread rather than the node.
- WHETHER FREEZING PROPAGATES INWARD. If a thread is frozen, is its Artifact frozen — i.e. does the CODE become harder to change too? That is either the most valuable part of the idea or the point at which it becomes unusable, and nothing here settles which.
- AND THE SHARPENING-VERSUS-WEAKENING PROBLEM IS UNCHANGED. Even on a frozen thread, adding a measurement is not the same act as removing a clause, and the graph still cannot tell them apart.

NOT DECIDED. The narrow first question recorded above — should a revision to a satisfied requirement leave a TRACE — remains the cheapest thing that moves toward this, and it is a prerequisite either way: a thread cannot be shown to have changed if its nodes can change without recording it.
properties.name: OPEN — should a requirement that is satisfied AND demonstrated become tuple-like: still changeable, but not without specific confirmation?
properties.rationale:
Captured from Anthony's tuple framing and from Alex's concern, which is field evidence from a second user evaluating reflow2 for real work — the worry is drift rather than deletion. It is recorded as a new node rather than folded into req:inviolable-intent because that requirement covers DECLARED inviolability (a KPP, opt-in, about a threshold) and this is EARNED (automatic, retrospective, about a requirement's text and state). The load-bearing measurement is that status is guarded and content is not: a satisfied requirement's statement grew by 4,770 characters in this session with zero ChangeEvents and zero Snapshots recording it.

SHARPENED the same day by Anthony's correction that the unit is the THREAD and the trigger is OPERATIONAL, which answers the counter-argument rather than dodging it: sharpening happens before fielding, and the calculus inverts after. Measured on reflow2's own design, 67 of 110 accepted requirements have a complete thread shipped in a deployed release — so this would place 61% of accepted intent under configuration control immediately, which is far more than the handful assumed when the cost was first guessed at.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-06: "maybe a .mcp.json could have the graph_id for reflow2, dynograph-foundation, and flo2...so when any design decision is made, reflow2 can utilize all 3 graphs?"

⭐ EXTENDED THE SAME DAY, AND THE EXTENSION IS WHAT MAKES IT AN ARCHITECTURE RATHER THAN A CONVENIENCE. Anthony's second pass: "projectC is dependent upon projectB which is dependent upon projectA and these are all managed by user1. say user2 is responsible for projectD which is dependent upon projectC. user2's .mcp.json should only have the graph_id for projectC and projectD, while user1's .mcp.json should have projectA, B and C. theoretically, you could link huge projects together with multiple users only managing their respective set of projects."

THE RULE THAT FALLS OUT OF HIS OWN EXAMPLE, and he did not state it explicitly: projectC appears in BOTH configs. So a graph_id in a config does not mean one thing — THE SAME GRAPH IS WRITABLE FOR ITS OWNER AND READABLE FOR ITS CONSUMER. user1 owns C and may write it; user2 depends on C and may only read it. The set a user holds is therefore {the graphs I own → writable} ∪ {the graphs I directly depend on → readable}, and that is not a flat list of equals — it is a list with a role per entry.

THIS RESOLVES THE TENSION THIS NODE WAS RECORDED TO NAME. Option (b) below was written as the conservative choice — one writable graph, N readable. Anthony's federation makes it the GENERAL one: N writable (the ones you own) and M readable (the ones you depend on), which degenerates to (b) for a single-project owner and to today's behaviour for someone with no dependencies. Option (a) — a flat list where every graph is equal — stops being the simple choice once the roles are visible, because it is the only one that has to answer "which of these three does this write land in".

⭐ THE SCALE PROPERTY, which is the real content of "link huge projects together": NOBODY HOLDS THE WHOLE DAG. Each user holds a LOCAL CUT of it — their own subtree plus one hop outward — and the cuts overlap exactly at the ownership seams. That is why it composes to arbitrary size without any user, machine or process ever loading the whole federation, and it is a materially different claim from "one process holds many graphs" (dec:one-process-many-stores), which is about a SERVER holding tenants. This is about a PERSON holding a neighbourhood.

⚠️ THE HONEST LIMIT, and it is the thing worth deciding rather than discovering: user2 sees C but NOT B or A. If user2's need in C turns out to require a change in B, user2 cannot see that and cannot even tell that B exists. The requirement has to RELAY — user2 asks C's owner, who then discovers it is really a B problem. Whether that is a feature (bounded blast radius, matching real ownership and real org charts) or a defect (a need can stall invisibly one hop out of view) is a genuine question. The bounded reading is probably right and is how every package ecosystem already behaves; the cost is that transitive needs travel at the speed of humans, which is exactly the friction Anthony opened this whole thread wanting to remove.

AND IT SHARPENS THE AUTHORITY QUESTION NEXT DOOR: the boundary of authority is EXACTLY the shared graph. Everything dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency asks — who may write intent into a design they do not own — is now localised to the overlap, C. It is not a question about the federation; it is a question about each seam in it, asked once per seam, between two named people.

IT ALSO MAKES OPTION (c) NEXT DOOR ACTUALLY WORK AT SCALE. "The upstream pulls rather than the downstream pushes" needs a reverse index — who declares a dependency on me — which today does not exist because req:design-dependencies-declared points downward only. Under this federation the reverse index is small and local: C's owner asks who declares a dependency on C and finds exactly user2's D, never the whole world.

RELATED AND ALREADY OPEN: dec:idea-cross-org-federation asks whether reflow2 should federate heterogeneous designs across ORGANISATIONS the way OpenMBEE does, rather than composing exports. Anthony's example is the same shape one scale down — across PEOPLE rather than organisations — which is useful, because it means the mechanism can be tried on two brothers and three repos before it has to survive two companies.

⚠️ IT ALSO PULLS AGAINST A DECISION MADE TWELVE HOURS EARLIER. dec:one-process-many-stores (proposed, 2026-08-05) has each client session ATTACHED TO EXACTLY ONE graph, and carries req:a-session-cannot-reach-another-designs-graph as a SECURITY property for flo2: project A's design must be unreachable from project B's session. Both can be true, but only if the distinction is stated rather than discovered later: MULTI-TENANT ISOLATION (strangers' projects on a hosted server, must not see each other) is not the same as COMPOSITION (one author's own interdependent designs, useless apart). The federation above makes the split cleaner than it first looked — isolation is between TENANTS, composition is within one tenant's declared neighbourhood — but nothing in the design says so yet.

IT LANDS ON AN OPEN QUESTION HE HAS ALREADY LEANED ON. dec:how-a-session-is-pointed-at-a-design (proposed) records his 2026-08-05 preference — "I like this approach of just pointing .mcp.json at the graph_id" — and the counter beside it: [BL-123] holds that the /mcp reconnect is the one step an autonomous agent cannot take, so config-file selection is the option an agent cannot exercise for itself. A multi-graph .mcp.json inherits that counter unchanged.

WHAT IS ALREADY BUILT, so the gap is smaller than the question sounds. cap:composed-analysis is REALIZED: two designs analysed together without either being written to, the other's ids namespaced into an in-memory graph, every finding attributed ours / theirs / seam. describe_designs (shipped 2026-08-05) answers what design lives at a path without opening it. So "reason across several graphs" is a call you can make today; what a config would add is that it happens BY DEFAULT and WITHOUT BEING ASKED.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN.

(a) A FLAT LIST OF graph_ids, ALL EQUAL. Closest to the first phrasing. Now the weakest, because the federation example shows the entries are NOT equal and this is the only option that must then answer "which one does a write land in" at every call site.

(b) ROLES PER ENTRY — owned/writable versus depended-on/readable, which is what Anthony's own example describes. Preserves single-writer per graph, preserves the isolation property's shape, matches how every dependency manifest already works, and degenerates gracefully for the one-project case. Counter: it does not by itself serve the flo2 case, because flo2's need is for something to be written INTO reflow2 — that is dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency, not this node.

(c) NOTHING IN CONFIG — composition stays an explicit call against a dependency declared in the manifest, where req:design-dependencies-declared already puts it. Cheapest and already built. Counter: an explicit call is one somebody has to remember to make, which is the failure req:no-idea-goes-quiet exists to reject.

(d) THE MANIFEST, NOT .mcp.json, IS THE RIGHT FILE — and the federation strengthens this considerably. reflow2 ALREADY declares its dynograph-foundation dependency this way, pinned and version-checked, with ver:design-dependencies-declared passing against the real thing. A DEPENDENCY IS A PROPERTY OF THE DESIGN, NOT OF THE MACHINE SOMEBODY READS IT ON: projectD depends on projectC no matter whose laptop is open, so putting it in .mcp.json — per-machine, and gitignored in this very repo — means every clone and every teammate re-states it, which is the shadow-list failure in a new costume. The counter, and it is real: the manifest says what the DESIGN depends on, while .mcp.json says what THIS PERSON is working on, and Anthony's user1/user2 split is genuinely about people. Those may both be needed — a committed manifest for the dependency edges, a per-user config for which subtree you have in hand.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SHARPENED 2026-08-12 — THE UNION FRAMING, AND THE FIRST TRIAL EVIDENCE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, thinking out loud, and he said "it is just an idea".

HIS WORDS: "as I own both reflow2 and flo2, I'd like to get to the point I can work in either project and changes I make in one project are automatically related to one another (maybe like there are external interface nodes that for a given session, allows you to treat the union of 2+ reflow2 graphs as one graph for that reflow2 session)."

⭐ DELIBERATELY SHARPENED RATHER THAN FORKED. This is the same question this node already holds; forking would be the near-duplicate the search-first rule exists to prevent. THREE THINGS ARE GENUINELY NEW in his framing:

1. **UNION, not read-across.** Everything above is about REASONING across graphs — compose, analyse, attribute ours/theirs/seam. He is asking for the graphs to BE one graph for the duration of a session, which is a stronger claim: not "I can see both" but "there is no seam to see".
2. **EXTERNAL INTERFACE NODES as the mechanism.** A named thing in each graph that says "this is where I join". The federation model above has roles per graph but no vocabulary for the join itself.
3. **AUTOMATIC RELATING ON WRITE.** "changes I make in one project are automatically related to one another" — the existing text is read-side. This is the write side, and it is where the cost lives.

═══ THE TRIAL EVIDENCE, 2026-08-12 — the first time pairing actually computed on this pair ═══

`pair_designs` was run for real, reflow2 against flo2's committed export. Result: **paired 0, conflicts 10, unmet_needs 5, dead_surface 2, candidates 1, unclassified 2 ours / 1 theirs.** Three findings, and all three argue FOR the union rather than against it.

⭐⭐ (A) THE SEAM COULD NOT COMPUTE, AND NOT FOR A FIXABLE REASON. Zero pairs — because flo2 models `cmp:reflow2-service` as a component it CONTAINS, providing `ifc:reflow2-design-api` to its own `cmp:tool-loop`. Pairing matches complements ACROSS a boundary; flo2 drew reflow2 INSIDE its boundary, so there is no boundary. That is a legitimate model (Anthony builds that half) and it makes the seam permanently uncomputable. **A UNION DISSOLVES THIS ENTIRELY** — if the two graphs are one for the session, containment is just containment and needs no complement.

⭐⭐⭐ (B) THE STRONGEST ARGUMENT FOR THE UNION, FOUND BY ACCIDENT: TWO GRAPHS CAN AGREE BY BEING IDENTICALLY WRONG. Both designs label the reflow2 boundary `medium: REST`; both MEAN MCP, and both say so in `spec` prose where nothing computes. Had the roles been complementary they would have PAIRED — on a shared falsehood — and reported a clean seam. The tool defends against `unspecified` reading as agreement; it has no defence against both sides stating the same wrong value. **A SHARED NODE CANNOT DISAGREE WITH ITSELF.** The entire class of seam-mismatch defects (medium, auth, transport_security, payload) exists only because the contract is TWO nodes that must be kept in agreement. One node has no agreement to maintain. That is the real argument for external interface nodes, and it is stronger than the convenience one Anthony opened with.

🛑 (C) BUT THE SUBSTRATE HE WOULD BE UNIONING IS THE WRONG ONE FOR THIS CONSUMER. A backtest replayed reflow2's history against the two places flo2's hand-written tracker went stale, and measured which signal would have caught them:
  - The TOOLSNAP diff caught both input-contract changes decisively and mechanically (`inputSchema.properties` {} → {contributor_id}).
  - The DESIGN EXPORT diff buried them: 1 relevant node in 70 changes, then 12 in 103.
  - NEITHER caught the result-shape change (`suggested_fix_type` → Option) — toolsnaps record `annotations, description, inputSchema, name` and NO output schema at all.
  - ⚠️ AND THE DESIGN EXPORT ACTIVELY LIED: `cap:owed-to-a-contributor` reads `in_progress` at v0.26.1, v0.27.0 AND v0.28.0, three releases after the capability shipped, because status moves only on the owner's word and nobody went back. A subscription built on it would have told flo2 "still in progress" about working code — worse than silence.
  ⇒ **flo2 consumes reflow2's TOOL SURFACE, not its DESIGN.** Unioning the design graphs joins the wrong two things for that dependency. It would be right for a sibling consuming reflow2's INTENT. So "link two projects" is at least two different links, and the union answers one of them.

═══ WHAT THE UNION NEWLY COSTS, which the read-side framing above never had to answer ═══

- **WHICH GRAPH DOES A WRITE LAND IN?** Option (a) above was already noted as the one that must answer this; the union makes it unavoidable rather than optional. A new node created "in the union" has no home until someone says which.
- **TWO STORES, TWO LOCKS.** `req:single-writer-graph` gives each directory an exclusive RocksDB lock. A session writing across a union holds two, and lock ordering between them is a real concurrency design, not a detail.
- **WHOSE EXPORT CARRIES A SHARED NODE?** If an external interface node is genuinely one node, both repos' exports either carry it (and now disagree on every unrelated commit) or neither does (and it lives nowhere durable). This is the phantom-drift problem at repo scale, and `dec:export-once-per-pr` exists because that problem is already hard within ONE repo.
- **WHO ACCEPTS INTENT IN THE OVERLAP?** `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` is unambiguous with one owner per graph. In a union owned by one person it stays simple — which is exactly why Anthony's own case is the right first trial — and it is undefined the moment the union spans two people.

═══ WHAT IS ALREADY BUILT TOWARD IT ═══

`compose_and_analyse` is REALIZED and does the READ-ONLY union today: it imports the other design into an in-memory graph, NAMESPACES their ids so nothing overwrites, throws it away, and attributes every finding ours / theirs / seam. So the union already exists for reads and is thrown away; his idea is that it persists for a session and accepts writes. The namespacing is the part that would have to change, because a shared node is precisely one that must NOT be namespaced apart.

NOT DECIDED. ⭐ THE CHEAPEST NEXT TRIAL, since it needs no new vocabulary: take the ONE boundary that should be shared (reflow2's `ifc:mcp-tools` and flo2's `ifc:reflow2-design-api`), and see what breaks if it is treated as one node rather than two — which export carries it, what happens when one side edits it, and whether the medium disagreement becomes impossible or merely relocated.

═══ SHARPENED AGAIN 2026-08-12 — MUTABLE / IMMUTABLE, AND THE TOOL THAT ALREADY DOES IT ═══

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING. Anthony, on what happens when he does NOT own the other project: "maybe I can still import, just all changes have to be in one side of the graph. basically, treat one side as unchangeable. this is like: mutable objects can change their internal state or value after creation, while immutable objects cannot be altered once they are created."

⭐ THE FRAMING COLLAPSES THREE OF THE FOUR COSTS THE UNION SECTION ABOVE RAISED, and that is why it is worth recording rather than merely noting:
  - WHICH GRAPH DOES A WRITE LAND IN? — gone. Only one side accepts writes.
  - TWO STORES, TWO LOCKS — gone. You hold one write lock; the other side is a document.
  - WHOSE EXPORT CARRIES A SHARED NODE? — gone. Yours does, marked foreign.
  - WHO MAY ACCEPT INTENT IN THE OVERLAP? — gone, and elegantly: you CANNOT move intent in a design you are structurally unable to write. `rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word` stops being a discipline someone must remember and becomes enforced by construction.

🛑🛑 AND IT IS ALREADY BUILT. `mirror_surface` (dec:nested-graphs option (c)) mirrors another design's published surface in as FOREIGN NODES stamped with the coordinate — `mirror_of`, `mirror_content_hash`, `mirrored_at`, `provenance: imported`. Its own description states the design choice that makes the union work: "foreignness is a property of the node rather than of the link", so local components provides/consumes the mirrored Interface with ORDINARY edges and the golden thread, propagate and every detector work unchanged. `mirrors` reads the coordinate back as "a dated claim about a VERSION of another design, never a live truth". COLLISIONS ARE REFUSED rather than merged.

⇒ Under Anthony's standing triage rule this half is SATISFIED and needs nothing new.

🛑 THE MEASUREMENT THAT REFRAMES THIS WHOLE THREAD, taken 2026-08-12: **ZERO MIRRORED NODES EXIST IN EITHER GRAPH.** No node in reflow2's design or flo2's carries `mirror_of`. `mirror_surface`, `export_surface`, `pair_designs`, `seam_report` and `mirrors` are all built, shipped, and have never once been run on a real pair and kept. That is precisely `cap:built-and-consumed-by-nothing`'s shape — built, correct, consumed by nothing — found on the linking layer the same day that detector shipped.

⇒ **SO THE CONCEPT WORK HERE IS NOT SPECIFYING SOMETHING TO BUILD. IT IS DISCOVERING WHY SOMETHING ALREADY BUILT WAS NEVER PICKED UP.** On today's evidence the answer is the bilateral precondition: mirroring needs the far side to have declared a published surface, and reflow2 declared no `required` interface at all until PR #130. Neither party gets value until both have paid.

⚠️ WHAT IMMUTABILITY DOES NOT SOLVE — it RELOCATES staleness into a refresh, and refresh is where the sharp edges are:
  - A mirror is a SNAPSHOT. Immutable means you cannot edit it; it does not mean it is current.
  - REFRESH REPLACES THE IMMUTABLE SIDE WHOLESALE — clean, like updating a lockfile.
  - BUT YOUR EDGES POINT INTO THEIR NODES. If they delete or rename something you consume, a refresh leaves your edges dangling — and reflow2 now REFUSES dangling edges outright. So a refresh can fail on referential integrity. Whether that is a refusal, a report or a gap is undecided and is the first thing a trial should exercise.
  - VENDOR OR REFERENCE? Does your committed export CARRY their mirrored nodes (self-contained and reproducible, but their churn appears in your diffs) or merely NAME them by `mirror_of` + `mirror_content_hash` (small, but your export alone is unreadable)? This is the vendoring-versus-lockfile question every package ecosystem faces. `mirror_content_hash` suggests the design already leans to the first with the second's guarantee.

THE CHEAPEST TRIAL, needing no new vocabulary and nothing enduring: mirror flo2's published surface into a SCRATCH reflow2 graph and run the tool that exists. Learn what the coordinate supports, then mirror a SECOND time with the far side moved, and see what happens to edges pointing at a node that changed.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
THE TRIAL PROPOSED ABOVE WAS RUN, 2026-08-12 — AND IT FOUND A DEFECT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

The section above ended: "mirror flo2's published surface into a SCRATCH reflow2 graph and run the tool that exists. Learn what the coordinate supports, then mirror a SECOND time with the far side moved." Done. Read-only against both real stores — flo2's graph was NEVER OPENED, because opening a store writes a schema stamp and would have silently upgraded his other project from 0.27.0; its committed export was imported into a scratch graph instead.

⭐ THE FIRST MIRROR IS CLEAN, AND THE BLACK BOX IS REAL. `export_surface` on flo2 gave 5 boundaries / 13 nodes exposed, 93 nodes and 201 edges WITHHELD as internal. `mirror_surface` took it: **13 nodes, 19 edges, ZERO collisions**, pinned to `mirror_content_hash sha256:0463d397…`. What arrived was 1 Project, 6 Components, 5 Interfaces, 1 Artifact, with **5 CONTAINS edges from `proj:flo2`** plus PROVIDES/CONSUMES/SPECIFIES — i.e. A PROJECT NODE CONTAINING ITS PARTS, with its published interfaces as ports. Then `cmp:service CONSUMES ifc:reflow2-design-api` was drawn as an ORDINARY local edge into a foreign node and worked exactly as the tool's description promises.

📌 TWO DETAILS THE DESCRIPTION DOES NOT SAY. Mirrored ids are NOT NAMESPACED — `ifc:reflow2-design-api` sits beside reflow2's own ids, and safety comes from collisions being REFUSED rather than from prefixing (unlike `compose_and_analyse`, which namespaces). And the COORDINATE IS NOT ON THE NODE: a mirrored node carries only `provenance: imported`; `mirror_of` / `mirror_content_hash` / `mirrored_at` live on the mirrored PROJECT, read back by `mirrors`. So a node cannot say whose it is without tracing to its Project, and `imported` is the same value a plain restore-from-backup sets — the two are indistinguishable at the node.

🛑🛑 THE SECOND MIRROR IS THE FINDING: **`mirror_surface` HAS NO REFRESH.** The far side was moved the way a real partner moves — `ifc:reflow2-design-api` renamed to `ifc:reflow2-tool-surface`, `medium` corrected REST → unspecified — and mirrored again:

    mirrored_nodes        1
    mirrored_edges        0
    collisions           12      <- everything from the first mirror
    mirror_content_hash  null

**Twelve of thirteen ids were refused as collisions WITH THE PREVIOUS MIRROR OF THE SAME DESIGN.** The refusal is correct and protective for a genuine cross-design clash, and its message says exactly that — "Two designs using one id for different things is a naming conversation between their owners" — but that is not what happened, and the guard cannot tell the two cases apart.

THE RESULTING STATE IS QUIETLY WRONG, which is what makes this worse than a plain failure:
  - the STALE `ifc:reflow2-design-api` is still present, still `medium: REST`, still the old name;
  - the renamed `ifc:reflow2-tool-surface` also arrived, with ZERO edges (`mirrored_edges: 0`), so it is orphaned;
  - the host's own `CONSUMES` edge STILL POINTS AT THE STALE NODE, and nothing said it moved;
  - **`mirrors` still reports the FIRST hash and `mirrored_at: 2026-08-12`** — so after a failed refresh the staleness register READS FRESH. The whole value of `mirror_content_hash` is the tool's own claim that "a newer surface with a different hash means this mirror is stale", and a silent no-op leaves the consumer believing they are current when they are two changes behind.

⇒ **RE-MIRRORING ONE `mirror_of` IS A DIFFERENT OPERATION FROM MIRRORING A NEW DESIGN.** One is "replace what I hold of theirs, at a new pin"; the other is "add a stranger, and refuse anything that clashes". Only the second is implemented, and the first is what a standing subscription is made of. This is the sharp edge the mutable/immutable framing predicted — immutability makes the first import clean and relocates the whole problem into refresh — and it is worse than predicted, because refresh is not awkward, it is absent.

📌 AND IT EXPLAINS THE ZERO-INSTANCE FINDING. The layer was built, exercised on a FIRST mirror, and never run twice — so the missing half was never visible. `cap:built-and-consumed-by-nothing` finds things nothing consumes; this is the adjacent failure, a capability consumed exactly once and therefore only half-tested.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED BY THIS TRIAL, so the result is not read wider than it is: whether a refresh SHOULD replace, merge, or refuse-and-report; what should happen to a host edge whose foreign target was renamed or withdrawn (reflow2 now refuses dangling edges outright, so a replace-style refresh has to answer this); and whether the host's committed export should CARRY mirrored nodes or merely NAME them by pin. All three are open.
properties.name: OPEN — should .mcp.json name SEVERAL graph_ids so one session reasons across reflow2 + flo2 + dynograph-foundation at once, and how does that sit against one-session-one-graph?
properties.rationale:
Captured under the brainstorm skill, 2026-08-06, and EXTENDED the same day when Anthony generalised his own example from three graphs to an arbitrary federation with per-user scopes. The extension was folded into this node rather than minted as a new one because it answers the SAME question — which graphs a session can see — at a larger scale; the skill's "several unrelated ideas mean several Decisions" does not apply to one idea getting sharper.

Kept SEPARATE from dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency deliberately, even though Anthony raised both in one breath: this is ACCESS (which graphs a session can see), that is AUTHORITY (who may write intent into a design they do not own). They have different right answers, and one node holding both could only ever be half-answered. The federation makes the split sharper rather than blurrier — it localises the authority question to each ownership seam.

The collaboration fact that bears on it and is new to the design: Anthony and his brother are split BY LAYER, not by project — Anthony on reflow2 core, his brother on the flo2 web app around it. That is not "many people on one project" (req:sessions-share-a-graph) nor "many projects at once" (req:many-designs-one-service); it is one owner per graph with the dependency running BETWEEN the owners, so the seam is simultaneously a technical boundary and a human one. req:many-people-and-many-projects-compose was written hours earlier assuming several people on one project and does not cover this shape. Anthony's user1/user2 example is the general form of the same thing.

What is NOT recorded here, because he has not said it: whether the per-user scope is meant to be a PERMISSION (user2 may not reach A and B) or merely a CONVENIENCE (user2 has no reason to load them). Those differ the moment anything is hosted, and reflow2 has no authentication to enforce the former.

SHARPENED 2026-08-12 with Anthony's union framing and the first trial evidence. The trial argues FOR it from an unexpected direction: two graphs agreed by being identically wrong about a shared boundary, and a shared node cannot disagree with itself. It also found the substrate objection — flo2 consumes reflow2's tool surface rather than its design, so unioning the design graphs joins the wrong two things for that particular dependency.

SHARPENED AGAIN 2026-08-12 with the mutable/immutable framing, which collapses three of the four costs the union framing raised and makes the authority rule enforced by construction rather than by discipline. The load-bearing finding is that `mirror_surface` already implements it and has ZERO instances in either graph — so this thread is diagnosing an unused capability, not specifying a new one.

THE TRIAL WAS RUN 2026-08-12 and found that mirror_surface has no refresh: a second mirror of the same design collides with itself, leaves the stale node and the host's edge to it in place, and leaves `mirrors` reporting the old pin — so the staleness register reads fresh after a failed refresh. That is the concrete blocker under every option in this node, because a federation of independently-moving projects is made of refreshes.

properties.decision: UNSETTLED. The instance is fixed; the class is not. Two dev_storyflow seats independently measured that the `brainstorm` skill instructed them to call `set_decision_status(proposed)` because "add_decision defaults to accepted" — behaviour that changed on 2026-07-25 and is dated in add_decision's own description — so a conscientious agent made a redundant write on every brainstormed idea. PR #102 corrected the text on 2026-08-08. WHAT REMAINS OPEN IS THE SHAPE OF THE GUARD, and three were offered: (a) let a skill ASSERT the defaults it relies on, so skill_lint fails loudly at the moment the default changes rather than the text aging quietly; (b) GENERATE the sentence from the tool's actual default at build time, so it cannot disagree; (c) forbid a skill from naming a default at all and require it to state the RELATION instead — "confirm the returned status is `proposed`" — which stays true across any default change and needs no new machinery. THERE IS AN OBVIOUS HOME: skill_lint.py already enforces that every tool a skill NAMES is served, and is run in CI on every push; asserting a default is the same kind of contract one field deeper.
properties.name: OPEN — when a served skill's text depends on a served tool's DEFAULT, should that dependency be asserted so the build breaks when the default moves?
properties.rationale: Worth a decision rather than a fix note because of what the reporters said about it, which generalises past this skill: a served skill and a served tool ship from the SAME BINARY and disagreed about that binary's behaviour — the one place this class of drift should be impossible. And the skill is the half a session reads BEFORE acting, so it is the half that silently teaches the wrong model; here it taught it with emphasis ("This call is not optional"), which is exactly the wording that survives a skim. Their formulation is the reusable one: A RULE PINNED TO A BEHAVIOUR MUST NAME HOW TO RE-CHECK IT, NEVER JUST ITS VERDICT. Reported 2026-08-08 by dragon Boss f96eccd3 and api-boss 5d608b85, both by RUNNING it and reading the echo; api-boss stated their own bound honestly, that they did not test whether the redundant call is harmful, only that it is unnecessary.

properties.decision:
🕐 DEFERRED 2026-08-14 BY ANTHONY — THE SHAPE ONLY, AND DEFERRED IS NOT DECLINED. Asked which form vertical linking should take, he chose to **fix `req:decomposition-covers-its-parent` FIRST and decide the shape after**: every option below makes decomposition more load-bearing, the coverage hole is already measured with a field instance, and settling a tier shape on top of a broken roll-up would bake the defect into precisely the boundary where nobody can see it.

⭐ **AND THE ASK IS NARROWER THAN "OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN" SUGGESTS — ANTHONY CLARIFIED WHAT ALEX MEANS:** *"I think my brother is more indicating that each tier is its own reflow2 graph that others are linked to vertically."* ⇒ **ALEX IS ASKING FOR OPTION (b): A GRAPH PER TIER, WITH VERTICAL LINKS BETWEEN THEM.** Not one graph with levels, and not a rendering. When this re-opens, (b) is the stated starting position rather than an open field — the others stay on the record as roads, not as equals.

⇒ WHAT IS SETTLED: nothing about the shape.
⇒ WHAT IS NOW LIVE WORK: `req:decomposition-covers-its-parent` (moved to **accepted** on his word) → `cap:decomposition-coverage-is-asked` (planned, `cmp:detect`). ⚠️ Its gap acknowledgement `decision:ack:1947285897ace4dc` — *"deferred on Anthony's word 2026-07-28… a handshake to design rather than a check to write"* — was WITHDRAWN, since a parked gap and a planned capability cannot both describe the same work.

🎯 **RE-ASK TRIGGER, NAMED SO THIS CANNOT DEGRADE INTO NEVER ASKED AGAIN** (the shape `dec:the-other-uaf-domains-wait-for-a-project-that-needs-them` set): re-open when the coverage check is BUILT and one of — (i) a real design is split across an authority boundary and someone needs a parent's number to mean something, (ii) `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` is settled, since binding-versus-visible is this question in disguise, or (iii) a second user asks for tiers.
⚠️ WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS DEFERRAL WRONG: someone building a tier hierarchy in prose or file layout while waiting — the workaround that looks like patience and costs exactly what the deferral was meant to avoid.
📌 NOT ANSWERED BY THE RENDERING ROUTE: `dec:idea-a-view-can-slice-by-altitude-not-only-by-aspect` covers what a reader is SHOWN. It composes with this and does not substitute for it — a first version of that node claimed otherwise and was corrected.

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Alex (`who:alex`) 2026-08-14, sharpened by Anthony's framing.

ALEX'S WORDS: *"I found myself wanting a top level graph and then graphs for the different components. The top level graph could hold information about the project as a whole and be aware of the graphs for the subcomponents of the graph (UI, API, e2e tests, etc.). In those graphs, we can put the fine details of those components, such as storing information about how migrations are performed in the database. The top level graph could contain domain knowledge that is relevant to all the graphs. This is the system of systems concept."*

ANTHONY'S FRAMING: *"instead of being peer-to-peer, this is more tier-to-tier. If peer-to-peer linking is 'horizontal', this idea is more 'vertical' between tiers… you could have a 'leadership' level that doesn't need to know every detail… a 'management' layer that knows more… a 'worker' graph that knows details. At each layer, it is probably the exchange of breadth for depth. In the military, we had 'strategic', 'operational', and 'tactical'."*

═══ ⭐⭐ WHY VERTICAL IS NOT HORIZONTAL REUSED ═══

**HORIZONTAL is an INTERFACE.** Two designs meet at a contract; neither contains the other; the coordinate is *"I designed against your published surface at this hash"* (`cap:mirror-surface`). A mirror is a REFERENCE.
**VERTICAL is a DECOMPOSITION.** The upper tier holds intent, the lower tier holds requirements decomposed FROM it, and delivery ROLLS UP — a containment-and-satisfaction relation with arithmetic attached.

⇒ **reflow2 HAS decomposition INSIDE a graph and mirroring ACROSS graphs. It does not have decomposition ACROSS graphs.** That is the gap, and the existing federation work does not close it.

═══ 🛑 MEASURED CORRECTION TO THE RECORD — the parent direction is NOT built ═══

`dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` asserts *"THE MECHANISM FOR THE PARENT DIRECTION ALREADY EXISTS… ANTICIPATED and BUILT, not missing."* **Too strong:**
  1. `report.rs` rolls delivery up via `decomposed_children` = `self.incoming(parent_id, DECOMPOSES)` (`graph.rs:1143`).
  2. Reads are scoped to the bound `graph_id` and `create_edge` resolves BOTH endpoints in scope — a `DECOMPOSES` edge between two graphs cannot be created at all.
  3. ⇒ **Nothing rolls up across a design boundary.** `cap:derived-completion` is verified WITHIN one graph.
  4. Mirroring does not rescue it: `export_surface` publishes published Interfaces, the artifacts that SPECIFY/REALIZE them, published Requirements and the Project — **no Verifications.** Delivery = satisfied AND realized AND PASSING CHECK, so **the evidence is exactly the part that does not cross.**
📌 That node warns *"READ THE EXPORT, NOT THE SUMMARY"* after making this error once, then makes it again a paragraph later about a different mechanism.

═══ ⭐⭐ THE TIER FRAMING TURNS A KNOWN DEFECT INTO A WORSE ONE ═══

`req:decomposition-covers-its-parent`: reflow2 rolls delivery UP and **never checks that children COVER the parent** — a parent split into two children addressing a tenth reports DELIVERED once both close. Measured instance: reflow's monolith split into 01a–01f, `context_management` and `self_improvement` present in all six originals, absent from all seven children, **unnoticed for months**.

🛑 **"EXCHANGE OF BREADTH FOR DEPTH" IS THE MECHANISM THAT HIDES IT.** A decomposition by SUBJECT drops what belongs to no single subject; trading breadth for depth is that drop made deliberately, tier after tier. Inside one graph a reader sees both sides. **Across an authority boundary they cannot: the strategic tier sees `delivered` and is structurally unable to see what fell between the children** — and it is the tier least likely to look.

═══ 📌 WHAT THE DESIGN ALREADY HOLDS ═══

  · `dec:nested-graphs` (ACCEPTED 2026-07-25) — a graph per OWNERSHIP boundary, `level`s inside; *a graph per system* rejected as a RULE because every seam costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check. **Alex's UI/API/e2e split is depth under one owner, so under today's rule it is ONE graph — which is exactly the rule his ask strains.**
  · **THE LEADERSHIP TIER IS ALREADY THERE, EXPRESSED HORIZONTALLY** — that decision calls `docs/org-scale-vision.md`'s *"one graph the whole company plans in"* a road not taken and replaces it with *"the CEO's objectives are one design that others MIRROR."* Anthony's point is that a mirror may be the wrong shape, and the roll-up finding says he is right: mirroring gives visibility, not arithmetic.
  · `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` — requirements already cross; the **Decision** cannot. Its unanswered question is this one in disguise: **is a mirrored Decision BINDING on the far side, or only VISIBLE?** Binding is what a tier means; visible is what a peer means.
  · `dec:idea-many-graphs-one-store`, `dec:idea-one-owner-many-projects` — both open, both the ownership rule strained by people with depth and no authority boundary.

🛑 MODELLING TRAP TO NAME BEFORE ANYONE BUILDS: `Component.level` (component → subsystem → system → system_of_systems → enterprise) is an **ASSEMBLY** ladder — *part of*. Strategic/operational/tactical is an **AUTHORITY and ABSTRACTION** ladder — a tactical design is not PART OF a strategic one, it REALIZES it. Reusing `level` conflates two relations, and `hierarchy_issues` already reads it the assembly way.

📌 UAF, CHECKED RATHER THAN ASSUMED: `dec:the-other-uaf-domains-wait-for-a-project-that-needs-them` names its re-ask trigger for the four DOMAINS (information, materiel, personnel, states), not for layering. **This note does not trigger it.**

OPTIONS — SHAPE DEFERRED, and (b) is what Alex is asking for.
(a) ANSWER WITH THE ACCEPTED RULE — one graph, `level`s, `cap:scoped-analysis`. Correct today; occurred to neither user.
(b) ⭐ **ALEX'S ASK** — VERTICAL AS A FIRST-CLASS RELATION: a graph per tier, cross-graph decomposition, intent down and EVIDENCE up. Cost: cross-graph edges, or a mirror carrying verification state; reopens `create_edge`'s endpoint invariant, which is deliberate and well-argued.
(c) VERTICAL AS MIRRORING, AS TODAY. Cheapest, already decided; the parent can compute nothing about its children.
(d) TIERS INSIDE ONE GRAPH — an abstraction ladder distinct from `Component.level`, tiers as a projection. No separate ownership or write locks, which is most of what a tier split is for.
(e) ⭐ **CHOSEN AS SEQUENCING, NOT AS SHAPE** — fix the coverage check first.

📌 ALEX'S OWN EXAMPLE IS STILL UNHOUSED: *"how migrations are performed in the database"* is not a requirement, capability or interface — operational know-how attached to a component, with nowhere to go today but an Artifact or a requirement's prose.
properties.name: DEFERRED, SHAPE ONLY — vertical (tier-to-tier) linking: Alex means A GRAPH PER TIER linked vertically (option b), and the FORM waits behind the decomposition coverage check
properties.rationale: Captured under the brainstorm skill, sharpened by Anthony's vertical/horizontal framing, deferred as to shape on his word, and then narrowed again when he clarified that Alex means a graph per tier rather than levels or a view. That clarification is recorded on the options list itself rather than only in prose, because the re-ask trigger will bring someone back to this node months from now and "options, none chosen" would hand them a blank field when the user has in fact stated one. The re-ask trigger follows the precedent `dec:the-other-uaf-domains-wait-for-a-project-that-needs-them` set, including naming what would make the deferral wrong. The measured correction to `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` lives here rather than being edited into that node, because withdrawing another node's claim deserves its own visibility rather than a quiet overwrite.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-14, extending Alex's system-of-systems note.

HIS WORDS: *"the graph is the systems engineering 'object' and can have all vertical tiers. However, when a user requests, give me the 'top level management' view, the agent should be able to get the info from the graph and render the user the requested 'view'. I don't know all the DoDAF and UAF views, but there is probably something for 'management' or 'vision'."*

⚠️ **CORRECTED TWICE WITHIN THE HOUR. BOTH CORRECTIONS ARE ON HIS WORD AND BOTH MATTER.**

**CORRECTION 1 — this does not answer Alex.** The first version claimed it *"may dissolve half of the tier question"* and read Alex's UI/API/e2e case as an altitude-view problem. Anthony: *"I think my brother is more indicating that each tier is its own reflow2 graph that others are linked to vertically."* Alex wants SEPARATE GRAPHS PER TIER — a storage question. **The altitude view neither answers nor replaces it.** They compose: a tier-split design still wants an altitude view inside each graph.
  · **ALTITUDE** — how much detail a reader is shown. A VIEW question. No new store, no seam. *This node.*
  · **OWNERSHIP / TIER** — separate graphs, vertically linked. A STORE question. *`dec:idea-a-top-level-graph-holds-what-the-component-graphs-share`, option (b).*
  📌 Kept on the record because an agent reading only Alex's words could build the view, declare the ask satisfied, and leave the real thing unbuilt — which is what this node nearly did.

**CORRECTION 2 — option (c) is CLOSED: the UAF/DoDAF catalogue does not belong in reflow2.** It originally proposed rendering CV-1/CV-2/CV-3/AV-1 as first-class outputs. Anthony: *"we purposefully did not define every UAF/DoDAF view as those are not appropriate for every design project AND reflow2 was meant as 'design anything' and 'build anything'… I left rendering the reflow2 graph to be able to store any design structure/content and left the agent the responsible party for 'rendering' the drawing."* **The division is deliberate: the graph stores any structure, the AGENT draws — mermaid, HTML, markdown, whatever suits.** `req:design-anything` (ACCEPTED) is what forbids binding a design-anything tool to one discipline's catalogue. See `dec:idea-a-view-that-does-not-apply-is-said-so-before-it-is-drawn` for the doctrine in full and for the idea it produced.

═══ ✅ MEASURED: TEN VIEWS EXIST, ZERO SLICE BY ALTITUDE ═══

`tools/render_views.py` renders `functional`, `flows`, `structural`, `traceability`, `released`, `decisions`, `evolution`, `provenance`, `fielded`, `budgets` — held to `dec:views-are-projections` (*"renderer fill-ins are defects"*) and `cap:bl-40` (no-extrapolation).

🛑 **EVERY ONE IS AN ASPECT VIEW: the whole design through one lens. None answers *"show me less."*** An altitude view trades depth for breadth by FILTERING what is shown — Anthony's *"exchange of breadth for depth"* done by the renderer instead of by a decomposition, and therefore **losing nothing**, since the detail stays in the graph. That is its one advantage over the tier-graph route, and it is not an argument against tier graphs, which exist for ownership reasons a view cannot supply.

📌 THE DoDAF MAPPING, KEPT AS CONTEXT AND NOT AS A BUILD TARGET (see correction 2): **CV-1 is titled "Vision"** and is the leadership-facing view with no reflow2 equivalent; **AV-1** is the executive summary; CV-2 taxonomy and CV-3 phasing are largely derivable from `Capability` + containment + Epochs, which `view_evolution` and `view_released` already partly cover. ⚠️ The exact UAF abbreviations were NOT verified against the spec and are deliberately not asserted. **The useful reading is that the MATERIAL for a leadership view is already in the graph — not that reflow2 should ship named standard views.**

═══ THE HARD PART ═══

🛑 **WHAT COMPUTES WHICH NODES ARE "TOP LEVEL"?** An altitude view is only honest if the filter derives from something the design already records. Candidates, none chosen: `Requirement.designation` (`published` vs `internal` — an audience distinction that already exists, and the strongest candidate), `priority`, `concern`, KPP status, distance from the Project root, an explicit tier property. **A filter chosen by the renderer rather than derived from the graph is precisely the "renderer fill-in" the doctrine calls a defect**, so this cannot be settled by taste.

🛑 MODELLING TRAP: `Component.level` (component → subsystem → system → system_of_systems → enterprise) is an **ASSEMBLY** ladder — *part of*. Management/vision altitude is an **ABSTRACTION** ladder. A subsystem is part of a system; a management view is not part of a worker view. Reusing `level` would make `hierarchy_issues` report nonsense.

OPTIONS.
(a) ALTITUDE VIEW DERIVED FROM AN EXISTING PROPERTY — most likely `designation`. Cheapest, no schema change, testable against the no-extrapolation standard.
(b) AN EXPLICIT TIER PROPERTY, projected on. `req:a-vocabulary-distinction-proves-it-is-read` demands a computation read it, which this supplies. ⚠️ If tier GRAPHS are ever built, this property and that boundary must not disagree about what a tier is.
(c) ~~RENDER THE NAMED DoDAF VIEWS AS FIRST-CLASS OUTPUTS~~ — **CLOSED on Anthony's word.** The catalogue belongs to the agent, not to reflow2.
(d) LEAVE IT — an agent can answer "show me the top level" conversationally from `graph_report`. Counter: unrepeatable between sessions. ⚠️ Note this is NOT the same as correction 2: leaving the DRAWING to the agent is doctrine, while leaving the FILTER to the agent's judgement is a renderer fill-in. The distinction is what separates this option from (a).

📌 RELATED AND SEPARATE: `dec:idea-document-generation` and `dec:idea-outward-docs-are-rendered-from-the-graph` ask what to DO with a rendered view; this asks whether the projection exists at all.
properties.name: OPEN — reflow2's ten views all slice by ASPECT and none by ALTITUDE, so "show me the top level" has no projection behind it (a SEPARATE need from tier graphs, and NOT a licence to hard-code the DoDAF catalogue)
properties.rationale: Captured under the brainstorm skill and corrected twice on Anthony's word within the hour — once for misreading Alex's ask as a rendering need, once for proposing that reflow2 ship the named DoDAF views. Both corrections are kept in the text rather than silently replacing it, following `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs`' precedent, because the two failure modes are worth seeing together: an agent that finds a cheaper adjacent problem and declares the original satisfied, and an agent that reaches for a familiar standard catalogue in a tool deliberately built not to have one. The second is the more likely to recur, since the catalogue is genuinely useful and the pull toward it feels like expertise rather than like a mistake. What survives both corrections is the measurement — ten aspect views, zero altitude views — and the open question of what could honestly compute the filter.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-14.

HIS WORDS, restating settled doctrine first and then adding the new part: *"we purposefully did not define every UAF/DoDAF view as those are not appropriate for every design project AND reflow2 was meant as 'design anything' and 'build anything' type construct. This is why I left rendering the reflow2 graph to be able to store any design structure/content and left the agent the responsible party for 'rendering' the drawing.
