WHAT IS AVAILABLE AND UNUSED: dynograph-vector ships an HNSW approximate-nearest-neighbour index (HnswConfig / HnswIndex / SearchResult, with filtered, batch and snapshot-persisted search) plus SIMD cosine similarity and the whole distance family. reflow2 uses none of it. search_design is BM25 lexical, and the schema carries embedding_field declarations on several node types that nothing populates.

THE CASE FOR: semantic search would find a requirement whose words differ from the query's. It would also strengthen resolution — the duplicate-detection path already has a fuzzy_then_vector strategy declared in the schema with the vector half unimplemented.

THE CASE AGAINST, and it is why this has stayed parked: embeddings need a MODEL, and reflow2-core is deliberately LLM-free and deterministic. An embedding provider at the core would break that, and putting it at the seam means a sidecar to install, version and keep in sync — which cuts against req:thin-install and the whole served-not-installed posture. Determinism is also load-bearing here: two runs of a detector must agree, and an ANN index is approximate by construction.

--- 2026-08-04, re-examined while building BL-186 (cap:corpus-ingest). Four things are now MEASURED rather than supposed, and one distinction is offered against the case-against. The question is still open and this update does not settle it. ---

1. THE PRODUCER EXISTS AND IS ANTHONY'S OWN. `embeddings-rs` (github.com/sligara7/embeddings-rs, local at a990e4d v0.1.1) is a Rust/ONNX parity sidecar for nomic-embed-text-v1.5 with a code-derived, drift-gated OpenAPI contract, written to pair with dynograph-foundation. That matters to the case-against: "a provider dependency" and "a local, self-hosted, contract-frozen sidecar you maintain" are not the same risk, and the deferral's stated reason was avoiding an external LLM provider.

2. THE WHOLE PATH EXISTS AND IS INERT — VERIFIED, not read from the earlier note. dynograph-storage has an embeddings column family with set_embedding / get_embedding / delete_embedding / scan_embeddings_by_type. dynograph-vector really does ship HNSW (crates/dynograph-vector/src/hnsw.rs) and SIMD cosine (distance.rs). reflow2's own schema declares embedding_field on Capability, Requirement, Question and others. reflow2's source contains exactly two matches for "embedding": a bidi-sanitizer comment and a doc comment saying "no embeddings". So the missing piece was never the model or the index — it is reflow2 calling any of it. embedding_field is another declared-and-read-by-nothing field, this time spanning four components.

3. NOT NEEDED FOR cap:corpus-ingest, AND ANTHONY SCOPED IT OUT ON 2026-08-04: "keep BL-186 lexical and ship it." The cost half of the corpus problem is candidate generation, which the BM25 index already in the served binary answers; embeddings would ADD a round trip per node, not remove one. The ordering half was a naming bug, fixed lexically. The folder driver needs no vectors.

4. WHERE IT WOULD ACTUALLY EARN ITS KEEP, and this is the honest limit of the lexical answer: req:corpus-ingest requires that "the same component named in forty specifications must converge on one node". Forty authors do not merely reorder tokens, they choose different words. token_sort_ratio cannot see "Read Cache" ~ "Local Store" at all — that is not a low score, it is invisible. The cases the scope doc names (Auth Service / Authentication Service = 84, Gateway / API Gateway = 74) are the EASY ones because they still share tokens. So shipping BL-186 lexical satisfies the requirement's ordering clause and its cost, and leaves its convergence clause satisfied only for documents that happen to share vocabulary. That limit should be stated to a user pointing reflow2 at a heterogeneous corpus rather than discovered by them.

5. THE DISTINCTION OFFERED AGAINST THE CASE-AGAINST: determinism is treated above as one blanket objection — "two runs of a detector must agree, and an ANN index is approximate by construction". That is strong for search_design and for anything feeding a gate. It is materially weaker for INGEST RESOLUTION, because under dec:ask-not-repair that path's output is a merge_candidate a human rules on, not a verdict. Approximate retrieval feeding a QUESTION is a different risk from approximate retrieval feeding a GATE. So the answer may not be a single yes/no: "yes, on the ingest resolution path only" would leave req:deterministic-core intact. Offered as a distinction to consider, not as advocacy — the req:thin-install objection stands unchanged either way, since a sidecar to install, version and keep in sync is a real change to the one-binary deployment story.

--- 2026-08-06: FIRST EXTERNAL EVIDENCE. Alex Sligar's 2026-08-05 survey of the "graph brain" ecosystem (relayed by Anthony), recorded here because it bears on the case-against and on nothing else in the node. Does not settle the question. ---

6. EVERY COMPARABLE SYSTEM IN THE FIELD IS HYBRID, NOT LEXICAL. Mem0 combines vector search with graph relations and key-value storage; Cognee's pipeline is ingest, chunk, entity/relationship extraction, then vector DB plus graph DB plus relational, queried by hybrid graph-and-semantic similarity; Zep/Graphiti, Letta, LangMem and LlamaIndex Memory all rest on vector retrieval. Not one of the surveyed systems is retrieval-lexical-only. That does not make lexical wrong — none of those systems has reflow2's determinism requirement, because none of them feeds a GATE, which is precisely the distinction drawn in point 5 — but it does mean the case-against can no longer include "nobody needs this": everyone building in this space has paid for it. The question narrows to whether reflow2's gate-feeding, one-binary posture is worth the retrieval quality it costs, and that is a real trade rather than an oversight.

7. WHAT THE COMPARISON DOES NOT SHOW: none of those systems has to answer a query the same way twice, and none of them exports a byte-stable artifact a CI gate diffs. So their unanimity is weak evidence about reflow2's core and strong evidence only about the ingest-resolution path — exactly where point 5 already located the weaker objection. The external evidence therefore sharpens the existing distinction rather than adding a new argument.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 adopt embeddings and the HNSW index, or stay on lexical search?
properties.rationale: Captured because the review found the HNSW index entirely unused and the question live only in prose. The honest status is "already parked, now visible" rather than "newly proposed". Updated 2026-08-04 after BL-186 forced the question in practice: the findings above are measured against the local checkouts of embeddings-rs and dynograph-foundation rather than recalled, and the per-path determinism distinction is new. Anthony's scoping call — BL-186 ships lexical — is recorded here so the decision to defer is visible on the node itself rather than only in the increment that deferred it. Updated 2026-08-06 with the first EXTERNAL datum: the whole comparable field is hybrid graph-plus-vector, which removes one leg of the case-against without touching the determinism or thin-install legs.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Nothing here is intent. Anthony, 2026-08-11: "since every reflow2 project will use git repo, then a project needs to shape its own governance rules for that project."

⭐ THE ARGUMENT IS UNIVERSALITY, AND IT IS WHAT MAKES THIS A PRODUCT QUESTION RATHER THAN REPO HYGIENE. `req:persistence` is ACCEPTED — the design lives in-repo alongside the code — so a git repository is not one deployment choice among many, it is the substrate every reflow2 project stands on. That makes the QUESTIONS predictable even though the ANSWERS are not: who may merge, what may land on the main line, when the design export is written, whether breaking any of it should stop a build. Every project will face them; each will answer differently.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, and the gap is in the TRIGGER rather than the vocabulary:
  · `cap:governance-proposal` — BUILT and shipping. Asks what breaking a rule should cost and writes
    `enforced` explicitly in both directions. But it is REACTIVE: it fires when somebody happens to
    state a rule. Nothing asks the question first.
  · `DesignRule` + three-state `enforced` + `unverified_enforced_rule` — the layer is there.
  · `req:a-project-records-how-it-ships` (proposed, Anthony 2026-07-31) — ADJACENT AND NOT THE SAME.
    That is the ordered RELEASE PROCEDURE, and its own text says the steps are not derivable from
    the graph. This is workflow AUTHORITY and TIMING, which is a different question with the same
    property: not derivable, project-specific, and currently unrecorded until someone volunteers it.
  · `genesis` captures deployment and platform context as Requirements — target platforms, the
    driving agent — and captures NOTHING about how the project's work reaches its main line.
  · `req:a-node-can-say-who-may-change-it` (proposed) — node-level authority, not merge authority.

📌 AND HIS OWN 2026-08-08 FRAMING ALREADY NAMED MERGING, in the entry that produced reflow2's governance layer: "every project will be managed differently and have differing sets of people running it with their own practices and POLICIES ABOUT MERGING AND WHO CAN MERGE and other governing mechanisms — but allowing reflow2 to setup a generic set of nodes/edges that allow a user or set of users to define their own project management policies/governance in graph form is something that I think would be really helpful." The capture half of that shipped. The half that would make a project actually reach for it did not.

⭐ WHY REACTIVE CAPTURE IS NOT ENOUGH, measured rather than argued. reflow2 itself has run for weeks with `rule:nothing-lands-on-main-directly` stated NOWHERE in its design until 2026-08-09 — that rule's own text records it: "it lived in an agent's memory file and in Anthony's head, and it was followed twice that day by a session reading it from neither." A reactive mechanism cannot capture a rule nobody thinks to state, and a rule everybody follows is exactly the one nobody states.

IDEAS, unranked:
(a) ASK AT GENESIS/ADOPT. A short set of workflow questions alongside the deployment ones, each landing as a DesignRule with its consequence stated. Reaches every project once, at the moment the repo is being set up anyway.
(b) ASK WHEN THE EVIDENCE APPEARS, not at bootstrap. A design that has gained a Release, or a second Contributor, or a second seat, has demonstrably reached the point where merge authority matters — and at genesis nobody has an opinion yet, which is the same objection that makes asking for feedback consent at INSTALL read worse than at UPDATE.
(c) SHIP A STARTER SET as advisory DesignRules the project edits or deletes — reflow2's own four, generalised. Fastest to value and the most dangerous: a default rule is an opinion nobody chose, which is precisely what `cap:governance-proposal` exists to prevent, and `req:defaults-do-not-assert` forbids.
(d) Nothing. The vocabulary is there; a project that wants governance can state it, and prompting risks manufacturing policy nobody needed.

⚠️ THE STRONGEST OBJECTION, and it is Anthony's own from a different day: `dec:proposed-requirements-pruned` dropped two requirements as "backlog hygiene dressed as product requirements", with the test being whether a requirement changes what anyone BUILDS. A prompt that produces four DesignRules nobody enforces has changed nothing and added four nodes. What would save (a) or (b) from that is the CONSEQUENCE question — governance-proposal's actual contribution — because a rule with a stated, chosen consequence does change what the build does.

⚠️ SECOND: the questions are only universal if they stay in PURE GIT. "Who may merge" is a forge concept on GitHub and a filesystem-permission concept on a bare remote; "what lands on the main line" is expressible in plain git and survives both. See dec:idea-should-reflow2-carry-its-own-git-discipline, where reflow2's own rule is stated entirely in GitHub's vocabulary and is partly unfollowable without one.

⚠️ THIRD, the scale objection: a solo project and a seven-session fleet need different answers, and asking a solo developer to state merge authority is asking him to gate himself — which is exactly why Anthony made reflow2's own branch-then-PR rule ADVISORY rather than enforced ("there is nobody to stop"). Any prompt must be able to accept "nobody, it is just me" as a real answer rather than an incomplete one.
properties.name: OPEN — every reflow2 project uses a git repo, so should reflow2 PROMPT each one to shape its own workflow governance rather than wait for someone to state them?
properties.rationale: Git is the substrate every reflow2 project stands on, which makes the governance questions predictable even though the answers differ per project. The capture half shipped and is reactive; nothing asks first. reflow2's own experience is the evidence that reactive is insufficient — its branch-then-PR rule existed nowhere in its design for weeks while being followed daily, because a rule everybody follows is the one nobody thinks to state.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-13, after taking a pile of Alex's feedback over the phone.

HIS WORDS: *"I told him to just git clone the repo and then run via his agent/session to add the feedback directly into the graph. Then he should git push. My idea would be that next time I git pull, I should have all his feedback in the graph?"*

⭐ **THE ANSWER IS YES, AND IT IS WHAT THE DESIGN IS BUILT FOR** — `dec:multi-writer-architecture` (no server, the file is the transport), the three-way merge, and the `parallel-work` skill all exist for exactly this. It is not a new mechanism; it is the intended one.

📌 SEPARATE FROM `dec:central-host`, which asks whether reflow2 gains a hosted MCP surface ALONGSIDE the repo file. That question is about REPLACING or supplementing the transport; this one is about whether the transport we already have is DEFENDED. A hosted surface would make all four steps below moot, which is an argument for that node rather than an answer to this one.

🛑 **FOUR STEPS HAVE TO HAPPEN, AND THREE ARE SILENT IF MISSED.** Checked against the repo rather than assumed:

  1. **ALEX MUST IMPORT FIRST, BEFORE HE WRITES ANYTHING.** A fresh clone has no `.reflow2/`, so his first reflow2 use MINTS A NEW DESIGN with a new `graph_id` — and his export would then be a different design that merely looks similar. Measured on the v0.30.0 cut: importing into an EMPTY store prints *"this store was empty, so it takes the imported design's name (reflow2)"*, so importing first preserves identity and writing first does not. **Silent either way.**

  2. **ALEX MUST EXPORT TO `docs/design/<project>.json` BEFORE PUSHING.** `.reflow2/` is gitignored, so his graph writes are invisible to git; pushing without exporting sends NOTHING and the push succeeds. ⇒ **THIS IS THE EXACT DEFECT HE HIT TODAY** (`fact:second-user-first-run-report-2026-08-13`): he could not find the committable record because a fresh install never made one. **His feedback plan depends on the thing that was broken, and would have failed silently before this morning's fix.**

  3. **HIS CLONE WILL NOT HAVE THE MERGE DRIVER.** `.gitattributes` declares `docs/design/reflow2.json merge=reflow2`, but its own comment says the driver *"needs [to be] defined once per clone (git deliberately does not let a repository configure an executable)"*. MEASURED: it IS configured in this clone, and **`tools/reflow2_init.py` does not install it** — grep for `merge.reflow2` / `gitattributes` in the installer returns nothing. So Alex gets git's LINE-BASED text merge on a 5 MB JSON graph document. The `.gitattributes` comment calls that *"safe — it just means you resolve the JSON by hand"*, which is true and is not a thing anyone will do.

  4. **ANTHONY MUST IMPORT AFTER PULLING.** `git pull` updates the FILE; the live graph is a separate store. `sync_status` reports `behind` and names the missing ids — and it **deliberately never auto-imports**, because *"import is an upsert and an unasked one would silently overwrite live work"* (`dec:ask-not-repair`). So the last step is a conscious act by design, and it is at least LOUD.

⇒ **THE PLAN IS RIGHT AND THE PATH IS UNDEFENDED.** Three of the four steps produce a successful-looking outcome when skipped: mint-instead-of-import, push-without-export, and a text merge on a graph.

═══ THE OPTIONS, none taken ═══

A — **NOTHING. Tell people the four steps.** The `parallel-work` skill already prescribes most of it. CHEAPEST; and this session is the evidence against it, because the skill exists and Alex still hit step 2 head-on. `req:a-discipline-is-delivered-at-the-tool-not-in-a-catalogue` says a catalogue cannot deliver a discipline that applies mid-flow.

B — **THE INSTALLER CONFIGURES THE MERGE DRIVER.** `reflow2_init.py` already writes `.mcp.json`, hooks and `.gitignore`; two `git config` calls close step 3 entirely. **The narrow, obviously-good one.** Costs: it must point at a binary path that exists on THAT machine — the same absolute-path problem `.mcp.json` already has and already solves.

C — **IMPORT-ON-FIRST-USE.** If a store is empty and a committed export sits beside it, adopt rather than mint. Closes step 1, and it is the behaviour the import path ALREADY has once somebody thinks to call it. ⚠️ Adopting a design because a file happened to be present is the silent inference `describe_designs` refuses; it would have to say loudly what it did.

D — **A PULL-SIDE NUDGE.** `sync_status` already computes `behind` with the ids; the loop hint could say it on the first call of a session rather than waiting to be asked. Closes step 4's discoverability without touching its deliberate manual-ness.

E — **A `sync` SKILL** covering all four steps as one named workflow, the way `link-projects` now covers linking. Cheap, and the same shape that just worked for a process nobody could reconstruct.

⚠️ **THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT WORTH KEEPING, AND IT ARGUES AGAINST C SPECIFICALLY:** every step here is silent-when-skipped, and the instinct is to automate all of them. But step 4 is deliberately manual on `dec:ask-not-repair`'s reasoning — an unasked upsert can overwrite live work — and step 1 has the same shape from the other side. **Automating an act because forgetting it is expensive is exactly how a tool starts making design decisions on somebody's behalf.** B and D add no inference and are safe; C infers.

📌 A PRACTICAL NOTE THAT IS NOT PART OF THE DESIGN QUESTION: Alex pushing to `main` directly would collide with `dec:export-once-per-pr` and the branch-then-PR practice. Either he opens a PR, or his feedback lands on a branch Anthony merges — worth telling him before he tries, since a rejected push is a discouraging first experience of contributing.
properties.name: OPEN — a collaborator clones, writes feedback into the graph, pushes; the other pulls and has it. Four steps make that work and three of them fail silently — how much should be automatic?
properties.rationale:
Recorded under the brainstorm skill: Anthony asked whether a plan would work rather than deciding anything, and the plan turns out to be the design's intended path with three undefended steps in it.

Worth keeping for the measurements rather than the idea, which is not new: the merge driver is declared in .gitattributes but NOT installed by reflow2_init.py (grep confirms), so a fresh clone silently falls back to git's line merge on a 5 MB JSON graph; and a fresh store mints a new graph_id unless the export is imported first, measured on the v0.30.0 cut when an empty store reported taking the imported design's name.

The connection worth not losing: step 2 of Anthony's plan is precisely the defect Alex reported this morning. His feedback route depends on the committable record existing, and before today's fix it did not — so the plan would have produced a successful push carrying nothing.

Kept separate from dec:central-host because that asks whether to add a hosted surface alongside the repo file, which would make these four steps moot; this asks whether the transport already in use is defended.

Options B and D are recorded as the safe ones and C as the risky one on purpose. Automating a step because forgetting it is expensive is how a tool starts inferring intent, and step 4's manual-ness is a decision (dec:ask-not-repair), not an oversight.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Nothing here is intent. Alex's idea (`who:alex`), relayed by Anthony 2026-08-11; his input is ADVISORY per rule:design-intent-moves-only-on-the-owners-word.

HIS WORDS: "You should put in an update that asks me if I want to collect feedback and store my decision in the graph or something. And put the skill in your skills. That way you get what you want."

TWO HALVES, AND ONE IS ALREADY DONE. The skill half is satisfied: `report-friction` is served and ships in the kit, one of eighteen — that he asked for it is itself recorded as evidence under fact:second-user-report-2026-08-11, because a user asking for an installed capability is the sharpest form of `req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session`. THE NEW HALF IS CONSENT: nothing in reflow2 asks whether a project is willing to send anything back, and nothing records the answer. Grepped 2026-08-11 — no consent, opt-in-to-feedback or telemetry machinery exists anywhere in the core or the surface.

⭐ WHY IT MATTERS MORE THAN IT LOOKS, AND IT IS NOT ABOUT COLLECTION. Every piece of field evidence reflow2 has was carried back by hand, by two people who happen to talk to each other. dec:idea-field-evidence-is-a-prioritisation-input asks whether that evidence should reach prioritisation; this asks whether the evidence ARRIVES AT ALL from anyone outside that circle. A prioritisation input with a single-digit number of sources is not a prioritisation input, and weighting by SOURCE INDEPENDENCE — the honest version of that idea — is impossible while every source is the same two households.

⭐⭐ AND ALEX'S FRAMING IS THE DESIGN, not a nicety. "ASKS ME... AND STORE MY DECISION IN THE GRAPH." Not a config flag, not an env var, not a default: a decision, asked once, on the record, revisitable. That is `cap:governance-proposal`'s shape applied to the consumer relationship rather than to a build rule, and it is exactly what `req:defaults-do-not-assert` demands of anything with a substantive default — silence must not read as yes, and it must not read as no either.

WHERE IT WOULD LIVE. `req:frictionless-update` is accepted ("install is one command, update is one word", modelled on Claude Code). The update path is the natural moment to ask: it already exists, it is already a place a human is present and consenting to something, and `reflow2 update` is queued work. Asking at INSTALL rather than UPDATE was considered and reads worse — at install nobody has used the tool yet, so there is nothing to have an opinion about.

IDEAS, unranked:
(a) A one-time ask at update, recorded as a Decision in the graph with the user's word. Revisitable, visible in the design, and it costs nothing when declined.
(b) Ask, but record it OUTSIDE the graph (a config file). Keeps the design clean of tooling state and loses the thing Alex specifically asked for — a decision he can see and change later.
(c) No ask. Keep `report-friction` as the only route and make it more discoverable instead. Cheapest and it does nothing about arrival rate.
(d) Ask, and additionally make the reporting one command. Alex's whole framing is "that way you get what you want", which reads as him volunteering — the bottleneck he is naming is that nobody asked him, not that he lacked a tool.

⚠️⚠️ THE HOLE THIS LANDS ON IS ALREADY NAMED AND STILL OPEN. `docs/partnership.md` lists DATA-PRIVACY MARKING among the three uncovered failure modes: "local-first by decision, and report-friction redacts by design; but NO FIELD IS MARKED SENSITIVE, so nothing can enforce redaction mechanically." A consented feedback channel makes that hole load-bearing. Consent to send is not consent to send ANYTHING, and today the redaction is a skill's discipline rather than a property the graph can check. This must not ship ahead of that.

⚠️ SECOND: consent recorded in a design that gets EXPORTED and committed is consent that travels. Whose consent is it when a second contributor pulls the repo? `req:a-node-can-say-who-may-change-it` (proposed) is the adjacent unbuilt piece, and this is a concrete case for it.

⚠️ THIRD, and it cuts against the whole idea: reflow2 is local-first by decision (`dec:repo-file-embedded` weighs "the user's design on a machine they do not control" AGAINST a service). Any channel that sends anything anywhere is in tension with that, and the honest version may be a channel that only ever produces a FILE the user chooses to send — which is what report-friction already does.
properties.name: OPEN — should reflow2 ask, once, whether a project wants to send feedback back, and record that consent in the graph?
properties.rationale: Every piece of field evidence reflow2 holds arrived by hand from two related sources, which is precisely why the prioritisation idea recorded beside it cannot weight by source independence. Alex's framing — ask once, record the decision in the graph — is the right shape and matches how this project already handles a rule's consequence. The blocker is that it lands squarely on the data-privacy-marking hole partnership.md names as uncovered, where redaction is a skill's discipline rather than anything the graph can enforce.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — Anthony thinking out loud, 2026-08-11. Nothing here is intent.

HIS FRAMING, in his words: "feedback that I've been giving back to from various projects... is clear demand signal of what needs prioritized... Obviously, this is demand signal for reflow2 itself; perhaps, in a general project, this would be akin to 'test reports', which should help prioritize which things need fixed immediately versus other desirements." And the sharpening that prompted it: two items in a fresh external report were things ALREADY ACCEPTED and unbuilt, so the report did not propose them — it CONFIRMED them, which is a different and more actionable signal.

THE MEASUREMENT, taken 2026-08-11 on this design:

  TemporalFact nodes                                    133
    of fact_type `defect`                               123   — every one basis: measured
    of those, whose text describes RECURRENCE            70   (instance / recurred / third time /
                                                               two projects / again)
  ranking computations that read any of them              0

`what_next` scores connectedness only: governed nodes (+1 each), those scheduled into an increment (+2), CONTRADICTS an accepted Decision (+2). `crates/reflow2-core/src/what_next.rs` never references TEMPORAL_FACT. The only readers anywhere are nodes.rs (constants), temporal.rs (the writer), preserve.rs (classification) and readiness.rs (forecasts). So reflow2 holds a corpus of 123 measured field observations and cannot let one of them move a priority.

⭐ THE WORKED EXAMPLE IS FROM TODAY AND IT COST FORTY MINUTES. `fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server` (2026-08-07) recorded a defect at basis `measured`, confidence 1, WITH ITS FIX WRITTEN IN ITS OWN EVIDENCE FIELD. A sibling fact counted three instances across two projects and two machines and noted the third "landed on the maintainer". A fourth instance hit on 2026-08-11 and blocked every graph tool. Between the diagnosis and the fix, FOUR DAYS, during which nothing ranked it — because a TemporalFact is not a Decision and `what_next` scores Decisions. The issue it was filed under was CLOSED with the finding unfixed.

⚠️⚠️ THE DECISIVE COUNTER-ARGUMENT IS ANTHONY'S OWN, AND IT IS ALREADY ACCEPTED. `dec:proposed-requirements-pruned` (2026-07-30) DROPPED `req:friction-has-a-severity-bar` and `req:friction-has-a-baseline` with this reason: "Both are backlog hygiene dressed as product requirements: THE ANSWER TO UNCONVERTED FRICTION REPORTS IS TO ACT ON THEM, NOT TO MODEL THEM." His stated test was whether a requirement changes what anyone BUILDS, and "how the project manages itself" does not. Any version of this idea has to answer that or it is a re-litigation.

THE ARGUMENT THAT IT IS NOT THE SAME THING, offered so he can judge it rather than be persuaded by it: the dropped pair were about REFLOW2 MEASURING ITSELF — a usability baseline, and a threshold at which reflow2's own friction becomes reflow2's own scheduled work. That is process. THIS is about whether ANY user's design can let measured field evidence — test reports, incident records, trial findings — reach the thing that says what to work on next. That is a product capability with a code citation, which is exactly what survived his prune. The honest counter to the counter: it is also convenient for me to say so, and he is the one who drew the "backlog hygiene" line in the first place.

IDEAS, unranked:
(a) Give `what_next` a term for measured evidence: a Decision or Requirement that a `defect` TemporalFact is ABOUT scores higher, and higher again when independent instances accumulate. Small, reuses the existing vocabulary, changes a ranking nobody has to trust.
(b) Do not touch the score; add a BAND. `what_next` already separates `marked` / `ranked` / `unexplored` / `shaping` precisely because they answer different questions. A fifth band — "things the field has told you about" — reports the evidence without pretending it is commensurable with connectedness.
(c) Model the confirmation case only, which is the narrow half Anthony actually pointed at: when external evidence lands on something ALREADY ACCEPTED AND UNBUILT, say so. That is a much smaller claim than ranking, and it is the one his example supports.
(d) Nothing. Act on the reports. This is his 2026-07-30 answer and it has not been shown to have failed — the spawn defect was not unranked because ranking was missing, it was unbuilt because nobody picked it up.

⚠️ THE TRAP, AND THE GRAPH ALREADY NAMED IT. `fact:the-stale-server-defect-recurred-to-the-people-who-wrote-it-down` carries its own caveat: "recurrence is not automatically corroboration — these three share a CAUSE rather than a METHOD, so they add weight to the COST, not to the diagnosis." A naive instance count would have read three findings-by-the-same-route as three independent confirmations. Whatever counts here must distinguish *found the same way twice* from *found two different ways*, or it manufactures confidence — the same failure as `dec:` on BM25 scores not being relevances.

SECOND TRAP: a count of reports is gameable by whoever writes the most reports, and reflow2's field evidence currently comes from a small number of closely-related sources. Weighting by SOURCE INDEPENDENCE is the honest version and is much harder than counting.

NOTE ON WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, so this is not built twice: `report-friction` writes the reports, `TemporalFact` holds them with `basis`/`confidence`, and the reconcile family (`reconcile_artifacts` / `_verification` / `_deployment`) already turns observations into findings. The gap is not capture and not vocabulary. It is that nothing carries any of it forward into what to do next.
properties.name: OPEN — should MEASURED FIELD EVIDENCE (friction reports here, test reports in any project) be an input to what to work on next?
properties.rationale: reflow2 holds 123 measured defect facts, 70 describing recurrence, and no ranking reads any of them — while a fully-diagnosed defect with its fix already written down sat four days and recurred. The generalisation to test reports is sound. What it must answer is Anthony's own accepted decision that friction prioritisation is backlog hygiene rather than product, and the graph's own warning that recurrence by the same method is not corroboration.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-06: "having somewhat independent reflow2 projects linked allows for requirements from one project to flow naturally to another without a user specifying we need to update package x because package y has a gap that only package x can fix. having reflow2 be able to do this automatically would be great."

THE WORKED EXAMPLE IS THIS REPOSITORY, AND IT WAS ENTIRELY BY HAND. flo2 hit a wall it could not climb from inside itself — a proposed Decision that nothing reported — and the fix had to land in reflow2. What carried it across was a human writing a markdown proposal in the flo2 repo, a human reading it, and an agent re-typing it as reflow2 nodes (chg:flo2-proposal-multi-graph-hosting). NOTHING IN EITHER GRAPH KNEW.

⭐ SHARPENED 2026-08-06 BY A CONCRETE CASE AND A SCALING ARGUMENT THAT CHANGES THE ANSWER. Anthony: "say my brother, who only has read access for reflow2, needs place a requirement upon reflow2 in order for flo2 to properly function... should my brother have the ability to add proposed ideas to reflow2 (write only for proposed, else read only) or should my brother place the external requirement in flo2 and when I open all 3 of my projects, it'll (the agent) see this requirement in the flo2 graph. I'm leaning towards the prior because say projectA (the one being depended upon) is huge and has multiple other projects dependent upon it and don't actually track any of the dependent projects/graphs, then option B may not function... think of it like a Google service is project A...they are not going to load every graph that is dependent upon them."

⭐ THAT ARGUMENT DEFEATS OPTION (C) BELOW, WHICH THIS AGENT HAD RECOMMENDED, AND THE REFUTATION IS RECORDED RATHER THAN THE RECOMMENDATION QUIETLY WITHDRAWN. "The upstream pulls rather than the downstream pushes" rests on the upstream being able to ENUMERATE ITS DEPENDENTS. A widely-depended-on design cannot: it does not know who depends on it, and would not load their graphs if it did. And DISCOVERY OF DEPENDENTS IS ITSELF A PUSH — either the upstream somehow learns of every consumer, or consumers register, and registering is a write. Pull cannot bootstrap itself. It survives only in the SMALL federation case Anthony described earlier (C's owner asking who declares a dependency on C, finding exactly D).

⭐ THE ANALOGY IS AN ISSUE TRACKER, NOT PUB/SUB. Anthony reached for "socket publish/subscribe". Pub/sub is the right shape for the OTHER direction and already exists: the upstream publishes its surface (export_surface, built), consumers mirror it (mirror_surface, built). The REVERSE channel in every real ecosystem is a tracker: you do not get write access to Google's codebase, you file an issue. ANYONE MAY FILE; ONLY MAINTAINERS TRIAGE. That is precisely "write only for proposed, else read only", and it scales because the upstream keeps ONE inbox rather than N graphs.

⭐⭐ IN SYSTEMS-ENGINEERING TERMS THIS IS NOT EXOTIC, IT IS THE NORMAL DIRECTION. flo2 is a CUSTOMER of reflow2; reflow2 is the SUPPLIER. A customer levying a requirement on a supplier is the most ordinary transaction in the discipline. Framing it as "writing into a design you do not own" made an unremarkable act sound like a violation.

⭐⭐ THE VOCABULARY IS ALREADY THERE, WHICH THIS AGENT PREVIOUSLY GOT WRONG BY NOT LOOKING. Checked against describe_schema, a Requirement already carries every field this needs: `source` ("who/what stated it — a user, a regulation, a stakeholder"), `provenance` with an `imported` value, `designation` published/internal so the downstream can mark what it publishes, `status` starting at `proposed` with only the owner's word moving it off (set_requirement_status), and AUTHORED_BY carrying role author/reviewer/approver. A levied requirement is expressible TODAY as: add_requirement (lands proposed) + authored_by <them> role=author + source "<their design>" + provenance imported. NOTHING IN THE SCHEMA NEEDS TO CHANGE.

⭐ AND IT IS ALREADY REPORTABLE, BY WORK MERGED THE SAME DAY. loop_status gained `unsettled_assigned_decisions` (PR #81, 2026-08-06) — a Decision left proposed while carrying an approver edge. The identical shape answers "a proposed Requirement from an external source is waiting on you". THE INBOX IS ALREADY COMPUTABLE; it has never been pointed at this case.

SO WHAT IS MISSING IS TWO THINGS: (1) TRANSPORT — how a node gets from their machine into this graph; (2) ENFORCEMENT — nothing stops a writer doing more than filing, because reflow2 HAS NO AUTHENTICATION and cannot acquire one without becoming a different product.

⭐ TRANSPORT ALREADY EXISTS, AND IT IS **GIT** — NOT ANY ONE PROVIDER.
⚠️ CORRECTED BY ANTHONY, 2026-08-06, and the correction matters because the first version of this node named GitHub: "we can probably use GitHub for this example, but not every project will use GitHub. every project is designed to use a git repo though so other git providers like gitlab can also work."

The mechanism is a BRANCH CARRYING A PROPOSED-STATUS NODE IN THE COMMITTED EXPORT, offered to the owner, who merges it or does not. Every primitive that needs is plain git — a branch, a diff, a merge — and reflow2's own three-way merge driver already operates on the export FILE, provider-agnostic by construction. A hosted forge (GitHub pull request, GitLab merge request, Gitea, Bitbucket) is one CONVENIENT UI over those primitives and supplies the review gate and audit trail for free; NONE OF IT IS REQUIRED. With no forge at all the same exchange works by `git format-patch` and email, `git request-pull`, or a shared bare repo over SSH — which is also what makes it usable where a forge cannot go, including the disconnected case dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments cares about.

THE LOAD-BEARING FACT: dec:multi-writer-architecture (accepted) already made the repo file the unit of exchange, and req:persistence puts the design inside the consumer project. So "the design travels as a file in a git repo" is not a workaround adopted for this feature — it is the architecture, and this transport falls out of it for free. ZERO NEW REFLOW2 CODE.

ITS LIMIT, STATED PLAINLY: it requires the filer to have a clone and a git workflow, which is exactly what flo2's non-technical contributors do not have — so for the HOSTED case flo2's own layer must be the mailbox, and that lands back on req:reflow2-consumable-as-an-image and dec:one-process-many-stores.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN — REORDERED BY THE ARGUMENT ABOVE.

(A) ⭐ ANTHONY'S LEAN: WRITE-ONLY-AT-PROPOSED. A consumer may create nodes at `proposed`, attributed and sourced, and may do nothing else — no accepting, no editing, no deleting. Expressible in today's schema, reportable by today's loop, transportable by plain git, and it scales because the upstream keeps one inbox rather than N graphs. Counter, and it is the honest one: reflow2 cannot enforce it. "Write only for proposed" is a property of WHATEVER HOLDS THE MAILBOX — a forge's branch permissions, a maintainer's judgement, or flo2's own layer — and calling it a reflow2 feature would be the same overclaim dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments warns about.

(B) THE REQUIREMENT STAYS IN THE DOWNSTREAM GRAPH and the upstream owner sees it when they open both. Anthony's own counter is decisive at scale: a heavily-depended-on design will not load its dependents' graphs and does not know who they are. Still fine for the two-brothers case, and it is what the composition machinery already supports with no new anything.

(C) THE UPSTREAM PULLS. Refuted above as a general mechanism. Retained for the small federation case only.

(D) A THIRD, PROGRAM-LEVEL GRAPH holding cross-project intent, with the others as composed children. dec:nested-graphs and cap:derived-completion anticipate the shape. Answers "where does shared intent live" rather than "how does a need travel", and adds a design to maintain.

⚠️ THE PREREQUISITE THAT STILL BOUNDS ALL OF IT: dec:linked-repos-poc was RUN 2026-08-06 and found reflow2 declares NO `required` interface at all, so nothing pairs across any seam. The channel this node is about has no labelled boundary to run along.

⚠️ AND THE CONSTRAINT FROM dec:idea-need-to-know-compartments: an automatic cross-graph write is a channel between compartments, and the safe direction is defined against SENSITIVITY, not against the dependency arrow. Option (A) is materially safer than any automatic flow precisely because a human files it and a human accepts it — the write is deliberate at both ends.

Captured under the brainstorm skill 2026-08-06, then SHARPENED twice the same day.

⭐ THREE CORRECTIONS TO THIS AGENT ARE PRESERVED IN THE NODE rather than edited away, because each was a different failure worth keeping visible.

(1) Option (C), upstream-pulls, was RECOMMENDED here and is refuted by Anthony's Google-service argument: pull requires enumerating dependents, a widely-used design cannot, and discovery of dependents is itself a push, so pull cannot bootstrap.

(2) This node previously implied the graph could not express a levied requirement. describe_schema shows it already can — `source`, `provenance: imported`, `designation`, `status: proposed` and AUTHORED_BY roles are all present. Same failure dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs corrected on 2026-08-05: asserting an absence from a summary instead of reading the surface. READ THE SCHEMA, NOT THE SUMMARY.

(3) The transport was first written as "a pull request... enforced by GitHub". Anthony corrected it: not every project uses GitHub, but every project uses a git repo. The distinction is not pedantic — coupling reflow2's answer to one vendor's feature would narrow a product whose whole persistence story (req:persistence, dec:multi-writer-architecture) is already vendor-neutral, and would exclude exactly the disconnected and self-hosted environments where the file-and-merge model is the ONLY workable one. The primitives are branch/diff/merge; a forge is a UI over them.

Kept SEPARATE from dec:idea-a-session-holds-several-graphs (ACCESS — which graphs a session can see) because this is AUTHORITY — who may write what, and at which status. The federation node localises this question to each ownership seam; this node is what happens at one.

The reframe worth keeping even if every option here is rejected: this is a CUSTOMER REQUIREMENT LEVIED ON A SUPPLIER, the most ordinary transaction in systems engineering.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony raised this at the very end of 2026-08-09 and it got no thinking because the session was out of context. Nothing below is intent; the options are recorded so the roads not taken survive.

ANTHONY'S QUESTION, and he brought the strongest counter himself: should reflow2's management and governance surface (rules, enforcement, claims/seats, epochs, releases, readiness, budget, ownership) live where it does, or become a sister package? HIS OWN COUNTER-ARGUMENT: **UAF does not separate them** — Architecture Management, Project, Standards and Strategic are all viewpoints inside one framework. That counter is strong and is engaged below rather than waved at.

--- OPTION A — STAY UNIFIED (status quo, no work) ---
One package, one vocabulary, one graph. FOR: proj:reflow2's objective is already "Keep a design coherent from concept THROUGH OPERATIONS" — the whole lifecycle is the stated scope, so a split narrows an objective held since genesis. The management surface is DEFINED BY READING DESIGN STATE: dec:release-trigger computes a cut from what is delivered, req:readiness-gates-the-roadmap computes the epoch from readiness rather than declaring it, req:plans-move-honestly puts plan movement on the record. None of that is a layer on top; it is a reader of the coherence graph, so a sister package would need full read access anyway — at which point ask what was actually separated. AGAINST: this is also the option that requires nobody to think, which is not the same as being right.

--- OPTION B — SPLIT INTO A SISTER PACKAGE ---
A second crate / MCP server with its own vocabulary, sharing the graph. FOR, and this is the real evidence: dec:bl-155 measured 40 of 132 served tools never called, and roughly SEVENTEEN of those forty are the management/governance/coordination family (claim_region, claim_report, release_claim, mint_seat, apply_merge, merge_designs, recall_resolutions, plan_epoch, set_epoch_status, arrival_delta, budget_report, add_flow, part_of_flow, performed_in, add_resource, add_environment, set_project_mode). The management half is measurably the least-exercised part of reflow2. Also: the natural users differ — governance's natural consumer is an agent fleet, design coherence's is a person designing. AGAINST, and it is the same datum read the other way: BL-155's own conclusion is that these tools are UNREACHABLE FROM ANY SKILL, not unwanted — "a capability nobody can find is worth what an absent one is worth". Packaging is not the cause of the non-use, so packaging is not the cure; a split would make them less reachable, not more. SECOND COST, concrete: a sister package collides with two ACCEPTED requirements — req:thin-install ("after setup, a project never has to change again for reflow2 to move") and req:no-setup-per-project ("setting up a project is not a step"). The split is not free; it is paid for in install friction the design already refused once.

--- OPTION C — SPLIT THE VOCABULARY, NOT THE PACKAGE ---
One binary; governance/management becomes a declared, optional PROFILE a project opts into. FOR: this is what UAF actually does, and it is where Anthony's counter is sharper than it first looks. UAF unifies VIEWPOINTS in one framework; it says nothing about whether one piece of software ships them. So the UAF precedent argues for one VOCABULARY and is silent on one PACKAGE — which suggests the question is a packaging question wearing a vocabulary question's clothes, and that separating the two axes may dissolve it. AGAINST: reflow2 has no profile mechanism today, so this is the option with the most unbuilt machinery behind it.

--- OPTION D — NEITHER: THE LINE IS MECHANISM vs POLICY ---
Not a package boundary at all. Mechanism lives in reflow2; policy lives in each project's own graph and reflow2 stays ignorant of it. FOR: this is the line the storyflow fleet drew after a month of operations, with the test "could a solo hobbyist, a two-person team and a regulated enterprise each express THEIR governance with this, without reflow2 having an opinion about which is right?" Their verdict sizes the missing work as small: "reflow2 models the DESIGN well and the DECIDING poorly — it does not know who may decide, what a decision covers, which rules can even be checked, or where else a rule is written down. Those four are what a governance layer is, and each is a small declarative field plus a report — NOT A SUBSYSTEM." You do not split a package off four fields. AGAINST: the same report notes DesignRule is "the least-connected type in the schema, which is odd for the one whose whole job is to bind other things" — so governance here is an underfitted corner, and calling the remaining work small may be measuring the part already understood.

--- WHAT THE GRAPH ITSELF SAYS, checked rather than assumed ---
reflow2's own functional decomposition (dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition, "reflow2's systems are functional, not its file tree") holds EIGHT systems — Agent Surface, Coherence Loop, Documentation, Human Channel, Intake, Design Store, Time & History, Vocabulary — and NONE of them is management or governance. There is no existing seam to split on. That cuts both ways and the honest reading of both is recorded: it means a split must invent a boundary the design never drew, and it means the absence of that boundary may be exactly why the area is tangled.

RELATED AND DELIBERATELY NOT MERGED: dec:idea-package-versus-shared-server asks a different packaging question (shared server vs self-contained package) on the same axis; rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party governs how any answer must be judged — by what it does for a consumer's project, never for this repo.

The storyflow fleet's trial-case report (2026-08-09, api-boss 05af57c1) supplies option D from a month of live operation. No option is recommended and none is promoted to intent.

RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — surfaced 2026-08-11 checking `docs/requirements-coverage.md`'s deferrals against the code rather than trusting its status column. Nothing here is intent.

WHAT WAS MEASURED. HEAL-3 says the catalogue is 8 of 13, with `unreachable`, `weak_connection`, `missing_link`, `missing_entity` and `missing_embedding` deferred. Grepping the core: the only hits for those five are a MODULE COMMENT at `crates/reflow2-core/src/heal.rs:27-29` and unrelated `unreachable!()` macros. So the five are genuinely absent — confirmed, not assumed.

⭐ BUT THAT COMMENT IS ITSELF STALE, WHICH IS THE SHARPER FINDING. heal.rs:27-29 reads: "Deferred (need `dynograph-graph` or the LLM): dead_end / unreachable / disconnected_community / weak_connection / single_point_of_failure / missing_link…". Three of those — `dead_end`, `disconnected_community`, `single_point_of_failure` — ARE BUILT and were being proposed as fixes until PR #147 narrowed them this same session. A comment naming what is missing has kept naming things that arrived.

⭐⭐ AND HEAL-14'S BLOCKER HAS EXPIRED. The row reads "⬜ Missing-intermediate Component for hierarchy — matryoshka (needs `Component.level`)". `Component.level` EXISTS: 3AX-9 is ✅, `hierarchy_issues` and `MissingIntermediateLevel` are in `crates/reflow2-core/src/hierarchy.rs` (5 references), and `missing_intermediate_level` is surfaced as a gap by `detect_gaps`. So the DETECTOR fires and the REPAIR was never written — `heal.rs` has zero references to it. The stated reason for deferring is gone and nothing noticed. This is the same shape as `cap:what-next`, whose blocker also expired unnoticed and which turned out to be buildable the moment anyone looked.

⚠️ THE COUNTERWEIGHT, and it is not optional: PR #147 (merged today) REMOVED HEAL's ability to propose `generate_bridge`/`generate_owner` for `disconnected_community`/`dead_end`/`orphan`, because inventing a relationship nobody designed is not a repair. A `generate_component` for a missing intermediate level is EXACTLY THAT SHAPE — inventing a subsystem to sit between a system and a part. So HEAL-14 may not be "unblocked and buildable"; it may be "unblocked and now forbidden by a rule accepted hours ago". `req:a-repair-suggestion-never-proposes-fabrication` is accepted. That tension is the actual question here and it did not exist when the row was written.

IDEAS, unranked:
(a) Fix the stale module comment and the stale HEAL-14 blocker note — pure record-keeping, costs nothing, and stops the next reader inheriting both errors.
(b) Decide HEAL-14 on the anti-fabrication rule: either the missing-intermediate repair is legitimate (the level is derivable from the two endpoints, not invented) or it is forbidden and the row should be RETIRED rather than left ⬜ forever.
(c) Retire the five never-built categories from the catalogue. The project's own test is "unused AND redundant → retire; unused AND not-redundant → defer, and say so" — nobody has re-asked which of the five is which since 2026-07-22.
(d) Nothing. 8 of 13 has been enough for every trial so far, and no friction report has asked for the missing five.

📌 THE META-POINT, which is the reason this node exists at all: `requirements-coverage.md` carries a BINDING deferral discipline — "a deferral that isn't written down is a silent stub, which this project treats as the same integrity breach as a silent drop." Three rows were checked today and three were wrong: SP-3b says ingest cannot be called from a session (it can), GS-17 says the polished PROMPT step is deferred (`gap_to_prompt` does it), 3AX-5 says TemporalFact usage is deferred (133 instances). The table goes stale in BOTH directions, and nothing computes on it. That is the argument for deferrals living where a detector can reach them — and equally the argument against trusting this table as the source for what to build.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony's question, 2026-08-16: "we used to have a planned capabilities increment / planned epochs within reflow2 — can we use these features within reflow2 to map out the triage fixes?" The reconnaissance and the options are mine.

THE SHORT ANSWER IS YES, THE MACHINERY EXISTS AND WORKS. Measured today: `plan_epoch` (future) is distinct from `add_epoch` (happened); `schedule_for` carries `modality: expected | required` with real teeth; `arrival_delta` computes five outcomes and stores none; 11 planned epochs and 27 SCHEDULED_FOR edges already exist. `arrival_delta` on `epoch:governance-becomes-expressible` returned six outstanding requirements AND volunteered "nothing is scheduled `required` … so there is no obligation to miss and it is NOT ready to cut. An increment that promises nothing has not been scoped." The tools are healthy and opinionated.

⭐ BUT THERE IS A BLOCKER THE QUESTION DOES NOT ANTICIPATE, AND IT IS THE WHOLE DECISION: `schedule_for` accepts `Requirement` or `Capability` ONLY. EVERY triage finding is a TemporalFact. So not one of them can be scheduled as it stands. The plan-increments skill says why this is correct rather than a limitation — "a plan is not intent … an item scheduled but never captured is a promise with no requirement behind it" — so the missing step is CAPTURE, not scheduling.

📌 AND THE SKILL ALREADY NAMED WHAT I WAS DOING: "if you are maintaining a numbered list of upcoming work in the conversation … that is a delivery plan living outside the graph." My ranked what-next list was exactly that, twice today, and it would have died with the session.

⚠️ EVIDENCE THAT THIS IS WORTH DOING PROPERLY RATHER THAN QUICKLY — reflow2's OWN plan has drifted, in precisely the shape the skill's §4 warns about. Of 27 SCHEDULED_FOR edges, ELEVEN still point at `rel:v0190`, `rel:v0200` and `rel:v0210`, all long shipped. Planned epochs sit at sequence 250–267 while arrived epochs reach 343. So the plan looks present and is answering nobody. Any new plan laid on top inherits that unless the stale half is dealt with.

THE OPTIONS FOR WHAT BECOMES PLANNABLE.

(a) A CAPABILITY PER FIX, at `status: planned`. Faithful to how features are tracked. ⇒ AGAINST: most of these are repair, not new function — "propose_heal stops mislabelling its scope" is restoring intended behaviour, and filing it as a capability inflates the capability count with maintenance and makes `unrealized_capability` noisier for months.

(b) A REQUIREMENT PER FIX, capabilities beneath where one is genuinely new. Faithful to the vocabulary: a fix is a statement about what must be true. ⇒ AGAINST: roughly a dozen findings would become a dozen requirements, which is a lot of intent minted in one act, and some are small enough that a requirement overstates them.

(c) ⭐ A REQUIREMENT PER THEME, several findings beneath each — and today's findings cluster harder than they look. At least four are ONE statement: "a report says whether a check was EXERCISED or had NOTHING TO EXAMINE." That covers propose_heal's vacuous zero, and it is not new doctrine — `chg:a-null-and-a-vacuous-zero-now-say-which-they-are` already did exactly this for scoped `detect_gaps`, and dev_storyflow named it a WIN. A second theme is "a reply says what it did not recognise", covering the undeclared property and the nearest-name suggestion. ⇒ AGAINST: theming is a judgement, and grouping wrongly buries a finding under a heading nobody searches.

(d) SCHEDULE NOTHING; leave them as facts and let the loop surface them. ⇒ AGAINST, and this is measured rather than argued: across this entire session `loop_status` reported the same 80 gaps and 16 defects and NEVER ONCE surfaced a triage item, because a defect FACT is not a gap. Doing nothing means they stay invisible to the loop that exists to say what is owed.

(e) EXTEND `schedule_for` TO ACCEPT A TemporalFact. Removes the blocker directly. ⇒ AGAINST: a fact is an observation, not work. Scheduling an observation is a category error, and it would let the design promise to deliver a measurement.

AND THE SECOND QUESTION, WHICH IS SEPARABLE: HOW MANY EPOCHS? One "triage fixes" epoch is easy to reason about and hard to argue with; two or three themed epochs (the detectors that misdescribe themselves, the write surface that accepts what it should question, the loop that cannot scope itself) carry more meaning and cost more to keep honest. `arrival_delta`'s own note argues for at least one `required` item per epoch, or it is not scoped.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the stale SCHEDULED_FOR edges to shipped releases should be cleaned first, retired deliberately, or left as the historical record they arguably are — that is its own decision and re-pointing them silently would erase the slip, which the tool explicitly warns against.
properties.name: OPEN — the triage findings are TemporalFacts and schedule_for takes only a Requirement or Capability, so nothing today can be planned. What becomes the plannable thing, and how many of them are there?
properties.rationale:
Anthony's idea; the blocker, the drift measurement and the five options are mine. Recorded rather than acted on because the choice mints intent.

⭐ SETTLED 2026-08-16 ON HIS WORD: "one triage fixes epoch, requirement per theme." That is option (c) for the plannable unit and ONE epoch for the container.

WHAT THAT RULES OUT, recorded because the roads not taken are the useful half: (a) a Capability per fix is declined — most of these are repair rather than new function and would inflate the capability count with maintenance; (b) a Requirement per fix is declined — roughly a dozen at once is too much intent minted in one act; (d) leaving them as facts is declined, and the measurement is why: `loop_status` reported the same 80 gaps and 16 defects all session and never once surfaced a triage item, because a defect FACT is not a gap; (e) extending `schedule_for` to accept a TemporalFact is declined as a category error — a fact is an observation, not work.

AND HE CHOSE ONE EPOCH over two or three themed ones — easier to reason about and harder to argue with, at the cost of the increment carrying less meaning in its name.

⚠️ WHAT THE RULING DOES NOT DECIDE, and was not asked: nothing is scheduled `required`. Every item goes in `expected`, because `required` is an obligation whose miss is a computed violation rather than a slip, and the plan-increments skill says to ask rather than assume. ⇒ `arrival_delta` will therefore report this epoch NOT ready to cut until somebody names at least one obligation. That is the tool being right, not a defect, and it is the next question for him.

AND THE STALE HALF IS STILL OPEN: eleven SCHEDULED_FOR edges still point at releases shipped long ago. This ruling adds a new plan beside them and does not clean them, deliberately — re-pointing them silently would erase the slip.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-08-09: \"how can we link reflow2 and flo2 — flo2 is dependent upon reflow2; we've discussed publisher → subscriber type relationships.\"

WHAT SEARCHING FIRST CHANGED, and it changed the question rather than answering it: most of the linking machinery is DESIGNED AND BUILT, and it has already been RUN on exactly this pair. dec:linked-repos-poc (executed 2026-08-06) composed reflow2, flo2 and dynograph-foundation in a throwaway in-memory graph and found ONE true positive unprompted — ifc:core-api (ours, `library`) against flo2's ifc:model-provider-api (`REST`), 80/100 name match, \"very likely the same contract, but they cannot be connected as either is currently built.\" Nobody told it the answer. So the publisher/subscriber SHAPE is not the open question; dec:pairing-role-placement settled where the role lives, cap:publish-surface and cap:mirror-surface are built, and dec:nested-graphs settled that separately-owned designs are separate graphs.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY OPEN IS THE TENSE. Every link so far has been a THING SOMEBODY RAN — a manual composition into a temporary graph, discarded afterwards. A subscription is a standing relationship: flo2 would be continuously answerable to what reflow2 currently publishes, and would learn when it moved. Nothing in the design says how that happens, and the two projects are on different machines, different release cadences and different owners.

THE OPTIONS, in Anthony's framing and with what is cheap or expensive about each recorded beside it rather than argued down:

(A) PULL AT THE EXPORT. flo2 vendors reflow2's committed export (or its published surface via export_surface) and re-composes on each reflow2 release. Cheapest by far, needs nothing new, and rides git which both already use. COUNTER: it is a snapshot, so flo2 learns about a moved contract whenever it next remembers to pull — which is the failure mode this whole question is about, one level up.

(B) PULL AT THE RUNNING SERVER. Once one process holds many designs (cap:graph-registry, reflow2_updates #1), flo2 could hold both graph_ids and ask across them live. COUNTER: gated on the largest outstanding piece of work, and dec:idea-a-session-holds-several-graphs is still proposed. Also flo2's graph_id is `1a97fc1f1de4d5d2` — an opaque mint beside two readable labels — so the addressing story needs a human-facing name first.

(C) A DECLARED DEPENDENCY EDGE BETWEEN DESIGNS, not just between nodes. reflow2 already has req:design-dependencies-declared (accepted, verified) for library versions; the analogue for designs would let a consumer say \"I depend on reflow2's published surface at version X\" and make a stale subscription COMPUTABLE rather than remembered. COUNTER: it is new vocabulary, and dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs and dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency are both still open about what may legitimately cross a design boundary at all.

(D) THE SEAM AS A GATE. flo2's CI composes against reflow2's published export and fails when a contract it consumes has moved — the ci-gate pattern pointed across a boundary instead of inward. COUNTER: it makes reflow2's release able to break flo2's build, which is a real coupling decision and Anthony's to make, not a technical detail.

⚠️ THE BLOCKER IS THE SAME FOR ALL FOUR, AND IT IS ONE MISSING LABEL. dec:linked-repos-poc found it and deliberately did not fix it: REFLOW2 DECLARES NO `required` INTERFACE ANYWHERE. Pairing matches complements, so with nothing required, nothing can ever pair — paired=0 on BOTH pairs, 15 of dynograph-foundation's interfaces and 5 of flo2's landing in dead surface. Its most dangerous number was `unmet_needs: 0`, which reads as \"nothing is missing\" and means \"we never said we needed anything\". Until reflow2 says what it requires, every option above links two designs that cannot be compared. That PoC called declaring them \"the cheapest next step\" — a handful of nodes — and left it to Anthony's word because it is design about reflow2's own boundaries.

AND A SECOND THING NO OPTION ADDRESSES, from reflow2_updates.md #7 (NOT DESIGNED): there are TWO version axes at this seam and only one negotiates. The MCP protocol version negotiates per connection; reflow2's 149-tool surface does not. The toolsnaps stop a surface change landing silently IN THIS REPO and tell flo2 nothing. Whatever subscription shape is chosen has to carry that, or \"clean module\" quietly becomes \"vendored fork\" — which dec:open-reflow2-as-core-module already names as the crux, with the cost falling on @ajs.

NOTHING HERE IS PROMOTED. The options are recorded as considered; the one decision genuinely waiting is whether to declare reflow2's `required` interfaces, which is small, unblocks all four, and is not an agent's to make.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ANSWERED IN PART 2026-08-12 BY A BACKTEST — THE SUBSTRATE IS NOT THE DESIGN EXPORT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

This node said the SHAPE was settled and only the TENSE was open. A backtest shows a third thing was open and unnoticed: WHAT THE SUBSCRIPTION WATCHES.

THE METHOD, and it is reusable: rather than build a mechanism and hope, replay real history against failures with KNOWN answers. `reflow2_updates.md` — flo2's hand-written tracker, the manual version of this subscription — went stale in two specific, dated ways. Each was given a window and three candidate signals were scored against it. Read-only; nothing was built.

  §4 CONTRIBUTOR-SCOPED loop_status. The doc was CORRECT when written (2026-08-09 10:21, against v0.26.1 — `loop_status_for` genuinely absent). It landed 3h later in PR #126 and shipped in v0.27.0. The doc became WRONG at its 2026-08-11 re-check. Window: v0.26.1 → v0.27.0.
  §7 THE SEAM CHANGES. `HealIssue.suggested_fix_type` went `&'static str` → `Option`, and five capture tools began REFUSING near-duplicates. Both v0.28.0-only. Window: v0.27.0 → v0.28.0.

RESULTS:

  signal                | §4 input contract | §7 capture refusals | §7 result shape
  design export diff    | 1 hit in 70       | 12 hits in 103      | NO — only "art:heal changed"
  toolsnap diff         | DECISIVE          | DECISIVE            | STRUCTURALLY BLIND

⭐ THE TOOLSNAP DIFF WINS OUTRIGHT ON INPUT CONTRACTS. For §4 it is mechanical and needs no interpretation: `inputSchema.properties` went `{}` → `{contributor_id: …}`. For the capture refusals, `distinct_from` appears with a description that explains the new refusal.

🛑 NOTHING SEES OUTPUT SHAPE. Toolsnaps record `annotations, description, inputSchema, name` — THERE IS NO OUTPUT SCHEMA. So a result-shape change is invisible to every signal reflow2 has, and it is exactly the half most likely to break a generated client.

🛑🛑 AND THE DESIGN EXPORT ACTIVELY LIES. `cap:owed-to-a-contributor` reads `in_progress` at v0.26.1, v0.27.0 AND v0.28.0 — three releases after the capability shipped — because status moves only on the owner's word and nobody went back. A subscription built on design-export status would have told flo2 "still in progress" about working code. THAT IS WORSE THAN SILENCE, and it fully explains how the hand-written doc went wrong: it was not carelessness, the design export AGREED WITH IT.

⇒ **DIFFERENT CONSUMERS NEED DIFFERENT SUBSTRATES.** flo2 calls reflow2's TOOLS; its contract is the tool surface. A sibling consuming reflow2's INTENT would want the design export. Treating "link two designs" as one thing conflates them, and option (A) above (pull at the export) would have watched the wrong artefact.

⚠️ AND THE WINNING SIGNAL IS NOT OBTAINABLE ACROSS THE SEAM. The toolsnaps ship in NEITHER `release.yml` NOR the kit. flo2 has already registered them as `art:reflow2-toolsnaps` with location "github.com/sligara7/reflow2 — tools/toolsnaps/*.json", i.e. GO READ THEM OUT OF OUR REPO. The strongest available signal requires a checkout of the upstream, which defeats consuming a released artifact. TWO CHEAP FOLLOW-ONS THE BACKTEST EARNED: publish the toolsnaps as a release asset, and record OUTPUT schemas in them.

═══ THE PAIRING TRIAL, same day — first time it computed on this pair ═══

`pair_designs` reflow2 → flo2: **paired 0, conflicts 10, unmet_needs 5, dead_surface 2, candidates 1, unclassified 2 ours / 1 theirs.** The blocker this node's PoC recorded (reflow2 declared no `required` interface) cleared in PR #130; reflow2 now declares 9.

  (a) ZERO PAIRS, NOT FOR A FIXABLE REASON. flo2 models `cmp:reflow2-service` as a component it CONTAINS. Pairing matches complements ACROSS a boundary; flo2 drew reflow2 INSIDE its boundary, so there is none. A legitimate model that makes the seam permanently uncomputable by pairing.
  (b) TEN CONFLICTS, NEARLY ALL SPURIOUS. reflow2's dynograph LIBRARY requirements name-matched flo2's REST endpoints at 62–83/100. The one true correspondence scored 61 and landed in `candidates`. Fuzzy names PROPOSE; only a person DISPOSES.
  (c) TWO DESIGNS CAN AGREE BY BEING IDENTICALLY WRONG. Both label the shared boundary `medium: REST`; both MEAN MCP and both say so in `spec` prose. Had roles been complementary they would have PAIRED on a shared falsehood. The tool defends against `unspecified` reading as agreement and has NO defence against two sides stating the same wrong value. A seam check verifies LABEL EQUALITY, never interoperability.

═══ THE GAPS IN LINKING, generalised so they apply to any two reflow2 projects ═══

 1. THE LINK IS NOT A THING. Nothing in either graph records the other exists. A link happens when a human hands two files to a tool: no identity, no owner, no pinned version, no lifecycle. `req:design-dependencies-declared` covers LIBRARY versions and has no analogue for DESIGNS.
 2. CORRESPONDENCE IS INFERRED, NEVER ASSERTED. No shared identifier space, so matching falls back on fuzzy names and re-guesses every run. A human should be able to say "my X IS your Y" and have it stick.
 3. AGREEMENT IS NOT INTEROPERABILITY (see (c) above).
 4. THE LINK IS A RUN, NOT A RELATIONSHIP — the tense problem this node opened with.
 5. THE COMPARISON HIDES ITS OWN SKEW. A 0.27.0 flo2 export was compared against a 0.28.0 reflow2 and nothing said so. ⭐ `dec:fix-the-comparison-before-pointing-it-earlier` step 2 ALREADY DECIDED "a comparison discloses its own confound" for the single-project case and has never been pointed at the cross-project one, which has the same confound and a worse one — the two sides are on different release cadences by construction.
 6. ONLY INTERFACES CROSS. A decision in A that invalidates a capability in B, a shared constraint, readiness gating — the vocabulary for crossing is one node type wide.
 7. READING IS SAFE; WRITING IS NOT. A comparison touches neither store. A propagated gap writes into a graph its owner never agreed to. The git-diff transport survives BECAUSE it never opens the store — a safety property, not an implementation detail.
 8. THE PRECONDITION IS BILATERAL AND NOBODY BUDGETS FOR IT. A seam is only as good as the least-labelled side, `internal` is the DEFAULT so an unlabelled project reports a confidently empty seam, and neither party gets value until both have paid. This is why the whole linking layer has zero instances.
 9. N > 2 IS QUALITATIVELY DIFFERENT AND ALREADY MEASURED. `fact:the-diamond-meets-at-dynographs-internals-not-its-interface`: reflow2 and dev_storyflow both depend on dynograph, one as a Rust library and one as REST. A naive pairwise check between the siblings reports ALL-CLEAR — confidently and wrongly — because the conflict lives BELOW both published surfaces. Shared-dependency conflict is a property of the graph, not of any pair in it. Linking N designs is not N-choose-2 links.
properties.name: OPEN — what makes the reflow2→flo2 link a STANDING subscription rather than a run somebody remembers to do?
properties.rationale:
Recorded via the brainstorm skill: one Decision per open question, at `proposed`, options in the prose, nothing promoted to intent without Anthony's word. Kept SEPARATE from dec:linked-repos-poc because that node records a RUN and what it proved; this one asks what the relationship should be going forward, which the PoC explicitly did not answer. Kept separate from dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs and dec:idea-gap-flows-to-the-dependency because those ask WHAT may cross a design boundary, while this asks WHEN and BY WHAT MECHANISM — one node holding both could only ever be half-answered.

PARTLY ANSWERED 2026-08-12 by a backtest against two dated failures with known answers: the substrate for a TOOL consumer is the toolsnaps, not the design export, whose status field lagged three releases behind a shipped capability. The method — replay real history against failures whose answer is already known — is more reusable than the finding.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — found 2026-08-11 by breaking CI with it. Nothing here is intent.

WHAT HAPPENED, and it is the cleanest possible demonstration. `cap:capture-registers-its-source` shipped, and the first thing it was pointed at was the document that actually drove reflow2's governance work: `dev_storyflow/reflow2_feedback.md`, in a SIBLING REPOSITORY. Registered as `art:storyflow-reflow2-feedback` with `location: ../dev_storyflow/reflow2_feedback.md`, plus DOCUMENTS edges to the seven governance requirements. Local gates passed. CI FAILED:

  FAIL  DRIFT  art:storyflow-reflow2-feedback: missing_artifact

CI checks out reflow2 alone, so the path resolves to nothing. `tools/reflow2_check.py` (line 615) reads `location` and FALLS BACK TO `name` when it is absent, then joins against `--root` — so there is NO WAY to register an out-of-repo source without failing the gate. Dropping the location does not help; it makes the check try the name as a path instead.

⭐ THIS IS `req:content-reaches-every-seat` FIRING ON THE THING BUILT TO SATISFY `req:no-idea-goes-quiet`. "A pointer resolves for everyone holding the design, not only for the machine that wrote it." A relative path into a sibling checkout resolves on exactly one machine. The two accepted requirements pull against each other in this case, and neither names the other.

⚠️ THE CASE IS NOT EXOTIC — IT IS ANTHONY'S NORMAL. His operating context is several partially-built designs across repositories and organizations, with the source material for one living in another. `req:many-people-and-many-projects-compose` (proposed) is the axis; this is a concrete instance of it landing on the artifact layer rather than the design layer.

IDEAS, unranked:
(a) An `external: true` / `reachability` marker on Artifact that tells `reconcile_artifacts` the file is deliberately not part of this checkout, so ABSENCE is expected rather than drift. Mirrors what `volatility` already does for expected CONTENT change — this is the same move for expected ABSENCE. Risk: absence is the one finding `set_artifact_intent` deliberately keeps at full severity, so this weakens the strongest signal in the reconcile family and needs its own argument.
(b) COPY the driving excerpt into this repo as a dated, attributed source document and register that. Honest, resolves everywhere, and is what `req:sources-are-kept-not-just-parsed` (accepted) arguably already implies — keep the source WITH the design. Cost: a copy can drift from its original, and nothing would detect that.
(c) Treat the other repo as a DESIGN rather than a folder, and reach it through the cross-design machinery (`req:design-dependencies-declared`, accepted) instead of the artifact layer. Cleanest conceptually; costs the most, and dev_storyflow's feedback file is not a design.
(d) Do nothing, and accept that a source outside the repo simply cannot be traced. Cheapest; it is also the status quo that made Anthony hand-point an agent at the file in the first place.

WHAT WAS DONE MEANWHILE: the artifact and its seven DOCUMENTS edges were REMOVED so the gate is honest, and the backward trace is once again absent. That is a retreat, not a fix, and it is recorded here so the retreat is visible rather than quiet. `cap:capture-registers-its-source` remains correct for the in-repo case, which is the case its own description scoped it to — it says nothing about reachability, and that silence is the actual defect in it.
properties.name: OPEN — how does a design register a source document that lives OUTSIDE its own repository?
properties.rationale: The capability shipped and its first real use broke CI, because the only source document that mattered lives in a sibling repo. Two accepted requirements — no-idea-goes-quiet and content-reaches-every-seat — pull in opposite directions here and neither names the other. Recording the fork rather than picking one, because option (a) weakens the strongest signal the reconcile family has and option (b) crosses a repo boundary; both are Anthony's calls.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — Anthony's question in his own words, 2026-08-11: "now the project has things that weren't supposed to be built - should they maintain, delete it accept the work done without a requirement?" Nothing here is intent.

THE SHAPE OF THE PROBLEM. Those three are a real disposition with real cost attached, and the graph has nowhere to put them. The two moves the tooling currently offers both lose information:

  (1) WRITE A REQUIREMENT FOR IT. The detect-and-ask skill warns against this in its own table: "The wrong move is to invent a requirement from the capability's own description: a requirement backed out of the thing that implements it is satisfied by construction and can never contradict anything." A retro-fitted requirement makes the gap disappear and makes the design lie.
  (2) `acknowledge_gap`. Files it under "reviewed and fine". Cannot tell "we accept this and will maintain it" from "we accept this and it is now debt somebody owns" from "this is scheduled for deletion" — three different futures, one record.

IDEAS, unranked:
(a) A disposition property/edge on the acknowledgement itself: accepted-and-maintained / accepted-as-debt / scheduled-for-removal, with an owner. Cheap if it rides on the existing acknowledge_gap Decision.
(b) Reuse the retire-from-design path for the delete branch and leave the other two to acknowledge_gap. Cheapest — no new vocabulary — but the accept-vs-debt distinction stays unexpressed.
(c) Treat it as an ordinary Decision the user writes by hand, governed by nothing new. Zero build cost; costs the ability to ASK "what unrequested work are we carrying?" across a design.

⭐ WHY THIS IS NOT A NICHE CASE, and it is Anthony's actual working context rather than a hypothetical: at NSLS-II he evolves a ~10-year-old bluesky stack where several organizations built partially-overlapping things because they could not wait for each other. Unrequested-but-built is the NORM on the brownfield path, not the anomaly. `req:accreted-intent-becomes-a-design` (proposed) is the adjacent capture; this is what to DO once it is captured.

RELATED BUT DISTINCT, so it is not folded in here: `req:the-design-says-what-was-built-and-never-used` (proposed) surfaces implemented effort nothing depends on. That is BUILT-AND-UNUSED. This is BUILT-AND-UNREQUESTED. A capability can be either without the other, and conflating them would produce a detector that answers neither question.

COUNTER-ARGUMENT: reflow2 is a design-coherence tool, not a project-management tool. dev_storyflow's own feedback rejected importing PMBOK/WBS structure for exactly this reason — "importing PM artifact structure would add a second, competing spine next to the golden thread." A disposition vocabulary is close to that line, and (c) is the option that respects it.
properties.name: OPEN — how does a project record what it DECIDED about work that was built without a requirement: maintain, delete, or accept?
properties.rationale: Anthony named three futures for unrequested work and the graph collapses all three into one acknowledgement. Recording the question keeps his framing intact; the ideas differ mainly in how much new vocabulary they cost.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony asked how to choose this after a capture pass hit it; nothing here is intent, and the options are mine unless marked otherwise.

MEASURED FIRST, because it changes the question.
