If rendering requires extrapolation, something is missing inside reflow2 — almost always. Decided 2026-07-19 (https://claude.ai/code/session_013aumVdHrRHu24cLirn6Cam); render_views.py, BL-40.

properties.decision:
Anthony's rule, 2026-07-31, drawing the line the content store needs and nothing had yet stated.

THE TEST, in his words: "the actual implemented design of something or its artifacts" stays NATIVE IN THE REPO. Everything that INFLUENCED the design without being its output goes in the CONTENT STORE.

  NATIVE IN THE REPO — the codebase reflow2 helps build, and anything that gets compiled, tested, shipped or read by a consumer. It is versioned, diffed and reviewed as code always has been; reflow2 changes nothing about it. A README or an ADR that ships WITH the product also stays native, because it is a product-facing artefact rather than an input — the rule is about role, not about whether something is prose.

  IN THE CONTENT STORE — a markdown file a user wrote describing a design aspect, a corpus of decision notes, a whiteboard photograph, a session transcript, a diagram an agent drew to explain a choice. These informed what got built and are not themselves the thing built.

THE EVIDENCE, AND IT IS WHY REFLOW2 EXISTS. storyflow began as one repo holding the codebase AND every markdown file recording Anthony's design decisions — now 900+ documents. Two costs, and the second is the one that matters:

  (1) NAVIGATION. The repo was a mess: design notes and source interleaved, and neither easy to move through.

  (2) RETRIEVAL, which is the deeper failure. In his words: "whenever I started implementing design, I had to remember where in those 900+ design documents something actually was" — they were not all in one folder, not consistently labelled, not structured so you could work out where anything lived. And worse: "some of my design choices were spread across multiple documents", so even finding the right document was not finding the answer.

  THE WORKAROUND TAKEN: a two-repo split — `storyflow` for the codebase, `dev_storyflow` for the design corpus (979 notes as of the 2026-07-20 adopt trial). It works, and it fixes exactly ONE of the two problems.

WHY THAT MAKES IT THE MOTIVATING CASE RATHER THAN THE SOLUTION. Separating the documents cures the mess and does NOTHING for retrieval. You still have to remember where a decision lives; a choice spread across five documents is still spread across five documents, now in a tidier folder. reflow2's claim is that the design record should stop being PROSE YOU NAVIGATE and become A GRAPH YOU QUERY, with the prose kept as provenance hanging off the nodes it produced. The content store is therefore NOT a neater `dev_storyflow`: the document goes to the store, what it SAID becomes nodes, and asking "where was this decided" becomes a query rather than an act of memory.

AND IT IS WHY CROSS-DOCUMENT IDENTITY IS LOAD-BEARING RATHER THAN A NICETY. "Spread across multiple documents" is precisely the case `req:corpus-ingest` was written for — the same thing named in forty specifications converging on ONE node with several provenance Fragments rather than forty near-duplicates. Anthony's 900 documents are the corpus that requirement describes, and this is the experience that motivates it.

THE FALSIFIABLE FORM, worth stating because it is checkable rather than rhetorical: IF REFLOW2 WORKS, STORYFLOW WOULD NOT HAVE NEEDED `dev_storyflow`. One repo, code native, the design in the graph, the sources in the store. If a user still ends up splitting their repo to stay sane, reflow2 has not delivered what this decision claims.
properties.name: The repo holds what the design PRODUCED; the content store holds what INFORMED it — and storyflow is the case that proves why
properties.rationale:
Recorded because the content store shipped without anyone stating what belongs in it, and a store with no placement rule fills up with whatever the first person guessed — after which the rule is set by accident.

The storyflow history is the valuable half rather than the rule. The rule alone reads as tidiness; the history says what tidiness is worth and where it stops helping. A user who had already tried the obvious fix, at real scale, and found it solved half the problem is much better evidence than an argument, and it is evidence from the author's own working life rather than a hypothetical.

The falsifiable form is deliberate. This project keeps finding declared properties nothing checks (`dec:edge-orthogonality`'s rule that a distinction earns its keep only if a computation reads it), and a doctrine about what goes where is exactly the kind of claim that can sit unexamined for a year. "Would storyflow have needed a second repo?" is a question someone can actually answer later.

properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.

For an epoch or increment that has ARRIVED there IS a past to point at, so the question is only which handle the graph stores. Three candidates, and they answer different questions rather than competing.

(a) GIT TAG (`epoch/2026-Q4`, `v0.18.0`). Human-readable, already the in-repo precedent — `rel:v0180` lives in the graph, tag `v0.18.0` lives in git, and nobody greps tags to learn what shipped. Cost: a tag is mutable and deletable, so a pin can quietly stop meaning what it meant.

(b) COMMIT SHA. Immutable and exact. Cost: opaque to a person, and says nothing about which repo it is in — useless on its own in a multi-repo ecosystem.

(c) THE EXPORT'S OWN `content_hash`. Every export already carries one, and `prev_content_hash` already chains them, so reflow2 HAS a version history of the design that owes git nothing. The same design exported on any machine hashes the same, which git cannot say of a commit. Cost: a hash identifies but does not LOCATE — you cannot fetch a document from its hash.

THE SHAPE THIS SUGGESTS: `content_hash` is the IDENTITY and the git ref is the ADDRESS. They answer "is this the same design?" and "where do I get it?", which are different questions, and storing both makes a third thing computable for free — if the tag later points at a commit whose export hashes differently, the pin has drifted, and that is exactly the kind of finding reflow2 exists to make rather than to suffer.

A SEPARATE QUESTION, and the one that decides how much is even needed: DOES REFLOW2 CREATE GIT REFS, OR ONLY RECORD THEM? Measured while thinking this through — reflow2 shells out to git NOWHERE. The merge driver is invoked BY git, never the reverse. So recording-only would preserve a property the tool currently has completely: it takes no clock, and it would take no VCS either. It could print the command it would have run. Creating tags would also mean write access to repos reflow2 does not own, which in an ecosystem of coupled repos is a different tool.

MULTI-REPO: one epoch does not pin one ref, it pins a SET — one per design — which is `req:version-combination-is-an-object`, already the recorded dependency of `req:epochs-can-be-planned`. So the pin is a version combination, not a string.
properties.name: OPEN — what identifies an arrived epoch's snapshot: a tag, a commit, or the export's own content hash?
properties.rationale:
Anthony's question (2026-07-30): how the mechanics of using git to capture snapshots would actually work. Recorded as options because he asked to think it through, not to be handed an answer.

The `content_hash` option is worth flagging because it was not in the original framing and it is already built: exports have carried `content_hash` and `prev_content_hash` since the lineage chain landed, and the gate already fails when the chain is broken. If identity is what is wanted, most of it exists.

properties.decision:
DECIDED by Anthony 2026-07-31. Both earlier states are preserved: the original four-way fork at `snap:epoch:arrival-delta:dec:where-content-lives`, the object_store amendment at `…:r2`.

THREE PARTS, all his word:

1. ADOPT `object_store` (Apache Arrow, originally InfluxData), LOCAL FILESYSTEM ONLY. The `fs` backend is a default feature and `InMemory` needs no feature at all; `aws`/`azure`/`gcp` stay OFF, which keeps `reqwest` and the crypto providers out of the tree. Cloud backends remain one configuration change away with no rework, because the whole point of the crate is that the backend is a runtime detail — so this is the smallest useful slice rather than a narrowing.

2. BLOBS ARE COMMITTED TO THE REPO. Chosen because it is the only option where the bytes are DISTRIBUTED BY THE SAME MECHANISM AS THE DESIGN: clone and you have everything, nothing to configure, nothing to be down, nothing to fall out of step. Every alternative is a second distribution channel, and a second channel is a second thing someone can skip — after which they see a design with holes in it and cannot tell. That is the failure `req:content-reaches-every-seat` exists to prevent. ACCEPTED COSTS, named rather than glossed: repo weight, and git handles binary churn poorly. Text — markdown, mermaid, HTML — diffs and compresses well and is most of what this will hold; raster images are the real risk and are the thing to watch first.

3. THE STORE LIVES IN `reflow2-mcp`, THE POINTER IN `reflow2-core`. Forced by a property worth keeping rather than chosen for taste: `object_store` is async and `fs` pulls tokio, while `reflow2-core` is deliberately synchronous — measured 2026-07-31, its entire dependency list is dynograph-{core,storage,graph,resolution,vector}, serde, serde_json, sha2, with no tokio, no async, no futures. So the core holds the CONTENT HASH, which is sync, deterministic and in-memory-testable, and `reflow2-mcp` does the I/O with the tokio it already carries through rmcp and hyper. Same split as `coverage_report`: the core computes, the surface touches the world.

WHAT MUST HOLD, unchanged by the answers: the pointer is a CONTENT HASH and never a path (`cap:session-memory` already recorded what a path costs — it "resolves for one person on one machine and silently misses for everyone on a shared graph"), and an unresolvable pointer FAILS LOUD and names itself (`req:no-silent-fallback`). Content addressing also keeps this reversible: because a blob can be verified wherever it came from, moving to a different distribution mechanism later changes how bytes are fetched and nothing about what the graph says.

STILL TO CHECK AT BUILD TIME, not decided away: `object_store`'s MSRV against the workspace's 1.94, and its transitive tree with cloud features off MEASURED rather than assumed. Per `dec:design-dependencies-declared` the dependency is DECLARED with its version and the features taken by name — a new crate in this tree is a recorded reliance, not a line in a Cargo.toml.

AND ONE THING DELIBERATELY LEFT OPEN: what bounds repo growth. A size cap that refuses oversized blobs loudly was offered and not taken, so nothing currently stops a large binary landing in the history where it cannot be removed without rewriting it. That is the first thing to revisit if the repo starts to hurt, and it is cheaper to add before there is history than after.
properties.name: Content lives in a content-addressed store behind object_store, local backend, COMMITTED to the repo
properties.rationale:
Settled in one pass because Anthony's research had already dissolved the hard part: once `object_store` makes the backend runtime configuration, "which storage" stops being an architectural commitment and only the git question remains — and that one turned out not to be about repo weight at all, but about whether the bytes travel the way the design already travels.

The placement was not a preference. It came from measuring `reflow2-core`'s dependency list and finding it genuinely free of async, which makes "put the store in the core" a decision to spend a property the crate has kept deliberately for a convenience it does not need. Reading the manifest answered in a minute what an argument about layering would not have settled at all.

The open item on repo growth is recorded rather than decided because the honest answer depends on evidence nobody has yet: what actually gets stored. A cap chosen now would be a number invented to feel safe — the asserting default `req:defaults-do-not-assert` exists to prevent — while a cap chosen after a month of real blobs would be measured. The cost of waiting is that git history is unforgiving, and that is exactly why it is named here rather than left to be discovered.

properties.decision:
CHOSEN BY ANTHONY, 2026-07-30: "yes, promote this intent." Option (d) of the brainstorm; the roads not taken are kept below.

THE DECISION. A design's forward-looking schedule — which capabilities and requirements are expected at which epoch or increment — lives in the graph and is reached by QUESTION, not by document. His acceptance test, in his words: "what capabilities are due to be released in epoch 5" and "what didn't we achieve that we were supposed to in increment 10?" Nothing is written into git as an epoch snapshot: no epoch branch, no per-epoch file, no rendered roadmap held as a record. "Let the agent/user figure out how to render the snapshot" — rendering is an OUTPUT, produced on demand and thrown away, never the record.

WHERE GIT KEEPS A REAL JOB, and it is narrower than the original idea: an ARRIVED epoch corresponds to real commits in real repos, so "what was actually deployed at epoch 3" pins a version combination (`req:version-combination-is-an-object`). Forward-looking plans describe GRAPH content and stay in the graph; backward-looking arrivals describe CODE and pin code. The information is in git either way, because the schedule lives in the graph and the graph is exported to `docs/design/reflow2.json` on every commit.

ROADS NOT TAKEN, kept because they were genuinely considered.
(a) EPOCH BRANCHES — his own original mechanism, 2026-07-28: "epoch branches: project_x:epoch_1 captures what we expect the graph to look like at epoch_1." A branch is the only place you can look at a future design whole, which is a real virtue. Not taken: checking out a branch normally makes the whole REPO reflect that state and there is no future code to reflect; a full export is 1.6 MB, so N epochs is N × 1.6 MB of near-identical JSON rewritten on every replan; branches invite merge semantics that do not apply; and a branch pointer moves silently, which is exactly what `req:plans-move-honestly` must be able to see.
(b) A FILE PER EPOCH ON MAIN — my recommendation, and NOT TAKEN BECAUSE IT WAS WRONG rather than merely less good. Its selling point was that `git log -p` on the file would give the plan's revision history for free. But the schedule lives in the committed export, which already has git history and its own `prev_content_hash` chain — so the property existed and the file was an artifact added to obtain something the design already had. That is the shape this project keeps finding in other designs, found here in my own advice.
(c) RENDER TO FILES — the generated form of (b), carrying the same redundancy plus a staleness obligation.

THE ARGUMENT THAT DECIDED IT. Both of his questions are QUESTIONS, not documents: a query answers them directly, while a file answers them only if someone rendered the right one at the right moment. And every materialised artifact acquires a staleness problem the moment the graph moves — `docs/design/reflow2.json` has a gate for it, `dataflow.html` has a check for it, and `docs/loop-model.json` demonstrated the failure the same day by becoming permanently unreproducible. Not materialising is the only way to have no drift at all.

MY EARLIER OBJECTION DID NOT HOLD, recorded because it was argued at length before being withdrawn: I claimed graph-only breaks readability for someone not running reflow2 (`req:design-reachable-without-the-repo`). It does not — the schedule is in the committed export, so it is reachable, merely not pretty, and prettiness is what on-demand rendering is for.
properties.name: The schedule lives in the graph and is queried; nothing is snapshotted into git
properties.rationale:
Anthony's idea, Anthony's lean, and Anthony's word to promote it. `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` was reworded on the same word, because it described indexing git refs and that is no longer what it means; its original text is preserved at `snap:epoch:planning-axis-intent:req:graph-indexes-snapshots`.

Worth keeping: the option that won is the one that ADDS NOTHING. No new file, no new branch, no new format, and — per the requirement it satisfies — largely no new storage, since epochs, Snapshots capturing incoming edges, and `compare_designs` already exist. The two rejected options both proposed materialising something, and both were arguing for a property the committed export already provides.

Also worth keeping, because it is a pattern rather than an incident: the file-per-epoch recommendation was mine, argued confidently, and wrong for the reason this project most often finds things wrong — it added a mechanism to obtain a property that already existed. Anthony's instinct to strip it back was better than my proposal to build it.

properties.decision: RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. When a plan moves during execution — "the motorcade slips thirty minutes" — somebody has to be told, and the question is who decides that. (a) SUBSCRIPTION, the way every coordination tool works: you join a channel, or somebody remembers to include you on the distribution. Cheap, familiar, and it fails one way every time — the person who most needed to know was not on the list, and nobody finds out until it matters. (b) DERIVED FROM THE BLAST RADIUS: propagate_from already returns who a change impacts, including which published boundaries it crosses, so the owners of the impacted regions ARE the distribution. Nobody maintains a list, nobody is spammed with changes that cannot touch them, and when the plan changes shape the distribution changes with it for free. (c) BOTH — derived by default, with an explicit watch for people who want a region they do not own. THE COUNTER-ARGUMENT TO (b), recorded beside it: a blast radius is only as good as the edges that exist, so an unrecorded dependency means a silent non-notification — which is the same failure as (a), reached by a different route, and arguably harder to notice because the mechanism looks principled. The mitigation is that a missing edge is already what detect_gaps hunts, so the honesty debt has an owner.
properties.name: OPEN — is notification computed from the blast radius, or subscribed to?
properties.rationale: This is the most distinctive idea in the 1000-planner exploration and the strongest reason reflow2 would belong in that problem rather than a chat tool with a plan attached: a FRAGO is a ChangeEvent whose blast radius is computed, and "who does this break" is a question reflow2 already answers. It is the same shape as every other answer in this project — computed, not remembered — and it inherits the honesty rules, so a notification would have to say what changed, what it impacts and what is now unresolved, never "the plan was updated". Kept separate from dec:live-tier because the mechanism choice is separable: (b) is worth building for a single team on the repo-file architecture, with no hosting at all, the moment anyone wants it.

properties.decision: Accepted the gap gap:034e96a2e1a7f4d0.
properties.name: Reviewed: gap:034e96a2e1a7f4d0
properties.rationale: Deferred on Anthony's word, 2026-07-28, with the rest of the reflow workflow review. Accepted and not dropped, and unusually concrete for a parked item: the mechanical half is specified in the requirement and needs no LLM — does every node type and edge type NAMED in a hint exist in the merged schema, and does every relationship a hint asserts have a corresponding edge type declared between those endpoints. Both are answerable from the schema alone and both would have caught the Anchor case, where two hints assert an Anchor-to-DriftEvent DEPENDS_ON with zero instances and no code path, while passing validate_schema.py cleanly. Deferred rather than built because it is coupled to dec:anchor-retire-or-implement: writing the check before deciding whether Anchor is retired, implemented or aliased would either red-light the build on a type about to be removed, or bless prose about to be rewritten. Decide the Anchor question first, then the check has a known-good corpus to run against. Also worth carrying forward: the check must not overreach — whether a hint's ADVICE is good stays a human question, and a linter that pretended otherwise would be the flattering default this design keeps refusing.

properties.decision: Accepted the gap gap:c628f709c27ad035.
properties.name: Reviewed: gap:c628f709c27ad035
properties.rationale:
LEFT OPEN ON PURPOSE — Anthony's call 2026-07-31. The requirement is HIS OWN idea, captured the same day; accepting this gap parks the MODELLING question, not the intent.

WHAT BLOCKS IT IS A REAL VOCABULARY PROBLEM, FOUND BY CHECKING AND RECORDED SO NOBODY RE-DERIVES IT. The first answer given was "reflow2 already has the vocabulary — model the release procedure as a Flow". THAT IS WRONG AS THE SCHEMA STANDS: PART_OF_FLOW is declared Capability -> Flow and accepts nothing else, so a Flow's steps must be Capabilities. "Bump the version in three files" is a chore, not a capability. Modelling seven release chores as seven Capabilities would put fake entries into the very set that coverage_report and the verification counts range over — 100 real capabilities plus seven chores makes every one of those reports quietly wrong, permanently. The correction is recorded here rather than edited over the earlier claim.

SO THE OPEN QUESTION IS ONE LEVEL DOWN, AND IT IS GENUINE: is a procedure step a first-class design object, or is it documentation the design POINTS AT? Making it first-class means widening PART_OF_FLOW to accept a step type — which MOVES THE STAMP and locks every older reflow2 out of the design, so it is a release-shaped decision, not a side edit. Pointing at it instead means writing the procedure as a document in the content store (which now exists) and referencing it from the Project — cheap, no schema change, but an agent reads prose rather than querying steps, which is most of what was asked for.

WHY NOT NOW: v0.20.0 was deliberately scoped to cap:changelog-view ALONE, and a schema change is not a side quest to slip in beside it. Nothing is lost by waiting — the requirement holds the reasoning and the derivability argument, and the seven recovered steps are written down outside the graph in the meantime.

THE ONE THING NOT TO DO is build it as a Flow of invented Capabilities to make this note go away. That would trade a visible open question for a silently wrong metric, which is the exact trade req:no-silent-fallback exists to forbid.

THE EVIDENCE STANDS AND IS NOT WEAKENED BY THE PARK: cutting v0.19.0 required reconstructing seven steps from `git show v0.18.0` plus a grep, and at least two of them — that an upgrade doc is owed ONLY when the schema stamp moves, and that the release manifest must be exhaustive with nothing computing it — were discoverable only from a past commit message.

properties.rationale: User (who:ajs, standing policy from 2026-07-23, applied again 2026-07-25): validation happens through the trials programme — docs/trials/ is where "built the right thing" is exercised against operational intent; formal validation-kind Verification nodes are not this project's tracking mechanism. Re-fired only because cap:kpp-proposal joined the set (38 → 39), and it is one of the clearest fits the policy has had. The three unit tests prove that a confirmed KPP is recordable, that an objective is never invented, and that the objective is never read as the threshold — every one of them a property of the WRITE PATH. What cannot be tested is the part that matters: whether the consequence question ("if it came in at 450 instead of 500, would that sink the project?") lets someone who has never heard the term recognise their own inviolable intent, and whether the agent asks about the right one candidate in a session instead of the loudest four. Both are answered by watching a real person answer a real question about their own project — the trials programme, and specifically the fleet-feedback trial — not by any fixture. The guard that IS testable is deliberately not claimed as verification either: nothing in Rust can stop an agent from setting category kpp on its own, because the tool cannot tell an agent's reading of the wording from the user's word. That guard lives in the skill's prose and in add_constraint's own description, and its failure would be visible as a KPP nobody remembers agreeing to.

properties.decision: Accepted the structural defect heal:4bd7c50f777fe56e.
properties.name: Reviewed: heal:4bd7c50f777fe56e
properties.rationale: ACKNOWLEDGED UNDER PROTEST, and the protest is the point: this contradiction IS resolved, and the detector cannot see it. dec:the-stranded-server-correction-stands is accepted, is edged GOVERNED_BY from both endpoints, and states exactly which clause of the older fact is withdrawn and why. That is precisely what the check-health skill says makes a contradiction go away ('two nodes joined by CONTRADICTS with no resolving Decision') and what every such issue's own suggested_fix_type asks for ('generate_decision'). It changed nothing: detect_defects returned the identical issue id afterwards. The detector reads the edge and never looks for the Decision — recorded as fact:defect-a-contradiction-cannot-be-resolved-only-acknowledged. So this acknowledgement is a WORKAROUND for a reflow2 defect, not a judgement that the disagreement is acceptable. It is chosen over the only alternative — deleting the CONTRADICTS edge — because deleting it would erase that reflow2's own graph carried a confident, untested claim for a day, and that history is worth more than a clean defect list. WHEN THE DETECTOR IS FIXED, this acknowledgement should be withdrawn (withdraw_defect_acknowledgement) rather than left standing, or the graph will record a resolved contradiction as a tolerated one forever.

A design is named by an id that resolves to a location — never by the path itself
properties.statement:
A DESIGN IS NAMED BY AN ID THAT RESOLVES TO A LOCATION. cap:select-graph-by-id frames it correctly — the server maps id to path — so the id is primary and the path is a storage detail. A surface that treats a filesystem path as the canonical identity forecloses object storage, where the location is a key and the identity rides as metadata.

ADVISORY — Anthony, 2026-08-09, splitting this clause out of rule:per-design-state-is-never-a-process-global and answering the enforcement question for both halves at once (gap:ba21fb8550a81e07): "Split it: clause 1 enforced, clause 2 advice."

WHY IT IS ADVISORY AND ITS SIBLING IS NOT, which is the reason the split was worth making rather than a hedge. The two clauses sit in OPPOSITE positions against the code. The no-globals clause is already satisfied — three runtime process-globals exist and two of them are legitimately process-wide — so a detector for it passes today and its only job is to stop the fourth one. This clause has no compliant surface at all: `--graph-path` is how a server is pointed at a design, `compare_designs` takes `base_path`, `describe_designs` answers about a path, and cap:select-graph-by-id is `planned` with nothing realizing it. An honest detector would therefore fail against the entire existing tool surface on the day it was written, and the only ways to make it green would be to block every build or to attach a check that proves nothing — which is precisely the failure the `enforced` tri-state was introduced to end (dec:does-enforced-default-to-gate-blocking: "a KPP that nothing checks is a comment").

So the flag says what is true: this is the project's rule, confirmed by its author, and no build has been stopped by it because nothing can yet tell compliance from the status quo.

WHEN IT SHOULD FLIP. The honest trigger is cap:select-graph-by-id becoming realized — once a surface exists on which a session names a design by id, "a NEW surface must not take a path as identity" becomes checkable against something other than the whole codebase. Until then this rule does its work at the moment of the decision it would break, which is the same mechanism rule:no-foreclosure runs on and the same reason that rule is also advisory.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: nothing about WHERE a design is stored, nothing about hosting, and nothing that requires the registry to be built. It only keeps the door open.

properties.name: A gate is run against the state it will be judged in — for the design export, that means AFTER committing
properties.statement:
Run a check against the state that will actually be judged, not against a working tree that is about to change. For `reflow2_check` specifically: **run it AFTER committing or amending, never before.**

WHY, MEASURED 2026-08-14 (`fact:the-lineage-gate-verdict-depends-on-when-you-run-it`): the lineage check compares the new export against the export committed at HEAD. Run before an amend it answers about a commit that is about to stop existing. The same file, byte-identical, FAILED at step 3 and PASSED at step 5 of one sequence — only `HEAD` moved between them.

THE GENERAL SHAPE: this gate always reasons about a PAIR of commits, and both of its known failure modes come from that pair differing between local and CI. `fact:the-local-lineage-gate-cannot-see-a-stacked-export` is the mirror image — the gate PASSING locally on a commit CI rejects, because CI checks out the PR merge commit where `HEAD~1` is main. Neither is a bug in the gate; both are a bug in when it is trusted.

ENFORCEMENT: **advisory, on Anthony's word 2026-08-14.** He was asked whether somebody who ran the gate early, trusted it and pushed should have been stopped, and answered that it is advice. The reasoning that supports it: a wrong local verdict is self-correcting, because CI checks out the merge commit and gives the authoritative answer either way — so this rule saves confusion and wasted cycles rather than preventing a bad landing. It also could not honestly be enforced: the ordering happens on a developer's machine and leaves no trace in the repository, so no check could see the violation.

DELIBERATELY NOT BOUND to a node with `GOVERNED_BY`. It shapes an operator's sequence rather than any design element, and `describe_schema` reports no edge type that models a DesignRule to what it governs here — the skill's instruction is to leave the edge out rather than assert one that is wrong.

properties.name: A lesson is generalised before it is built — reflow2 is not tuned to the project that happened to reveal the problem
properties.statement:
When a defect is found in one design, ask what the GENERAL form is before building anything. A detector, threshold or guard fitted to the project that happened to expose the problem makes reflow2 better at that project and worse everywhere else.

ANTHONY'S WORDS, 2026-08-14: *"I don't want to be hyper focused on solving this by creating another requirement which then causes another issue later on. I don't want this to become like a decision tree where it is so specialized to some training data that it is no longer generalizable."*

⭐ THE PRINCIPLE ALREADY EXISTED IN THREE PLACES AND HAD NO HOME — which is why it kept being re-derived and re-failed:
  · `req:the-tool-finds-its-own-blind-spots` (accepted): *"a detector that reaches zero findings by only asking questions the graph can already answer HAS BEEN TUNED TO THE INSTRUMENT. Satisfying this requirement by adding checks that happen to pass is the failure mode, not the fix."*
  · BL-5's lesson, in a `detect.rs` comment: **a loud detector needs a different QUESTION, not a tuned number.**
  · `dec:idea-silence-is-reported-not-inferred`, where the concern was raised again.

THREE MEASURED INSTANCES OF THE FAILURE, each found by a person or agent working by hand rather than by any check:
  1. `chg:orphan-decision-degree-zero` (2026-08-01) — a clean bill from every detector; zero-degree nodes counted by hand. **One detector was added for that one case.**
  2. `req:the-tool-finds-its-own-blind-spots` (2026-08-07) — six blind spots, all found by hand.
  3. 2026-08-14 — 43 live planned capabilities invisible to every tool (`fact:the-build-list-is-suppressed-by-realized-via-component`); an agent had to leave the graph and grep the tree.

📌 THE POSITIVE FORM, because a rule stated only as a prohibition is hard to act on: `granularity_report` is the pattern to copy. It answers a judgement-shaped question — *is the build coarser than the design?* — with **no threshold and no severity**, by comparing against THIS design's own distribution and refusing a verdict. `BL-42`'s `realized_via_component` guard is the counter-example: it solved a real noise problem measured on one storyflow adopt trial and created greenfield-increment blindness that nothing recorded for six weeks.

ENFORCEMENT: **advisory, on Anthony's word 2026-08-14.** He was asked whether shipping a check tuned to one design's data should stop the build, and answered that it is advice. That is the honest answer: *"is this overfitted?"* is a judgement about why code was written, which is not a property the graph can see — so an enforced version would owe a detector nobody could write, leaving a 0.6 finding open forever. **Advisory here means findable and quotable in review, not weak.**

properties.name: [BL-135] State the FAILURE MODE, not the rule — the guardrail principle, evidenced by a blind trial, and written nowhere
properties.statement:
State the FAILURE MODE, not the rule — the guardrail principle, evidenced by a blind trial, and written nowhere

*The strongest general finding from the 2026-07-31 case study, and the only one that is about how this project WRITES rather than what it computes.* An agent designed a whole project through reflow2 without knowing the guardrail docstrings were deliberate behavioural interventions. It read them as ordinary API prose, formed its own view of what they were for, complied, and praised the phrasing in its log without suspecting it was aimed at it — a blind trial, and they worked. It then ranked the eight that changed its behaviour, most effective first: set_artifact_checksum's *"silent accept does not exist: it is how a design erodes into fiction over N fix cycles while reporting zero gaps"* (named the single strongest intervention in the surface — it produced a named ChangeEvent for all nine artifact updates that would otherwise have been silent re-registrations); genesis's *"do not invent a brief on my behalf"* (held through THREE blank briefs with a detailed solicitation sitting in the directory, preventing the largest failure available — fabricated requirements phrased in the customer's own language, which are unusually hard to spot later); add_constraint's *"criticality is a claim about consequence, so ask the user first"*; set_requirement_status's *"promoting it yourself forges their signature"*; delete_edge's *"a link that WAS true and stopped being true is design history, not an error"*; describe_schema's *"validating is not the same as meaning what you intended"*; set_project_mode's *"the default records that nobody has chosen"*; and the stop hook's *"bookkeeping is not the loop"*. The extractable rule, in its words: it complied more readily where it was told what goes wrong if it did not, because that let it evaluate the reasoning rather than obey it — and agree. *"Ask the user first"* alone would have been weaker than the version naming the consequence. Equally informative: the interventions that did NOT need to exist — nothing had to stop it over-modelling or creating Components at genesis, because the skills sequenced the work so those temptations arrived when the right move was already obvious. The work: write the rule where descriptions are written (AGENTS.md), with this ranked evidence, so it is a standard rather than a habit — and consider a skill_lint check that a guardrail sentence names a consequence. The counterexample is already filed: [BL-124] shows a guardrail whose reasoning is the same quality as the rest and whose IMPLEMENTATION contradicts its intent, which the case study called the highest-value fix in its document. Good wording does not survive a mechanism that defeats it. CORROBORATED FROM INSIDE THE OTHER PROJECT, which is the strongest form the evidence could take: that session adopted the same pattern in its own code without being told to, and it caught a real error — a guardrail written two entries earlier asserted that all calibration anchors miss in the same direction, and when the same agent later fitted a coefficient to one anchor, the assertion failed with its own text: *"anchors now disagree in direction; the models were probably tuned to fit one of them."* Written before the mistake, and it named the cause. The principle is not a style preference about API prose; it transfers to any assertion a person will read at the moment they are getting something wrong. Their honest division of labour is worth carrying into the docs alongside it: *reflow2 is where reasoning persists; tests are what stop you being wrong* — which is also the argument for the out-of-scope line on [BL-126]. Size S

properties.name: [BL-212] A folder of documents carries no recoverable chronology, so EVOLVES_INTO and SUPERSEDES — both directional — can never b
properties.statement:
A folder of documents carries no recoverable chronology, so EVOLVES_INTO and SUPERSEDES — both directional — can never be drawn from a corpus

*Found 2026-08-04 while capturing [req:accreted-intent-becomes-a-design].* The vocabulary for "someone changed their mind over years" is already there and is entirely unused for this: CONTRADICTS carries alignment: opposing\ | supporting with confidence and evidence, EVOLVES_INTO is literally *"source is an earlier form that becomes target over time"*, SUPERSEDES/OBSOLETES retire on the record, and TemporalFact holds a time-bounded assertion with VALID_FROM/VALID_TO. All of it needs to know which document came FIRST, and a folder cannot say. File mtimes lie (checkout, copy, sync all rewrite them), a document corpus may have no git history at all, and the dates inside documents are prose. This is the exact inverse of the bug fixed in this same increment: there, arrival order wrongly decided the canonical NAME and the fix was to stop consulting order; here order genuinely carries meaning and there is no way to learn it. So the honest default is that a corpus ingest draws CONTRADICTS (symmetric, needs no direction) and NEVER EVOLVES_INTO/SUPERSEDES (directional) unless a human or an explicit in-document date supplies the arrow — which makes "you changed your mind here" answerable and "this replaced that" a question. Candidate signals worth measuring before choosing: an explicit date in frontmatter or filename, git log --follow --diff-filter=A first-commit date where a repo exists, and the corpus's own supersession language ("replaces", "superseded by"). Do not infer the arrow from mtime. Size S

properties.name: [BL-41] Graph text is data, never instructions — and nothing says so
properties.statement:
Graph text is data, never instructions — and nothing says so

S half done, 2026-07-19 — the standing rule is stated in the three places an agent looks: a section in the consumer AGENTS.md, one line in each of the eight skills at the point where it starts reading graph text, and the server's get_info instructions (so a session that loads no skill still gets it in the handshake). The one genuinely uncovered LLM failure mode in [partnership.md](partnership.md): every skill tells the agent to read node text and act on the design, and a hostile or careless statement rides that trust. Bounded today (single user, local graph); real the day a graph is shared (BL-12) or an adopted repo's prose flows through INGEST (BL-27). Mechanical mitigation (provenance-aware trust, quoting boundaries — [BL-12](#bigger-threads) sketch idea 2 is its design seed) is M and should wait for a real multi-writer case

properties.name: Design information lives in the graph, not in documents
properties.statement:
This project does not store design information in documents. What a document would have said belongs in the graph as typed nodes. Anthony's word, 2026-08-15: "we no longer use documents to store info. should be in graph" — and, on the buildup of two feedback files captured only partially, "we can't let this buildup occur again".

ENFORCEMENT IS HIS EXPLICIT ANSWER, NOT AN INHERITED DEFAULT. Asked what should happen if somebody added a markdown file holding design information — good content, tests passing — he chose STOP THE BUILD over advice and over leaving it unstated.

═══ WHY, IN HIS WORDS (2026-08-15, the reasoning behind the rule) ═══

THREE ARGUMENTS, and each has a measured precedent in this project or a neighbouring one:

(1) DOCUMENTS GET FORGOTTEN AND ARE HARD TO MAINTAIN. His example is this project's own: "like our initial backlog file of tasks for reflow2 kept growing and growing". That is `dec:backlog-is-retired` — 218 rows and 592 KB before it was retired into the graph on 2026-08-07, with an accepted decision violated and re-derived three times in the session that finally fixed it.

(2) A CORPUS OF THEM PILES UP FASTER THAN ANYONE READS IT. "what scared me was a corpus of feedback docs piling up. In dev_storyflow, I think I had 900+ documents of records that we're now having to go through slowly." The fear is not the first document; it is the nine hundredth, and the fact that the reading debt arrives long after the writing felt free.

(3) A DOCUMENT IS NOT SEARCHABLE THE WAY THE GRAPH IS. "documents are external and require grep to see contents (assuming markdown files, but that isn't always the case) — having in the graph is immediately searchable." The parenthesis is the sharp part: `search_design` works on any node, while grep only works on text formats, and a PDF, a spreadsheet or a drawing is opaque to it entirely.

═══ THE EXCEPTION HE STATED, WHICH SCOPES THE RULE ═══

⭐ "unless they are like a manual for using the designed system". THAT IS THE LINE: a document that is a DELIVERABLE OF the designed system — a user manual, an operator's guide — is not design information and this rule does not reach it. What the rule forbids is design information ABOUT the system living outside the graph.

⭐ AND A CONCESSION HE OFFERED UNPROMPTED: "If there was a way to put a pointer in the graph to the external document, that might be okay, but I think it is cleaner if we don't have external docs." A pointer is `Artifact.location` and `Fragment.content_ref`, both of which already exist and are exactly that — so the concession is already implementable, and he is stating a PREFERENCE for cleanliness over it rather than a prohibition on it.

═══ THE COUNTER HE RAISED AGAINST HIMSELF ═══

"The counter in some ways is something like dev_storyflow that did maintain a lot of records of the design." Recorded because he raised it and because it cuts: the same 900+ documents that are now a reading debt are also a design record that survived, and no graph held it at the time.

═══ THE LIMIT HE NAMED, AND IT IS THE REAL BOUNDARY ═══

From the acquisition world he works in: "in some designs, actual design reviews are done and official direction to proceed and other formal docs are required (coming from the US Air Force and US Space Force, documentation is required — maybe we can eventually get to where the graph tracks authorizations to proceed or other official acquisitions documents are in the graph and organizations trust the graph to hold such docs and therefore, keeping external docs is no longer needed — but I don't think we are there yet)."

SO THE RULE IS STATED FOR THIS PROJECT AND IS NOT YET CLAIMED TO GENERALISE. Whether reflow2 could become the system of record an organisation trusts for formal authorisation is open in `dec:idea-can-the-graph-be-the-official-record-an-organisation-trusts`, recorded separately because it is a question about the product rather than a rule about this repository.

⚠️ THIS RULE OWES A DETECTOR AND CANNOT HAVE ONE YET, because two things must be scoped before a check could tell a violation from ordinary work:

(1) SCOPE. 187 markdown files are tracked outside `docs/design/`. AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, COORD.md, REFLOW2.md, README, CHANGELOG and every served SKILL.md are documents, and several are load-bearing instructions the project cannot function without. The manual exception above narrows this but does not settle it: served SKILL.md files are closer to "a manual for using the designed system" than to design information, and nobody has ruled.

(2) A CONFLICT WITH THE SCHEMA'S OWN DESIGN, measured 2026-08-15: `Fragment.content_ref` is "a pointer to the source content RATHER THAN INLINING IT", and Fragment carries no field for a document's text. `Artifact.location` and `DOCUMENTS` share that assumption. AND THE FEATURE THAT WOULD HAVE CLOSED IT WAS BUILT AND WITHDRAWN: `cap:content-store` held "the source documents a corpus was extracted from", was `realized` and verified, and was discontinued on his word on 2026-08-09 for zero use across three projects (`dec:the-content-store-is-discontinued`). That discontinuation left `req:sources-are-kept-not-just-parsed` accepted and unsatisfied ON PURPOSE, with a `design_artifacts` folder — a folder of documents — named as the intended replacement and still unbuilt. THIS RULE AND THAT REQUIREMENT CURRENTLY POINT IN OPPOSITE DIRECTIONS, six days apart, both on his word.

properties.name: Design intent moves only on the owner's word — an agent may propose anything and settle nothing
properties.statement:
A NODE THAT ASSERTS INTENT REACHES A SETTLED STATE ONLY BECAUSE ANTHONY SAID SO. An agent may create, draft, measure, argue and recommend without limit; it may not move a Requirement off `proposed`, mark a Decision `accepted`, or record a rule's enforcement on his behalf. Alex is a genuine design contributor and second user (`who:alex`), and his input is ADVISORY — it informs and gates nothing.

ENFORCED — Anthony, 2026-08-09, answering the consequence question directly ("if a session recorded a decision as accepted without you saying so, should that stop the build, or is it advice?"): stop the build.

⭐ THE ASYMMETRY IS THE FINDING, and it was not predicted. Asked the same question about the branch-then-PR process rule minutes earlier, he answered ADVICE. So in a one-developer project the PROCESS rule is self-discipline and the AUTHORITY rule is inviolable — the opposite of the naive expectation that a solo project needs no authority modelling because there is only one person. What one person needs protection from is not another person; it is an AGENT WRITING IN HIS VOICE. That is a data point for `req:a-node-can-say-who-may-change-it` from the simple end of the scale, where every other data point so far came from a multi-agent fleet.

WHAT IT OWES, stated plainly rather than quietly closed: a DETECTOR. `unverified_enforced_rule` will fire at 0.6 and stay until a PASSING Verification is attached — a `planned` one does not silence it. NO CHECK IS ATTACHED TODAY, deliberately: the governance-proposal skill's standing warning is that attaching a check to close a finding is green-washing, and a passing check that tests nothing is a lie the graph cannot see.

=== THE DETECTOR SPEC, CORRECTED 2026-08-09 — READ THIS BEFORE WRITING THE CHECK ===

⚠️ THE FIRST SPEC WAS WRONG AND IS PRESERVED IN THE SNAPSHOT AT `epoch:detector-spec-cannot-name-a-forked-identity`. It read: "every Decision at `accepted` carries an AUTHORED_BY edge to `who:ajs`." THAT CHECK WOULD HAVE BEEN QUERYABLE AND WRONG, because the owner exists as TWO Contributor nodes and both carry live edges.

MEASURED ON THIS GRAPH, 2026-08-09, 7 Contributors under TWO id conventions (`ctr:` and `who:`):
  @ajs        → `ctr:anthony` (8 edges)  AND  `who:ajs` (161 edges)
  claude-code → `ctr:claude-fable` (11 edges) AND `who:claude-code` (39 edges)
A check keyed on `who:ajs` alone would either fire false violations on everything attributed to `ctr:anthony`, or pass while the owner's authority is silently split across two identities. The second failure is the dangerous one: it reports green.

⭐ WHY THIS IS THE RULE'S PROBLEM AND NOT A TIDINESS ONE. dev_storyflow filed exactly this hours before it was found here (finding ⑮ of their generalized set, api-boss `80c01d1f`, sharpened by a correction from storybug Boss `47accf78`): "a governance layer built on a forked attribution namespace inherits the fork, AND GAINS CONFIDENCE WHILE DOING IT." They hit it trying to encode a tri-boss ruling as three approver edges and could not, because two of three approvers each matched two nodes and the third had no Contributor node at all. Their conclusion travels: edges that are queryable and wrong are STRICTLY WORSE than prose that is honestly informal.

THE CORRECTED SPEC, in two parts, and the first is a PRECONDITION rather than a step:

(1) PRECONDITION — THE FORK MUST BE RESOLVED OR DECLARED FIRST. Either the duplicate identities are merged (a `DUPLICATES` edge with `basis: asserted`, which per dec:ask-not-repair is the only basis licensing a merge, and the merge is Anthony's call because it is destructive), or the check is given an explicit, recorded set of ids that mean the owner. WHAT IT MUST NOT DO IS HARD-CODE THE FORK SILENTLY — a check listing two ids without saying why is a check that has absorbed a defect and made it permanent.

(2) THE CHECK ITSELF, once (1) holds: every Decision at `accepted`, and every Requirement moved off `proposed`, carries an AUTHORED_BY edge to a Contributor the design recognises AS THE OWNER — resolved through (1), never by matching an id literal in the check's source. `loop_status` already computes the mirror image (a `proposed` Decision whose named approver has not answered); what is missing is the inverse — a SETTLED node with nobody's name on it.

📝 HOW IT WAS FOUND, recorded because the mechanism generalises: the same session that wrote the wrong spec also minted two new `who:` Contributors WITHOUT searching the namespace first, and landed on the documented convention only by copying the neighbouring `who:alex`. storybug Boss named this precisely — `who:` is not one convention among equals, it is the form `add_contributor`'s own parameter description gives as its example, so the deviations are deviations from a documented convention that no schema, validator or detector defends. And the deviation path is COPYING A NEIGHBOUR, not carelessness — so any fix that assumes authors read the parameter description will miss it.

ALREADY PARTLY MECHANIZED, which is why enforcement is not a bluff: `add_decision` lands at `proposed`; `add_requirement` lands at `proposed`; `dec:certainty-derived` derives a requirement's certainty from status × provenance because every move off `proposed` records the user's word; `set_requirement_status`'s own guardrail says promoting it yourself forges their signature; and `dec:three-party-checks` states the division — the LLM speaks, the graph remembers and counts, the human decides. The rule names the policy those mechanisms serve, which until now was implemented everywhere and stated nowhere.

HONEST BOUND: the tooling resists the violation but cannot presently REPORT one, which is exactly the gap the enforcement flag now makes visible instead of leaving to good behaviour — and, until the precondition above is met, the gap cannot be closed correctly rather than merely closed.

properties.name: Feedback sources are triaged in a stated order: dev_storyflow first, Alex level with it, music_graph after
properties.statement:
ANTHONY'S WORD, 2026-08-16, stated in passing while asking for a triage sweep: "dev_storyflow is a higher priority" and "any un-addressed feedback from my brother should be addressed — it is right up there in importance next to dev_storyflow". Recorded because it is a STANDING ordering, not a one-off instruction for that sweep, and because a future session with three logs and finite attention will otherwise re-derive it wrongly or read them in whatever order they were handed over.

THE ORDER: dev_storyflow first — Alex level with it — music_graph after.

WHY IT IS NOT ARBITRARY, inferred and marked as inference rather than as his stated reasoning: dev_storyflow is the fleet Anthony runs himself, so its log is his own usage at scale and arrives fastest; Alex is the SECOND HUMAN USER, and a second user's friction is the only evidence reflow2 has about anyone who did not build it; music_graph is a single consumer project whose reports, while excellent, have so far concentrated on one surface (restore and setup). ⚠️ HE DID NOT SAY THIS — he stated the order and not the grounds, and a later session should not quote the reasoning back to him as his.

WHAT IT DOES NOT MEAN, since a priority order is easy to over-read: it is not a quality ranking. music_graph's F23 was the most consumer-blocking defect of the whole increment and was fixed first, before this ordering was stated. Priority here is about which log to READ when there is not time for all of them, not about whose findings matter.

📌 `enforced: false` DELIBERATELY, and the reason is that no check is possible: nothing in the graph knows which log a session read, or in what order. So this is guidance for a reader and must not be raised as an unverified enforced rule.

⚠️ THIS NODE WAS CREATED WRONG THE FIRST TIME AND THE ERROR IS RECORDED RATHER THAN QUIETLY FIXED: it was written with `enforcement: "advisory"`, a property the schema does not declare. It was ACCEPTED AND STORED, echoed back, and the enforcement gap fired anyway — which is what exposed it. See `fact:defect-an-undeclared-property-is-stored-without-complaint`.

AN INPUT TO AN OPEN QUESTION: `dec:idea-is-there-a-feedback-intake-skill-and-is-it-a-router` asks whether reflow2 should have a feedback skill that routes external input. If that is ever built, THIS is a thing it would need to know and has nowhere to read.

properties.name: Every fix is judged by what it does for somebody else's project — this repo is the test rig, not the target
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-06: "most changes we do here are not for the sake of reflow2 itself (though we often apply reflow2 tools/skills on itself). so when we fix something, it must be from the perspective that we are improving reflow2 for anybody that may use it in their project."

THE RULE: when a defect is found while working on reflow2's own design, the fix is judged by what it does for a CONSUMER — a project that installed reflow2 and whose authors will never read this repository. Improving reflow2's own repo state is not the objective; it is the evidence.

DISTINCT FROM THE DOGFOODING RATIONALE, and the two are easy to conflate. req:skill-use-survives-a-long-session records that using the skills on this project is the INSTRUMENT that finds defects. This rule says how to judge the FIX once the instrument has fired. One is about detection, the other about the target. Both are needed, and only holding the first produces a beautifully-instrumented repository that has fixed nothing for anybody.

THE FAILURE MODE IT FORBIDS, which is subtle because it looks like completion: find a hole, patch it HERE, mark the requirement met, and leave every consumer with the hole. The repo goes green, the design says the need is satisfied, and nothing is true of anyone else's project.

THE WORKED EXAMPLE THAT PROMPTED IT, same day, and it is the clearest test of the rule available. Asked whether anything runs `reconcile_dependencies`, the first answer was "reflow2's own CI does not" — accurate, small, and actionable by adding a step to this repo's workflow. Applying this rule reframed it: `reflow2_check.py` is THE GATE THAT SHIPS TO EVERY CONSUMER IN THE KIT, and it reconciles ARTIFACTS but never DEPENDENCIES. Same underlying fact; the second framing is the one worth acting on, and only the second one fixes anything for anybody. Adding a CI step here would have satisfied the first reading and left req:design-dependencies-declared unenforced in every project that installs reflow2.

HOW TO APPLY IT, concretely: when a finding is written, ask where the fix lands. If it lands in `.github/`, `tools/build_design_graph.py`, or anything else that exists only because reflow2 develops itself, ask what the CONSUMER-facing equivalent is — the served tool surface, a skill, `reflow2_check.py`, the kit, the installer, a tool DESCRIPTION. If there is no consumer-facing equivalent, that absence is usually the real finding.

WHY IT IS A RULE AND NOT A REQUIREMENT: it constrains how every other change is judged rather than describing behaviour anything can satisfy, which is the same shape as rule:no-foreclosure. Nothing verifies it; it is applied by whoever is deciding what to build, and its evidence is the framing of the findings that follow it.

THE COUNTER-PRESSURE, recorded so the rule is not applied blindly: reflow2 IS a real project with real operational needs, and some work genuinely is for this repo alone — the release procedure, the export discipline, COORD. The rule does not forbid that work. It forbids MISTAKING it for product work, and it forbids closing a consumer-facing requirement with a repo-facing fix.

properties.name: Build nothing today that forecloses growing into a hosted, multi-user, multi-project service
properties.statement: Anthony's reframe, 2026-07-25, of what to do with the GitHub-MCP study's larger lessons: rather than hold them as a roadmap of features to build, hold them as a rule about what NOT to do now — do not take a shortcut today that would make it impossible for reflow2 to become what GitHub's MCP server is. A roadmap ages badly and gets stale in a document nobody reads; a non-foreclosure rule is checkable at the moment of the decision that would break it, which is the only moment it matters. THE SPECIFIC FORECLOSURES, from reading github-mcp-server (each one a shortcut that is tempting precisely because there is one writer today): (1) IDENTITY IN A GLOBAL. Authority must arrive with the caller and be read from the request, never stashed in a process-wide variable or resolved once at startup — GitHub constructs a fresh server per request in stateless mode for exactly this reason, and their lockdown cache carries the warning that a viewer-scoped lookup shared across requests runs under the wrong user's credentials. (2) INVENTING AUTHORITY. reflow2 must never become the thing that decides who may read what; it delegates to an authority that already exists, on GitHub's stated principle that a server must not let anyone reach more than they could reach without it. Building an account system would foreclose that by making reflow2 the authority. (3) TREATING THE SINGLE-WRITER LOCK AS A CONTRACT. One RocksDB handle is an implementation fact; the day it is a promise in a tool description or a skill, concurrency becomes a breaking change rather than a build. (4) CONFIG THAT WIDENS. Per-request configuration must only ever NARROW what the deployment allowed — GitHub's headers can restrict within static bounds and can never re-include what was excluded, and any read-only surface that a header can talk out of read-only was never read-only. (5) ONE GRAPH ASSUMED EVERYWHERE. graph_id already exists on every node and edge and is pinned to a constant; code that assumes the constant rather than reading the field is the foreclosure, not the constant itself. (6) TRUSTING TEXT BY ITS LOCATION. Once a design can arrive from someone else, text is untrusted because of where it came from, not because of which field it sits in — so the trust boundary belongs at ingress, before anything reads it. WHAT THIS RULE IS NOT: it is not a licence to build the hosted service, and not a reason to add abstraction now. Every item above is a constraint on shortcuts, satisfiable by writing the simple version carefully — the point is that the simple version stays a strict subset of the eventual one, so nothing has to be undone. ENFORCEMENT DECIDED 2026-07-25 (Anthony: "go with your recommendation"): ADVISORY, `enforced: false`, and deliberately so. VIOLATES_RULE is a vocabulary item no detector reads, so declaring this gate-blocking would promise a check that does not exist — the exact failure the KPP work was built to end ("a KPP that nothing checks is a comment"). The rule is the project's rule, confirmed by its author; the flag says only that no build has been stopped by it yet. It flips to enforced the day a detector can read a foreclosure from graph state — the honest first candidate being (4) and (5), which are mechanically checkable, unlike (2), which is a judgement about architecture.

properties.name: Nothing lands on main directly — branch, open a PR, get the gates green, then merge
properties.statement:
EVERY change reaches main through a branch and a pull request. The PR is what makes CI run at all (`ci.yml` is `on: push` for main only, plus `on: pull_request`), the gates must be green before merge, and the branch is deleted by the merge.

ADVISORY — Anthony, 2026-08-09, answering the consequence question as the governance-proposal skill puts it ("if somebody pushed straight to main with a good change and passing tests, should the build have stopped them?"): advice, record it, do not gate.

WHY ADVISORY IS THE HONEST ANSWER HERE AND NOT A HEDGE. This project's governance is one developer with occasional feedback from one other person (Anthony, 2026-08-09: "the management/governance is just me, a single developer with occasional feedback from my brother Alex on it"). There is nobody to stop. A gate on this rule would be the sole author gating himself, which buys no protection and costs a detector — and `dec:does-enforced-default-to-gate-blocking` exists precisely to stop a convention recorded in passing from asserting it could fail somebody's build.

WHAT A DETECTOR WOULD LOOK LIKE, recorded so the option stays open rather than being forgotten: assert every commit on main is a squash-merge from a pull request. Feasible, and it becomes worth writing the day a second person can push here.

WHY IT IS RECORDED AT ALL, WHICH IS THE POINT. Until 2026-08-09 this rule existed NOWHERE in the design — `dec:export-once-per-pr` was recorded, `req:pr-is-a-delta` was recorded, and the rule they both presuppose was not. It lived in an agent's memory file and in Anthony's head, and it was followed twice that day (#132, #133) by a session reading it from neither. That is `req:a-rule-knows-where-else-it-is-written-down` firing on this repository: no authoritative copy, only restatements.

THE TRAPS THAT TRAVEL WITH IT, because they cost real time and are not derivable from the rule: (1) a feature branch gets NO CI until a PR exists, so open the PR as a DRAFT to start CI and mark it ready only on green; (2) merging deletes the branch, and pushing that name again recreates it with no PR and no CI; (3) a rebased commit can carry a green that belongs to a DIFFERENT commit — verify the check run's head SHA against the PR head (`fact:defect-a-rebased-commit-keeps-a-green-that-belongs-to-another-commit`); (4) a STACKED PR merges into its base branch, not main, and if that base was already squash-merged the content is stranded while GitHub still reports MERGED.

properties.name: Per-design state never lives in a process-global
properties.statement:
STATE THAT BELONGS TO A DESIGN LIVES ON THE DESIGN HANDLE, NOT IN A `static`. cap:graph-registry names the metadata that must become per-graph rather than per-process; every new process-global that is secretly per-design adds another line to that migration. Legitimately process-wide state is fine and exists today — the seat registry and the serve-shared mode flag are facts about the PROCESS, not about a design. The test is not 'is it a static' but 'would this need a different value for a second design open in the same process'.

ENFORCED — Anthony, 2026-08-09, answering the enforcement question as it was put to him (gap:ba21fb8550a81e07, "should the build have stopped them, or is that advice?"): "Split it: clause 1 enforced, clause 2 advice."

WHY THIS HALF CAN CARRY ENFORCEMENT AND ITS SIBLING CANNOT — the whole reason the split happened, and it was MEASURED BEFORE THE DECISION RATHER THAN AFTER. A violation of this clause is mechanically visible, because a process-global is a declaration in the source. The codebase holds exactly three runtime process-globals, all in crates/reflow2-core/src/identity.rs: the process's own seat id (`seat_id`, line 357), the attached-seat registry (`ATTACHED_SEATS`, line 486), and the shared-mode flag (`SERVES_MANY_SESSIONS`, line 578). The last two are the ones this rule's own text already calls legitimately process-wide. So enforcement stops nothing today and costs nobody a build; what it stops is the FOURTH one — which is exactly the erosion this rule was written against, one convenient global at a time, invisible until the migration.

WHAT THE CHECK ACTUALLY DETECTS, AND WHAT IT DOES NOT. ver:no-per-design-process-globals is an allowlist over runtime `static` / `OnceLock` / `OnceCell` / `thread_local!` declarations in the crates' `src` trees. It FAILS when a global appears that the allowlist does not name, so the cost of adding one is stating why it is not per-design. It CANNOT judge whether a struct field is correctly scoped: the per-design metadata that rides on `ReflowService` today (graph_path, write_gen, read_hint) is not a global and the check has nothing to say about it — that is cap:graph-registry's work, and its absence is planned, not a violation. A check that claimed otherwise would be the green-washing the governance skill warns about: attaching a passing check to silence a finding rather than to detect a fault.

THE CLAUSE THAT LEFT: "a design is named by an id that resolves to a location — never a path" is now rule:a-design-is-named-by-an-id-not-a-path, and it is ADVISORY. It was split out rather than dropped because the two clauses sit in opposite positions against the code — that one has no compliant surface today, so an honest detector would fail against the entire existing tool surface, and the only ways to make it pass would be to block everything or to attach a check that proves nothing.

EVIDENCE, 2026-08-09, from Anthony's question about running reflow2 behind a web app at 1k / 100k / 1M tenants (dec:idea-a-hosted-tier-of-many-single-writer-tenants). This costs nothing today and is expensive to retrofit, and the failure mode is erosion rather than a decision. reflow2's own design measured 1,828 nodes = 3.8 MB export vs 33 MB store, which is what makes hold-many-designs-per-process the architecture rather than an option.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: nothing about WHERE a design is stored, nothing about hosting, and nothing that requires the registry to be built. It only keeps the door open.

properties.name: Success is read from the authoritative object, never from a tool's local exit code
properties.statement:
When a command acts on something outside itself — a remote service, a subprocess, a pipeline, a build artifact — read the OUTCOME from the authoritative object, not from the wrapper's exit status. A tool reporting failure on its local half is not evidence the act failed, and a zero exit is not evidence it succeeded.

FOUR MEASURED INSTANCES, all on this project, all 2026-08-14 or earlier:

1. **`gh pr merge` — FIVE TIMES on 2026-08-14.** It printed `git: 'remote-https' is not a git command` and a fast-forward warning, which reads exactly like a failed merge. **The merge had already succeeded server-side every time**; what failed was gh's LOCAL post-merge sync. The authoritative read is `gh pr view <n> --json state,mergeCommit`. ⚠️ Retrying on the apparent failure is how a branch gets merged twice or force-pushed over.

2. **`fact:a-piped-gate-reports-the-pipes-exit-code-not-the-gates`** — `cargo test --workspace | grep | tail` was reported as passing. **A pipeline's exit code is its LAST command's**, so that zero belonged to `tail`. Caught only because 20 suites / 250 tests looked low against the real 103 / 1,138. Redirect the gate to a file and read `$?` from the gate itself.

3. **🔴 NEW 2026-08-14 — A GREEN TEST SUITE IS NOT EVIDENCE THE BINARY DOES THE THING.** Building `cap:nudge-absence-says-why`, all 19 unit tests passed while `target/debug/reflow2-mcp` was still the PREVIOUS build: **`cargo test --lib` compiles the library and its test harness, not the executable target.** A live call against that binary still returned the old answer. Only `cargo build -p reflow2-mcp` then re-running the live call showed the change. **The suite was authoritative about the library and silent about the artifact a user runs, and those are different objects.**

4. **🔴 NEW 2026-08-14 — A CORRECT SOURCE FILE IS NOT EVIDENCE OF WHAT IS SERVED.** Skills are embedded into the binary by `build.rs` at COMPILE TIME, so editing `getting-started/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` changes what is served only after a rebuild. `skill_lint` passing and the three trees being byte-identical say nothing about the running server. The authoritative read is asking the rebuilt binary: `get_skill` and check the body.

⭐ **WHAT 3 AND 4 ADD TO THE RULE, AND IT WIDENS THE DETECTOR IT OWES:** the first two instances are about EXIT CODES; these two are about BUILD ARTIFACTS. Same shape — the value you read is not the value you think you are reading — but a check that only scans for piped gates and CLI exit codes would miss both. **A detector for this rule has to cover "was the thing you measured the thing a user gets?" as well as "was the status you read the status of the thing you ran?"**

THE SHAPE ALL FOUR SHARE: **the misreading looks exactly like the answer you wanted.** That is why advice was not enough — AGENTS.md already tells agents to read results sceptically, and all four happened anyway.

ENFORCEMENT: **ENFORCED, on Anthony's word 2026-08-14** — asked whether breaking it should stop the build, he said stop the build. He is the first person to choose an enforcement value on this project deliberately; `dec:does-enforced-default-to-gate-blocking` records that reflow2's other four enforced rules acquired that state from a default nobody chose.

🛑 **WHAT THIS RULE OWES, STATED RATHER THAN QUIETLY SATISFIED.** An enforced rule raises `unverified_enforced_rule` at severity 0.6 until a PASSING Verification detects violations of it. **No check is attached, and none should be attached to close the finding** — `governance-proposal` is explicit that a passing check which tests nothing is a lie the graph cannot see. The finding stays open until a real detector exists.

✅ THE EXIT-CODE HALF IS CHECKABLE FROM THE REPO: a gate piped through `grep`/`tail`/`head` before its status is read, or a remote-acting CLI whose exit code is taken as the outcome — `tools/` and `.github/workflows/` are both in-repo and greppable. ⚠️ **THE BUILD-ARTIFACT HALF MAY NOT BE**, since "did you rebuild before you measured" leaves no trace in the repository. That asymmetry is worth knowing before somebody attaches a check that covers half the rule and reads as covering all of it.

properties.name: Exactly one commit on a branch writes the design export, and it should be the last
properties.statement:
A branch may hold as many commits as it likes. EXACTLY ONE of them may write `docs/design/reflow2.json`, and it should be the last one. Export straight onto the committed file rather than exporting elsewhere and copying it in — the lineage link is built from whatever file is already at that path.

ENFORCED, AND THAT IS A MEASUREMENT RATHER THAN A JUDGEMENT. Breaking this ALREADY stops the build: `tools/reflow2_check.py` fails with `FAIL LINEAGE` and CI goes red. It did so twice on 2026-08-11 in one day's work. So `enforced: true` records what the project already does, not a consequence anybody chose today. ⚠️ Anthony has NOT been asked the consequence question for this rule — `cap:governance-proposal` exists to ask it and was not run. If he would rather this were advisory, the flag is wrong and the CI gate is what should change, not the flag.

WHY THIS RULE EXISTS SEPARATELY FROM THE REQUIREMENT IT SHADOWS, which is the whole point of adding it. `req:the-export-is-serialised-rather-than-socially-enforced` (accepted) says the SOFTWARE must detect a severed chain, and it is fully traced: `art:check` satisfies it and `ver:gate-suite` verifies that artifact. That thread is about what reflow2 BUILDS. It says nothing about what a CONTRIBUTOR must do, and the governance layer — `unverified_enforced_rule`, which scans DesignRules — could not see this policy at all, because the policy was expressed only as a requirement on the tool.

⇒ THE DETECTOR WAS REQUIRED AND BUILT; THE BEHAVIOUR WAS A CONVENTION WITH NO GOVERNANCE NODE. Anthony, 2026-08-11: "reflow2's own rules shouldn't be tracked by hand, but by some governance rules." This is that rule, made first-class.

HOW TO FOLLOW IT, recorded because it is not derivable and it cost about ten hand-driven cycles in a single day: restore the committed file first (`git checkout origin/main -- docs/design/reflow2.json`), then `export_graph` ONCE, then commit — folding into the existing commit with `--amend` if the branch already has one. ⚠️ A LINEAGE FAILURE REPORTED LOCALLY IMMEDIATELY AFTER EXPORTING IS EXPECTED AND IS NOT THE DEFECT: the local gate compares against HEAD's committed export while CI compares against the primary branch's, so amend first and re-check. The reverse also holds — a local OK after a rebase is not proof, because the three-way merge driver merges CONTENT correctly and cannot repair LINEAGE, which is a property of the file-to-file chain.

SCOPE, stated because the sibling rule does not state its own and is partly unfollowable without a forge. THIS RULE IS EXPRESSIBLE IN PURE GIT: one commit per branch touches one file. It needs no pull request, no forge and no review model. A PR is merely where CI happens to notice, which is why the rule survives on a bare remote where `rule:nothing-lands-on-main-directly` does not.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SAY: nothing about who may merge, nothing about branch naming, and nothing about review. Those are separate conventions and this rule deliberately does not smuggle them in.

properties.name: reflow2's own design always trails what reflow2 can catch — and that lag is the mechanism, not a failure
properties.statement:
A TOOL CAN ONLY CATCH WHAT IT HAS ALREADY BEEN TAUGHT TO CATCH. So reflow2's own design will always contain the class of defect reflow2 is about to learn to detect, and the implementation will always sit behind the detector it is growing. That is the definition of self-hosting, not evidence that anything is wrong.

Anthony, 2026-08-11, in his own words: "we are designing reflow2 using reflow2, so there is always a lag in implementation behind what reflow2 would catch."

WHAT THE RULE ACTUALLY BINDS, which is REPORTING rather than building. A finding of the shape "reflow2 did not catch X in its own design" is not an indictment and must not be written as one. The accurate reading is "X is now catchable, for everyone". Both sentences describe the same measurement; only the second is true about the situation. An agent that writes the first teaches the next reader that the project is failing at the exact moment it is working.

⭐ THE LAG IS THE MECHANISM, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Every defect reflow2 finds in its own design is one CONSUMERS WERE ALREADY EXPOSED TO and could not see. The stranded-server defect fixed on 2026-08-11 had hit two other projects before it reached the maintainer, and was reported independently by a third the same week. reflow2's own design is the canary: it is the first place a missing detector shows up as pain, because it is the design under the closest observation. That is why `rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party` works in practice rather than only in principle — the self-host generates the finding, and the third party is who the fix is FOR.

HIS SECOND HALF, recorded because it is the reason the arrangement is worth its cost: "the kind of cool thing is that because we are using reflow2 to develop itself, we get to see first hand how the things we develop/implement actually work immediately on reflow2 itself - kind of like an immediate feedback."

MEASURED THE SAME DAY, and the shape of the evidence matters. `cap:search-first-at-the-tool` shipped with seven purpose-built tests, all passing and mutation-checked three ways. Within minutes CI surfaced a false-positive class NONE of them held: two requirements with three-word statements refused as near-duplicates, found by an unrelated suite exercising a REAL usage pattern. The synthetic cases came from what an author imagined; the correction came from actual use. A test suite structurally cannot supply that, and the self-host does it for free and immediately.

WHAT THIS RULE DOES NOT LICENCE. It is not an excuse for a defect that was already detectable and was missed — those are ordinary misses and the graph should say so plainly. The lag it forgives is specifically the one between a detector EXISTING and the design it was built from being clean. Nor does it license fixing things here and calling them shipped: `rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party` still governs, and its named failure — patch it here, mark the requirement met, leave every consumer with the hole — is unaffected by this rule and is the more common error of the two.

ENFORCEMENT: NOT STATED. `DesignRule.enforced` is genuinely three-state and absent means nobody has said, which is the honest record here — Anthony has not been asked whether breaking this should stop a build, and it is a rule about how to READ a finding, so no detector could evaluate it. Asking the consequence question is `cap:governance-proposal`'s job and has not been done for this rule.
