There is no state in which some capabilities are frozen pending a decision while the rest of the work proceeds. reflow could do this. Its rigid-mode resync offered the user two options, and option B was: "Document each drift item as change request, add to context/change_requests.json, BLOCK implementation of drifted features, continue with non-drifted work." The RESYNC_to_P1 path for major drift in rigid mode likewise says "BLOCK until change request approved" — a targeted freeze, not a stopped project. WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN IT SOUNDS. On a system being evolved incrementally against functional production code — Anthony's actual case at NSLS-II, a ten-year-old bluesky stack evolving on the fly — "stop everything until this is resolved" is almost never the right answer, and "carry on regardless" is never the right answer either. Partial blocking is the only response that matches how the work actually proceeds: quarantine what is contested, keep delivering what is not. It is also what makes a gate survivable in a shared repo, where one contested capability currently reddens the build for everyone. WHAT reflow2 ALREADY HAS, so this is a smaller change than it appears: the graph can already say which capabilities are affected (propagate_change gives the blast radius; scope + claim_region give "the part I hold"), and status/proposed already expresses "not agreed yet". What is missing is that nothing READS those to scope a refusal — the gate asks one global question and gives one global answer. OPEN: whether a partial block is advisory (reported, not enforced, per dec:report-dont-judge) or actually refuses writes against the frozen region, and whether the frozen set is computed from the drift's blast radius or named by the user. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it.

properties.name: A design can see where its build stopped following it
properties.statement: Where the build holds as one artifact what the design holds as several distinct capabilities, reflow2 shall report that disagreement as an observation measured against the design's own distribution — never against an absolute size, never as a defect, and without ruling on which side is wrong.

properties.name: Unbounded build iteration is noticed and surfaced — a HARD STOP is one option, not the requirement
properties.statement:
REASSESSED 2026-07-28, same day, on Anthony's instruction not to treat reflow's workflows as canon. First written as "the build loop is bounded, and exhausting the budget forces a return to the design", which took reflow's halt-and-resync as the requirement rather than as one candidate mechanism. The name now separates the two.

THE REAL GAP, which stands on its own: reflow2 MEASURES design erosion under repeated build rounds and never ACTS on it. The erosion trial asks the sharp question — after N rounds of test-fails/fix-code/accept, does the design still describe what it should — and is a regression gate, so the decay is known and quantified. Nothing ever interrupts. A session can iterate indefinitely and reflow2 will faithfully record the drift afterwards. That is a real hole, whatever the response turns out to be.

WHY THE HARD STOP IS DOUBTFUL AS THE ANSWER. reflow halted after three P3/P4 loops and forced a resync to architecture. Three objections. (1) It is PHASE-SHAPED: "go back to P2" presumes there is a P2 to go back to, and reflow2 has layers of a golden thread, not phases. (2) A hard stop is a poor fit for the operating context this project exists for — continual evolution against functional production code, where halting the work is rarely the right answer and is exactly the move that gets a discipline abandoned by the people it is meant to help. (3) Any fixed count is arbitrary. reflow at least ASKED for it (phases/P0_setup elicits the budget, default 3, range 1-10, alongside the mode and drift tolerance) which is better than compiling it in — but eliciting an arbitrary number does not make it meaningful, only chosen.

WHAT IS MORE LIKELY RIGHT, and it fits the discipline reflow2 already committed to. dec:report-dont-judge says report and ask rather than decide; the loop nudge and cap:read-loop-hint already surface debt when it is real without blocking anything. The natural shape here is the same: NOTICE that the build has been iterating without the design moving, and SAY SO with evidence — which is a computed observation, not a threshold. The evidence is already available: unresolved DriftEvents accumulating, a design_holds/design_updated history that confirm.rs can already read as dishonest (five holds with zero design edits), coverage moving the wrong way. Escalation, if any, belongs to req:drift-rolls-up-to-a-score, which was reassessed the same day for the same reason.

DISTINCT FROM cap:budget, which rolls a RESOURCE budget against a Constraint (mass, cost, power). Whatever is built here is about the design PROCESS, and reflow2 has no vocabulary for that.

Worth keeping from the review, because it answers the obvious objection that any of this is waterfall legacy: reflow's own P5_operations phase_definition states "P5 is typically ongoing" and routes production issues back_to_P3_P4 as "a new development cycle". Even the phase model reflow2 inherited did not assume termination. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows; reassessed the same day.

properties.name: A claim names its owner, and a claim with no live owner is reported stale
properties.statement: A claim records the session that made it (its harness session id — assigned out of band, so it cannot race), and claim_report distinguishes a claim held by a live seat from one left behind by a session that closed. Liveness is computed from the owner, not asserted by the claim: a claim nobody is working is a ghost that makes the overlap report lie.

properties.name: Design stays coherent across its lifecycle
properties.statement: When anything changes in any phase, the ripples are found and surfaced.

properties.name: Pair two designs by complementary role, so the seam is computed rather than hand-wired
properties.statement:
Anthony's idea (2026-07-27), and the analogy he reached for is load-bearing rather than decorative: RNA strands pair because the bases are COMPLEMENTARY — adenine with uracil, guanine with cytosine — never like-with-like. Applied here: each boundary declares a ROLE — it publishes, it subscribes, it does both, or it is not external at all — and each project publishes only its publish-or-both boundaries with an id and a description. Combining two designs then starts mechanically: match every publisher against every subscriber, associate them, and treat the pair as ONE graph for every ordinary reflow2 check — gaps, defects, god nodes, surprising connections. The pairing is what makes composition cheap; everything after it already exists (cap:composed-analysis).

DECIDED 2026-07-27 (dec:pairing-role-placement, accepted on Anthony's word): the role lives on the INTERFACE, extending `designation`, not on every node. A Component both publishes and subscribes, so a per-node role collapses to `both` and pairs with everything — the `both` value was the tell that the attribute was on the wrong noun.

WHAT REFLOW2 ALREADY HAS. `Interface.designation` is the publish flag (`internal | published`, defaulting to internal because publishing is a commitment). `export_surface` emits published Interfaces plus the Components either side and withholds the rest. `PROVIDES` and `CONSUMES` carry the two roles at the edge level. The publish half works end to end.

WHAT IS MISSING, and it is the whole idea: THE SUBSCRIBE SIDE IS NOT DECLARABLE. A design says what it OFFERS; it cannot say what it NEEDS from outside in a form another design can be matched against. Today a need is a CONSUMES edge pointing at an Interface the consumer modelled INSIDE ITS OWN design — so a match only happens where the consumer already guessed the provider's contract and named it compatibly. Without that half there is no complementary strand.

THREE OUTCOMES, ALL USEFUL: a publisher matched to a subscriber (the seam, computed); a publisher nobody subscribes to (dead surface); a subscriber nothing publishes (an unmet need — the loudest signal there is). Two publishers of one key is a fourth: a duplicated provider, a conflict rather than a match.

THE PAIRING KEY IS NOT NAME ALONE — AMENDED 2026-07-28 AFTER A REAL TRIAL. Complementary role plus a matching key was the first draft, and the dynograph-foundation session refuted it from the provider's side within an hour of the channel opening. Their design carries three `medium: REST` boundaries: `ifc:rest-v1` (TCP, JWT), `ifc:uds` (Unix socket, JWT, `transport_security: physical`) and `ifc:ops-probes` (PUBLIC AND UNAUTHENTICATED BY DESIGN, because an orchestrator's liveness check cannot hold a credential). Under role-plus-medium alone, a consumer declaring "I require REST" pairs against all three — including the unauthenticated probe surface. That is not a near-miss; it is the pairing rule confidently producing a wrong and security-relevant answer.

So base-compatibility is `medium` PLUS `transport_security` PLUS `auth`. Every one of those is already a property on Interface, put there by req:interface-spec-complete; the fault was leaving them out of the key, not a missing field. And the analogy survives the correction better than it started: adenine–uracil is two hydrogen bonds, guanine–cytosine three. COMPATIBILITY WAS NEVER A SINGLE POINT OF CONTACT.

A mismatch on those axes must be REPORTED AS AN INCOMPATIBILITY, never dropped as a non-match. "You publish this, I need this, and we cannot be connected the way either of us is built" is exactly the finding worth having, and silence would hide it.

NAMES ARE STILL FUZZY. `auth-api` against `AuthService` is the Bob/Bobby/Robert problem, already solved once: ingest's two-band resolution (below fuzzy_threshold = no match, between = a reported candidate, above auto_merge_threshold = act) plus the token-subset pass that catches `Gateway` vs `API Gateway`. Reuse that rather than inventing a second matcher, and ASK about the middle band (dec:ask-not-repair).

UNLABELLED MUST NOT READ AS `non_external`. A boundary nobody classified silently counting as internal means a design that never did the labelling pairs with nothing and reports a clean seam — the blindness cap:coverage exists to end. The pairing report must count and name what carries no role, as coverage_report does.

properties.name: Whether intent has been delivered is computed from the golden thread, never asserted
properties.statement: A requirement's completion must be derived from evidence already in the graph — something satisfies it, and that capability is realized and its check passes — not set by hand on the requirement itself. A hand-set "done" is a claim that outlives the truth: it survives the capability regressing, the artifact drifting, the verification starting to fail, and it degrades exactly as silently as an unreconciled checksum. Derived completion also makes the reverse question answerable without anyone maintaining it: what fraction of accepted intent is actually delivered, and which requirements are believed-done on evidence that no longer holds. The same rule applies to the rest of the lifecycle: a requirement that stopped being satisfied must be able to say so, rather than remaining green because nobody revisited it.

properties.name: Import one design into another and analyse the whole
properties.statement: reflow2 must be able to bring a dependency's design into a consuming design and run its ordinary analysis over the combined whole, so that composition problems appear as ordinary gaps rather than requiring a bespoke comparator. WHAT BLOCKS IT TODAY IS CONCRETE, not vague: import_graph writes every node under its ORIGINAL id with upsert semantics, so importing design Z into design A means Z's `cap:store` silently overwrites A's `cap:store`. It was built for layering a design onto itself — its own doc says an export can be layered onto a design it references — and using it to compose two DIFFERENT designs would corrupt the consumer without saying so. The other two composition mechanisms do not do this either, and it is worth being exact about why: mirror_surface deliberately imports only the published SURFACE and keeps it foreign, and merge_designs is a three-way merge of two versions of the SAME design. So a fourth thing is needed — a NAMESPACED import where both designs coexist and are separately identifiable. TWO THINGS THAT MUST NOT BE LOST. First, the combined graph must never be mistaken for the consumer's own design: every imported node stays attributable to where it came from, and an export of A must not start shipping Z's internals. Second, project-level detectors would now reason over both designs, so a consumer would see gaps belonging to its dependency — noise that would get the whole feature switched off. cap:scoped-analysis already narrows detection to a region and reports what it left out, so scoping the combined analysis to the seam is the likely answer rather than a new filter. NOTE THE TENSION WITH dec:nested-graphs, which chose a graph per ownership boundary precisely because edges cannot cross stores: this does not overturn that decision — the designs stay separately owned and separately released — but it does mean a THIRD, analysis-only composition alongside the two that exist.

properties.name: What the graph computes reaches the quality axis it informs
properties.statement: Where reflow2 computes something that bears on a quality axis, it shall report that evidence against the axis by name, and shall say plainly of each axis whether a design graph can inform it at all — never deriving a score, never re-judging a finding the computation that produced it declined to call a defect, and never ruling on which side is right where a computed signal and an asserted assessment disagree.

properties.name: Several people can plan against one design without colliding
properties.statement: A team, not a single author, must be able to work on one design at the same time: each person able to see what the others hold, to work in a scope that does not collide with theirs, and to have genuinely overlapping work surfaced as decidable conflicts rather than silent last-writer-wins. Whether this extends to simultaneous editing with live presence, or stops at non-colliding parallel work with good merges, is deliberately not asserted here — it depends on an architecture question that is still open, and the weaker form may be what teams actually need.

properties.name: A pointer resolves for everyone holding the design, not only for the machine that wrote it
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-07-31: "as one of the features we've worked on previously was that multiple people could use reflow2, may have to think about how the blob contents can be made available to multiple users of reflow2 on multiple machines? Maybe the git repo also backs-up the blob contents?"

THE REQUIREMENT: any seat holding the design must be able to resolve a pointer to its bytes, or be told plainly that it cannot. A design where half the diagrams open for one person and not the other is worse than one with no diagrams, because the first person cannot tell that the second is missing something.

WHY IT IS THE HARDEST PART OF THE CONTENT STORE, and why it belongs as its own requirement rather than a footnote to `req:content-store-for-what-the-graph-points-at`: the graph already solved distribution by being a FILE — `dec:multi-writer-architecture` chose a repo file plus merge-on-pull precisely so that cloning gets you the design and no service is needed. Blobs do not inherit that for free. A content store that lives only where it was written recreates the exact failure `cap:session-memory` already names about machine-local paths, one layer up: it resolves for one person and silently misses for everyone else.

THIS IS ALSO WHERE THE COMMITTED-OR-GITIGNORED QUESTION IS ACTUALLY DECIDED. `dec:where-content-lives` asks it as a repo-weight trade-off; read through this requirement it is not really about weight at all, it is about whether the bytes are DISTRIBUTED BY THE SAME MECHANISM AS THE DESIGN. Anthony's own suggestion — let the git repo carry the blobs — is the option that makes distribution automatic and identical to how the design already travels, at the cost of repo size and git's poor handling of binary churn. The alternative is a second distribution channel, which means a second thing to configure, be down, or be out of step.

WHAT MUST HOLD EITHER WAY: an unresolvable pointer FAILS LOUD and is nameable (`req:no-silent-fallback`), and content is addressed BY HASH so a blob fetched from anywhere can be verified as the right one — which also makes several distribution mechanisms interchangeable rather than requiring one to be chosen forever.

NOT SETTLED HERE: the mechanism. That stays with `dec:where-content-lives`, which this requirement reframes rather than answers.

properties.name: The graph holds pointers; a content store holds the bytes — narrative, transcripts, diagrams and drawings travel WITH the design
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-07-31: reflow2 should capture session context — the conversation itself — as a narrative snapshot recorded in the graph, the way storyflow already does it. "storyflow has a blob storage setup to actually store all narrative context and pictures, etc, and then the dynograph-foundation just records the pointer to that storage. The benefits is that any session context and generated artifacts or user provided diagrams/drawings can be stored as part of the reflow2 and are persistent."

THE SPLIT IS THE REQUIREMENT: the graph stores a POINTER and the bytes live in a content store beside it. The graph stays small, diffable and queryable — the properties `dec:repo-file-embedded` chose it for — while the things that are large, binary or verbatim stop being second-class.

WHAT THIS UNLOCKS THAT NOTHING ELSE DOES: user-provided DIAGRAMS AND DRAWINGS. The design vocabulary is entirely textual today, and a hand-drawn architecture sketch or a whiteboard photo is exactly the kind of intent that never survives a project — it lives in someone's phone and is gone when they leave. `Artifact` can name a file on disk but nothing carries its content, so a diagram is a path that rots.

IT ALSO FIXES A FLAW THE DESIGN ALREADY NAMED. `cap:session-memory` models the session transcript as a Fragment pointing at `~/.claude/projects/<slug>/<uuid>.jsonl`, and states the problem in its own words: "a path stored as identity resolves for one person on one machine and silently misses for everyone on a shared graph." A content store IS the answer to that — content-addressed bytes travel with the design instead of referring to one person's filesystem. The requirement should be read as completing `cap:session-memory`, not competing with it.

THE CONSTRAINT THAT MUST SURVIVE, from that same capability: a pointer to a 3 MB transcript is a RECEIPT, not documentation. Storing the raw conversation must not become the excuse that stops takeaways being distilled into Decisions and findings — "it is all in the transcript" is the same failure as "it is all in the backlog file", one level down. The store makes the receipt durable; it does not discharge the obligation.

PRIOR ART, and it is a sibling rather than a stranger: storyflow already runs this and shares the dynograph-foundation substrate underneath, so the question is what to import, not what to invent. AGENTS.md rule 6 permits exactly this direction — mine the sibling repos for ideas, land the work here.

DELIBERATELY NOT SETTLED HERE: where the bytes actually live. That is a genuine architecture fork against `dec:repo-file-embedded`, and it is recorded separately as `dec:where-content-lives`.

properties.name: Context cost is MEASURED and budgeted, not estimated at design time
properties.statement:
REASSESSED 2026-07-28, same day, on Anthony's instruction not to treat reflow's workflows as canon. First written as "context consumption is modelled so a path that will not fit is knowable before it is walked", arguing from reflow's design-time estimation. The FINDING is mine and stands; reflow's MECHANISM is the weak half, and the name now says which.

THE FINDING, measured against reflow2's own design and independent of any prior art: DEPENDS_ON declares a coupling-weight facet whose schema comment states its purpose — "weight is a STRENGTH (higher = tighter); invert to a cost for shortest-path/closeness" — and over 3,250 edges, 232 carry weight_basis while ZERO carry weight, frequency or data_volume. The facet is declared and wholly unpopulated, which also explains req:edge-defaults-do-not-assert rather than merely repeating it: weight_basis asserts "estimated" over an absent weight because weights were meant to be there.

WHY DESIGN-TIME ESTIMATION IS THE WEAK PART. reflow made context_consumption a function attribute and the primary edge weight, published estimation guidelines (read_workflow_file 5000-15000 tokens, generate_architecture 5000-15000, and so on), summed along paths, and flagged CRITICAL above 160k. Three problems. (1) The estimates go stale the moment anything changes and nothing ever re-derives them, so the graph accumulates confident numbers nobody has checked — the shape this project keeps rediscovering. (2) They are model-specific: 160k was reflow's environment, tokenisers and context windows differ, and hardcoding one number as a law is the asserting default req:defaults-do-not-assert forbids. (3) Real consumption is dominated by what static structure cannot see — how much a tool actually returns, how many rounds a negotiation takes, what the user pastes in. A statically-summed path cost would be precise and wrong.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WANTED, and reflow2 already has most of the vocabulary. MEASURE rather than estimate: real sessions produce real costs per tool call and per skill, and weight_basis already distinguishes estimated / evidence / measured — further evidence the facet was designed for observed values, not guesses. Then BUDGET at runtime against what is left, which composes with cap:bounded-reads (a read that would not fit answers with a bounded page and says what it left out) and cap:tool-search (finding a tool on a surface too large to hold) rather than replacing them. A measured cost also feeds req:friction-has-a-baseline honestly, since "this got more expensive across a release" is a regression the baseline should catch.

An estimate is defensible only as a SEED for something never measured, and must read as estimated — which is exactly what weight_basis is for. Fixing the edge default and populating the facet remain two answers to one question and should be decided together. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing 99-meta_analysis.json; reassessed the same day.

properties.name: What an agent cannot infer must travel on the tool, not only in the skill it may never load
properties.statement:
The parts of a skill that are reflow2 CONVENTION — not general good sense — must be reachable from the tool surface itself, because a capable agent reconstructs most of a skill and silently loses the rest.

THE ASYMMETRY THIS RESTS ON, observed 2026-07-31: reading `detect-and-ask` after having worked without it, roughly its first and last steps had already been done unprompted (call `detect_gaps`; re-run it to confirm). What had NOT been done was every reflow2-specific step in between — the `gap_to_prompt` handshake, `answer_question`, and the distinction between answering a gap and acknowledging one. A competent model infers the general shape and drops the local convention, and the loss is INVISIBLE: you cannot know which part of a skill you failed to load.

So the fraction worth relocating is precisely the fraction a model would never guess. A tool description that says "answering a gap and acknowledging it are different acts, and an answered-but-unacknowledged gap stays open" costs one sentence and cannot be skipped, because the schema arrives with the call.

THE TENSION, named rather than glossed: `dec:skills-served` chose to serve skills from the server so they always match the running version and nothing in a consumer's repo goes stale. That is right, and this does not reverse it. It says the IRREDUCIBLE MINIMUM also rides the tool, where it is unskippable, and the served skill keeps the depth, the worked examples and the reasoning. Two homes for two jobs, not a copy.

THE COST TO WATCH: tool descriptions are context an agent pays for on every session, and `cap:tool-search` exists because the surface is already too large to hold. So this must be a sentence per tool at most, chosen for what cannot be inferred — not a second copy of the skill wearing a different hat.

properties.name: A whole corpus of existing specifications can be brought into the design in one pass
properties.statement: Where a system's intent already exists as a large body of written specifications, reflow2 must be able to take the whole corpus — a folder, not a file — and produce one coherent design from it, with every claim still pointing back at the document it came from. The load-bearing requirement is identity ACROSS documents: the same component named in forty specifications must converge on one node rather than forty near-duplicates, and where convergence is uncertain the user is asked rather than the nodes being silently merged. Ordering must not decide meaning — which file happened to be read first must not determine the canonical name of anything.

properties.name: The design can state that two parts must agree, and check it — correspondence as a first-class rule
properties.statement:
NOT FROM reflow. Raised 2026-07-28 from the architecture-description standard ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010, after Anthony's instruction to bring judgement rather than treat reflow's workflows as canon. reflow had nothing resembling this; the gap is visible only against the standard practice reflow2 exists to serve.

42010 models an architecture description as Stakeholders holding Concerns, Viewpoints that frame those concerns, and Views governed by viewpoints — and then the piece that does the work: CORRESPONDENCES between elements of different views, governed by CORRESPONDENCE RULES that state what must hold between them, so consistency is a checkable claim rather than a hope. reflow2 has the projection half and not the correspondence half. dec:views-are-projections is right and is stronger than anything in reflow (a view is a pure projection of the graph; renderer fill-ins are defects), but a projection guarantees only that a view does not invent — it says nothing about whether two projections of the same design agree where they overlap.

WHAT reflow2 HAS TODAY IS A HANDFUL OF HARDCODED CORRESPONDENCES. cap:seam-incompatibility says when two linked designs disagree at a boundary. reconcile_artifacts, reconcile_deployment and reconcile_verification each compare the design against one facet of reality. The unvalidated_capability, status_contradiction and unprovided_interface gaps are each a fixed rule about what must agree with what. Every one is a correspondence rule expressed in Rust, invisible to the user, and unextendable: a team cannot say "in OUR design, every Component with concern=safety must have a Verification of kind=validation performed in a non-simulation Environment" and have it checked. The rules that exist are the ones the maintainer thought of.

WHY IT MATTERS HERE SPECIFICALLY. The operating context is several organisations with competing, partially-built designs that were never meant to interoperate, delivered as increments. That is the situation 42010's correspondence machinery was written for: A's view and B's view describe overlapping reality with different vocabulary and different concerns, and what makes integration tractable is being able to STATE the correspondence and then compute whether it still holds as both sides move. Hand-wiring each such rule into the tool does not scale past the maintainer's imagination.

AND IT WOULD GIVE Requirement.concern A READER. concern is the sharpest item in the 2026-07-28 sweep — an enum carrying the ILS/SME vocabulary (logistics, sustainment, safety, security…), single-valued at `core` on 67 of 67, with no writer on the MCP surface and no reader anywhere, so "which are the safety requirements?" answers `none` rather than `unknown`. It is dead because nothing consumes concerns, and nothing consumes concerns because there is no stakeholder-concern-viewpoint chain for them to feed. Building the chain is what would make that property mean something, rather than deleting it.

OPEN and not decided: whether a correspondence rule is authored as data (a small predicate over node types, properties and edges, evaluated by the detector machinery) or remains code with only the VOCABULARY made explicit; whether Stakeholder is a new node type or Actor grown up (Actor already carries actor_type including `stakeholder`, and is currently counted in report.rs and read nowhere — see req:scenarios-are-modelled); and how a user-authored rule avoids becoming a way to make the tool assert things nobody checked, which dec:report-dont-judge would forbid.

properties.name: The design must be able to say how much of the system it has never modelled
properties.statement: reflow2 must be able to report the portion of a real system that no node in the design has ever claimed, so that the thinness of a recovered or evolving model is measurable rather than merely felt. An empty gap list must mean "the design is coherent AND it covers the system", not "the design is coherent about the fraction it happens to know". The report says what is unclaimed and how large it is; it never scores the design, never blocks, and never treats coarse-but-honest modelling as a deficiency — a single opaque Component legitimately claims everything beneath it.

properties.name: Recording an open question must never assert that it was settled
properties.statement: A Decision's status must not be set on the user's behalf. Recording a choice someone is still facing — an open question, a brainstormed option, a decision point held for later — must land as `proposed`, and reaching `accepted` must be a separate, deliberate act. Found as friction 2026-07-25: add_decision defaults to `accepted`, so six open questions recorded in one session each landed as settled and needed correcting immediately afterwards. This generalises dec:certainty-derived from requirements to decisions, and the reason is the same: an accepted Decision is what where-am-i reads back to the user as "what you decided", what the fork layer treats as binding, and what the KPP contradiction check reads as a trade already made. A musing recorded as a reasoned choice is therefore worse than a missing record — it is a false one, attributed to them. Evidence it was systemic rather than one slip: the correction had become a standing note carried across sessions, and the brainstorm skill had to instruct it in prose ("this call is not optional"), which is a defect with a bandage on it.

properties.name: A decomposition is checkable against what the parent held, because delivery rolls up whether or not the children cover it
properties.statement: reflow2 rolls delivery UP a decomposition and never checks that the children COVER the parent. report.rs:566 is explicit: if a requirement has decomposed children, it is delivered if and only if every child is delivered — "let children = self.decomposed_children(requirement_id)?; if children.is_empty() { return Ok(false); } for child in &children { if !self.requirement_is_delivered_within(child, depth - 1)? { return Ok(false); } } Ok(true)". Nothing anywhere asks whether the children, taken together, amount to the parent. So a parent split into two children that address a tenth of it reports DELIVERED the moment both close, in the coverage number this project treats as ground truth (req:completion-computed: delivery is computed from the golden thread, never asserted). THE CONCRETE INSTANCE, and it is not hypothetical. This was first noticed on 2026-07-28 as a modelling risk, when DECOMPOSES was rejected as the edge type for two new requirements precisely because decomposing req:defaults-do-not-assert (ten measured instances) into two children would have reported it delivered with eight outstanding. Reviewing 01-systems_engineering.json the same day turned that risk into a field observation: reflow's own monolithic workflow was decomposed into 01a through 01f, and TWO CROSS-CUTTING TOP-LEVEL BLOCKS DID NOT SURVIVE. context_management (operations counter, degradation signals, refresh sequence, pre-operation checklist) and self_improvement (retrospective questions, metrics, improvement backlog) are present in all six monolithic workflows — 00-setup, 01-systems_engineering, 02-artifacts_visualization, 03-development, 04-testing_operations, feature_update — and absent from every one of 00a, 01a, 01b, 01c, 01d, 01e and 01f. Cross-referenced against workflow_master's phase assignments, context_management survives in roughly two of about sixteen live workflows. The discipline lived in every original file and largely did not make it into the decomposition, and nothing noticed for months. THE MECHANISM OF THE LOSS IS THE GENERAL CASE: a decomposition by SUBJECT drops what belongs to no single subject. Cross-cutting content has no natural child to land in, so it lands in none. That is exactly the failure a coverage check would catch and a roll-up will never notice, because the roll-up only ever asks whether each child is done. WHAT IS NOT BEING ASKED FOR: automatic refusal, or an LLM judging sufficiency. The honest form is a question put to the user at decomposition time — "does this set of children cover the parent, and what did the parent hold that none of them do?" — with the answer recorded, so a later reader can tell a deliberate narrowing from an accident. That fits the pattern the project already uses for gaps: report and ask, per dec:report-dont-judge, never decide. Note also the interaction with req:requirement-lineage, which distinguishes decomposed from derived: a DERIVED requirement adds new technical necessity and is not expected to cover anything, so any check must apply to decomposition alone. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing 01-systems_engineering.json. Anthony's word: capture it.

properties.name: A default must not assert what nobody chose
properties.statement:
FOUND BY A DELIBERATE SWEEP, 2026-07-28, asking the question `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` implies but does not answer: what ELSE does the schema claim that no computation checks? The sweep was Anthony's call after the same defect shape appeared six times in three days.

THE MEASURED FINDING. Ten properties are materialised onto every node by the store's schema defaults and appear ZERO times in the entire Rust source — not in a detector, not in a report, not in a test. Measured against reflow2's own 860-node design:

- `Requirement.concern` — `core` on 67 of 67
- `Capability.tier` — `operational` on 84 of 84
- `Component.tier` — `operational` on 53 of 53
- `Capability.is_entry_point` / `is_exit_point` — `false` on 84 of 84
- `Constraint.concern`, `DesignRule.enforced`, `Actor.actor_type`, `EnvironmentRule.mandatory`, `EnvironmentRule.rule_type`, `Flow.tier` — likewise defaulted, likewise unread

Single-valued across the whole design, every one. A property that never varies is not carrying information; it is asserting one.

THE WORST INSTANCE, and the reason this is intent rather than tidiness. `Requirement.concern`'s enum is core / logistics / sustainment / safety / security / cost / schedule / manufacturability / usability / environmental — and the schema's own description says logistics and sustainment are there to carry "the ILS considerations an SME surfaces". That is the systems-engineering angle this project exists to serve, encoded in the schema and then asserted away: every requirement claims `core`, there is NO WRITER for it on the MCP surface (only the `create_node` escape hatch — the same shape as the KPP `objective` finding), and nothing reads it. So "which of these are the safety requirements?" cannot be answered, and the graph does not answer "unknown" — it answers "none".

THE RULE, AND IT IS ALREADY PROVEN HERE. `Interface.medium` defaulting to `REST` was fixed on 2026-07-28 for exactly this reason, and `ver:interface-spec` states the principle in the form it should now generalise: "UNRECORDED FIELDS READ AS `unspecified` NOT `none` — the flattering default would tell a consumer an unspecified contract is open." So: A DEFAULT MAY RECORD ABSENCE; IT MAY NOT RECORD A CHOICE. Where a property has a substantive default nobody selected, the default becomes `unspecified` and silence reads as silence.

WHY IT IS NOT MERELY COSMETIC. `export_surface` publishes a design's boundary to another design; a mirrored surface carrying `tier: operational` and `concern: core` ships assertions nobody made across a seam, which is the same failure `req:publishable-promise` was raised for one layer down. And the moment any future computation DOES read one of these — the SME view `concern` was designed for — it reads a value the schema invented.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT, and it is what stops this being a blanket rewrite: a default that records a genuine absence is CORRECT and must stay. `provenance: authored` and `status: proposed` are real defaults meaning a real thing. The test is whether the default names a CHOICE among alternatives (tier, concern, rule_type) or the ABSENCE of one — only the first kind lies. Changing a default is also not retroactive: nodes written before the change keep the value they were given, so a sweep of existing designs is a separate, deliberate act.

SIBLING FINDINGS FROM THE SAME SWEEP, recorded here rather than lost. (1) Fifteen properties are WRITTEN and never consulted — the sharpest is `DriftEvent.severity`, written from `kind.severity()` at three call sites while ranking independently re-derives it via `severity_rank(kind)`, so the stored copy can silently diverge from the mapping that actually governs; also `DesignEpoch.sequence`, which COORD entries quote as meaningful ("epoch:v0180 at sequence 210") and nothing orders by. (2) `req:supporting-is-not-conflict` is an instance of ITSELF: it carries `concern: core`, one of the properties nothing reads.

properties.name: Design anything, not only software
properties.statement: Software, hardware, a document, a process — the vocabulary stays neutral.

properties.name: A system's design can be a unit of its own that composes with the designs around it
properties.statement: Anthony, 2026-07-25, promoting the idea he had been thinking out loud about: "being able to have multiple repos that are linked by interface specifications (reflow2 could take both graphs and figure out how to resolve differences between those two repos to ensure they work together)... the idea would allow teams to focus in their most immediate concern and let the interface take care of how it works with all the other systems/components." The intent is that a design need not be one document for one program: a team owning a system can hold ITS design as a unit — its own store, its own lifecycle, its own published surface — and that unit composes with the systems around it through the interfaces between them, so the day-to-day view is genuinely local and the cross-system agreement is carried by the contract rather than by everyone reading everything. Four things follow, each a real obligation rather than a detail. The link between two designs cannot be an edge, because the schema validates both endpoints of every edge and they live in different stores; it must be a COORDINATE that names the other design, the node in it, and the version of it being built against. A parent's view of a composed child must ROLL UP the child's evidence — what it delivers and what it has proven — or a requirement satisfied inside the child fires as unsatisfied in the parent forever. That view is a dated claim about a VERSION of the child, never a live truth, so staleness is part of the model and not an afterthought. And the seam becomes the place where two teams genuinely collide, which is precisely where the merge machinery does not yet reach. This restates in the design what BL-45 recorded on 2026-07-20 from the same author, and it is deliberately silent on federation-versus-one-graph, which is dec:nested-graphs.

properties.name: Declare which version of another design you depend on, not just record what you took
properties.statement: A project that composes with another design must be able to DECLARE which version of it that dependency is on — a tag, a commit, a release — in a checked-in manifest a person edits, the way Cargo.toml, pyproject.toml, pixi.toml or uv.toml declare code dependencies. Anthony's framing, 2026-07-27: when two projects evolve separately you need to know which version yours depended upon. WHAT ALREADY EXISTS IS THE OTHER HALF, and the distinction is the whole point. cap:mirror-surface already RECORDS the coordinate after the fact — mirror_content_hash is the content hash of the surface document a mirror was made from, and mirrored_at dates it, deliberately as a dated claim rather than a live truth. That is what you GOT. A manifest is what you MEANT: human-meaningful (v0.11.0, not a 64-character hash), authored rather than derived, reviewable in a diff, and readable before any graph is opened. HAVING BOTH IS WHAT MAKES THE CHECK POSSIBLE: declared-versus-mirrored answers 'am I actually composing against the version I said', and declared-versus-upstream answers 'has what I depend on moved since'. Either question is unanswerable with only one of the two halves. THE MANIFEST MUST ALSO RECORD WHICH REFLOW2 WROTE IT (Anthony, same day) — the same discipline the export stamp already follows, and for the same reason: a manifest is read by a binary that may be older or newer than the one that produced it, and a file that cannot say which vocabulary it was written against forces the reader to guess. reflow2 already refuses rather than guesses when an export's stamp is unreadable; the manifest should be no weaker. The manifest must also survive the case where the dependency's design is not available at all, because declaring a dependency you cannot currently resolve is a normal state and silence about it would be the failure.

properties.name: A durable design knows its own name, and remembers it across opens
properties.statement: A design that composes with others must have a stable identity of its own, remembered beside the store rather than supplied on each open. Found while building cap:mirror-surface on 2026-07-25: every reflow2 graph carried the same hardcoded graph_id, so no design could tell another design from itself — mirroring had to refuse a surface whose source id equalled its own, and with one constant that check could never pass. `open_in_memory_as` fixed it for library and test use; the durable case is unsolved and is deliberately not half-built, because the id namespaces every stored key: an on-disk graph reopened under a different name would find nothing, and one reopened under the DEFAULT name after being created with another would silently present an empty design. So identity has to live where the provenance stamp already lives (the sidecar beside the store), be written once at creation, and be REFUSED rather than defaulted when a later open disagrees with it — the same shape as the schema stamp refusing a graph a binary cannot read in full. Two consequences follow. Identity must be stable across machines, or the same design mirrored from two places reads as two designs; and it must be distinct by default, since two projects both called the design's default name would mirror into each other and the collision guard would report every node as a clash. This is rule:no-foreclosure item 5 arriving as real work rather than as a hypothetical.

properties.name: Someone without the repo can reach a design, read it, and contribute to it
properties.statement: Anthony and his brother work on each other's ideas from opposite coasts, and today the only way to reach a design is to clone the repository that carries it. The intent is that a design can be made reachable to a named collaborator without handing them the code: they can read what it says, ask it questions, and contribute intent back — the collaboration is on the DESIGN, which is often the part a second person can help with before they know anything about the implementation. Two things this must not become. It must not make the design's home ambiguous: whatever hosts a shared copy, the repo file stays the durable record, or a hosting outage becomes a design outage (req:persistence, dec:repo-file-embedded). And it must not silently widen who can write: reaching a design is not the same as authoring in it, so a contribution must be attributable to a person (the Contributor layer, which exists) and the reach must be granted rather than assumed. Whether this is served by git remotes that already span both coasts, by a hosted service, or by both, is the open question recorded as dec:central-host — this requirement states the need, not the machinery.

properties.name: Where a design admits it, design its simulator too — and test there first
properties.statement: A design usually has to operate in an environment. Where it is reasonable to build a simulated version of that environment — or a digital twin of the design itself — reflow2 should treat THE SIMULATOR AS SOMETHING TO BE DESIGNED, not as an implementation detail that appears later, and should support a progression: exercise the design in simulation first, iron out what that reveals, then move to progressively more realistic tests and only then to real fielding. The payoff is risk removed before it is expensive: an issue found in simulation costs a rebuild, the same issue found in the field costs a deployment and sometimes a system. THE CAVEAT IS PART OF THE REQUIREMENT, not a footnote — not every design admits a meaningful simulation, and a tool that insisted on one would produce elaborate fictions for the designs that do not. So the first question is whether a simulator is feasible and worth it for THIS design, asked rather than assumed, and a design that answers no must be able to say so on the record without being nagged.

properties.name: The core is deterministic and LLM-free
properties.statement: The runtime core must be free of LLM and provider dependencies and neutral to the interaction surface; LLM reasoning enters only behind a sync, object-safe seam.

properties.name: Drift is reported with its direction and its meaning, not just its magnitude
properties.statement: When the design and the build diverge, reflow2 must say which way and about what — not merely that a file's contents moved. Three things follow. Direction: a system that has grown capability the design never recorded is a different condition from one whose design overstates it, and today both arrive as an identical checksum change, so understatement is invisible exactly where it is largest. Meaning: the report must say what the design now claims wrongly, because asking someone to decide whether the design still holds while telling them only that bytes changed puts the entire burden of finding the delta on the person least likely to have time for it — which is how the design goes stale despite a mechanism designed to stop it. And write-back: where the design was recovered from documents, bringing the design up to date must be able to reach those documents, or the source everyone actually reads stays wrong while the graph quietly becomes right.

properties.name: Escalation from drift is computed — but probably NOT from a single scalar
properties.statement:
REASSESSED 2026-07-28, same day, on Anthony's instruction not to treat reflow's workflows as canon. This requirement was first written as "drift rolls up to one number, and how far the work retreats is computed from it", arguing from reflow's scalar drift_score. That argument was too credulous and the name has been changed with it. What follows keeps the real question and demotes reflow's answer to one option among several.

THE REAL QUESTION, which stands on its own: when the design and the build have diverged, nothing in reflow2 says HOW FAR BACK the work should go. Per-event dispositions answer "what do we do about this divergence"; nothing answers "is the accumulated divergence bad enough that we should stop adding to it and revisit the allocation, or the intent?" That question is real and unanswered.

WHY THE SCALAR IS THE WEAK PART. Collapsing heterogeneous drift into one 0.0-1.0 number destroys precisely the information that decides what to do: a missing artifact, a spec mismatch and an undocumented addition are different problems with different responses, and their average is not a thing. reflow's thresholds (below 0.3 keep building, 0.3 to 0.5 revise allocation, at or above 0.5 revise intent) are invented numbers with no derivation given, and its retreat targets are phase-shaped because reflow had phases. Adopting the scalar would also collide with dec:certainty-derived: a confident aggregate computed from a base the code already disagrees with is an assertion dressed as a measurement.

reflow2 IS ALREADY AHEAD HERE AND SHOULD NOT REGRESS. Drift is disposed of PER EVENT — design_holds or design_updated — so a session can hold the design on one divergence and update it on another, which reflow's single global mode could not do. And confirm.rs audits whether the dispositions are honest: "five design_holds claims with zero design edits is a very different confirmation history from one design_updated". That history is a better signal than any scalar, because it is evidence rather than an estimate. If escalation is built, it should read the disposition history, not an average.

THE PRECONDITION STILL HOLDS whatever shape is chosen: DriftEvent.severity is one of the WRITTEN-and-never-consulted properties the 2026-07-28 sweep found — written from kind.severity() at three call sites while ranking re-derives it via severity_rank(kind) — so any computation over stored severity reads a value the code already contradicts. Settle the single-source question first.

WHAT IS ACTUALLY WANTED, stated without borrowing reflow's mechanism: a computed, evidence-backed answer to "should we keep building or go back, and back to WHAT" — where the destinations are layers of the golden thread (realization, allocation, intent) rather than phases, and the trigger is drawn from what the graph can already prove (unresolved DriftEvents by kind, the design_holds/design_updated history, coverage moving the wrong way) rather than from a number nobody can derive. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows; reassessed the same day.

properties.name: The driving agents are coding agents, not humans
properties.statement: The primary consumers are Claude Code and grok build (plus OpenCode/Copilot), which reach the system as MCP tools plus an installed skill kit. The human is reached only through the agent.

properties.name: Edge properties default like node properties do, and the sweep never looked at them
properties.statement:
The 2026-07-28 schema sweep behind req:defaults-do-not-assert measured NODE properties — ten of them across Requirement, Capability, Component, Constraint, DesignRule, Actor, EnvironmentRule and Flow. It never looked at EDGE properties, and the same defect is there. FOUND BY TRIPPING OVER IT: creating a DEPENDS_ON with no properties at all returned {"optional": false, "weight_basis": "estimated"} — materialised while capturing a requirement about exactly this.

MEASURED, not inspected, over the 3,226 edges of reflow2's own design. Nineteen edge properties carry a schema default. Four are single-valued wherever they appear, matching the default and never varying: ALLOCATED_TO.weight_basis = estimated on 96 of 96, DEPENDS_ON.optional = false on 123 of 123, PROVIDES.weight_basis and CONSUMES.weight_basis = estimated on 3 of 3 each.

THE SHARPEST FINDING IS WORSE THAN A DEFAULT THAT NEVER VARIES: it is a default that describes a value which does not exist. `weight_basis` is documented as "How the weight was set: an LLM estimate, grounded in evidence, or measured from telemetry." 225 edges carry weight_basis — ALLOCATED_TO 96, DEPENDS_ON 123, PROVIDES 3, CONSUMES 3 — and ZERO of them carry a `weight`. Every one of those edges states the provenance of a coupling strength that was never recorded. Note that variation does not rescue it: DEPENDS_ON.weight_basis genuinely varies (evidence on 70, estimated on 53), so it passes the single-valued test the node sweep used, and it is still describing nothing. The node sweep's own test — "a property that never varies is not carrying information" — is necessary but NOT sufficient on edges, because a property can vary and still refer to an absent value.

DEPENDS_ON.optional = false on 123 of 123 is a plain instance of the original rule: it asserts that every dependency in the design is MANDATORY, which is a real architectural claim and nobody made it.

LATENT, and it will assert on first use: ten defaulted edge properties sit on edge types with zero instances in this design — ANNOTATES.resolved, CAUSES.basis (`correlational`), CAUSES.validation_status, CLAIMS.depth, COMPLIES_WITH.verified, PART_OF_FLOW.weight_basis, SUPPLEMENTS.grounding (`extrapolated`), and VIOLATES_RULE.proposer / severity / status. VIOLATES_RULE.severity defaults to `high`, so the first rule violation anyone records will claim high severity unprompted. CAUSES.basis defaulting to `correlational` is the same shape one level up, and the edge's own hint says "Do not assert `causal` without a mechanism" — the schema warns against asserting the strong value while defaulting the weaker one.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT FROM THE PARENT APPLIES UNCHANGED: a default recording genuine ABSENCE is correct and must stay; only a default naming a CHOICE among alternatives lies. AUTHORED_BY.role (author 63 / approver 7 / reviewer 2) and CHANGED.accepted_baseline (true 232 / false 188) both vary and both carry information — they are not in scope. Also unchanged: altering a default is not retroactive, so edges already written keep what they were given and a sweep of existing designs is a separate deliberate act.

Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it. Not yet decided is whether `weight_basis` should default at all, or be absent until a weight exists — which is the same question ver:interface-spec answered for Interface.medium.

properties.name: An epoch can be planned, not only recorded
properties.statement: The temporal axis must run forward as well as back, in TWO PAIRED VIEWS of the same architecture (Anthony, 2026-07-28: 'in systems engineering, I think this would be 2 views of the same system'): increments in TIME — epochs, what the architecture is expected to be at epoch_1..n — and increments in CAPABILITY — what each small, frequent release adds, the release-fast-in-small-increments practice now common in industry (his brother's project ships ~2 minor releases a week). Both views must exist, each comparable as a delta: any two epochs, any two increments, or either against the present. With many moving parts — an ecosystem of coupled repos, each with its own graph — an epoch or increment must pin the set of per-repo design versions it means, or the question 'which epoch are we talking about?' has no answer, which is the failure this exists to prevent. Original idea 2026-07-28 ('epoch branches: project_x:epoch_1 captures what we expect the graph to look like at epoch_1'), amended the same day with the two-views framing. THE ATOM, Anthony's distillation 2026-07-28: the roadmap is a SATISFACTION SCHEDULE — a mapping of requirements to the epoch or increment where they are satisfied: 'in epoch 1, requirements A and B are satisfied; in increment 3, requirements C, D and E are expected to be satisfied; in epoch 27, KPP 1 is required to be satisfied.' His own verbs carry the three modalities the mapping must distinguish: ARE satisfied (recorded history — the backward direction the graph already does), EXPECTED to be satisfied (a plan, carrying confidence that decays with horizon per req:plans-move-honestly), and REQUIRED to be satisfied by (an obligation whose miss at arrival is a computed violation, the scheduling face of a KPP — content inviolability from req:inviolable-intent gains a deadline dimension).

properties.name: Evidence carries the date it was taken, so a measurement can be aged rather than believed forever
properties.statement:
Where the design records that something was MEASURED, it must also record WHEN — so a report can say "measured, but a long time ago" instead of presenting a stale number as current.

THE OBSERVATION IS `fact:defect-a-measured-contribution-carries-no-date-so-it-is-believed-forever` (music_graph F22); this is the intent behind fixing it.

THE ASYMMETRY IS THE ARGUMENT, and it is reflow2's own doctrine applied unevenly. `ver:evidence-quality` has a whole TIME axis — an accept dated after the check reports STALE, a re-run after the accept is current, and an undated side is UNKNOWN and counted rather than silently passed. `Artifact.last_confirmed_at` exists for exactly this, and its description says a confirmation "says nothing changed" so it is stored as a dated property. ⇒ Dating evidence is settled practice for Verification and for Artifact, and absent from the one number a KPP verdict rests on: the CONSTRAINS edge declares `note`, `contribution` and `basis` and NO DATE.

MEASURED THEIR SIDE: a contribution recorded as 6.9 fps with `basis: measured` against a 40 fps minimum, while the true measured value was 55.06. The number was right when taken and had been wrong for days. Their framing is the one to keep — "an estimate stays an estimate, but a measurement is a statement about a system at a moment."

⚠️ `basis: measured` IS THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE CLAIM THE SCHEMA OFFERS AND THE ONLY ONE THAT DECAYS. An estimate does not go stale; a measurement does.

NOT DECIDED, and both are real: whether the date belongs on the edge or on a separate observation node — the same question `Artifact.last_confirmed_at` answered by choosing the property, on the grounds that confirmations are high-frequency non-events; and whether ageing against the contributors' artifact checksums is sound, since a contribution can go stale with no file changing.

A SECOND, SMALLER ITEM IN THE SAME REPORT, kept because it cost them real time: a MINIMUM budget returns `within` while a contributor is `unstated`. That is defensible — a missing number can only improve a minimum — but the asymmetry is unexplained in the payload and read as a bug. The verdict is right and does not say why it is right.

properties.name: A passing check says what part of the space it actually covered
properties.statement: When a check verifies a claim, the design must be able to say what the check held fixed and what it varied. A capability whose every passing check pins the same parameter, and whose design declares it independent of that parameter, must read as narrowly proven rather than as proven. Where no check states its scope the answer must be that the scope is unstated — reported and counted, never read as full coverage, because silence about coverage is how a check that only ever ran at one point of the space reads as if it ran everywhere.

properties.name: reflow2 explains what it is and how to run it before it explains what it believes
properties.statement: Someone arriving at reflow2 cold must learn, in plain language and before any philosophy, what it physically is and how it runs on their machine: a binary they run locally, a design graph kept as a file in their own repository, and a coding agent that talks to it over MCP. They must then find where the agent instructions go and two or three concrete uses — starting a design from nothing, recovering one from a system that already exists, and asking what breaks if something changes. The doctrine that makes reflow2 worth using is not the entry point to it.

properties.name: Once the design points at content, the export must say what it does NOT carry — a pointer with no bytes fails loud, not quietly
properties.statement:
FOUND BY IMPACT-CHECK, 2026-07-31, before any content-store code was written. `propagate_from cap:content-store` reported three boundary crossings — `ifc:core-api`, `ifc:graph-export`, `ifc:mcp-tools` — and the export one changes what an existing contract MEANS.

THE CONSEQUENCE. Blobs travel in git (`dec:where-content-lives`); the export document carries only pointers. So the moment content exists, `export_graph` stops being a complete design transfer: hand someone the JSON on its own — email it, drop it in a ticket, move it between machines — and every diagram, transcript and source document silently fails to resolve. Today the export IS the whole design, which is why `dec:export-door-spof-accepted` calls it "an accepted single door"; after content, it is the whole design MINUS whatever the graph points at.

THE REQUIREMENT: an export that references content must say so, and a consumer holding an export without the bytes must be able to TELL. The shape most consistent with what already exists is a manifest of referenced content hashes carried in the export beside the stamp — the stamp already records the vocabulary a document was written with, and this records the content it depends on. Then "do I have everything?" is a set comparison rather than a discovery made when a diagram fails to open.

WHY IT CANNOT BE LEFT TO CONVENTION: `req:content-reaches-every-seat` requires an unresolvable pointer to fail LOUD and be nameable, and `req:no-silent-fallback` says the same one layer down. A design that renders quietly without its pictures satisfies neither — and the person who cannot see the diagrams is exactly the person who cannot tell they are missing.

DELIBERATELY NOT SPECIFIED HERE: whether the export should also be able to EMBED content for transfer (self-contained at the cost of size), or only ever declare it. That is a separate question and should not be answered by implication.

NOTE ON PROVENANCE: raised by the agent from an impact-check, not by Anthony. It is `proposed` and wants his word.

properties.name: Project.domain is written and never read — but a framework registry is probably the wrong fix
properties.statement:
REASSESSED 2026-07-28, same day, on Anthony's instruction not to treat reflow's workflows as canon. This was first written as "which modelling framework is in use must be a recorded choice", arguing from reflow's framework_registry.json. On re-reading, the DEFECT is real and the PRIOR ART's solution is doubtful; the name has been changed to say so.

THE DEFECT, which stands on its own: Project.domain is free text, written by genesis, and read by nothing — it is on the write-only list from the 2026-07-28 sweep. reflow2's own Project carries domain = 'software'. Either something should read it or it should not be collected, and that is true regardless of what reflow did.

WHY reflow's ANSWER IS PROBABLY WRONG, stated plainly because the first version of this node treated it as the model to copy. (1) The terminology mapping is largely COSMETIC. framework_registry.json maps node to 'service' / 'gene' / 'agent' / 'species' and edge to 'interface' / 'interaction' / 'relationship' over one universal graph. Renaming the same structure does not change what can be computed about it, and it introduces a translation layer between what the user says and what the graph holds — a layer that can drift, and that every reader must now traverse. (2) The load-bearing claim is a SMELL, not a feature. reflow's LESSON-01 says "framework choice determines which NetworkX analyses are available". Analyses should be available based on WHAT THE GRAPH CONTAINS, not on a declared label: a cycle detector should run wherever there are dependency edges, whoever calls them interfaces or interactions. Gating capability on a self-declared category is how a user gets the wrong answer for a reason they cannot see. reflow2's one universal vocabulary with computations keyed to STRUCTURE is very likely the better design, and adopting a registry would be a regression dressed as a feature.

WHAT SURVIVES FROM reflow: only the rule, and reflow2 already has it. LESSON-01's real content — "Do NOT default to UAF" — is req:defaults-do-not-assert, independently arrived at. The supporting CONTRADICTS edge to that requirement stays correct; the framework registry is not the mechanism it implies.

WHAT SHOULD ACTUALLY BE DECIDED, and it is smaller than a registry: does anything read Project.domain, and if not, does it become unspecified-until-stated (per ver:interface-spec's rule for Interface.medium) or leave the schema entirely? A plausible middle path worth weighing separately: domain as a hint to EXTRACTION and phrasing — what vocabulary the agent uses when talking to the user and reading their documents — without ever gating which computations run. That keeps the honest part of reflow's insight (a biologist should not be told about 'services') and discards the part that would make analyses conditional on a label. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing 00b-framework_selection.json; reassessed the same day.

properties.name: Usability is measured against a baseline, so getting harder to use is detectable
properties.statement: reflow2 regression-gates whether its DETECTORS still work and has no equivalent for whether a person or agent can still get THROUGH the process. tools/phase_trial.py seeds a realistic graph, injects the divergences P3/P4/P5 are each meant to catch, scores whether the graph noticed, sits at 13/13, exits 0 and works as a regression gate; the erosion trial asks the sharper version, whether the design still describes the system after N rounds of test-fails/fix-code/accept. Both measure the machinery. Neither measures the EXPERIENCE of driving it, so reflow2 could become materially harder to use across a release and every gate would stay green. report-friction's own text concedes the consequence: "Everything reflow2 knows about its own weak points came from someone writing down what fought them. Those were staged trials; ordinary use produces better evidence and CURRENTLY LOSES ALL OF IT." THE PRIOR ART, from reflow's 97-GAN-inspired-test.json, and its structure is the transferable part rather than its specifics. Execution was separated from evaluation: one agent drove the workflows BLIND — "Agent B should NOT see expected outputs" — while a second read the transcript afterwards, categorised what went wrong and found root causes rather than symptoms, asking of each "why did this occur, how did it manifest, how frequently, what is the fix effort". Results aggregated to metrics, compared against a stored baseline, and regression was called out explicitly: "if new version performs worse than baseline, that's a P0 issue." The cadence was stated — periodically, or before a major release. THE BLINDNESS IS THE LOAD-BEARING PART and the easiest to lose: an evaluator who knows the expected output cannot see the friction, because it reads the intended path into whatever happened. reflow2's real trials (brownfield ophyd-service, greenfield aidrone, brainmaker) already produce this evidence and it is what taught reflow2 most of what it knows — but they are occasional, hand-run, and not comparable to each other, so nothing can say whether the last release made anything worse. Depends on req:friction-has-a-severity-bar: a baseline needs countable, classified findings to be a baseline OF something. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it.

properties.name: Friction is classified and has a bar at which it becomes work
properties.statement: reflow2 collects friction with no vocabulary for it and no threshold at which accumulated friction becomes scheduled work, so reports pile up and nothing converts them. THE EVIDENCE IS IN THIS REPO, twice over. (1) The eight brainmaker friction items in feedback.md — from a real genesis pass over a 47-component decomposition — are still not in docs/backlog.md. Observed, written down, and never converted. (2) Friction findings with nowhere to live are being crammed into node NAMES: ver:kit-manifest-agrees is literally named "... (friction 2026-07-25: reflow2's own manifest is four releases stale and nothing noticed; unwritten)" and ver:tools-reject-unknown-args carries "(friction 2026-07-25, unwritten)". When a finding has no home it ends up in a name string, and "unwritten" in a Verification name is a backlog entry in hiding. THE PRIOR ART, from reflow's 97-GAN-inspired-test.json: friction was classified into a fixed taxonomy of twelve categories — tool_workflow_misalignment (tool output does not match the documentation), missing_documentation, automation_incompatibility (requires human interaction, fails unattended), missing_tools (workflow references something that does not exist), ambiguous_instructions, template_issues, path_resolution_issues, plus five for the hierarchical machinery. Each finding was prioritised against stated criteria rather than judgement: P0 BLOCKING, "workflow cannot proceed without manual intervention or workaround"; P1 HIGH VALUE, "causes significant friction (5+ minutes wasted) or happens frequently"; P2 POLISH. And there was a bar: p0_issues_count > 0 OR (p1_issues_count > 3 AND friction_overhead > 15%) converted the pile into a fix cycle. The specific numbers are reflow's and are not the point; the point is that a stated bar exists, so friction stops depending on someone feeling that there is enough of it. NOTE WHAT reflow2 ALREADY DOES BETTER and must keep: report-friction's redaction discipline (tool names and argument SHAPES, node TYPES not ids, counts not contents, errors with ids masked) has no counterpart in reflow's loop, because reflow's ran on its own repo where there was no third party's design to protect. reflow2 installs once per machine into other people's projects, so any classification scheme must carry that discipline with it. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it.

properties.name: Install is one command, update is one word
properties.statement: A consumer installs reflow2 with a single command from a stable public URL (curl | bash or the platform equivalent) and updates with a single short command; releases are frequent and very minor, so updating is routine and cheap rather than an event. Modeled on the Claude Code installer/update experience the user named as the target (2026-07-20).

properties.name: The functional vocabulary must compute something or not be declared
properties.statement: reflow2's schema declares a functional-analysis vocabulary that nothing in the core reads: Capability.is_entry_point and Capability.is_exit_point (schema/functional.yaml:20, both defaulting to false), plus inputs, outputs and capability_type. Only Flow.entry_point is actually read. add_capability cannot write any of them, so they are reachable only through the create_node escape hatch, and no detector consults them. Found 2026-07-28 by comparing reflow2 against the original reflow's system_of_systems_graph_v2.py (2,146 lines, NetworkX): three of that tool's five FUNCTIONAL-mode gap detectors are unimplementable in reflow2 purely because of this — unreachable_functions needs is_entry_point, dead_end_functions needs is_exit_point, unexplained_outputs needs outputs. The service-mode analysis DID come over and in better form (cycles, communities, centrality, orphans, unimplemented services, orphaned interfaces all have reflow2 detectors); the functional mode did not. The schema was ported and the computations were not, which is req:defaults-do-not-assert at the scale of a whole workflow: a property defaulting to false asserts 'this capability is not an entry point' on every node in the design, and nobody chose that. Anthony's word 2026-07-28: add it. Recorded after the originating session was killed by an OOM before it could write. The honest resolutions are to compute against the vocabulary or to remove it — storing it while nothing reads it is the shape this project keeps rediscovering (BL-96 inviolable-intent, BL-106 last_run_at, the temporal axis before BL-70). Sibling of req:defaults-do-not-assert, which is parked as deferred.

properties.name: Every artifact traces to the intent it serves
properties.statement: Traceability runs from concept through operations without a break.

properties.name: The graph can catch up after unrecorded change
properties.statement: When work arrives from elsewhere — a git pull bringing commits made on another machine or by a session that never touched this machine's live store — the design must be able to catch up on demand, in two layers. LAYER 1, THE RECORD: a machine's live store is a long-lived cache of the committed export (req:stale-seat-knows states the write-side guard; this is the read side). After a pull, the store must take on the pulled record's changes: fast-forward when only the record moved, three-way merge (base = the last export both sides share, from git history) when both moved — never a blind overwrite in either direction. LAYER 2, THE CODE: commits in the pull that changed the project without updating the graph must then be walked against the synced graph through the ordinary two-sided drift questions. Catching up is an interrogation, never a bulk import: the graph re-earns coherence, it does not absorb whatever happened. Anthony's scenario, 2026-07-28 (amending his first wording of today): 'I have been working reflow2 from a home computer mostly; I'm doing this in another session on a different computer. When I get home I'd like to git pull the latest, then run delta and it should reconcile any deltas with what it had. I often don't restart the claude code session at home, so the graph it has will be in whatever state I left it.'

properties.name: The graph answers "as of epoch n" itself — a design's own time axis is not a git lookup
properties.statement:
A user must be able to ask the design a temporal question and get an answer, without going to git, without knowing a ref, and without anyone having rendered a document first. "What capabilities are due to be released in epoch 5?" and "what didn't we achieve that we were supposed to in increment 10?" — Anthony's own two questions, 2026-07-30 — are the acceptance test.

REWORDED 2026-07-30 ON ANTHONY'S WORD, and the change is substantive rather than editorial, so the original is preserved at `snap:epoch:planning-axis-intent:req:graph-indexes-snapshots`. This requirement was first written as an INDEX: "the graph tracks its own snapshots — which epoch_n or increment_n a thing belongs to, and WHERE THAT SNAPSHOT LIVES (the git ref)". That framing assumed the snapshot was a thing sitting in git that the graph pointed at. It is not, and the intent behind the original sentence is better served without it.

WHY THE INDEX FRAMING WENT. His stated intent never changed: "a user shouldn't have to remember which git branch a particular epoch or increment is in." Storing plan slices in git and indexing them satisfies the letter of that. Storing nothing in git satisfies it absolutely — there are no branches to remember because nothing was put in one. His words on 2026-07-30: "we could do this completely in the graph without git. We are just using git as a means to render a snapshot in time… let the agent/user figure out how to render the snapshot."

WHAT THIS REQUIRES, and it is a query surface rather than a file format. The graph must be able to answer, for any epoch or increment: what is scheduled to be satisfied by it; what was actually satisfied when it arrived; and the delta between those. The temporal machinery to do this already exists in part — epochs, Snapshots that capture a node's incoming and outgoing edges, and `compare_designs` — so this is largely a matter of reading what is already recorded rather than recording something new.

WHAT IS DELIBERATELY NOT MATERIALISED. No per-epoch branch, no per-epoch file, no rendered roadmap held as a record. Every materialised artifact acquires a staleness problem the moment the graph moves, and reflow2 has three live examples of paying that cost (`docs/design/reflow2.json`'s gate, `dataflow.html`'s check, and `docs/loop-model.json`, which became permanently unreproducible on 2026-07-30). Not materialising is the only way to have no drift. Rendering stays an OUTPUT — `render_views.py` may emit an epoch view whenever a person wants one, as a disposable projection, never as the record.

THE INFORMATION IS STILL IN GIT, WHICH IS WHY NOTHING IS LOST. The schedule lives in the graph, the graph is exported to `docs/design/reflow2.json`, and that file is committed. So a teammate without reflow2 can read it, and "what did the plan say in March" is answerable by `git log -p` on that one file plus the export's own `prev_content_hash` chain. The earlier objection — that graph-only breaks `req:design-reachable-without-the-repo` — does not hold: the information is reachable, it is merely not pretty, and prettiness is what on-demand rendering is for.

WHERE GIT KEEPS A REAL JOB, narrowed to where the thing being pinned actually lives in git: an ARRIVED epoch corresponds to real commits in real repos, and "what was actually deployed at epoch 3" is a question about the product, not the plan. That pin is a version combination (`req:version-combination-is-an-object`), and it is the backward direction only. Forward-looking plans describe graph content and stay in the graph; backward-looking arrivals describe code and pin code.

The in-repo precedent still holds and still shows the division: `rel:v0180` lives in the graph, tag `v0.18.0` lives in git, and nobody greps tags to learn what shipped.

properties.name: A design survives replacing the container it was served from — state lives on a volume, and a store is never separated from its identity sidecar
properties.statement:
Raised by @ajs from flo2, 2026-08-05, and flagged in the proposal as THE PART TO GET RIGHT. A reflow2 design is not configuration that can be rebuilt. It is the product. Baking any of the following into an image means losing every design on the next deploy.

THE GRAPH DIRECTORIES. .reflow2/graph is a RocksDB directory — live database files, not a snapshot. Under multi-graph hosting there will be many, so the volume wants a graphs root with one directory per design beneath it, and the registry maps graph_id to a path under that root.

THE SIDECAR FILES, ON THE SAME VOLUME AS THE STORE THEY DESCRIBE. graph.id.json (identity), graph.meta.json (version and schema stamp), the sync marker and the rendezvous file all live BESIDE the store, not inside it. Separating a store from its identity sidecar is the silent failure identity.rs warns about: a design opened under an id it was not created with finds nothing and PRESENTS AS AN EMPTY DESIGN rather than erroring. In a container, where paths are easy to get subtly wrong, this is the failure to design against — the design is still on disk and reflow2 opens an empty one beside it reporting nothing wrong.
