THE CONTENT STORE, WHICH NEEDS A DECISION RATHER THAN A DEFAULT. --content-path defaults to ./reflow2-content and its doc comment says to point it at a directory inside the repo, because blobs are committed so they travel with the design. A HOSTED SERVER HAS NO REPO, so that assumption does not hold and the hosted case needs its own answer — most likely a second volume, or object storage. This is deliberately left open rather than guessed.

THE VOLUME TYPE IS NOT A DETAIL. RocksDB's exclusive lock is a filesystem lock, and network filesystems honour those unreliably — NFS especially. The volume must be a real block device or a local volume. A lock that silently fails to exclude is how two processes end up writing one store, which is the corruption case the entire single-writer design exists to prevent, and it fails with no error saying so.

THE ACCEPTANCE TEST IS A CONTAINER REPLACEMENT: stop the container, start the new image against the same volume, and every design is still there and still ITSELF — the graph_id is unchanged and no design opens empty.

properties.name: Gaps become questions, not guesses
properties.statement: Where the design is underspecified, the system must ask the human in plain language and record the answer, rather than silently choosing a default.

properties.name: The install asks which agent harness this project uses, and writes harness-specific files for that one only
properties.statement:
`init` asks which agent harness(es) will open this project and installs the harness-specific files for those alone, instead of writing every supported harness's configuration unconditionally. The harness-neutral half of the install is unaffected and always written: the instruction file, the committed design export, the ignore rules and the merge attributes.

THE ANSWER MUST BE SUPPLIABLE WITHOUT A PROMPT, and this is part of the requirement rather than a refinement of it. A non-interactive caller — CI, a scripted install, an `adopt` run — must be able to name the harness on the command line, and a run with no tty must never block waiting for an answer. An install that hangs in CI is a worse defect than the one being fixed.

THE PROMPT MUST NOT BE THE ONLY WAY TO CHANGE THE ANSWER. `init` is re-runnable, and a project that later adds a second harness must be able to say so and get that harness's files without reinstalling or hand-editing.

WHY ASKING RATHER THAN DETECTING, since the cheaper option was available and rejected: a brand-new repository carries no evidence of which harness will open it, and that is precisely when `init` runs. Inferring from what is present therefore guesses, and a wrong guess is SILENT — the user receives a configuration their tool never reads, with nothing to indicate anything is missing.

Raised by Alex (`who:alex`) 2026-08-14 as a first-run report on a real work project; settled by Anthony the same day on `dec:idea-init-asks-which-harness-and-installs-only-that`, over a recommendation to detect instead.

properties.name: Design intent is read back into a long build, not only the debt the loop is owed
properties.statement:
A long build session forgets what it was trying to build. reflow's countermeasure was explicit: workflow_master.json takes an architecture_anchor at the P2-to-P3 transition — checksums over the service/functional/interface/graph specs plus captured fields design_intent_summary, key_decisions, constraints, service_count, function_count — and then RE-INJECTS it at three moments: phase_transitions, resync_protocol, and every_N_iterations with N = 5. Its llm_instructions make the purpose plain, on_phase_entry: "Read architecture_anchor from working_memory.json ... Remind yourself of design intent and constraints."

reflow2 HAS a periodic re-injection mechanism and it carries different cargo. cap:read-loop-hint surfaces loop DEBT when it is real — what capture/detect/ask/decide steps are owed — and the Stop hook nudges when graph writes finish without a loop check. That is valuable and is not this. Debt says what you OWE; intent says what you were TRYING TO BUILD. A session can be perfectly clean on debt and still have quietly stopped building the thing the design describes. The vocabulary for the payload largely exists — Snapshot is the checksummed baseline (14 instances against Anchor's zero, see dec:anchor-retire-or-implement), Decision carries key decisions, Constraint carries constraints — so the gap is the RE-READING, not the recording.

THE TRIGGER QUESTION, AMENDED 2026-07-28. This requirement was captured with one thing open: what triggers a re-injection in a system with no phase counter to count iterations against. Reviewing 01-systems_engineering.json answers it, and the answer is two mechanisms rather than one.

(1) A COUNTER. Its context_management block runs an operations counter with threshold 5, tracked in working_memory.json as operations_since_refresh, incremented "after each real operation (file creation, tool execution, artifact generation)" and forcing a refresh at 5. Note the same number as workflow_master's every_N_iterations, so the cadence is consistent across reflow rather than picked twice.

(2) SIGNALS, which is the part with no reflow2 counterpart at all. reflow named the OBSERVABLE SYMPTOMS of context degradation so an agent could notice its own state rather than only counting: "Asking about system name (it's in working_memory.json)", "Forgetting current step", "Working in wrong directory (pwd != system_root)", "Using wrong template format", "Creating artifacts in wrong locations", and "Implementing features not in service_architecture.json" — that last being DRIFT caught behaviourally, from what the agent is about to do, rather than by diffing artifacts after the fact.

The response was a fixed 8-step refresh: PAUSE, VERIFY PWD, SAVE STATE, RELOAD (workflow file, definitions, templates), READ (current focus and progress), CONFIRM (state the system name, workflow, step and next action back), RESET the counter, RESUME. Plus a pre-operation checklist carrying one line worth keeping verbatim: "Verify not about to generate report/summary (do real work)" — an explicit guard against the agent drifting into producing summaries instead of doing the work.

So the trigger is not either/or: a counter bounds how long you can go WITHOUT re-grounding, and signals catch degradation that arrives faster than the counter. A counter alone re-injects on a healthy session and misses a fast collapse; signals alone never fire on the slow drift that has no symptom yet.

STILL OPEN after the amendment: which of reflow's signals survive translation. reflow2 has no pwd, no working_memory.json and no template format, so "wrong directory" and "wrong template" do not port — but "implementing features not in the design", "forgetting what was decided", and "asking for something the graph already holds" all do, and the last is directly observable at the tool boundary. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing the original reflow workflows. Anthony's word: capture it, then amend it.

properties.name: The past is never overwritten
properties.statement: Updating the design to match the build must not erase what was intended.

properties.name: A published interface carries enough to check compatibility, not just prose
properties.statement: When a design publishes an Interface, the published spec must carry the things two systems actually have to agree on, in a form a computation can compare — not a free-text blob a human has to read. The user's six characteristics: (1) ARCHITECTURAL STYLE AND PROTOCOL — the technology (REST, gRPC, GraphQL, WebSockets; RS-232, PCIe, CAN bus) and the communication paradigm, synchronous request-response versus asynchronous event-driven; (2) DATA STRUCTURE AND TYPES — payload serialization (JSON, XML, protobuf, raw binary) and a schema saying which fields are mandatory, their types, and their formatting constraints; (3) OPERATIONS AND ENDPOINTS — where to send a request (URL, port, memory address, function name) and what actions are permitted (HTTP verbs, RPC methods, read/write commands); (4) AUTHENTICATION AND SECURITY — how identity is verified (API keys, OAuth2, TLS certificates, cryptographic signatures) and how data is protected in transit and at rest; (5) ERROR HANDLING AND STATE CODES — the status vocabulary and a consistent failure structure the consumer can parse automatically; (6) PERFORMANCE AND CONSTRAINTS — rate limits, throttling, maximum concurrency, and timeout thresholds. THE POINT IS NOT COMPLETENESS FOR ITS OWN SAKE: it is that two designs cannot be checked for INCOMPATIBILITY at their seam unless the seam is described in comparable terms. Today reflow2 structures roughly one and a half of these six (medium, and designation) and puts the rest into one free-text `spec` string or nowhere at all — so mirror_surface can link two designs and still not tell you they disagree.

properties.name: Intent that must hold no matter what is recorded as inviolable, and a violation is computed, not remembered
properties.statement: A design must be able to record intent that no downstream decision may trade away — a key performance parameter, in the acquisition sense: a threshold that, if missed, fails the effort regardless of how well everything else went. Inviolable intent is distinct from a Requirement (a goal to achieve, tradeable against other goals) and from a Constraint (a limit imposed on the design). reflow2 must (a) let that intent be stated with its threshold and, where it applies, its objective value; (b) COMPUTE a violation rather than rely on anyone remembering — an accepted Decision, an allocation, or a change whose blast radius contradicts a KPP must be surfaced loudly and above ordinary gaps; and (c) show a KPP crossing in impact analysis BEFORE the edit is made, not after it has been committed. A KPP that nothing checks is a comment.

properties.name: Invoked as an MCP server over stdio
properties.statement: The user-facing surface is the reflow2-mcp binary spoken to over stdio, installed into a consumer project by tools/reflow2_init.py, which merges rather than overwrites existing agent configuration.

properties.name: The design says which interfaces are the published boundaries, and computations read that distinction
properties.statement: Some interfaces are the boundary a system is known by; most are internal plumbing. The design must be able to say which — and the distinction must earn its keep by being read, not merely stored (dec:edge-orthogonality). From the MOSA guidebook Anthony supplied (OUSD(R&E), February 2025), whose entire discipline turns on designating modular system interfaces and then holding them stable and open, and independently from BL-45's system-of-systems thread, which found the same hole from the other side: nothing marks an Interface external-facing, so "visible to others" versus "mine to change" is undeclarable. Two independent routes to one missing property. What must read it, or the designation is decoration: a change that crosses a published boundary is a different risk from one that stays behind it, and impact analysis should say which it is BEFORE the edit; a design that publishes a surface should be able to export exactly that surface and nothing internal; and a composed design (req:design-composes) links through published boundaries, never through another system's internals. What this must NOT become: an assertion that a boundary is stable. Whether a published interface has in fact held is a matter of evidence — its drift history — not a property anyone sets.

properties.name: The install must land its pointer where the agent will actually read it
properties.statement:
FOUND IN USE, 2026-07-28: Anthony installed the kit into dynograph-foundation, opened a session there, reconnected the MCP server, and reported that no reflow2 skills appeared. The server was healthy and holding the graph. The kit was invisible.

THE CAUSE, and it is the SAME DEFECT CLASS `reflow2_init.py` already documents having been bitten by, in the opposite direction. `INSTRUCTION_FILES` adds a pointer line to every instruction-file convention THAT ALREADY EXISTS, and creates `AGENTS.md` when the project owns no such file. dynograph-foundation had neither `AGENTS.md` nor `CLAUDE.md`, so a fresh `AGENTS.md` was written — correct by the agents.md convention, and not the file Claude Code reads first. The installer's own comment records the storyflow case: "storyflow carries CLAUDE.md and no AGENTS.md, so the installer saw nothing to protect, wrote a fresh AGENTS.md, and left the file Claude Code actually reads with no mention of reflow2 — the whole kit invisible on the primary path." That fix protected an existing `CLAUDE.md`. It did not cover a project that has NO instruction file at all, which is the ordinary state of a repo that has never been agent-worked.

SO THE RULE IS NOT "protect what exists" BUT "reach what reads". A greenfield or never-agent-worked repo is the common case for adopt, and it is exactly the case where the installer currently produces a file the primary harness may never open.

THE SECOND HALF, which the same session surfaced: the SKILLS ARE SERVED and correctly so, but the eight slash commands that make them usable (`/gaps`, `/health`, `/where`, `/req`, `/decisions`, `/debt`, `/brainstorm`, `/kpp`) live only in reflow2's own `.claude/commands/` and ship in no kit. So every consumer project loses the ergonomics, and a user who has worked in reflow2's repo experiences the consumer install as broken rather than as thin. The commands are pure pointers — each says "use skill X" and hardcodes no path — so they do not carry the staleness that `dec:skills-served` was written to prevent. Whether to ship them is nonetheless a decision that touches that decision's reasoning, and is Anthony's to make rather than mine.

WHAT "INSTALLED CORRECTLY" HAS TO MEAN. Not "the files were written" — the install reported success in the failing case. It has to mean the agent, in a fresh session, is told reflow2 exists on the path its own harness actually reads.

properties.name: Linking two projects is a process reflow2 serves, not one an agent improvises each time
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-13: "are we tracking notes for a process that we can reuse when a user wants to link 2+ reflow2 projects" — asked after reflow2 and flo2 had been linked twice, and the honest answer was NO.

⭐ WHAT WAS TRACKED WAS FINDINGS, NOT PROCESS. `epoch:linking-two-designs` (seq 325) records that the work happened and what running it found; `fact:reflow2-flo2-seam-measured-2026-08-13` records today's numbers; `dec:idea-defined-pair-types-so-two-projects-combine-by-lookup` holds the open mechanism question. **Nothing said HOW.** Measured the same day: 19 served skills, and none covered it — `link-artifacts` is files-to-capabilities inside one design, `parallel-work` is several people on ONE design. A user saying "link projectA and projectB" got an agent improvising, twice.

WHY A SERVED SKILL IS THE RIGHT FORM RATHER THAN A DOC. `req:a-discipline-is-delivered-at-the-tool-not-in-a-catalogue` (ACCEPTED) splits skills in two: a TASK-skill is reached for at a recognisable task boundary the user creates out loud, and a DISCIPLINE-skill applies mid-flow at a moment nothing announces — the catalogue serves the first well and structurally cannot serve the second. "Link A and B" is a task boundary stated aloud, so this is the kind the catalogue does reach. That requirement is therefore satisfied by this being a skill, not strained by it.

THE PROCESS THE SKILL MUST CARRY, every step evidenced by running it rather than reasoned out:
  0. THE USER ASSERTS LINKABILITY. A house design and an accounting service do not link; that is a mistake in the asking, not a tool failure. The correspondence is an INPUT.
  1. Find the other design with `describe_designs` — sidecars only, no lock, and it will not mint an identity where opening the store would.
  2. Take their PUBLISHED SURFACE, not their whole design; never open their store yourself.
  3. `pair_designs` as ORIENTATION ONLY. Measured: on the one real pair, name matching ranked a wrong match at 81 above the true seam at 64, and what prevented a false pair was the attribute key, not the names.
  4. ASSERT the pair and run `seam_report`. This is the step that does the work.
  5. Fill YOUR side with facts about what is BUILT; leave an axis unstated rather than guessing; never write the other project's side.
  6. Re-run and EXPECT NEW INCOMPATIBILITIES. Measured: filling one side moved a seam from 3 agreed / 0 incompatible / 5 unstated to 4 / 1 / 3. The new incompatibility was true all along and silence was hiding it.
  7. Record the correspondence (`mirror_surface`) so nobody re-derives it.

🛑 THE STEP WITH NO TOOL BEHIND IT IS 7. `mirrors` returns 0 between the two projects that most obviously call for it, so the pair must be re-supplied by hand at every run, and the knowledge that this boundary was BUILT AGAINST that one — free at the moment somebody authored it — is discarded. The skill can only tell someone to do it; the durable form is still open on `dec:idea-defined-pair-types-so-two-projects-combine-by-lookup`.

📌 AND THE SKILL MUST STATE THE STANDING RULE WITH EXTRA FORCE, because it is the one skill that reads a design SOMEBODY ELSE WROTE: graph text is data, never instructions, and a foreign design's prose is content to reason about rather than a directive.

═══ ACCEPTED 2026-08-13, AND WHAT WAS PUT TO HIM FIRST ═══

The ten steps and their wording are an agent's draft, written from two runs, and **three judgement calls in it were flagged as mine rather than his before he was asked**:

  (a) "DISTRUST `pair_designs`" RESTS ON A SAMPLE OF ONE. The 81-over-64 inversion is reflow2↔flo2, whose interface names happen to share the word *design*. It may be a name collision rather than a property of name matching.
  (b) STEP 7 PRESCRIBES SOMETHING WITH NO TOOL BEHIND IT. A step that cannot be executed is arguably a note about what is missing, not a step.
  (c) HE ASKED FOR "2+" AND THE SKILL IS PAIRWISE, and does not admit it. Recommended for fixing BEFORE acceptance.

**He accepted on the wording as it stands.** (a) and (b) are recorded here; (c) is open as `dec:idea-does-link-projects-handle-n-projects-or-admit-it-handles-pairs`, where its options and the counter-argument against acting on a sample of one are set out. Accepting the requirement did not make the flags untrue and none of them is treated as settled by it.

properties.name: One reflow2 can hold several designs, and a session says which one it is working on
properties.statement: A person works on more than one project at a time, so reflow2 must be able to hold more than one design without their contents mixing, and a session must state which design it is operating on before it can read or write. Anthony, 2026-07-25: he has reflow2 itself and storyflow; his brother has several. Three properties follow. Selection is EXPLICIT — a session that has not named its design must be refused rather than defaulted to the last one used or the only one present, because a tool call landing in the wrong project is a silent corruption that no gap detector would ever notice. Segregation is enforced by the store, not by convention: every node and edge already carries a graph_id, which is exactly the primitive this needs, and today it is pinned to the constant "reflow2" — so the mechanism exists and is unused, the same shape as the temporal axis and the inviolable-intent vocabulary before them. And the identity of a design must be stable across machines, so the same project reached from two places is one design rather than two that happen to share a name. This is deliberately silent on where the designs live: one process per design and one holding many are both answers to it, and that is the hosting question, not this requirement.

properties.name: Many people on one project AND many projects at once — the two axes must hold TOGETHER, which neither accepted requirement says
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-05, stating what flo2 actually is: "a web app that has reflow2 as its core service... you will probably have multiple people working simultaneously on the same project - and secondly, you could have multiple different projects going on through the web app simultaneously. reflow2 needs to support both."

BOTH AXES ARE ALREADY ACCEPTED INTENT, SEPARATELY. Axis one is req:sessions-share-a-graph — "several sessions on one machine work the same design at the same time" — accepted, and already realized: cap:shared-sessions is VERIFIED, serving many sessions from one process over --http, and it satisfies single-writer rather than working around it because one server means exactly one writer. Axis two is req:many-designs-one-service — "one reflow2 can hold several designs, and a session says which one it is working on" — accepted, and deliberately silent on where the designs live.

WHAT IS MISSING IS THE COMPOSITION, AND IT IS NOT IMPLIED BY EITHER. Nothing in the design states that N people across M projects works — only that N people on ONE project works, and that M projects can be held. The cross product is a distinct claim with distinct failure modes, and flo2 is the first consumer that needs it.

THE CONCRETE QUESTION THE COMPOSITION RAISES, which the flo2 proposal does not answer: LOCK GRANULARITY. req:sessions-share-a-graph requires that "reads must not queue behind each other (the graph sits behind a lock that today serialises everything)", and cap:shared-sessions met that by moving the graph from a Mutex to an RwLock — PER PROCESS, holding one graph. Once one process holds many graphs, a per-process lock would make a write on project A block reads on project B, which is a cross-tenant performance coupling that neither requirement forbids because neither one can see it. The registry map itself must not become the new serialisation point. The property that has to hold: concurrency is per-design, so activity on one project is invisible in the latency of another.

RELATED BUT NOT THE SAME AS ISOLATION. req:a-session-cannot-reach-another-designs-graph is about CORRECTNESS and security — project A's design must be unreachable from project B's session. This requirement is about CONCURRENCY — project A's traffic must not degrade project B's. A design can have either without the other, and a hosted service needs both.

NOTE ON WHAT "MANY PEOPLE" NOW MEANS. req:sessions-share-a-graph was written for "several sessions ON ONE MACHINE" (Anthony, 2026-07-26, six concurrent sessions on his own box). flo2 makes them several people on several machines reaching one hosted process, which keeps the single-writer property intact — there is still exactly one writer, the server — but changes who the seats belong to and puts req:seat-per-client under real load rather than local load.

properties.name: The governance mode is chosen, visible and changeable — it is the one asserted default that is actually acted upon
properties.statement:
Project.mode decides whether the design or the implementation is the source of truth, and reflow2 applies it by default, never asks for it, and provides no way to change it.

THE MEASURED STATE, 2026-07-28. genesis.rs takes mode OPTIONALLY — "if let Some(mode) = opts.mode" — and its own comment states the consequence: "Scaffold the Project (schema applies mode=flexible, status=active when unset)". project_mode_of falls back to "flexible" again on read. The string "mode" does not appear anywhere in crates/reflow2-mcp/src/service.rs, so there is no set_project_mode and no setter of any kind on the served surface; after genesis it is reachable only through the create_node escape hatch — the same shape as the KPP objective finding and Requirement.concern. And reflow2's OWN Project carries mode = flexible, which nobody chose.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN THE TEN PROPERTIES IN THE ORIGINAL SWEEP, and the difference is the whole point. Those defaults are asserted AND UNREAD — Requirement.concern sitting at core on 67 of 67 is inert, carrying no information and driving nothing. This one is asserted AND ACTED UPON: heal.rs:431 reads it, and in rigid mode HEAL only proposes and never auto-applies. So req:defaults-do-not-assert has, in this property, its first instance where the invented value changes what the system DOES. flexible is not a neutral setting either: in the vocabulary reflow2 inherited it means the architecture is NOT the source of truth, the implementation drives the architecture, and the response to drift is to update the design to match the build. That is a governance decision. reflow2 — a project whose thesis is that the design is the memory — is currently running in the mode that says the implementation drives the design, not because anyone decided so but because opts.mode was None.

THE PRIOR ART IS A MODEL, NOT A FAILURE — CORRECTED 2026-07-28, same day. This requirement was first written claiming that reflow defined development_mode, required it as the P0-to-P1 prerequisite, read it in resync_protocol and tested for it in 97, but that NO WORKFLOW STEP ANYWHERE SET IT. That claim was wrong, and the error was method rather than reasoning: the search covered workflows/*.json and did not recurse into workflows/phases/. reflow DOES elicit it, and does so better than reflow2. workflows/phases/P0_setup/phase_definition.json carries a development_mode_configuration block whose own description reads "This is where the critical development mode choice is made", and it puts a labelled question to the user — "What type of project is this?" — with two options carrying real descriptions: flexible, "Personal / Exploratory / Agile — architecture can evolve with implementation, design is a living document"; and rigid, "Enterprise / Approved / Regulated — architecture is locked after approval, implementation must conform, changes require formal approval". It then asks TWO follow-ups: if rigid, what level of drift is acceptable (none 0%, minimal 10%, or threshold-only, "threshold requirements locked, objectives flexible"); and always, "How many development/test iterations before forced architecture review?", default 3 over a range of 1 to 10. So all three governing values — mode, drift tolerance and iteration budget — were ELICITED per project rather than assumed, and the numbers that appear hardcoded elsewhere in reflow are the defaults of questions actually asked.

The correction strengthens this requirement rather than weakening it. The comparison is no longer "both systems have the same hole" but the sharper one: reflow asked the user three questions before letting the project proceed, and reflow2 asks none of them and cannot be told the answers afterwards.

THREE THINGS THIS REQUIRES, and they are separable. (1) The value is CHOSEN — genesis asks, or the mode reads as unspecified until someone says, per the rule ver:interface-spec already sets for Interface.medium: a default may record absence, never a choice. reflow's phrasing is worth reusing; it asks about the PROJECT ("what type of project is this?") rather than about a setting, which is what makes it answerable by someone who has never heard of the field. (2) The value is CHANGEABLE — a project's governance legitimately moves as it matures, exploratory to controlled, and today it cannot; brainmaker reported this from the field, half-right, since the sharper fact is that genesis does not set it at all, it defaults it. (3) The value is VISIBLE — a mode that silently changes HEAL's behaviour should be readable in the reports that say where the design stands.

What rigid should MEAN beyond heal.rs:431 stays open and parked separately on Anthony's word; this requirement is the prior question, because rigid cannot mean anything useful while the mode is unchoosable and unchangeable. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing 00a-basic_setup.json; prior-art claim corrected the same day after reviewing workflows/phases/.

properties.name: Modularity is computed from the design, not asserted by the architecture diagram
properties.statement: A design that calls something a module must be able to be CHECKED on it. From the MOSA guidebook's conformance criteria (Table D-1: "demonstrate severable modular components"; components "encapsulated, cohesive, loosely coupled"), reframed to reflow2's own rule that a claim is derived from evidence rather than set by hand — the same move already made for requirement certainty and for delivery. The operative test is severability, and reflow2 already owns the machinery: if the blast radius of a change inside a part stops at that part's published boundaries, the part is severable; if it leaks past them, the part is not modular whatever the diagram says. Cohesion and coupling are already computed (community structure, the modularity score, the god-component finding) — the gap is severability, which needs req:key-interfaces to know where a boundary is. Two guards. This reports, never scores: a coarse-but-honest module is not a defect, and a single opaque part legitimately encapsulates everything beneath it (dec:report-dont-judge). And the vocabulary stays neutral (req:design-anything) — the acquisition community's words for these criteria belong in a VIEW over the computation, never in the schema, or reflow2 will have adopted one domain's language as its own.

properties.name: A session that has no design graph is told so, in band
properties.statement: When reflow2 cannot open the graph — another session holds the single-writer lock, or the graph was stamped by a different reflow2 — the MCP server must still complete the handshake and carry the reason where the agent will read it. Exiting at startup makes the outage indistinguishable from "reflow2 was never configured for this project", and an agent that concludes that skips the design-first process for a reason nobody recorded. Field-reported by the StoryFlow fleet, 2026-07-25.

properties.name: An idea in the graph stays connected to whether it was built and to where it was written — the user never hunts for the source document again
properties.statement:
Once an idea or requirement is in the design, reflow2 must keep it connected in BOTH directions without the user remembering it exists: FORWARD to the design and implementation that serve it (or the visible absence of any), and BACKWARD to the document and location it was written in. The user must never again have to recall that they wrote something, hunt for the file, and hand-point an agent at it.

ANTHONY, 2026-08-04, IN HIS OWN WORDS: "I put in dev_storyflow probably hundreds of ideas (some of which may be requirements) - I always struggled of translating these ideas into design and implementation. It was always manual process of me trying to find the document or documents that I had written the idea/requirement in and then purposefully point the agent to it. my hope is that by putting this in the graph, that these requirements are automatically linked to design and implementation (kind of a core feature of reflow2)."

WHAT "AUTOMATICALLY LINKED" MUST AND MUST NOT MEAN, because the obvious reading of his words would break the product. reflow2 must NOT auto-draw SATISFIES/REALIZES edges from similarity: the adopt skill's central discipline is that "a requirement backed out of the implementation that satisfies it is satisfied by construction — it can never contradict anything, so a graph of those can never say anything," and auto-linking would make every captured idea read as delivered and the completion reading say 100% forever. Edge PREDICTION is a live open question and deliberately framed as a question rather than a repair (dec:idea-missing-edge-prediction, proposed). What must be automatic is the INVERSE: an idea nothing implements FIRES AND KEEPS FIRING (unsatisfied_requirement — "a Requirement has no SATISFIES from any Capability", verified in detect.rs), and an idea that IS implemented is reachable to its file paths through the existing thread — Requirement <-SATISFIES- Capability -ALLOCATED_TO-> Component <-REALIZES- Artifact. The backward half is already carried by ingest: every extracted node gets YIELDED to its provenance Fragment, whose content_ref holds the blob hash plus the agent's locator (dec:agent-navigates-content).

⭐ THE RESTATEMENT THAT MATTERS, AND IT IS NOT THE PROBLEM AS FIRST DESCRIBED. The stated pain is retrieval — "I could not find the document." The operative pain is VISIBILITY: an idea written eighteen months ago was invisible until he happened to remember it existed. Auto-linking would restore that invisibility under a friendlier name, because a linked idea reads as handled. Staying LOUD until ruled on is therefore the requirement, and cheap retrieval is its by-product rather than its point.

DISTINCT FROM ITS TWO NEIGHBOURS, on the same pattern req:accreted-intent-becomes-a-design uses to separate itself from req:corpus-ingest. req:corpus-ingest is CONVERGENCE (forty specs naming one component resolve to one node). req:accreted-intent-becomes-a-design is INGEST (a contradictory, never-built corpus becomes a design at all). THIS one is what the design owes the user AFTERWARDS — it is satisfied or violated long after ingest has finished, and it is violated silently. req:golden-thread (accepted) states the thread must not break; this states that an idea's END of that thread must be loud when the thread does not reach it, which is the case a corpus makes normal rather than exceptional.

Status deliberately `proposed`: Anthony's framing captured in his words and awaiting his confirmation of the wording. The reading above ("loud, not linked") is MY restatement of what he asked for and is the part most worth his challenge — he asked for automatic linking and is being told the opposite is what serves him.

properties.name: The user never needs systems engineering
properties.statement: The graph carries the discipline; the user answers plain questions.

properties.name: Setting up a project is not a step — reflow2 is installed once per machine
properties.statement:
FROM ANTHONY, 2026-07-28, twice in one session and the second time as scope: "we need to make this as easy as possible. it is getting too hard to just start a project and then there are multiple steps after just to get it working" — and then, decisively: "my brother is using reflow2 on his machine. I'm using it another machine and this machine to develop it and use it. this isn't a fix for just this machine - it is a fix to make this easy for all users that ever use reflow2 from now on."

WHAT HE HAD MEASURED, on a real project (brainmaker) minutes before saying it: install the binary, run a per-project installer naming an absolute path into a reflow2 checkout, restart the agent, then type a slash command that had never shipped. Four steps to reach the first design action, three of them after the install, and the last one failed.

THE OBSERVATION THAT MAKES IT SOLVABLE: none of reflow2's per-project footprint is per-project in NATURE. `--graph-path .reflow2/graph` is relative to the working directory, so ONE registration still gives every project its own graph. The slash commands are pointers at served skills, so one global copy carries nothing that can go stale. The loop hooks are the same script in every project. What is genuinely per-repo is only the committed design export, and a pointer file for a repo whose OTHER contributors' agents must be told reflow2 governs it.

SO THE REQUIREMENT IS: after a one-time machine install, a user starts designing any project by opening their agent in a directory and asking — no installer, no config, no restart, no per-project step of any kind. Setup that survives per project is a defect, not a feature.

THE COUNTERWEIGHT, and it is what makes this honest rather than merely convenient: a machine-wide install must cost a directory that will never be designed exactly NOTHING. No graph created, no hook output, no state written. Most directories on a machine should stay untouched, and they must stay untouched by construction rather than by the user avoiding them.

properties.name: No silent fallbacks or drops
properties.statement: Failures and skipped work are surfaced loudly, never swallowed.

properties.name: The loop nudge covers the session that never touches the graph
properties.statement: A session that edits code while making zero reflow2 calls must receive the same one-time Stop nudge as one that writes the graph unchecked: the nudge arms on the harness's file-edit events (Edit/Write), not only on reflow2 write events. Today loop_nudge.py counts only mcp__reflow2__ writes, so the total-bypass session — the agent that ignores the design brain entirely — passes the Stop hook silently. Constraints carried over: the hook never reads the graph (single-writer lock), blocks once and never twice, and names what is owed (loop_status; impact-check before further edits, link-artifacts after) rather than demanding a ritual call; an edit-count threshold bounds false positives on typo/docs sessions. (BL-90, BL-74 family.)

properties.name: The path the coherence loop relies on to interrupt an agent is proven to interrupt one
properties.statement: The Stop-hook nudge and the read-side loop_hint are the only mechanisms that make the loop self-correcting, and nothing proves they reach a live agent: the existing suite tests the nudge script given its inputs, not that the hook is installed and fires. Prove the path end to end in a real session, and give it a backstop for when it is absent — a mechanism relied on to interrupt you is worthless until observed doing so.

properties.name: Someone who did not build the system can be told where a new piece of work belongs
properties.statement: A person inheriting a mature design must be able to ask "we need to add this — where does it go?" and be answered from the graph: which existing part should own it, what the change would touch, which decisions already govern that area and must not be casually contradicted, what intent it must not break, and who authored the reasoning so they can be asked. Answering "what is this system and what has been decided" is necessary but not sufficient; the requirement is satisfied only when the second question — where and how do I add to it — is also answered, and when the answer says honestly which parts of the real system the design does not cover.

properties.name: Whether this is one design or several is a question asked once, not a consequence of where init was run
properties.statement: reflow2 decides the boundary of a design by FILESYSTEM LAYOUT: a design is whatever lives under one directory's .reflow2/graph, fixed by wherever someone ran init, and nothing ever asks whether that is the right boundary. Genesis creates one Project and proceeds. THE PRIOR ART, from reflow's 00-setup.json: S-04-decision is a first-class decision point named "System-of-Systems Decision" — determine, before anything is built, whether this is a system-of-systems integration project. If yes, S-04 decomposes the concept into multiple independent systems: analyse the SoS requirements, DEFINE SYSTEM BOUNDARIES ("clarify which capabilities belong to which system"), IDENTIFY INTEGRATION POINTS ("understand how systems will interact"), and create a separate directory per identified system so each gets its own design. The question was asked once, at the start, and answered on the record. reflow2 HAS THE MACHINERY AND NOT THE QUESTION, which is the whole of this requirement. compare_designs, cap:composed-analysis (analyse two designs together without merging them), cap:mirror-surface (compose by mirroring the other's published surface), cap:seam-incompatibility (say when two linked designs disagree at a boundary), cap:merge-designs, cap:design-dependencies-declared, req:complementary-pairing and req:version-combination-is-an-object all assume the split already happened and someone else decided where. Nothing helps make that decision, records it, or revisits it. WHY IT IS NOT ACADEMIC: the operating context this project is built for is several organisations with competing, partially-built, differently-motivated designs, and an ecosystem of coupled repositories each carrying its own graph. In that world "is this one design or three, and where are the seams?" is the first real design decision, it is made implicitly today by where a directory happens to sit, and it is the one decision that determines whether all the composition machinery above ever gets used. NOTE THE TENSION TO RESOLVE, recorded rather than glossed: reflow2 deliberately installs once per machine and makes a directory with no design cost nothing (req:no-setup-per-project, cap:latent-surface). Asking a question at genesis must not become a setup step, which is exactly what that work removed. The likely shape is therefore not a prompt but a detector — notice when one graph is carrying what looks like several systems, or when several graphs are describing one, and ask THEN, which is the report-and-ask pattern the project already uses. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing 00-setup.json. Anthony's word: capture it.

properties.name: A gap arrives as YOURS, because the graph can say who owns the thing it is about
properties.rationale: THE EVIDENCE IS A NUMBER THAT NEVER MOVED. The fleet maintains an ownership matrix in markdown — ~25 rows mapping each component/surface/process to the boss who owns it and the bus where changes get flagged. The graph already holds the components; it cannot say who owns one. So detect_gaps BROADCASTS: every one of 7 attached sessions received the same '69 gaps / 26 defects / 20 / 20', almost none of it theirs. FIVE CONSECUTIVE SEATS REPORTED THOSE IDENTICAL NUMBERS AND NOT ONE MOVED — because debt addressed to everyone is addressed to no one. Their framing: with an OWNED_BY edge a gap could arrive as 'yours' rather than 'the graph's', and the rollup could say '12 of 69 are in regions you own'. That single change would convert their biggest standing number from wallpaper into a work queue. COMPOUNDS WITH A SECOND REPORTED DEFECT: fact:defect-an-aggregate-gap-hides-partial-progress — a gap naming 48 capabilities is one item, so a worker who closes it for one capability sees the total stay put. Unaddressed debt that also cannot register progress is doubly inert. WHAT ALREADY EXISTS HERE, and this requirement should be judged against it rather than beside it: cap:owed-to-a-contributor is already `in_progress` and holds exactly this thesis — but its chosen first cut is narrow (loop_status counting proposed Decisions carrying an AUTHORED_BY role=approver edge), which answers 'what has a named person been asked to settle' and NOT 'which of these gaps are in the part of the system I own'. The fleet's ask is the second one. Its own description records the larger shapes as considered-but-not-chosen. THE INPUT MAY ALREADY BE IN THE GRAPH TOO: claim_region records what a seat holds, computed as a propagation region from a seed — and the fleet's separate #5 ask notes 'nothing else consumes it'. So a seat-scoped loop_status may be reachable from claims without any new edge type at all, which is worth weighing before adding OWNED_BY. NOTE the deliberate constraint cap:owed-to-a-contributor already records and that this requirement must not overturn silently: notification is out of scope — the server never initiates a message, verified against the service rather than assumed, and a consumer polls.
properties.statement: The design graph SHALL be able to record who owns a component, surface or process, and the loop's reporting SHALL be answerable in terms of that ownership — so debt reaches an addressee instead of broadcasting. Requested as the #1 fleet-specific gap by dev_storyflow's api-boss 5d608b85 on 2026-08-08, ranked by what would have saved them the most: 'this is the biggest fleet-specific gap and it is not on anyone's list.'

properties.name: The design persists in-repo alongside the code
properties.statement: The graph lives at ./.reflow2/graph inside the consumer project, so the design travels with the repo; export/import is deterministic so a backup under git shows what actually changed.

properties.name: A plan is a dated claim whose movement is on the record
properties.statement: A planned epoch or increment is a claim about the future, and its reliability decays with horizon — Anthony, 2026-07-28: 'the further out you plan your epochs, the more volatile they are, almost like what the Black-Scholes model was created for. There will always be a delta between what was planned for a particular epoch and what was actually delivered when we arrive at it.' Three obligations follow. (1) A planned claim carries its confidence, and far claims carry less — the ANTICIPATES edge's existing confidence property (0.0-1.0) is the vocabulary hook. (2) Arriving at an epoch produces the planned-vs-delivered delta as a matter of course, and REPLANNING IS RECORDED: when a planned epoch's content moves, the plan's own change is a dated event on the record, so 'what did we believe at the time?' stays answerable — the same axis-Z discipline the as-built record already gets. (3) Firmness is two-dimensional and the dimensions move independently: a KPP (req:inviolable-intent, cap:kpp) is inviolable in CONTENT — it cannot be weakened to make a plan work — but may SLIP IN TIME to a later increment or epoch, and the slip is a recorded dated event, never a silent re-pin; ordinary requirements may flex in both content and time as factors affect the project. Evidence for the open dec:plan-time-axis question of whether scheduled time becomes a first-class axis. PARTIAL SATISFACTION AT ARRIVAL (Anthony, 2026-07-28, raised as a nuance, not decided): 'what happens if a requirement is only partially satisfied? Does the part that was not satisfied get transferred to the following epoch/increment, or is it discontinued?' The candidate mechanism is already in the design: a partially-met requirement is DECOMPOSED (req:requirement-lineage — the split is on the record, both children knowing their parent), the satisfied child closes at this epoch, and the remainder's fate is the one question that must be ASKED, never defaulted: transferred (re-pinned to a later epoch, a recorded slip) or discontinued (retire-from-design's discipline — dropped on the user's word, with the reason). The status vocabulary already carries both answers (deferred / dropped). He expects further nuances of arrival semantics; the modalities and rules here are an open list, not a closed one.

properties.name: Runs on Linux and macOS developer machines
properties.statement: Target platforms are Linux and macOS. Consumers must not pay a RocksDB C++ rebuild for a routine reflow2 update; the core runs on an in-memory backend with RocksDB opt-in.

properties.name: A proposed change can be read as a delta before it lands
properties.statement: A pull request is a delta that has not happened yet. For a project under design control, the design must be able to read a candidate change (a PR branch, a patch) the same way delta reads a landed one — which artifacts would drift, and which capabilities, interfaces and requirements those artifacts realize (propagate from the touched set) — but STRICTLY READ-ONLY: a review reports what the change would mean to the design and never writes an accept, because accepts record what IS, and a PR is not yet. When the PR touches a published or consumed interface, the report must say so by name, because that is the part of the diff a reviewer cannot see from the code alone. Anthony's scenario, 2026-07-28: at his job (a founding site of the Bluesky project, blueskyproject.io), 'just today I got a request to review a PR on bluesky-httpserver — delta would see the difference between the current version and what the PR adds/changes.' The cross-repo half of his scenario — bluesky-httpserver is tightly coupled with bluesky-queueserver; does the PR affect the other repo? — is deliberately NOT this requirement: it is the standing composition thread (req:seam-incompatibility, req:composed-analysis, dec:linked-repos-poc), where the delta review's touched-interface list becomes the input to a seam check against the coupled design's mirrored surface.

properties.name: A published surface must be able to carry a behavioural promise, not only structure
properties.statement:
FOUND BY A REAL TRIAL, 2026-07-28, and it is reflow2's defect rather than either project's: the dynograph-foundation session, publishing its offer to the reflow2 session, could not express the one commitment its consumer most needed.

THE MECHANISM, exactly. `export_surface` emits published Interfaces, the Components either side of them, and the contract artifacts. It withholds everything else as internal — including every Requirement, deliberately, because a consumer has no business reading its dependency's internal intent. But BEHAVIOURAL COMMITMENTS LIVE IN REQUIREMENTS. So the document reflow2 offers as "the published surface" carries structure and no promises, and there is no way to publish one.

THE CONCRETE CASE. reflow2's own Cargo.toml asserts, in a comment, that dynograph's `open_rocksdb` "fails loud (foundation contract), rather than silently falling back to memory". That is a real, load-bearing promise — a silent fallback to an in-memory store would lose a consumer's data with no error. dynograph's graph HAS it, as an accepted Requirement ("A build without RocksDB must work, and must fail loud rather than fall back"). The provider holds the promise, the consumer depends on the promise, and the surface export cannot carry it between them. So it lives where it is useless: a prose comment in the consumer's build file, on the wrong side of the seam, where the provider will never see it change.

WHY THIS IS WORSE THAN A MISSING FEATURE. A published surface that structurally cannot contain half of what a published surface is for will be *believed* — it says "published surface" on the tin, it counts what it withheld, and it looks complete. A consumer reading it concludes the provider promises nothing behavioural, when in fact the provider promises plenty and simply cannot say so.

TWO WAYS OUT, and they are not equal. (1) A prose companion document alongside the export — cheap, and it sits outside every check reflow2 has, so it drifts exactly like `docs/endpoints.md` did in the provider's own repo. (2) A `designation` on Requirement, the way Interface already carries one, so a behavioural promise can be marked publishable and travel with the surface — the export machinery, the withholding count, and the drift checks all then apply to it unchanged. Option 2 is the recommendation: it reuses the mechanism whose semantics are already settled (`internal` by default, because publishing is a commitment nobody should make by accident) rather than inventing a second, unchecked channel.

NOT A LICENCE TO PUBLISH REQUIREMENTS WHOLESALE. Most requirements are internal intent and must stay withheld. The designation is opt-in per requirement, exactly as it is per interface, and the default stays `internal`.

properties.name: A read reminds the agent of loop debt at the moment of attention
properties.statement: The agent should be reminded of outstanding coherence-loop debt while it is looking at the graph mid-session — not only at SessionStart (fires once) and Stop (fires at the very end). Reads (scan_nodes, get_node, search_design, graph_report, …) are the agent's first and most frequent action, so a read that returns while the loop is owed something is a well-timed place to surface it, closing the gap between the two existing triggers. This is the read-side sibling of the write tools' loop_hint and a member of the BL-74 "fire on a trigger, not on virtue" family: the reminder must ride a call the agent already makes, so remembering reflow2 does not depend on the agent's discipline under operational load.

properties.name: Reading the design does not require owning it
properties.statement: A session that cannot take the write lock should still be able to READ the design — orientation, detectors, reports — rather than having no design brain at all. RocksDB supports this (open_for_read_only, open_as_secondary) but dynograph-storage does not expose it, so this needs an upstream change to a tag-pinned dependency. Six concurrent sessions on one machine is the actual working pattern, and today five of them get nothing.

properties.name: The epoch an increment can deliver on is computed from readiness, not declared
properties.statement: An increment's delivery epoch shall be DERIVED from the readiness of the technologies it is gated on: the earliest epoch by which every gating technology reaches the level stated for it, with the answer naming the technology and level that decided it. Readiness is an OBSERVATION (a TRL/MRL level 1-9 about an enabling technology) and the gating threshold is a JUDGEMENT stated by the user — reflow2 shall never supply a default threshold, and an increment with no stated threshold shall report as ungated rather than as ready. A projected level shall be distinguishable from a measured one wherever it is read.

properties.name: Every element of a design is a black box with inner function and interfaces, nested as deep as the design needs, in any domain
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-07, in his words: treat everything in design as a systems-engineering BLACK BOX that has some inner functionality and an interface with other black boxes. Inside a black box may be a series of other black boxes making up the parent black box, and this continues down further and further as the design needs — system-of-systems level, then systems level, then component level, and so on. This should apply to just about any design project, from code projects to biology projects. Secondly, graph theory is then applied over which functions are allocated to which systems.

HE ADDED, AND IT IS THE POINT OF RECORDING THIS: "I'm a little surprised that reflow2 does not have this as it was one of the primary things I designed it for." So this requirement is not new intent — it is ORIGINAL intent that had no node, which is the failure mode this project has hit before (dec:idea-backlog-belongs-in-the-graph: accepted, invisible, violated, re-announced as new). Two prior answers in that conversation told him the recursive model was largely absent, and that was WRONG; the measurement below is the correction.

WHAT ALREADY EXISTS, measured 2026-08-07 rather than recalled: the vocabulary is complete and the backbone is real. Component carries a `level` (48 at `component`, 8 at `subsystem`), CONTAINS nests Component inside Component (42 edges), ALLOCATED_TO puts capabilities on components (138 edges), and the graph-theory half is built and running — evaluate_allocation computes modularity, god-components and misplaced capabilities; cap:hierarchy checks decomposition levels; req:analyse-at-any-level already requires that any level be analysable on its own; req:decomposition-covers-its-parent already requires a decomposition to be checkable against what the parent held. DECOMPOSES exists as an edge type and is UNUSED (0 instances) because CONTAINS carries it.

WHERE IT FALLS SHORT OF THE STATEMENT, and all three are measured:
1. DEPTH IS TWO, not "as deep as the design needs". Project -> 8 subsystems -> 42 components, max depth 2, nothing above system-of-systems and nothing below component. The schema does not bound this; the population does. And 14 components are roots — 6 ordinary components sit outside every subsystem, so the tree is not even complete at the depth it has.
2. THE INTERFACE HALF IS ~9% POPULATED. 5 Interface nodes and 5 PROVIDES / 5 CONSUMES edges for 56 components. "An interface with other black boxes" is the half that makes a black box a black box, and it is almost entirely unmodelled — the same fact the trajectory reports as `seams 0% (0/73)`.
3. THE DOMAIN CLAIM IS UNTESTED OUTSIDE SOFTWARE. Every calibration number behind the granularity guidance comes from code (110k LOC -> ~78 nodes; reflow2's own 34k LOC -> ~100 nodes). The adopt skill does explicitly claim non-code subjects and carries a table for them, but nothing has exercised "code projects to biology projects".

THE ASYMMETRY THIS EXPOSES, offered as reasoning rather than as settled: the standing guidance is one Interface per contract and one Artifact per meaningful unit, never per endpoint, file or function. For software that is defensible because the fine grain is REDUNDANTLY AVAILABLE — a compiler, an LSP and a type checker each hold element-level truth exactly and continuously, so a graph copy would be worse and staler. For a building, a satellite or an organism there is no compiler: nothing else holds "this penetration weakens this member", so the fine grain is not redundant, it is the only copy. The same rule may therefore be right for code and wrong for physical design, and reflow2 applies it uniformly.

WHAT WOULD SATISFY THIS, so it is not read as satisfied by the vocabulary alone: an arbitrary-depth nesting that is exercised beyond two levels, both sides of every contract modelled at each level so a change at one level propagates across siblings at that level (the electrical-drawing-affects-structural case he gave), and the allocation analysis reading something other than a perfect score over an empty structure.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SHARPENED 2026-08-12 — THE CROSS-GRAPH READING, WHICH NOBODY HAD DRAWN OUT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

Anthony, working the linking trial: "kind of getting to a place where we can do a bottoms-up approach of systems engineering where your system or system-of-systems is the composition of a bunch of independently developed and linked, but are federated, reflow2 projects that are the components or systems of the higher level project."

⭐ THIS REQUIREMENT HAS TWO READINGS AND ONLY ONE HAS EVER BEEN CONSIDERED.

  WITHIN A GRAPH — Component CONTAINS Component, `level`, matryoshka. This is what the statement above is about, and reflow2 already models itself as 8 `sys:*` components over 45 components.

  ACROSS GRAPHS — a WHOLE DESIGN, separately owned and independently developed, is a black box in a larger system. Same recursion, one level up, at an OWNERSHIP boundary rather than a containment one. Nothing in this requirement or its measurement addressed this, and it is what his framing adds.

⭐⭐ AND THE CROSS-GRAPH BLACK BOX ALREADY EXISTS — MEASURED, NOT ASSUMED. A mirror of flo2's published surface into a scratch reflow2 graph (2026-08-12, first time `mirror_surface` was run on a real pair) brought in 13 nodes: 1 Project, 6 Components, 5 Interfaces, 1 Artifact — with **5 CONTAINS edges from `proj:flo2`** plus PROVIDES/CONSUMES/SPECIFIES. So a mirrored design lands as A PROJECT NODE CONTAINING ITS PARTS, with its published interfaces as the ports: structurally a black box with an interface, sitting alongside the host design's own. The SHAPE this requirement asks for is therefore present across graphs as well as within one. What is absent is that NOTHING ASKS whether the thing just mirrored is a system in a larger one, and NO ANALYSIS RECURSES across that boundary.

⚠️ TOP-DOWN AND BOTTOM-UP ARE DIFFERENT PROBLEMS, and only the first was ever designed for. `req:one-design-or-several-is-asked` records reflow's S-04-decision — the System-of-Systems question asked BEFORE anything is built, which decomposes a concept into N designs, one directory each. That is TOP-DOWN: one owner, coordinated ids, boundaries designed together, released together. Anthony is describing BOTTOM-UP: N designs that already exist independently, from which the SoS emerges by linking.

EVERY GAP THE 2026-08-12 LINKING TRIAL FOUND IS A BOTTOM-UP GAP, and top-down composition would have had none of them:
  - ids are uncoordinated, so correspondence falls back on fuzzy names that re-guess every run;
  - boundaries were never agreed, so flo2 models reflow2 as a component it CONTAINS and pairing has no boundary to pair across;
  - release cadences differ by construction, so every comparison carries a version skew nothing discloses;
  - labelling is a bilateral precondition neither party gets value from until both have paid — which is why the whole linking layer has ZERO INSTANCES in either graph.

🛑 TWO THINGS BLOCK THE BOTTOM-UP READING, both concrete:
  (1) NO REFRESH. Found 2026-08-12 by running `mirror_surface` TWICE. The second mirror of the SAME design collided with itself — 12 of 13 ids refused as collisions, `mirrored_edges: 0`, `mirror_content_hash: null` — leaving the STALE node in place with the host's own CONSUMES edge still pointing at it, while `mirrors` continued to report the FIRST hash. So the staleness register reads FRESH after a failed refresh, which is worse than never refreshing. Re-mirroring one `mirror_of` is a DIFFERENT OPERATION from mirroring a new design ("replace what I hold of theirs at a new pin" versus "add a stranger and refuse clashes"), and only the second is implemented. A federation of independently-moving projects is MADE OF refreshes.
  (2) THE SoS-LEVEL INSTRUMENTS REPORT GREEN OVER EMPTINESS. `graph_report` says "Modularity 1.00 across 45 components; 0 misplaced", and `fact:defect-allocation-health-is-green-over-an-empty-structure` already records that this is computed over almost no dependencies. At system-of-systems level that is the `unmet_needs: 0` failure again — a confident number over an unpopulated structure — and this requirement's own closing line already demands "the allocation analysis reading something other than a perfect score over an empty structure".

📌 WHAT THIS DOES NOT CHANGE: `dec:nested-graphs` already settled that separately-owned designs are SEPARATE GRAPHS linked by mirroring, so the architecture for the cross-graph reading is decided and this is not a proposal to revisit it. What is added here is that the recursion this requirement asks for and that decision's composition mechanism ARE THE SAME THING at different scales, which neither node says.

properties.name: reflow2 can say which of its own skills and tools a session reached for — recorded automatically, reported without judgement
properties.statement:
reflow2 RECORDS which of its own skills were fetched and which tools were called in a session, automatically and without the agent's cooperation, and reports it as a fact rather than a verdict.

WHY IT IS FIRST, AND THIS IS THE WHOLE ARGUMENT FOR THE ORDERING: `req:a-discipline-is-delivered-at-the-tool-not-in-a-catalogue` proposes to raise a rate that HAS NEVER BEEN OBSERVED. `dec:bl-155` measured TOOL calls — 6,095 across 46 retained transcripts, 40 of 132 tools never called — and there has never been an equivalent for `get_skill`, which is server-side and trivially countable. **Ship the hints first and there is no way to tell whether anything changed; the project would be optimising a number it cannot see.** So this is not the interesting work and it goes first anyway.

AUTOMATIC, NOT A TOOL — and the reason is self-defeat rather than convenience. A tool must be CALLED, and the population most worth measuring is precisely the one least likely to call it: an agent that forgets `revise-design` forgets `log_usage` too. The measurement would be biased toward the sessions that need no measuring. Every MCP call already passes through the server, so the server records without being asked. Anthony reached this himself while proposing it (\"maybe a tool is not the right option\").

REPORTS, DOES NOT DIAGNOSE — his constraint, and already this project's doctrine: `dec:report-dont-judge` holds that the confirmation ledger reports claim history and never judges a claim. Same shape one domain over.

⚠️ WHAT IT CAN AND CANNOT MEASURE, stated up front because reporting the wrong one would be the exact false confidence the loop exists to prevent: **it measures FETCHES, NOT COMPLIANCE.** A skill can be followed correctly from memory without ever being fetched — this session followed revise-design's snapshot-first step without loading it — and a skill can be fetched and ignored. BL-155's own caveat travels: absence is WEAK evidence, and `set_project_mode` appeared as text in ten transcripts with zero recorded calls despite having been used. A rising fetch count is evidence that the routing changed, never evidence that the discipline held.

WHERE THE LOG LIVES is deliberately NOT settled here — `dec:how-should-reflow2-log-its-own-usage` holds that question, with the recommendation (beside the store, not in the graph) and its precedent (the shared-mode rendezvous and log already sit beside the store rather than inside it).

SOURCE: Anthony, 2026-08-09 — \"something that automatically logs usage and issues (doesn't diagnose, just logs)\".

properties.name: reflow2 is consumable as a pinned, versioned container image, so a consumer needs no Rust toolchain and reflow2 needs no knowledge of their deploy
properties.statement:
Raised by @ajs from flo2, 2026-08-05. flo2 wants to consume reflow2 as a pinned image rather than installing it, so that nobody building the web app needs a Rust toolchain and nobody maintaining reflow2 touches flo2's deploy. It is what lets a second contributor (@alex) consume reflow2 without building it.

THE JOB ITSELF IS SMALL AND IS NOT NEW MACHINERY. release.yml already builds a per-platform binary matrix (linux-x86_64, macos-arm64, macos-x86_64) and packages the consumer kit; a container is one more job in that workflow. Build for linux/amd64, and linux/arm64 too if flo2 may land on arm hosts. Tag the image with the reflow2 version already in [workspace.package], so a consumer pins a version rather than chasing latest. Publish to a registry flo2 can pull from. Run as a non-root user, and make sure the mounted data volume is writable by that uid — the commonest way a first container run fails. There is no Dockerfile in the repo today, so this starts from nothing.

TWO RUNTIME SETTINGS A SERVER NEEDS AND A LAPTOP DOES NOT. (1) The idle timeout does not belong on a hosted server: --idle-timeout defaults to 120 minutes and exists, per its own comment, because holding the lock blocks every CLI use of the graph — right for a developer's machine, wrong for a service, where the container exiting on idle looks like a crash loop to an orchestrator. The timeout is carried by the shared-server path, and the explicit --http branch constructs its surface with no SharedServer attached, so it appears not to apply there; which mode the container runs must be confirmed and the behaviour pinned rather than inherited. (2) Binding and reachability: the container must bind a routable address rather than loopback, and --http-allow-host is DNS-rebinding protection, NOT authentication. The image must be deployed on a private network behind flo2's gateway, and that expectation belongs in the image's own documentation so nobody deploys it thinking it defends itself.

READINESS. The rendezvous sidecar is written only AFTER the store is held and the port is bound, which makes it an honest readiness signal: if it exists, the server got all the way up. A healthcheck can use that, or an equivalent endpoint. What a healthcheck must NOT do is report ready before a cold open finishes — opening a large design builds its full-text index and takes seconds, not milliseconds.

properties.name: Someone can read what reflow2 is on the open web, without cloning it or installing anything
properties.statement:
ANTHONY, 2026-08-14, sequenced explicitly AFTER the next release: *"post release, i'd like to do something like this for: To show your repository's HTML files on a live web page like username.github.io, use GitHub Pages."*

WHAT IS ASKED FOR, stated only as far as he stated it: reflow2's repository publishes a live web page on GitHub Pages, reachable at a public URL, so a reader meets the project without cloning the repo, installing the binary, or running an agent. Today every description of reflow2 lives in files you must already have checked out.

HE SUPPLIED A MECHANISM SKETCH AND IT IS NOT TAKEN AS SETTLED, because he prefaced it with "something like this": `index.html` at the repository root, Pages configured to deploy from a branch (`main`, folder `/root`). ⚠️ THE ROOT PLACEMENT IS THE PART TO RE-EXAMINE RATHER THAN IMPLEMENT — this repository's root is a Rust workspace (`Cargo.toml`, `crates/`), and GitHub Pages also serves from `/docs` or from an Actions deploy, both of which keep generated HTML out of the build root. Which mechanism is right is a decision, not a transcription.

📌 ALREADY PRESENT AND WORTH KNOWING BEFORE ANYTHING IS BUILT: `docs/loop-dag.html` is the repo's one existing HTML page, and `tools/render_views.py` already renders design viewpoints as pure projections with a CONFESSIONS list for anything the graph cannot supply.

⚠️ WHAT THE PAGE SHOWS IS NOT STATED AND IS NOT INFERRED HERE. That question is `dec:idea-what-is-on-reflow2s-public-page`, and it is the one that decides how much work this is.

Status stays `proposed`: this is his word about wanting it, and the wording is not yet confirmed.

properties.name: Released equals designed
properties.statement: At release the design must describe what was actually released.

properties.name: A requirement knows where it came from: stated, decomposed from a parent, or derived from a decision
properties.statement: Requirements multiply in two different ways and reflow2 must tell them apart, because they behave differently. An ORIGINAL requirement is the stakeholder's own word. A DECOMPOSED requirement is a 1:1 split of a parent into smaller testable pieces, adding no new information — so satisfying every child satisfies the parent, and a parent's delivery is therefore derivable from its children rather than needing its own capability. A DERIVED requirement is new technical necessity that nobody asked for, created because of a design decision — so it traces to that DECISION, not to a parent goal, and if the decision is ever re-opened the derived requirement may cease to have any reason to exist. Three consequences follow. Delivery must roll up a decomposition tree instead of treating every requirement as an independent leaf. Re-opening a decision must be able to say which requirements existed only because of the road taken. And the distinction must survive the loss of the person who made it: an original requirement is the only kind whose loss loses intent, because decomposed and derived ones can be regenerated from what they came from, and that is precisely why the link back must be recorded rather than remembered.

properties.name: A restructuring is certified, not asserted
properties.statement: When a design change claims to move structure while holding function invariant, reflow2 shall decide that claim from the two as-designed records alone — reporting whether anything in the function layer (Capability, Requirement, Flow, Actor, Constraint, Project) was added or removed, and whether any link lying wholly inside that layer was added, removed or changed — and shall refuse to certify a divergence it cannot classify, answering indeterminate rather than passing it silently. A link shall be judged function-bearing by its endpoints and never by its type alone, because one edge type carries different meaning at different endpoints.

properties.name: A gap acknowledgement must expire when the thing it judged changes, not only when the SET of affected nodes changes
properties.statement:
`acknowledge_gap`'s own tool description promises: "If the gap's affected nodes later change, the review expires and the gap returns for a fresh judgement." That promise is only half kept. A gap id hashes its `gap_source` and its affected node IDS, so the review expires when the affected SET changes membership — and never when the affected NODES change content.

FOUND BY TRIPPING OVER IT, 2026-07-30, minutes after the requirements involved were accepted. `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` and `req:plans-move-honestly` were both parked on 2026-07-28 with their `unsatisfied_requirement` gaps acknowledged, each reason reading "Deferred on Anthony's word … scheduled for a later increment rather than built now." Anthony then accepted both as intent on 2026-07-30 and neither raised a gap, because a review written about a DEFERRED requirement silently went on suppressing the gap for an ACCEPTED one. Two requirements he had just committed to were invisible as open work.

THE SHARPER INSTANCE IS THE SAME NODE. `req:graph-indexes-snapshots` was reworded in the same session, off git-ref indexing and onto answering temporal questions in the graph. Its acknowledgement's rationale still reads "the graph owns the MAP from epoch/increment to the git ref that holds it" — so an accepted review was left justifying a requirement that no longer says that, and nothing noticed. A review that outlives the wording it reviewed is worse than no review, because it reads as a human having agreed to something they never saw.

WHAT CHANGES SHOULD EXPIRE A REVIEW, and this is the part to decide rather than assume: a status move (proposed → accepted is the case that bit), a statement rewrite, or any property the review's reasoning depended on. The honest difficulty is that reflow2 cannot know which properties a free-text rationale depended on, so the candidate rules are (a) expire on any property change to an affected node, which is safe and noisy; (b) expire on status change plus statement change only, which is targeted and guesses; (c) record what the review was made AGAINST — a content hash of the affected nodes at review time — and expire when that hash moves, which is the same mechanism `set_artifact_checksum` already uses for as-built drift and needs no guessing about which properties mattered.

(c) LOOKS RIGHT AND IS ALREADY A PATTERN HERE: an artifact's registered checksum is exactly "what I accepted, as it was when I accepted it", and a mismatch is reported rather than assumed harmless. A review is the same shape one level up.

NOT THE SAME DEFECT AS `req:set-scoped-acknowledgement-keys-on-its-rule`, and worth stating because they are mirror images and a fix for one could easily break the other. That requirement was about acknowledgements expiring TOO EAGERLY — a project-level rollup whose member set grows on every capability, so a standing judgement could never carry. This is the opposite failure: a per-node review that does not expire when it should. One is a false alarm, the other a false silence, and the pair suggests the underlying model — expiry keyed on an id hash — is too blunt for both.

Captured 2026-07-30 while promoting the planning axis to intent. The two stale acknowledgements found were withdrawn immediately so the accepted requirements show as open work; this requirement is about the mechanism, not those two instances.

properties.name: The open structural-defect list means still-needs-attention
properties.statement: A structural defect that has been reviewed and consciously accepted must move out of the open list into a reviewed one — not deleted, not hidden — the way an acknowledged gap already does. Found as friction 2026-07-25: detect_defects reports the same six findings every run, all six carrying recorded Decisions explaining why they stand, so a genuine seventh would arrive into a list nobody reads carefully and the count is the only signal. reviewed_gaps already keeps this promise for gaps on the stated grounds that "a list that can never reach zero gets skimmed"; the defect side makes the same promise in its docs and does not keep it. Two properties carried over from the gap side: the acceptance records WHY, as a real node that outlives the session, and it expires when the affected nodes change, so an accepted defect comes back for a fresh look rather than staying quietly accepted forever.

properties.name: The roads not taken are preserved and forkable
properties.statement: reflow2 preserves not only what was decided but what was considered and rejected: every Decision keeps its unchosen alternatives as first-class, forkable siblings, and any past decision can be re-opened at its epoch and a different branch taken from that point. The design is a navigable decision tree, not only a linear history — the extension of req:intent-preserved from 'the past is never overwritten' to 'the roads not taken are never lost either.' The unchosen option and its rationale are stored; the alternative's consequence design is computed on demand by replay, never eagerly maintained.

properties.name: An operational scenario is a design object, so validation has something to point at
properties.statement: reflow2 has no vocabulary for a scenario, a use case, or an operational thread. Grepping the whole schema for scenario, use_case, persona, journey and operational_view returns nothing. The consequence is not a missing view; it is that VALIDATION HAS NOTHING TO POINT AT. Verification.kind already distinguishes verification (built right, meets the spec) from validation (the right thing, meets the operational intent) and the unvalidated_capability gap already reads that distinction — but the design cannot state what the operational intent IS. That is why, on 2026-07-28, 67 capabilities were acknowledged as verified-but-not-validated with the reason "validation is tracked OUTSIDE this graph": the real evidence is the brownfield ophyd-service trial, the greenfield aidrone trial and sustained fleet use, all of which live in prose in docs/trials-private/. They live in prose because there is no node they could attach to. A scenario is precisely the missing anchor — a named narrative of an actor achieving something through a sequence of steps, which is what a passing validation would be a validation OF. THE PRIOR ART: reflow's 00-setup.json required THREE foundational documents before any design work began — SYSTEM_MISSION_STATEMENT.md (purpose, objectives, key stakeholders), SUCCESS_CRITERIA.md (measurable criteria, performance, functional and non-functional requirements), and USER_SCENARIOS.md ("detailed user scenarios, user personas, use cases, user journey maps"). Two of the three map onto reflow2 cleanly: the mission statement onto Project.objective, the success criteria onto Requirements plus the KPP machinery of req:inviolable-intent. The third maps onto nothing. THE PIECES EXIST AND ONE OF THEM IS HALF-DEAD, which is why this is a vocabulary gap rather than a missing subsystem. Flow is fully implemented — flow.rs carries add_flow, part_of_flow with step_order, and flow_report, realizing cap:model-process — so an ordered sequence of capabilities is already expressible. Actor is not: in the entire core it appears ONCE, at report.rs:35 inside SNAPSHOT_TYPES, where it is counted and nothing more, and INTERACTS_WITH — the relationship Actor's own schema hint describes ("Actors sit at the boundary; they INTERACT_WITH Capabilities or Flows and often originate Requirements") — has no reader anywhere. So the actor half of a scenario is declared and unread, another member of the family with req:functional-vocabulary-computes. WHY IT MATTERS PARTICULARLY HERE: operational scenarios are a standard viewpoint in the practice this project exists to serve (DoDAF OV-1 and OV-6, UAF), not a nicety. And a scenario is also the natural home for the behavioural-equivalence question held open the same day — "does the new implementation still do what the old one did" is answered by replaying a scenario against both, which is what reflow's 01f migration workflow did with golden tests. Found 2026-07-28 reviewing 00-setup.json. Anthony's word: capture it.
