Interoperability failures are overwhelmingly SEMANTIC — the same concept under two names, two units, two precisions — and none of that is expressible. `con:pairing-stops-at-the-boundary` already records the ceiling in the graph's own words: pairing sees boundaries, not the types that cross them. That constraint is this requirement's evidence.

NOT SPECIFIED HERE: whether this is a full entity-relationship layer or something much thinner, and whether reflow2 should model entities itself or only carry a locator to an external schema — `dec:agent-navigates-content` (the agent navigates content, the graph records where it landed) is an argument for the thinner answer, and the trade is not settled.

properties.name: Physical resources are modellable — supply, sparing, maintenance and consumption, which `Resource` does not mean
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-07, from the UAF audit, asked as "what if I said create/render me a logistics view": there is no logistics vocabulary, and the type whose name promises it means something else entirely.

THE TRAP, MEASURED: `Resource` exists, and its only instance is `dep:dynograph-foundation` with `resource_type: design-dependency`, carrying a provider URL, a version, a feature list and the file it was declared in. It models a SOFTWARE DEPENDENCY. `REQUIRES_RESOURCE` has one instance and means "this design depends on that library". Of the four missing domains this is the one most likely to be assumed covered, because the name is already taken by something else.

WHAT CANNOT BE SAID TODAY: a consumable and its consumption rate; a spare and its provisioning quantity; a maintenance action, interval or turnaround; transport, storage or shelf life; what a system needs to keep operating as opposed to what it needed to be built. A logistics view has no nouns to draw.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND reflow2: software has no materiel, so this costs nothing here and is load-bearing for every physical programme — which `reflow2-real-operating-context` and the adopt skill both say are in scope ("a satellite, a building or a fleet cannot live in a repository — its drawings, specs, models and analyses can").

NOT SPECIFIED HERE: whether the existing `Resource` type is generalised with a wider `resource_type` vocabulary or a separate type is added beside it. The first is cheaper and risks conflating a build-time dependency with an operational consumable; the second is cleaner and costs a type. That is a decision, and it should be made rather than defaulted.

properties.name: People are modellable inside the design, not only around it — organisation, role, and who performs a function
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-07, from the UAF audit: the Personnel domain has NO vocabulary in reflow2. Two people-shaped types exist and neither is this — `Contributor` is who authored the design, `Actor` is who the designed system serves. Both sit outside the system being designed.

WHAT CANNOT BE SAID TODAY: which role performs a function; the organisation a function belongs to; a post, a competence, or a responsibility assignment; who is accountable for a component. So an organisational view, a manning view, or a responsibility matrix has nothing to project from — and "which function is allocated to which system" (already answered by ALLOCATED_TO) has no counterpart for "which function is allocated to which PERSON or ROLE".

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND reflow2, which is the reason this is a requirement and not a curiosity: reflow2 itself is a tool with an agent and one user, so people barely appear inside its design and their absence is invisible here. Almost every non-software project has people IN the design — a beamline has operators, a satellite programme has crews and controllers, a hospital system has clinicians. `rule:fixes-are-judged-by-the-third-party` says fixes are judged by what they do for somebody else's project, and this is a gap only somebody else's project would feel.

NOT SPECIFIED HERE, deliberately: whether this is one node type or several, whether a role is a first-class node or a property on an edge, and whether reflow2 should follow UAF's Post/Role/Competence split or a simpler shape. Those are design questions and picking one now would foreclose them.

properties.name: Behavioural state and its transitions are modellable, distinct from lifecycle status
properties.statement:
Anthony, 2026-08-07, from the UAF audit: there is no state machine anywhere in the schema, and a whole UAF model-kind column depends on one.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MAKES THIS A REAL GAP RATHER THAN A NAMING ONE: reflow2 has plenty of `status` fields — a Requirement is proposed/accepted/deferred/dropped/met, a Capability is planned/realized/verified, a Verification is planned/passing/failing. Every one of those is a LIFECYCLE status: where a design element has got to in its own maturation. None of them is a BEHAVIOURAL state: a mode the designed thing is in while it operates. And no transition is modelled between any of them — the enums are values, not a graph, so even the lifecycles cannot be projected as a state diagram.

WHAT CANNOT BE SAID TODAY: that a detector is in acquiring / idle / faulted; that a vehicle is in launch / cruise / re-entry; that a protocol connection is in handshake / established / draining; which event causes which transition; which states are safe to be interrupted in. A state view is not expressible, and neither is "what modes must this interface work across".

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND reflow2: reflow2 is a request-response tool with no operating modes to speak of, so the absence costs nothing here and everything on anything with modes. Anthony's own current case is one — a beamline instrument has states, and the analysis stack behaves differently in each.

NOT SPECIFIED HERE: whether states attach to Components, Capabilities or both; whether a transition is an edge or a node; and whether lifecycle status should be unified with behavioural state or kept firmly apart. Kept apart is the likelier answer and is still a decision, not an assumption.

properties.name: A returning session can ask what happened while it was gone
properties.rationale: SESSIONS TODAY DETECT THAT THE GRAPH MOVED BY RE-RUNNING A ROLLUP AND SEEING A DIFFERENT NUMBER — the reporter calls this the worst possible detector, and the record bears it out: a worker checking in reported gaps 55->69 and defects 12->26 between two check-ins hours apart and, correctly, COULD NAME NO CAUSE. WHY IT IS ACUTE RATHER THAN CONVENIENT, and this is the part that generalises past their fleet: their sessions are EPHEMERAL BY DESIGN — they die on context exhaustion constantly and are replaced by a fresh seat that cold-starts from files. A returning seat's FIRST REAL QUESTION is 'what happened while I was gone', and there is no way to ask it. This sits directly under their stated primary use of reflow2, which is not design capture at all but DURABLE MEMORY ACROSS SESSION DEATH. THE RAW MATERIAL MAY ALREADY BE PRESENT: ChangeEvent exists as a node type and AT_EPOCH/OCCURS_DURING pin events in time; what is missing is the query. Worth checking whether this is a reporting surface over existing data rather than new machinery. RELATED ASKS THAT MAY SHARE A MECHANISM: claim visibility without polling (an overlapping claim never reaches the peer, so claim_report must be polled — the reporter's phrase is 'advisory should still be observable'), and the per-node revision in req:a-node-carries-a-revision. All three are forms of 'tell me what moved'.
properties.statement: The graph SHALL answer 'what changed since time T, and by whom' — writes by other seats over an interval — as a query, rather than leaving a session to infer movement by re-running a rollup and noticing a different number. Requested as the #3 fleet ask by dev_storyflow's api-boss 5d608b85, 2026-08-07.

properties.name: The design can say what to work on next, and why that and not something else
properties.statement: A person returning to the design must be able to ask "what is the most pressing thing to work on?" and get an answer computed from the design itself, with its reasoning visible — not a hand-maintained ordering in a file. The answer must rank an unmade decision ABOVE the work that waits on it, because being told to build something blocked on a choice only the human can make is worse than being told nothing. It must distinguish what is undecided from what is unbuilt from what is misshapen, since those need different actions from different people. And it must be a projection over the graph, never a stored list: a second place where priority lives is a second place for it to go stale, which is the failure the whole backlog-in-the-graph move exists to end.

DISTINCT FROM `fact:defect-a-schema-narrowing-orphaned-live-edges-and-no-export-is-ever-imported`, which measures the breakage. THIS asks what the vocabulary should say, and the answer decides whether a real edge is repaired or destroyed.

THE CASE. `ver:side_e_slo_gate_unwired_2026_08_09` VERIFIES `con:side_e_perf_slos_are_enforced_nowhere` — a check that measures whether a performance constraint is actually enforced. `schema/verify.yaml` lists `to: [Capability, Requirement, Artifact, Component, DesignRule]`, so the edge is unimportable and their export has not restored since at least 2026-08-11.

⭐ IT READS AS A LEGITIMATE MODELLING NEED, NOT A SLIP. A Constraint is "a limit or rule the design MUST respect" — a latency budget, a mass cap, "no PII leaves the device". Asking whether a limit HOLDS is the most natural thing anyone would want to check about it, and it is exactly the question `budget_report` answers arithmetically for the numeric case. A Verification is how this design records that something was CHECKED. Refusing to connect them says a limit may be stated and computed but never independently verified.

AND THE ASYMMETRY IS ODD ON ITS FACE: `DesignRule` IS in the list, and `unverified_enforced_rule` exists precisely so a gate-blocking rule owes a passing check. A Constraint is the DesignRule's sibling — the imposed limit beside the chosen one — and the same argument for verifying one applies to the other. Nothing in the schema explains why they were split.

THE OPTIONS:

(a) ADD `Constraint` TO THE TO-LIST. Repairs their export, needs no data migration, and makes the vocabulary say the thing it appears to mean. COUNTER: the list was derived FROM live edges as evidence of use, and adding a type because one edge exists is the same reasoning that produced the incomplete enumeration — one edge is not a demonstrated need.

(b) MIGRATE THE EDGE AWAY — a check about a Constraint could instead verify the Capability that honours it, or the DesignRule that expresses it. COUNTER, and it is `rule:never_shape_a_field_to_satisfy_an_instrument` from their own repo: reshaping real design to satisfy a validator is how a graph bends into fiction, and the edge was legal when written.

(c) RE-DERIVE THE WHOLE LIST ACROSS EVERY KNOWN GRAPH and take the union — the census the original change should have run, now with three real designs to run it against rather than one. COUNTER: it settles this instance without settling the rule, and the next narrowing repeats it.

(d) RESTORE `to: "*"` FOR VERIFIES. COUNTER: the enumeration was added for a reason recorded in the file, and reverting discards that.

⚠️ WHAT MUST NOT HAPPEN, and it is the reporter's point: nobody deletes those two edges to make an import succeed before this is answered. `Project` is the other unlisted type and may well be a genuine mistake — the two should be judged separately rather than as a pair.

{"decision":"RE-OPENS the settled choice that a claim's region is COMPUTED from a seed and a depth rather than stored as a node list. The existing rule is deliberate and stated in the tool itself — 'the region is COMPUTED from seed+depth rather than stored as a node list, so it follows the design as it changes' — and its benefit is real: a stored list goes stale the moment the design moves, which is the failure a claim board exists to avoid. The question re-opened is whether that is the ONLY shape a claim may take, or the default one. PROPOSED SHAPE, from the reporter: allow a claim over an explicit node LIST or over a QUERY, alongside seed+depth. A query would keep the follows-the-design property that motivated the original choice, which is the reason to prefer it over a bare list. NOT YET DECIDED — recorded so the trade is visible rather than re-derived.","name":"OPEN — a claimed region is computed from seed+depth, and a cross-cutting duty is not a radius: does a claim also take a list?","rationale":"Because the cost is now measured rather than argued. dev_storyflow w-aa0607ff, 2026-08-08: their lane was 'cold-test the retrievability of nodes another session mined', spanning two unrelated slices — there is no seed whose depth-2 radius is that work. They claimed a representative node and put the truth in the `note`, which means claim_report's PROSE was right while its STRUCTURED answer was wrong for them. That is the specific failure mode a structured board is supposed to remove. THE STRONGER EVIDENCE IS BEHAVIOURAL, AND IT IS THREE FOR THREE: both prior workers on the same lane skipped claim_region entirely and kept a text file of document paths instead, because a flat list described their actual region better than the graph could. A tool losing to a text file is the same shape as the finding that drove the read-half increment — 'today a document BEATS the graph for making a decision, and that is a fair fight the graph loses'. Cross-cutting duties (audit, cold-validation, a sweep over everything of one kind) are a general category, not one team's oddity, and the radius cannot express any of them. Counter-argument to weigh before deciding: a claim is ADVISORY and never a lock, so the cost of a wrong region is a colleague misreading who holds what, not a corrupted write — which is an argument for keeping the mechanism simple. Against that: an advisory board whose structured field is routinely wrong is how a signal gets trained into being ignored, which is the same objection raised against permanently-live seat liveness.","status":"proposed"}

{"basis":"measured","confidence":1.0,"fact_type":"defect","statement":"`add_change_event`'s `change_type` ENUM HAS NO VALUE FOR A DEFECT FOUND IN THE FIELD, SO RECORDING ONE FORCES A SMALL FICTION. Hit here on 2026-08-08 recording the DUPLICATES/merge fix. The enum is `requirement_creep | new_feature | test_failure_fix | performance_optimization | refactor | scope_change | constraint_change | environment_change | deprecation | resync | baseline_established`. The change being recorded was a defect REPORTED BY A USER of the built system — dev_storyflow's fleet — and diagnosed here. No test had failed; there was no test at all, which was part of the defect. `test_failure_fix` was chosen as the nearest fit and the event NAME says explicitly that no failing test existed, so the ledger is not silently wrong — but the structured field still says something untrue and only the prose corrects it. WHY THIS IS NOT PEDANTRY, and the schema itself makes the argument: `baseline_established` exists precisely because forcing a record-only change through `refactor`/`test_failure_fix` 'writes a fiction into the ledger that exists to prevent fiction' (its own description, BL-157). That reasoning applies unchanged one category along. THE DISTINCTION WORTH KEEPING if a value is added: a defect found by a CHECK and a defect found by a USER are different provenance for the same repair, and reflow2 already cares about that difference everywhere else — `set_provenance` grades authored/inferred/reconciled, and `cap:independent-evidence` refuses to let evidence a value was fitted to count as validating it. FIX SHAPE: add `defect_fix` (or `field_report_fix`); or, smaller, let the event carry a `reported_by`/`found_by` property so the how-it-was-found is structured rather than narrated. NOTE THE MILD IRONY, recorded because it is the same class the fleet reported six times: this is a structured field that answers a slightly different question than the writer's, and the only thing preserving the truth is prose beside it — which is exactly fact:defect-verification-evidence-is-prose-so-passing-can-contradict-itself, one node type over.","subject_id":"cap:loop-status","valid_from":"2026-08-08","value":"{\"observed\":\"2026-08-08, recording chg:duplicate-merge-needs-a-human-20260808\",\"enum\":\"requirement_creep|new_feature|test_failure_fix|performance_optimization|refactor|scope_change|constraint_change|environment_change|deprecation|resync|baseline_established\",\"chosen\":\"test_failure_fix, with the event name stating that no failing test existed\",\"precedent_in_schema\":\"baseline_established was added for exactly this reason (BL-157): forcing a record-only change through a code category writes a fiction into the ledger\",\"fix_shape\":\"add defect_fix/field_report_fix, or a structured reported_by/found_by property\",\"related\":\"fact:defect-verification-evidence-is-prose-so-passing-can-contradict-itself - same shape, different node type\"}"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL — Anthony thinking out loud, 2026-08-08. Nothing here is intent and nothing has been chosen. THE IDEA, his words: \"the allocation of functions to systems/services should be done as late as possible (agreeing that doing it at genesis is too early). I feel like doing it at the last possible moment before functional allocation to system/service is the right call.\" It is the answer he reached to a caution raised against the sibling idea (dec:idea-the-ility-chooses-the-allocation-graph), which proposed ASKING at genesis what quality attribute the system is for: the objection was that at genesis you frequently do not know yet, and premature commitment can cost as much as late discovery. His resolution keeps the question and moves WHEN it is asked — not at genesis, but at the moment allocation actually has to be committed. WHAT THIS WOULD MEAN CONCRETELY: the quality-attribute question rides the ALLOCATION event rather than the project's beginning, so a design accumulates requirements and capabilities freely and is asked what it is optimising for only when something is about to be bound to a component. THE HOOK MAY ALREADY EXIST, and this is the cheap part worth checking before anything is built: `unallocated_capability` is already a detected gap, so the graph can already see capabilities that exist and are bound to nothing. The transition from \"capabilities exist, none allocated\" to \"the first allocation is being made\" is observable from graph state alone, which is the same state-not-history discipline dec:loop-status-state-not-history already commits to. If that is the trigger, nothing new needs remembering. OPEN SUB-QUESTIONS, none answered here: (a) is the moment per-PROJECT or per-CAPABILITY — a mature design allocates new capabilities continuously, so \"the last responsible moment\" may recur rather than happen once, which would make this a repeating prompt rather than a milestone; (b) does deferring allocation conflict with reflow2's own trajectory model, where `allocation` currently reads 100% and sits ahead of the `seams` frontier at 0% — if allocation is supposed to be late, a design showing allocation complete and seams empty may be describing a real inversion rather than healthy progress; (c) what happens to a design that never reaches the moment, since a demonstrator may sit unallocated forever and be right (maturity_report already refuses to say where a design SHOULD be). COUNTER-ARGUMENT, recorded beside rather than against: the last-responsible-moment principle assumes the cost of deciding late is lower than the cost of deciding wrong, which holds when deferral is free — and here it may not be, because artifacts get written against an assumed structure long before anyone calls `allocate`. If real files already embody a de facto allocation, then \"deferring the decision\" defers only the RECORD of it, and the graph would be late to something the build already did. That is the same as-designed-versus-as-built gap that granularity_report exists to surface, and it argues the trigger should watch ARTIFACTS appearing rather than the `allocate` call.","name":"OPEN — is allocating functions to systems/services something to defer to the last responsible moment, and can reflow2 tell when that moment has come?","rationale":"Recorded under the brainstorm skill, separately from the ility idea, because the two are genuinely different questions — WHAT drives allocation and WHEN it happens — and can be answered independently; one node holding both could only ever be half-answered. Worth keeping because it converts a raised objection into a design position rather than losing it: the caution was \"at genesis you do not know yet\", and this answers it without abandoning the question. The `unallocated_capability` hook and the artifacts-versus-allocate-call counter-argument are the two things a later session would otherwise have to re-derive.","status":"proposed"}

{"description":"At an epoch or release, answers \"what didn't we achieve that we were supposed to?\" — every scheduled item returned as delivered, deferred (and where to), discontinued, or OUTSTANDING (still due here, not delivered, and nobody has said which of the previous two it is — the question to put to the user rather than default). Work scheduled after the baseline comes back separately, because a delta measured only against the plan cannot see the work that was not in it. `required` claims that did not land are reported as computed violations rather than slips — the scheduling face of a KPP. The baseline is the target's FIRST snapshot with every later one as the movement trail, so a total slip stays visible across repeated replans; where no snapshot exists the plan never moved and the live edges are the baseline. NOTHING IS STORED: the plan lives in the snapshots and delivery is computed from the golden thread, so writing the outcome down would create a second source of truth able to disagree with the first (`dec:arrival-delta`, `req:completion-computed`).","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"What was planned against what arrived, computed and never stored","provenance":"authored","status":"realized","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"A committed plain-text manifest mapping content hash → original filename → what references it, so a design that points at stored content can say what it does NOT itself carry. Makes \"do I have everything?\" a set comparison for someone holding only the export, and makes a blob change legible in `git log` as a readable name rather than a hex path. Paired with `.gitattributes` marking the blob directory `binary`, which stops git attempting diffs it cannot produce and — the part that matters — stops line-ending conversion silently corrupting a PNG on a CRLF checkout. Governed by `dec:content-manifest`; delivers `req:export-says-what-it-cannot-carry` and makes `req:content-reaches-every-seat`'s fail-loud promise checkable by a person rather than only by the tool. PLANNED.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Say what content the design depends on, in names a person can read","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"Content hash → readable name → what references it, so a design that points at stored content can say what it does NOT itself carry. `missing` names content the graph references and this checkout lacks — the case someone handed the export alone hits, where a diagram that will not open becomes a named finding instead of a silent absence. `orphaned` is the reverse: bytes stored and referenced by nothing, which is how a store grows without anyone deciding to (and the reason `dec:where-content-lives` left repo growth deliberately open).

DERIVED, NEVER STORED, and that is the design rather than an optimisation. The manifest is computed from the graph plus a directory listing; a manifest kept as its own record would be a second source of truth about what the design references and would drift the first time someone updated one and not the other. Rendering it to a committed markdown file is a PROJECTION — the same relationship `dec:views-are-projections` already sets for every other view.

THE READABLE NAME IS THE FRAGMENT'S `title`, not a filename stored beside the hash. The graph already requires a title, so there is no second place for names to live and nothing to disagree with the design about what a thing is called. `referenced_by` carries the Fragment AND what it annotates or yielded, so "what is this picture for?" is answerable from the manifest without opening anything.

A LOCATOR AFTER THE HASH TRAVELS VERBATIM and is never parsed (`dec:agent-navigates-content`) — `sha256:…#L412-L440` resolves to the same blob and reports `L412-L440` untouched. A `content_ref` holding a plain PATH from before the store existed is not treated as content at all, so legacy references do not read as missing blobs.

Needed a FOURTH store function, `list` — named rather than slipped in, because `dec:content-store-implementation` argued for three. That argument was about `object_store`'s path/prefix/pagination semantics, which immutable content addressing does not need; enumerating a flat set of addresses is a different thing, and orphan detection is impossible without it. `list` skips anything whose name is not a hash, so a stranded temp file or the committed manifest is never mistaken for content.

Paired with `.gitattributes` marking the blob directory `binary` — which stops git attempting diffs it cannot produce and, the part that matters, stops line-ending conversion silently corrupting a PNG on a CRLF checkout. REALIZED; `ver:content-manifest` passing, served as `content_manifest`.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Say what content the design depends on, in names a person can read","provenance":"authored","status":"realized","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"A content-addressed store for what the graph cannot hold inline — session transcripts, mermaid diagrams, HTML mockups, user-supplied drawings and photographs, and the source documents a corpus was extracted from. The graph records a CONTENT HASH; the bytes live in the store; an unresolvable pointer fails loud and names itself rather than rendering a design quietly missing its pictures. Built on `object_store` (Apache Arrow) with the local filesystem backend and cloud features OFF, so there is no service to run and cloud backends stay one configuration change away. Blobs are COMMITTED to the repo, which makes them travel exactly as the design does — clone and you have everything (`dec:where-content-lives`). The store itself lives in `reflow2-mcp` because `object_store` is async and `reflow2-core` is deliberately synchronous; the core holds only the hash, which is sync, deterministic and testable in memory. PLANNED.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Store bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"A content-addressed store for what the graph cannot hold inline — session transcripts, mermaid diagrams, HTML mockups, user-supplied drawings and photographs, and the source documents a corpus was extracted from. The graph records a CONTENT HASH; the bytes live in the store; an unresolvable pointer fails loud and names itself rather than rendering a design quietly missing its pictures.

HAND-ROLLED AND SYNCHRONOUS, IN `reflow2-core` (`dec:content-store-implementation`). `put(bytes) -> hash`, `get(hash) -> bytes`, `exists(hash)` over `sha2` (already a core dependency) and `std::fs`. Zero new crates, no async runtime, deterministic and testable without one. `object_store` was measured and recorded as the documented UPGRADE PATH rather than adopted: 36 crates new to reflow2, ~24 of them URL/ICU machinery a local store never calls, buying a feature set — paths, prefixes, listing, multipart, conditional writes — that immutable content addressing does not have.

THREE PROPERTIES THE BUILD MADE REAL, each pinned by a test and two of them mutation-checked. (1) `get` VERIFIES the bytes against the hash they are stored under and REFUSES a mismatch rather than returning it — a content hash nobody checks is only a filename, and the claim that a blob fetched from anywhere can be trusted once it verifies rests entirely on this. (2) A hash is interpolated into a path, so anything that is not exactly `sha256:` plus 64 lowercase hex is refused BEFORE it reaches the filesystem; `../../etc/passwd` is a malformed hash, not a missing file. (3) Writes are temp-then-rename within the shard directory, so a process that dies mid-write leaves nothing or a whole blob — and a stranded temp file is unreachable as content because its name is not a hash.

Blobs are COMMITTED to the repo, so they travel exactly as the design does (`dec:where-content-lives`). Reading INTO stored content is not this capability's job and never becomes one — the agent navigates, the graph records an opaque locator reflow2 never parses (`dec:agent-navigates-content`). REALIZED, `ver:content-store` passing.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Store bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash","provenance":"authored","status":"realized","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"When a planned epoch's content changes — a requirement moves out of epoch 5, a date slips, confidence drops — the movement itself is recorded and dated, rather than the plan being silently rewritten to look as though it always said the new thing. Whether that is sufficient, or whether planned epochs need a revision chain of their own, is undecided. Approved for build by Anthony 2026-07-30, superseding the 2026-07-28 park.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"A plan's movement is dated, so what we believed back then stays answerable","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"The answer to \"what is the most pressing item?\" once the backlog lives in the graph. It is NOT detect_gaps and NOT check-health, and the distinction is the design: detect_gaps asks what the design has not yet decided, check-health asks what shape is wrong, and this asks which of the agreed things to do now. Three different questions needing three different actions, often from three different people. Composed rather than invented — BL-85 already specifies the form (\"a backlog_report / roadmap projection, a view, never a second source of truth\"), BL-68 supplies readiness and risk-to-completion (\"the roadmap is a risk-burndown schedule\"), BL-40 is the projection layer, and the long narratives stay as documents-linked artifacts rather than being crushed into properties. THE RANKING RULE THAT MATTERS MOST: an unmade decision outranks the work waiting on it. A proposed Decision with things GOVERNED_BY it is a blocker, and pointing someone at blocked work is worse than saying nothing, because it looks like progress. Measured 2026-07-24, this is not hypothetical: dec:multi-writer-architecture blocks two nodes, so the honest answer to \"what is next\" right now is a decision only the human can make, not a build task. PREREQUISITE, and the reason this cannot usefully ship first: today ZERO accepted requirements lack a satisfying capability, so \"what is unbuilt\" is unanswerable from the graph — everything accepted is allocated to something. Distinguishing allocated from delivered needs cap:derived-completion (BL-104). Until that lands, this view can rank what is undecided and what is misshapen but is blind to what is merely unfinished. PLANNED.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Say what to work on next, as a projection with its reasoning shown","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.

Anthony, 2026-07-30: "as we march forward in time, we can measure the delta of what was actually achieved/realized versus what was planned for that epoch. For instance, in epoch 3 we had planned for capability A, B, C. However, when we actually got to epoch 3 in time, we only achieved A & C, and B was discontinued or deferred to epoch 4."

FOUR OUTCOMES PER SCHEDULED ITEM, three of them his and one the complement he did not name:
  - DELIVERED — the plan held (A and C).
  - DEFERRED — still intended, the date moved (B to epoch 4).
  - DISCONTINUED — no longer intended at all. Distinct from deferred in the way `retire-from-design` already distinguishes them: one is a date change, the other is a withdrawal, and conflating them either loses a commitment or embalms one.
  - DELIVERED BUT NEVER PLANNED — the complement. Work that arrived which nobody scheduled. Usually the most informative quarter of the delta, because unplanned work is where the estimate actually went, and a report that omits it makes a schedule look better than it was.

THE TRAP, and it is the same shape as the snapshot bug fixed on 2026-07-28. If deferring B simply RE-POINTS its schedule edge from epoch 3 to epoch 4, then when epoch 3 arrives the graph says epoch 3 was only ever about A and C — the slip is invisible and the plan has silently rewritten its own history. That is precisely what `req:intent-preserved` forbids, and precisely what the second-revision-overwrites-the-first defect did to snapshots. So REPLANNING MUST BE A RECORDED CHANGE, NOT AN EDIT.

A MECHANISM THAT NEEDS NOTHING NEW, given what was verified while thinking this through: a Snapshot captures a node's INCOMING edges as well as its outgoing ones. So snapshotting the EPOCH captures every schedule edge pointing at it — the whole plan for that epoch, in one snapshot, in one call. Replanning becomes `record_change` on the epoch, which is exactly the operation the 2026-07-28 fix made safe to do twice in one epoch.

WHAT IS COMPUTED VERSUS STORED. The delta is COMPUTED, never written down, for the same reason "ARE satisfied" is: `req:completion-computed` says delivery is computed from the golden thread and never asserted. At arrival, compare the last snapshot of the epoch's schedule (what was planned, as of before it moved) against what the thread says is delivered. Nothing about the outcome is stored; the two inputs already exist.

WHAT FALLS OUT ONCE IT IS COMPUTABLE — a schedule-performance profile per epoch: hit rate (planned and delivered over planned), slip (how many deferred, and by how many epochs), attrition (how many discontinued), and unplanned (delivered but never scheduled).

AND THE PAYOFF WORTH NAMING, because it closes a loop this project opened the same day. `req:plans-move-honestly` wants a planned claim to carry confidence that decays with horizon — Anthony's Black-Scholes analogy. Once several epochs have arrived, that confidence can be MEASURED rather than asserted: "historically, items scheduled three epochs out land 40% of the time." That is the same argument that retired `req:context-is-a-modelled-quantity` on 2026-07-30 — an estimate is defensible only as a seed for something never measured — applied in the direction where the measurement is actually available, because unlike context cost, schedule performance is observed every time an epoch arrives.","name":"OPEN — what happens when an epoch arrives, and what the planned-vs-delivered delta is computed from","rationale":"Anthony's idea, in his own example, recorded while the thinking is still open.

Two things added beside it rather than in place of it: the fourth outcome (delivered but never planned), because a delta that only reports against the plan cannot see the work that was not in it; and the re-pointing trap, because the obvious implementation of "defer B to epoch 4" is an edge edit, and an edge edit is exactly how the plan would come to lie about what it once said.

The mechanism note is a measurement, not a preference: snapshots were confirmed to capture incoming edges, so the epoch-snapshot approach needs no new machinery.","status":"proposed"}

WHY IT IS A FORK AND NOT A CHOICE OF LIBRARY: `dec:repo-file-embedded` and `dec:multi-writer-architecture` both chose a repo file over a hosted service, and their strongest argument was that no service means nothing to run, nothing to authenticate against, and nothing to be down. A content store is the first thing reflow2 would hold that a git-diffable JSON file is genuinely bad at — megabyte transcripts and binary images — so this is where that decision gets its first real test.

THE OPTIONS, none preferred yet:
  (a) A CONTENT-ADDRESSED DIRECTORY BESIDE THE EXPORT, committed to the repo. Keeps the no-service property exactly, and content-addressing is already this project's idiom (`dec:export-hash-chain` takes self-authenticating repos from AT proto; `set_artifact_checksum` already hashes). Cost: repo weight, and git is poor at binary churn — the objection is real and measurable rather than aesthetic.

{"decision":"OPEN, raised by `req:content-store-for-what-the-graph-points-at`. AMENDED 2026-07-31 after Anthony researched the Rust ecosystem and proposed `object_store` (Apache Arrow, originally InfluxData). The original four-way fork is preserved in the snapshot at `snap:epoch:arrival-delta:dec:where-content-lives`.

WHAT THE RESEARCH CHANGES, and it is more than picking a library. The fork assumed the choice was WHERE — repo, beside the repo, or an external service — and that choosing the service re-opened `dec:repo-file-embedded`. `object_store` presents ONE trait over local filesystem, in-memory, S3, GCS, Azure and HTTP/WebDAV, so the backend becomes RUNTIME CONFIGURATION rather than an architectural commitment. Written once against the trait, reflow2 defaults to local and the no-service property is kept intact, while anyone who wants durability configures a cloud backend without reflow2 knowing or caring. That is exactly the resolution option (c) hypothesised — "possibly only for the OPTIONAL half" — arriving as a property of the library rather than as a compromise.

VERIFIED, not taken from the summary: `fs` (LocalFileSystem) is a DEFAULT feature and `InMemory` needs no feature at all; the cloud backends are behind `aws`/`azure`/`gcp` and are NOT default, and with them off the crate avoids pulling `reqwest` and the crypto providers. The in-memory backend also mirrors reflow2's own `open_in_memory` testing idiom, so tests need no filesystem.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE, and this is the residue that still needs Anthony's word: whether the local blobs are COMMITTED TO THE REPO or GITIGNORED. That is a git question, entirely orthogonal to which crate does the I/O, and it is the one that decides whether a diagram travels with a clone. `object_store` is indifferent to it. Options (a) and (b) from the original fork therefore survive unchanged; (c) and (d) are largely absorbed.

THE REAL COST, which the ecosystem summary does not mention and which bites here specifically: `object_store` IS ASYNC, and `fs` pulls tokio — so even the local-only case requires a runtime. `reflow2-core` is deliberately SYNCHRONOUS: measured 2026-07-31, its entire dependency list is dynograph-{core,storage,graph,resolution,vector}, serde, serde_json and sha2, with no tokio, no async and no futures anywhere. Putting the store in the core would drag a runtime into the one crate that has kept itself deterministic and surface-agnostic.

THE PLACEMENT THAT KEEPS THAT PROPERTY, and it follows the architecture already in place rather than inventing a rule: the CONTENT HASH lives in the core — sync, deterministic, in-memory-testable, exactly what a pointer is — and the STORE lives in `reflow2-mcp`, which already carries tokio through rmcp and hyper. This is the same split as `coverage_report`, where the core computes and the agent supplies what it observed, and the same reason the core is described as neutral to the interaction surface.

STILL TO CHECK BEFORE ADOPTING: `object_store`'s MSRV against the workspace's 1.94, and its transitive tree with cloud features off measured rather than assumed. And per `dec:design-dependencies-declared`, a new dependency is DECLARED with its version and the features taken by name, not just added to a Cargo.toml.

WHAT ANY ANSWER MUST HOLD, unchanged: the pointer is a CONTENT HASH and not a path, because `cap:session-memory` already recorded what a path costs — "a path stored as identity resolves for one person on one machine and silently misses for everyone on a shared graph". And a missing blob must fail LOUD and be nameable (`req:no-silent-fallback`).

THE QUESTION NOW, narrowed from the original: adopt `object_store` with a local default — and do the local blobs get COMMITTED, so a clone carries the diagrams, or GITIGNORED, so the repo stays light?","name":"OPEN — where the bytes behind a pointer live; object_store dissolves most of the fork and leaves one git question","rationale":"Amended rather than answered, and the amendment is worth more than the original because it narrows the question instead of adding to it: a four-way architectural fork became one crate choice plus one git question.

The general shape is worth keeping. The original fork treated "external blob store" and "no service" as opposed, and they are only opposed if the storage backend is baked into the design. A library whose whole purpose is to make the backend a runtime detail removes the opposition rather than resolving it — which is a reminder that some design forks are artifacts of assuming an implementation, and dissolve when the implementation space is actually surveyed.

The async finding runs the other way and is the reason this is still not a trivial adoption: it was found by measuring `reflow2-core`'s dependency list rather than by reading about the crate, and it constrains WHERE the code can go regardless of which backend is chosen. Anthony's research answered the storage question; the constraint it collides with was already in the repo.","status":"proposed"}

THE MEASUREMENT, taken 2026-08-04. `docs/backlog.md` is 3,350 lines / 581,031 bytes across 132 rows. Of the 8 rows filed in one session (BL-205..212), SIX are referenced by ZERO graph nodes. The file is not a registered Artifact, so `coverage_report` does not count it and no checksum tracks it. FOUR things were re-derived in that same session that were already written down somewhere: BL-205 (third rediscovery), `dec:export-once-per-pr` (accepted, invisible, violated and then re-announced as new), BL-70's alternatives family (nearly re-proposed), and dev_storyflow's hand-made doc-intent scope table (re-derived worse from filenames).

THE FRAME IS ALREADY ACCEPTED AND THE BACKLOG VIOLATES IT. `dec:what-lives-where` states the rule: "the design record should stop being PROSE YOU NAVIGATE and become A GRAPH YOU QUERY, with the prose kept as provenance hanging off the nodes it produced." It carries a falsifiable test — "IF REFLOW2 WORKS, STORYFLOW WOULD NOT HAVE NEEDED dev_storyflow… If a user still ends up splitting their repo to stay sane, reflow2 has not delivered what this decision claims." THE SAME TEST GENERALISES AND REFLOW2 CURRENTLY FAILS IT ON ITSELF: if reflow2 works, reflow2 would not need a 581 KB markdown backlog. It is also the exact failure the dev_storyflow api-boss measured in that fleet's MEMORY.md — "an index that must be read IN FULL to be useful has a hard ceiling", 20 KB against a 17 KB limit with everything past the line silently invisible. The backlog is 29 times that size.

WHY IT HAS RESISTED THE OBVIOUS FIX — A BACKLOG ROW IS NOT ONE THING. Reading the eight rows from one session, they are at least four: (i) DEFECTS AGAINST SHIPPED CAPABILITIES (BL-205 loop_status too large, BL-206 the gate's truncated sweep, BL-208 the inert CI guard, BL-209 the blind orphan detector); (ii) UNBUILT WORK (BL-186 the folder driver, BL-211 genesis-from-a-folder); (iii) OPEN DESIGN QUESTIONS (BL-207's fix-shape fork); (iv) DISCOVERED LIMITS (BL-212, chronology cannot be recovered from a folder). Three of those four already have a home: unbuilt work is a Capability at `planned` behind a Requirement, an open question is a `proposed` Decision — which is what this very node is — and a discovered limit is a Constraint or DesignRule.

⭐ THE ONE THAT HAS NO HOME, AND IT IS THE LARGEST CATEGORY: a defect found by USING the tool. reflow2 has no way to say "this capability is built, VERIFIED, and does not do what it claims." `Verification` answers whether a check passes — and every one of BL-205/206/208/209 sat under a passing check. `DriftEvent` answers whether the code moved away from the design — and in all four cases the code and the design AGREED, and both were wrong. HEAL's issues are computed from graph shape, not recorded observations, so they vanish between runs. That absence is why these rows land in markdown: there is nothing to write them to.

OPTIONS, none chosen. (a) ROUTE EACH ROW TO THE TYPE IT ALREADY IS and add no vocabulary. Cheapest, and it works for three categories of four. Counter: for the defect category it loses the finding — "this is broken, here is the measurement, here is how it was found" becomes "here is a need", which erases the evidence and reads as intent rather than as a bug. (b) A `Finding`/`Defect` NODE TYPE carrying claim, evidence, when observed, and what it bears on. Counter, and it is strong: this project has proposed a node type and WITHDRAWN it after measuring TWICE in one week (`Attestation` → `TemporalFact`, `Hazard` → `DesignRule` + `CONSTRAINS`), so the prior against new vocabulary is heavy — and `TemporalFact` ("a time-bounded assertion true only between two epochs") may already be the shape, since a defect is exactly "this was true of the build from epoch X until the fix". (c) EVERYTHING BECOMES A PROPOSED DECISION. Counter: 132 proposed Decisions would swamp `where-am-i` and the decision list, and most rows are not forks between real alternatives. (d) KEEP THE MARKDOWN BUT DERIVE IT FROM THE GRAPH rather than maintaining it by hand. In-house precedent exists and is unused for this: `dec:views-are-projections` ("a view is a projection of the graph; renderer fill-ins are defects") and `tools/render_views.py` already render DoDAF-flavoured views into docs/viewpoints.md. The backlog is simply not one of them. Counter: this solves RETRIEVAL and not CAPTURE — it only helps once the content is in the graph, so it composes with (a)/(b) rather than competing. (e) DO NOTHING AND ACCEPT THE COST, recorded so it is a choice rather than a default: the backlog is readable by a human today, and the re-derivation cost, while real, has been paid without anyone stopping work.

WHAT MUST NOT BE RE-DERIVED WHEN THIS IS PICKED UP: `dec:what-lives-where` (the accepted rule and its falsifiable test), `dec:views-are-projections` plus `tools/render_views.py` (the rendering half already exists), [BL-198] (a serialized default is indistinguishable from a choice — the same "what does the graph actually record" family), and [BL-209] (22 Decisions invisible because `AUTHORED_BY` counts as attachment — a graph-native backlog would land straight into that blind spot and must not).","name":"OPEN — should the backlog stop being a 581 KB markdown file and become graph nodes, and what is missing before it can?","rationale":"Captured under the brainstorm skill at Anthony's request. The load-bearing content is the taxonomy and the single gap it exposes: three of the four kinds of backlog row already have a node type, and the fourth — a defect in a capability that is built, verified and wrong — has none, which is why those rows have no choice but to be prose. Recording the measurement (581 KB, 6 of 8 rows with zero graph representation, four re-derivations in one session) so the next session argues from numbers rather than from the impression that the file is getting long.","status":"proposed"}

--- ADDED 2026-08-04, ANTHONY ASKED WHAT A NODE AND AN EDGE CAN ACTUALLY HOLD. THE ANSWER IS THE CONSTRAINT THAT SHAPES EVERY OPTION ABOVE, AND IT IS MEASURED. ---

WHAT A NODE CAN HOLD. The schema's whole type system is `string` (170 declarations), `enum` (89), `float` (34), `bool` (10), `int` (7). There is NO dedicated text type and NO `max_length` anywhere in any schema file — `string` IS the narrative field and it is unbounded in practice: the `decision` property of this very node runs to several thousand characters without complaint. Every type carries at least one narrative-shaped field (`Decision.decision` + `.rationale`, `Requirement.statement`, `Capability.description`, `Component.purpose`), and Decision requires only `name` and `decision`. AND THE SCHEMA IS ADDITIVE: dynograph-core's own test is named `extra_properties_allowed` — "Extra properties should be allowed (schema is additive)" — so a property the schema never declared is stored rather than refused. It validates the TYPES of declared properties and enforces the required ones; anything else passes through.

WHAT AN EDGE CAN HOLD. More than assumed: 44 of the 60 edge types carry properties, across 46 distinct property names, and several are free text — `note`, `evidence`, `rationale`, `diff_summary`. SIXTEEN CARRY NOTHING, and they are all bookkeeping or temporal: AT_EPOCH, HAS_SNAPSHOT, VALID_FROM, VALID_TO, ABOUT_ENTITY, OCCURS_DURING, PERFORMED_IN, and — worth noting against [BL-212] — PRECEDES. The edge that would say "this document came before that one" can carry no evidence for the claim.

⭐ THE STING, AND IT IS WHY THIS BELONGS ON THIS NODE RATHER THAN AS TRIVIA: ONLY 52 PROPERTIES IN THE ENTIRE SCHEMA ARE `fulltext: true`, and those are the only ones `search_design` indexes. The distribution is name 20 · description 12 · statement 5 · summary 3, then singletons: rationale, decision, purpose, question, evidence, intent, effects, design_intent, criteria, context_setter, answer, title. So `Decision.decision` IS indexed and — measured — `Decision.rationale` is NOT. Every "why" written into a rationale field is stored and unsearchable. The same is true of any extra property invented under the additive rule: stored, not indexed, not returned by `describe_schema`, read by no report. That is this project's recurring declared-and-read-by-nothing shape one rung worse, because it is UNDECLARED and read by nothing.

THE CONSEQUENCE FOR EVERY OPTION ABOVE: UNLIMITED PROSE IN A NODE IS GREP BY ANOTHER NAME. What makes the graph queryable rather than navigable is the `fulltext:` flag, the typed properties and the EDGES — not the narrative. Moving the backlog into nodes therefore helps only to the extent a row becomes STRUCTURE: which capability the defect bears on (an edge), what was measured (a typed property), whether it is still true (a status or a temporal bound), with the prose hanging off that as explanation rather than as the record. A row moved in as one long `description` rebuilds `backlog.md` inside the graph with worse ergonomics and no gain — and that failure would be invisible, because it would look like progress.

AND IT PUTS A NUMBER ON THE DEPENDENCY WITH `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption`: with 52 lexically-indexed fields and no vector half, "query the graph" today means ranked keyword search over names, descriptions and statements. Better than grep — cross-node, ranked, no filename needed — but the same KIND of retrieval. The ceiling on "an agent can work from the graph alone" is set by that open question, so the two ideas should be weighed together rather than separately.

WHAT MUST NOT BE RE-DERIVED WHEN THIS IS PICKED UP: `dec:what-lives-where` (the accepted rule and its falsifiable test), `dec:views-are-projections` plus `tools/render_views.py` (the rendering half already exists), [BL-198] (a serialized default is indistinguishable from a choice — the same "what does the graph actually record" family), and [BL-209] (22 Decisions invisible because `AUTHORED_BY` counts as attachment — a graph-native backlog would land straight into that blind spot and must not).","name":"OPEN — should the backlog stop being a 581 KB markdown file and become graph nodes, and what is missing before it can?","rationale":"Captured under the brainstorm skill at Anthony's request. The load-bearing content is the taxonomy and the single gap it exposes: three of the four kinds of backlog row already have a node type, and the fourth — a defect in a capability that is built, verified and wrong — has none, which is why those rows have no choice but to be prose. Recording the measurement (581 KB, 6 of 8 rows with zero graph representation, four re-derivations in one session) so the next session argues from numbers rather than from the impression that the file is getting long. Extended 2026-08-04 with the data-model constraint Anthony asked for — free text is unbounded and the schema is additive, but only 52 properties are indexed and `rationale` is not one of them, so the answer turns on how much of a row becomes structure rather than prose. Note the irony worth keeping: this rationale is itself unsearchable.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS A MEASURED DEFECT PLUS AN OPEN QUESTION. Found 2026-08-05 by the FIRST REAL TRIAL of cap:corpus-ingest, over six architecture documents from dev_storyflow. Nothing here is settled, and the fix shape is genuinely open.

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT, AND IT IS THE WHOLE FINDING. `dynograph_resolution::token_sort_ratio`, which `ingest::fuzzy_match` uses on node NAMES, against the auto-merge threshold of 90:

  95  dynograph-vector   vs dynograph-core        <- SILENTLY MERGED
  94  dynograph-storage  vs dynograph-core        <- SILENTLY MERGED
  93  dynograph-extract  vs dynograph-context     <- SILENTLY MERGED
  91  dynograph-server   vs dynograph-query       <- SILENTLY MERGED
  89  dynograph-engine   vs dynograph-core        (asked)
  84  Auth Service       vs Authentication Service (NOT merged, NOT asked at Component's 90/80 bands)

THE THRESHOLD IS EXACTLY BACKWARDS FOR THE NAMES REAL SYSTEMS USE. Sibling modules sharing a prefix — the near-universal convention — score 91-95 and are merged without asking. The canonical duplicate the feature exists to catch, `Auth Service` ~ `Authentication Service`, scores 84 and is not. `docs/scope-corpus-ingest.md` asserted "90 on a token-sorted ratio is near-identity"; MEASURED, IT IS NOT.

THE IMPACT, MEASURED ON ONE DOCUMENT: dynograph.md declares NINE crates. After ingest the graph holds FIVE. FOUR CRATES — 44% of the architecture — WERE SILENTLY DESTROYED (dynograph-core, dynograph-vector, dynograph-query, dynograph-extract are gone as named nodes). And the survivors ASSERT SOMETHING FALSE rather than merely being incomplete: `cmp:dynograph-core` now carries the name "dynograph-storage", because the merged node keeps the first id and the longer name. The longer-name rule is BL-186's own #73 fix working exactly as designed — the defect is the merge, not the naming.

⭐ THIS IS NOT A CORPUS DEFECT AND THE TRIAL NEARLY MISDIAGNOSED IT. The first reading blamed the new corpus driver. Isolating dynograph.md and ingesting it ALONE reproduces it exactly: 9 in, 5 out, 4 merges. So this is PRE-EXISTING IN `ingest` and has been true of every single-document ingest since fuzzy dedup landed. The corpus layer is only the first thing to put enough same-family names in front of it for the loss to be visible. Everything this project has ingested one document at a time may carry it.

WHY NOBODY SAW IT: reflow2's own design uses prose names ("The graph handle is an accepted single point of failure"), not prefixed identifier names. `dev_storyflow` is a CODEBASE, so its architecture documents are full of `foo-bar` sibling crates. Self-host was structurally incapable of surfacing this — the same shape as BL-199, and the second time that shape has explained a long-invisible defect.

DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS `dec:ask-not-repair` IN PRACTICE WHILE OBEYING IT IN FORM. The ruling says suspected duplicates are asked, never silently merged; the 90+ band is treated as "not a suspicion" and acts. The measurement says the 90+ band CONTAINS the very cases most in need of asking, so the rule is honoured and its purpose defeated.

OPTIONS, NONE CHOSEN. (a) RAISE THE AUTO-MERGE THRESHOLD. Cheap, and wrong on its own: 95 was a sibling pair, so there is no threshold that separates them by score. (b) NEVER AUTO-MERGE — every match becomes a question, and the corpus batching (BL-186) is what makes that affordable. Honest and expensive; the 11-candidate band in the same trial was 11/11 FALSE POSITIVES, so a user would be answering "no" a great many times. (c) A DISCRIMINATOR BEYOND THE SCORE — refuse to merge when the names differ by a whole token that neither contains ("core" vs "storage" are not variants of each other, while "Auth" vs "Authentication" is a prefix). This targets the actual failure and is the option worth designing. (d) EMBEDDINGS as the tiebreaker in the band, which `dec:idea-embeddings-adoption` already asks about — and this trial is the strongest evidence yet FOR it, because the lexical signal is not merely weak here, it is INVERTED. (e) MAKE IT LOUD RATHER THAN CORRECT — keep merging but report every merge for review. Weakest alone, necessary in any case.

MY OWN DEFECT, FOUND BY THE SAME TRIAL AND FIXED BY NOBODY YET: `CorpusReport.fuzzy_merges` is a `usize`. The single-document `IngestReport` carries `Vec<FuzzyMerge>` and its doc comment says "auditable, never silent" — the corpus aggregate reduces that to a COUNT, so at exactly the scale where silent merges matter most, WHAT was merged is unrecoverable from the report. That is a regression I introduced in BL-186 and it should be fixed before anyone runs a real corpus.

NOT MEASURED, AND IT BOUNDS EVERYTHING ABOVE: what this does to the other 1,118 documents. The trial was SIX documents chosen for topical overlap. The 44% figure is one document's crate list, not a corpus-wide rate.","name":"OPEN — auto-merge at 90 silently destroys SIBLING components and misses the duplicates it exists to catch; the threshold is backwards for real naming conventions","rationale":"Filed the moment the trial produced it, with the scores rather than the impression, because "fuzzy matching is too aggressive" is the kind of claim that decays into folklore and then gets re-argued from scratch. The six numbers are reproducible from `dynograph_resolution::token_sort_ratio` directly.

Recorded as its own node rather than as an amendment to `cap:corpus-ingest` because the capability is not where the defect lives — isolating a single document proved it is `ingest`'s, and attaching it to the corpus capability would have embalmed the misdiagnosis the trial itself corrected.

The self-criticism about `CorpusReport.fuzzy_merges` is on the node deliberately: the trial's most useful property was that it could show WHAT converged, and the shipped report cannot. Recording that where the fix will be read is worth more than recording it where it would be flattering.","status":"proposed"}

{"description":"The surplus half of DETECT. Every existing gap asks what is MISSING; this asks what is SURPLUS — realized or verified, and downstream of nothing.

THE SIGNAL, computable from the graph as it stands: a Capability at `realized`/`verified` with no incoming DEPENDS_ON, no PART_OF_FLOW into any Flow, and no Actor INTERACTS_WITH. The same shape generalises to a Component whose Interfaces nothing CONSUMES, and to an Artifact realizing only capabilities that are themselves unconsumed.

⚠️ THE WORDING IS THE FEATURE, not a caveat on it. The graph knows DESIGN-LEVEL demand and nothing about runtime usage, so the honest finding is \"NOTHING IN THIS DESIGN CONSUMES X\" — never \"X is unused\". A feature real users call daily whose consumer was never modelled produces exactly the same graph shape as a dead one, and a detector that did not say so would confidently recommend deleting working code. Reported as a FACT rather than a gap for the same reason granularity_report and surprising_connections are: which side is wrong is the user's to say.

WHY IT IS NOT unmotivated_capability: that fires on a capability satisfying no REQUIREMENT — a question about intent, gated on requirements existing at all. A capability can satisfy a requirement perfectly and still be consumed by nothing, and that is the expensive case, because the paperwork is complete and the code is dead.

DELIBERATELY NOT COVERED HERE: runtime usage. dec:bl-155 and dec:idea-measure-the-surface hold that question, and answering it needs telemetry rather than the graph.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"A built thing that nothing in the design consumes is surfaced, and says so as a design-completeness finding rather than a verdict on the system","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"The capture half of governance, mirroring cap:kpp-proposal one layer along. An agent notices the shape of a rule — \"we always…\", a convention the build already follows but nothing records, a choice about HOW rather than WHAT — and asks the user what breaking it should cost, in language needing no vocabulary: \"if somebody pushed straight to main, should the build have stopped them, or is that advice?\" The answer is written to `enforced` EXPLICITLY in both directions. That is the load-bearing part: `enforced` defaults to true, so leaving it unset does not mean advisory, it means gate-blocking — and a rule that reaches that status by silence then owes a detector it never agreed to, which is exactly how all four of reflow2's own enforced rules got there. Also states what an enforced answer costs (unverified_enforced_rule, 0.6, until a PASSING check exists) and refuses the shortcut its own proposers warned about: never attach a verification to close the finding, because a graph node green-washes exactly like a document.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"A rule the project follows is captured with its consequence stated, not inherited from a default","provenance":"authored","status":"planned","tier":"operational"}

{"description":"A content-addressed store for what the graph cannot hold inline — session transcripts, mermaid diagrams, HTML mockups, user-supplied drawings and photographs, and the source documents a corpus was extracted from. The graph records a CONTENT HASH; the bytes live in the store; an unresolvable pointer fails loud and names itself rather than rendering a design quietly missing its pictures.

HAND-ROLLED AND SYNCHRONOUS, IN `reflow2-core` (`dec:content-store-implementation`). `put` / `get` / `exists` over `sha2` and `std::fs`. Zero new crates in the core, no async runtime. `object_store` was measured and recorded as the documented UPGRADE PATH rather than adopted: 36 crates new to reflow2, ~24 of them URL/ICU machinery a local store never calls, buying a feature set — paths, prefixes, listing, multipart, conditional writes — that immutable content addressing does not have.

REACHABLE FROM A SESSION as `content_put` / `content_get` / `content_exists` (`req:the-store-is-reachable-from-a-session`). That requirement exists because this capability was first marked `realized` while NOTHING COULD CALL IT — complete in the core, tested, carrying a passing check, and unreachable by every agent and person who would use it. Content arrives as `text` or `base64` (JSON carries no raw bytes), exactly one, and the store's root comes from `--content-path` rather than being derived from `--graph-path`, because the graph lives under a gitignored directory and blobs are COMMITTED so they travel with the design.

FOUR REFUSALS, which is where this earns its keep — each pinned by a test, two mutation-checked. `get` VERIFIES bytes against the hash they are stored under and refuses a mismatch: a content hash nobody checks is only a filename. A malformed hash is refused BEFORE it reaches the filesystem, since a hash is interpolated into a path. Passing both `text` and `base64` is refused rather than resolved by picking one. And a server with no store configured says so instead of inventing a directory — where blobs live is a decision about the consumer's repo.

Writes are temp-then-rename, so a process that dies mid-write leaves nothing or a whole blob, and a stranded temp file is unreachable as content because its name is not a hash. Reading INTO stored content is not this capability's job and never becomes one — the agent navigates, the graph records an opaque locator reflow2 never parses (`dec:agent-navigates-content`). What belongs here versus natively in the repo is `dec:what-lives-where`. REALIZED; `ver:content-store` and `ver:content-surface` passing.","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Store bytes beside the design and point at them by content hash","provenance":"authored","status":"realized","tier":"operational"}

{"decision":"UNDECIDED. Anthony, 2026-07-25: COORD.md was invented so he and his brother could coordinate; the claims layer shipped the same day; and reflow2 is developed by using reflow2 on itself, so the question is whether the markdown board should now be a graph read. WHAT WOULD ACTUALLY CHANGE, because it is less than it sounds: `claim_region` records a Contributor holding a seed node to a depth, `claim_report` computes the region and the overlaps, and both travel in the committed export exactly as COORD.md travels in git — so visibility is unchanged, and the gain is that the region is COMPUTED from the design (it follows the graph as the design moves) rather than being a hand-typed list of file paths that goes stale silently. WHAT WOULD BE LOST, and it is the part worth deciding rather than assuming: COORD.md is readable by a human with no reflow2 and no binary, it shows up as a diff in a pull request, and it holds the merge-conflict doctrine for the shared records — none of which a graph read does. The sane split, if this is taken: claims in the graph for WHO HAS WHAT, COORD.md retained for the conventions and the conflict doctrine, and the in-progress table deleted rather than maintained in two places, since two places for the same fact is the failure the backlog-in-the-graph move exists to end.","name":"OPEN — does reflow2's own claim board move from COORD.md into the graph?","rationale":"Raised as a dogfooding question, which is how most of this project's real findings have arrived — and it is a genuinely good test of the claims layer, because reflow2's own two-person collaboration is the only live multi-writer case that exists. Held proposed because a claim board is a coordination mechanism between two people, and switching it unilaterally would mean one of them silently changing where the other must look; that is Anthony's brother's call as much as his. The prerequisite is honest: nobody has used claim_region for real yet, so the first move is to run it on one real piece of work and see whether claim_report says something a person would have said.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"DECIDED by Anthony 2026-08-02, option 3 of three: the sweep is everything the version-control system tracks, minus NAMED exclusions echoed back with the rule that excluded them. No vocabulary change, no new property, no new node type — so the schema stamp does not move, which on this project is what locks out older binaries. (The node id says `declared` because that was the QUESTION; the answer is `derived`. Kept as a stable handle rather than re-minted, since `cap:coverage` is already GOVERNED_BY it.) ANTHONY'S REASONING, WHICH CORRECTS THE WEAKNESS THIS OPTION WAS RECORDED WITH. The objection on file was that deriving from a repo 'says nothing for a design whose subject is a fleet, a document set, or hardware', against `req:design-anything`. That conflated two different things. THE SUBJECT SYSTEM and THE DESIGN'S ARTIFACTS ARE NOT THE SAME THING, and a sweep only ever covers the second. A satellite, a building, a fleet cannot live in a repo — but its drawings, specs, models, analyses and requirement documents can, and normally do. In his words: 'while a hardware system, for example, can't live within a git repo, its design artifacts can. obviously, for all non-code projects, this is the case.' So the derived scope is not a code-only convenience; it is the general case, and it is MORE clearly right for hardware than for software, because there the artifacts are all there is to sweep. CODE IS THE SPECIAL CASE, NOT THE NORM — and it is special by being MORE than the norm, not less: 'code based projects are the system and can be inspected by the agent as well as the design'. For a codebase the repo holds the subject system AND the design artifacts at once, so a sweep sees both; for everything else it sees the artifacts, which is all a coverage question ever asked about. He also expects that exceptional case to be the majority of reflow2's use, which is why it must not be mistaken for the rule the design is built on. WHAT THIS GENUINELY CANNOT DO, which is a different limitation from the one it was charged with: a design artifact that is NOT under version control — a CAD file on someone's machine, a spec in a wiki, a drawing inside a PLM system — is invisible to a derived sweep. That is not fatal, because the seam already answers it: `coverage_report` takes caller-supplied observations, so an agent that can reach a PLM or a document store sweeps it and hands the paths over exactly as it hands over a repo listing. Derivation is the DEFAULT, not a restriction on what may be observed. WHAT IS STILL OPEN AND WAS NEVER THIS: `cap:coverage` records that the sweep is not persisted, so `detect_gaps` cannot raise coverage from graph state the way `unresolved_drift` is raised from a recorded `DriftEvent`. That deferral survives this decision untouched — it was never the fix for the blind quadrant, and it still needs a node to record a sweep in and a staleness rule (the `cap:freshness` precedent).","name":"Coverage scope is DERIVED from version control — because a sweep covers the design's artifacts, never the subject system","rationale":"Anthony's word, given 2026-08-02 in answer to the three shapes put to him. Recorded with his argument rather than just his choice, because the argument is the part that would otherwise be lost: it is not merely a preference between three costs, it identifies an ERROR in how option 3 was described to him — the artifact/subject conflation — and that error is what would have made a later reader re-open a settled question. The two rejected shapes are kept in the record deliberately (ADR discipline): (1) a scope property on Project/Component, cheap but with no history and nowhere to date a sweep; (2) a first-class node recording a sweep and its scope, which would have closed the persistence deferral in the same move but costs a schema change and pulls in the staleness decision. Both remain available as an OVERRIDE for a subject version control cannot enumerate — this decision fixes the default, not the ceiling.","status":"accepted"}

{"decision":"reflow2's own decomposition is the seven functional systems a design-graph tool IS — vocabulary, store, coherence-loop, human-channel, time-history, intake, agent-surface — with the 38 Rust modules re-parented under them as implementation. The as-built crate grouping (reflow2-core / -mcp / kit) is retired from the as-designed view.","name":"reflow2's systems are functional, not its file tree","rationale":"The self-model had been recovered backwards from the file tree, so its 38 Components were the Rust module list and the domain primitives a design-graph product fundamentally is — node and edge types — appeared nowhere (BL-83). A functional carving comes from the product's purpose (a genesis input), not the code, and cuts across crate boundaries, so adopt on the code can only re-derive the module view. Derived with the user, 2026-07-23. The retired crate view is recovered by adopt-on-a-copy (BL-83b) and the divergence measured by compare_designs (BL-83c).","status":"accepted"}

{"description":"When a requirement is decomposed, reflow2 raises the coverage question rather than answering it: what did the parent hold that no child holds? The answer is recorded, so a later reader can tell a DELIBERATE NARROWING from an ACCIDENTAL DROP — today both look identical, and both report DELIVERED once the children close.

Reports and asks, never judges (`dec:report-dont-judge`). It does not refuse a decomposition, and it does not put an LLM in charge of sufficiency — the honest form named on the requirement is a question put to the user with their answer written back, the same shape every other gap uses.

APPLIES TO DECOMPOSITION ONLY, not to derivation: a DERIVED requirement adds new technical necessity and is not expected to cover anything, and `cap:requirement-lineage` already holds that distinction (original / decomposed / derived).

Distinct from `cap:derived-completion`, which computes delivery UPWARD from the golden thread and is verified. {"description":"Given a filesystem path to a design store, report which design is there — its stable graph id, its label, whether that identity was minted or adopted, and the schema stamp the store carries — WITHOUT opening it, locking it, or writing anything. The paired half of discovery: the agent walks the tree and finds `.reflow2` directories (file navigation, which reflow2 does not do), and this answers what each one IS, so a person can be shown a menu before anything is created.

WHAT IT PREVENTS, measured: a session at the root of `hxm_program` was told "this directory has no design yet" and minted a THIRD graph while two populated ones sat one and two directories down. The agent could have listed the paths; nothing could say what they were.

BUILT 2026-08-05 as `describe_designs`, served on BOTH the full surface and the LATENT (no-design) surface — the latter deliberately, because a session with no design is the exact moment someone is about to create one, and a discovery tool only reachable after a design exists would arrive too late. Takes a LIST of paths, because the caller is sweeping a tree and one round trip per candidate is the wrong shape for a menu.

⭐ TWO DEVIATIONS FROM `dec:describe-a-design-without-binding-to-it`, BOTH FORCED BY THE CODE AND BOTH IMPROVEMENTS ON WHAT WAS ASKED FOR.

(1) NO NODE COUNTS. The decision said the report would carry "node counts by type". It cannot, and the reason is the whole design: `DesignGraph::open_rocksdb_with_provenance` WRITES `<path>.meta.json` via `check_and_stamp` and MINTS `<path>.id.json` via `identity::resolve` when the store has none. So counting would mean opening, and opening an unnamed store would NAME IT — inspecting a design would create the thing it was asked to look for. Identity and stamp answer *which design is this and how old is its schema*, which is what choosing between designs actually needs; size is not worth minting an identity to get.

(2) NO `busy` STATE, AND IT IS NOT MISSING. The decision flagged "must distinguish busy from absent" because a store held by a running server is exclusively locked. That turned out to be MOOT: everything reported comes from the two sidecar files beside the store, so nothing is ever locked and a design another session is writing right now describes perfectly. The requirement was met by removing the condition rather than by handling it.

THE STATES IT DOES REPORT, and the distinction that carries the value: `design` (named from its sidecar), `unnamed` (something is there whose identity cannot be read without opening — reported as such rather than named by the act of asking), `opted_in` (directory exists, nothing written yet), `absent` (nothing here). SOMETHING-UNNAMED MUST NEVER READ AS NOTHING-HERE, because "no design here" is the sentence that starts an unwanted one. Every row also carries a plain-language `reading`, because a bare enum makes the caller invent the meaning.

SHIPPED WITH THE INSTRUCTION THAT MAKES ANYONE CALL IT. `reflow2_start_design`'s description previously ended "it is safe to call when unsure" with no mention of looking around — the sentence behind the accident. It now requires a nearby sweep first and says why, and its payload tells a caller who skipped the check to say so immediately, while the recovery is still a deletion rather than a merge. A tool no skill tells anyone to use is this project's own recurring defect ([BL-152], [BL-178], [BL-197], [BL-204]); shipping the tool without the instruction would have been the fifth.

WHAT IT DOES NOT SETTLE: how a session is then POINTED at the chosen design (`dec:how-a-session-is-pointed-at-a-design`, open — with `dec:pointing-a-session-is-project-scope-only` as the working field answer).","is_entry_point":false,"is_exit_point":false,"name":"Say what design lives at a path, without binding to it","provenance":"authored","status":"verified","tier":"operational"}

OPTION A — leave it. Cheapest, and defensible: a rule worth recording is usually a rule you mean. Cost: reflow2's own four enforced rules all reached that status by silence, and none of them was a deliberate choice. OPTION B — flip the default to false.
