{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Whether the kit is actually used is measured, not inferred from whether the design looks tidy","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"Nothing in reflow2 records whether its skills were used, so the only reason this whole family of findings exists is that a user asked an agent directly and the agent answered honestly. That is not a mechanism.

WHAT MAKES IT ACUTE: a design can look healthy while the kit is barely being used. This session ended with 0 gaps, 0 defects, a clean loop and a green gate — and two skills loaded out of eight. `detect_gaps` measures whether the DESIGN is coherent; nothing measures whether the PRACTICE is. The report-friction skill already concedes the wider version of this in its own words — ordinary use produces better evidence and currently loses all of it — and `req:friction-has-a-baseline` was dropped, so there is no standing measurement at all.

THE HARD CONSTRAINT, which is why this is a requirement and not a fix: `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` says loop debt is computed from graph state and NEVER from run history, straight out of the BL-74 fleet trial. Any naive answer here — log which skills were called — is exactly the run-history reasoning that decision rejects, and a study that comes back recommending it has not read the decision.

THE DISTINCTION THAT MAY RESOLVE IT, offered as the open question rather than the answer: that decision governs what the LOOP may reason from when it computes debt. It does not obviously govern what the KIT may report about ITSELF as a product — the difference between "this design owes you three gaps" (must be state-derived, must be true of the graph as it stands) and "reflow2 was installed here and its skills were loaded twice in nine hours" (a fact about the tool's adoption, not about the user's design). Whether that distinction is real, or a rationalisation for the thing the decision forbids, is the question — and it must be settled before anything is built, not discovered afterwards.

BOUNDARIES THAT HOLD EITHER WAY: whatever is measured must respect report-friction's redaction discipline, which has no counterpart in the prior art — tool names and argument SHAPES, node TYPES not ids, counts not contents — because reflow2 installs into other people's projects, and the thing being measured is the user, not the design.","status":"deferred"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"Skill use is triggered by the situation, not remembered — the rungs cover loop debt, and skills fire on things the graph cannot see","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"An agent's use of reflow2's SKILLS must not decay over a session while its use of the TOOLS holds. Measured on reflow2's own repo, 2026-07-31, in a long session: `loop_status` was called unprompted throughout and every write went through `record_change`, two-sided checksum accepts and one-export-per-commit — but exactly two skills were loaded all session, and both only because the user typed a slash command. `impact-check`, `link-artifacts`, `capture-intent`, `revise-design`, `check-health` and `report-friction` were never loaded. THE THREE BL-74 RUNGS ARE ALL `verified` AND THIS STILL HAPPENED, which is the finding: they are working as designed and do not reach this.

THE STRUCTURAL REASON. The rungs compute LOOP DEBT — a property of graph state, which is what `dec:loop-status-state-not-history` correctly insists on. Skills fire on SITUATIONS: about to change code, just wrote a file, the user just shared an idea. The graph cannot see any of those, so the trigger mechanism covers one half of the problem and structurally cannot reach the other. That is why `impact-check` was dropped hardest — nothing in the system knows an edit is coming, and by the time the graph could tell, the edit has happened and the blast radius is a post-mortem rather than a check.

WHAT COST SOMETHING, honestly: `impact-check` was never run before changing `snapshot_node`, `delete_edge` and `delete_node`; the blast radius was reasoned about by hand instead of computed. `link-artifacts` was never loaded and a stale `art:nodes` checksum was nearly shipped — caught only by grepping after the export, which then required restoring the export and redoing it. `check-health` cost nothing, because `detect_defects` was run bare and did catch the island.

CANDIDATE MECHANISMS, in the order the evidence supports, NOT a decided design. (1) Extend the PostToolUse hook from COUNTING writes to matching SHAPES — a file edit with no ChangeEvent in the window means impact-check, an artifact checksum drift means link-artifacts. `req:nudge-covers-bypass` already arms the nudge on file-edit events and already names impact-check and link-artifacts, and is `verified`; what is missing is the shape-matching, not the trigger. (2) A refusal, where refusing is honest — reflow2's strongest mechanism, proven three times in this session alone — but only where skipping is genuinely wrong, because a guard that punishes correct work is the failure this project keeps naming.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THIS SESSION: BL-74 called this adoption-critical and found it in the author's own fleet, self-reported by the driving agent. This is the same failure observed from inside, on a session with MORE context about reflow2 than a consumer's agent will have — so it is likely a best case rather than a typical one.","status":"accepted"}

{"concern":"core","designation":"internal","kind":"functional","lineage":"original","name":"A second revision of a node in one epoch must not overwrite the first snapshot","priority":"medium","provenance":"authored","statement":"req:intent-preserved says the past is never overwritten. Snapshot identity currently breaks that rule whenever a node is revised TWICE within a single epoch, and the loss is silent.\\n\\nOBSERVED 2026-07-28, by doing it rather than by reading the code. req:build-loop-is-bounded was amended once (chg:iteration-budget-was-elicited, correcting the iteration budget to an elicited value) and later the same day amended again (chg:build-loop-shape-reassessed, demoting the hard stop). Both used record_change against the same epoch:reflow-workflow-review. The snapshot id is deterministic per (epoch, node) — snap:epoch:reflow-workflow-review:req:build-loop-is-bounded — so the SECOND record_change wrote over the first. compare_designs reported it under supporting.changed with base = the original statement and other = the first-amended statement: the snapshot now holds the INTERMEDIATE state, and the state the node held before any amendment survives only in git, in an export committed earlier.\\n\\nWHY THIS IS WORSE THAN AN ORDINARY BUG. Nothing failed and nothing warned. record_change returned a prior_snapshot both times and looked identical from the caller's side. The design's own history simply lost a version while reporting success, which is precisely the silent-overwrite failure the revise-design discipline exists to prevent — and the discipline was followed exactly. A user doing careful work by the documented procedure loses history and is never told.\\n\\nIT ALSO BREAKS THE STATED TEST OF A GOOD REVISION. The revise-design skill ends with it: \\\"afterwards, someone reading the graph can answer what did this say before, when did it change, and why — without git archaeology.\\\" After two amendments in one epoch that is false: answering it for the first amendment requires git archaeology, which is the exact fallback the skill promises to remove.\\n\\nTHE SHAPE OF THE FIX IS A CHOICE, and none of the options is obviously right, which is why this is recorded rather than patched. (a) Make snapshot identity per REVISION rather than per (epoch, node) — e.g. include the ChangeEvent id, which is already unique per revision — so every record_change mints a distinct snapshot and HAS_SNAPSHOT becomes one-to-many. Truest to req:intent-preserved; grows the graph faster and makes \\\"the snapshot for this epoch\\\" ambiguous where readers currently assume one. (b) REFUSE a second record_change against the same node in the same epoch, directing the caller to open a new epoch. Cheap and loud, and it forces epoch hygiene, but epochs are meant to bound a round of WORK, not a single edit, so this pushes an unrelated concern onto the caller. (c) Keep one snapshot per epoch deliberately, meaning it holds the state at the START of the epoch, and make the second call a no-op rather than an overwrite. Preserves the original, loses the intermediate, and needs the semantics stated somewhere they are currently only implied.\\n\\nWhichever is chosen, the silence is not defensible: if a revision cannot be snapshotted without discarding an earlier one, the call must say so. Found 2026-07-28 while amending requirements from the reflow workflow review; the amendments themselves are the evidence.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"UNDECIDED, and RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony, 2026-07-25, explicitly not convinced by the collaboration design and thinking out loud: \"could you have small/mini reflow2 graphs inside itself... coming from a system of systems engineering approach, reflow2 may lay out the graph and how all the systems need to interact and where there are gaps, but what if we now had a mini-reflow2 graph for each system? And a mini-mini-reflow2 of the components in the system... the idea is that reflow2 has the tools to analyze the graph at each level and ensure there are no gaps and that it works with the higher level systems or system-of-systems.\" WHAT IS ALREADY TRUE, because it changes what the idea is asking for. Levels exist and are already checked: Component.level is an enum of component / subsystem / system / system_of_systems / enterprise, CONTAINS between Components is the axis-Y spine, and hierarchy_issues already reports level_mismatch, missing_intermediate_level and orphan_level — the carburetor-to-body problem, imported from chain_reflow's matryoshka insight (docs/three-axes.md). And the multi-graph primitive exists unused: every node and edge carries graph_id, pinned to the constant \"reflow2\". So the question is not whether reflow2 can express nesting. It can. The question is whether a level should be a SUBTREE of one graph or a GRAPH OF ITS OWN. THREE OPTIONS. (a) ONE GRAPH, ZOOM BY LEVEL — today's shape. What is missing is not nesting but SCOPING: no read takes a subtree as its subject, so detect_gaps and graph_report always answer for the whole design. Adding a scope argument is a filter, not an architecture, and it delivers most of what was asked — the tools analysing each level. (b) A GRAPH PER SYSTEM, COMPOSED — Anthony's idea. It buys four things one graph cannot: an independent write lock per system, which is a different and stronger answer to the collaboration problem than region claims, because separate graphs are PHYSICALLY separate where a claim is only advisory; an independent lifecycle, so a subsystem can be released, adopted or handed to a vendor on its own; selective publishing, which is exactly req:design-reachable-without-the-repo; and per-level scale, since detectors run over hundreds of nodes instead of tens of thousands. (c) A GRAPH PER OWNERSHIP BOUNDARY, LEVELS INSIDE EACH — the hybrid, and the shape federated systems engineering actually uses: you split where AUTHORITY splits, not where the hierarchy happens to have a layer. THE FOUR HARD PARTS of (b), each one real: the golden thread cannot cross a store boundary, because the schema validates both endpoints of every edge — so a parent's Component pointing at a child's design needs a typed COORDINATE (graph id + node id + the export's content hash at the moment the reference was made), which is precisely the choice dec:fork-point-address already made for fork points over a native ref layer. Gap detection goes blind at the seam: a parent requirement whose satisfying capability lives in a child graph would fire unsatisfied forever unless the child's evidence rolls up — and that roll-up is cap:derived-completion's computation applied one level higher, which is encouraging rather than novel. Freshness becomes load-bearing: a parent's view of a child is a claim about a VERSION of that child, so it is a dated examined claim and never a live truth (the cap:freshness and confirmation-ledger shape). And the seam becomes the new collision point: two people changing the interface across the boundary still collide, now in the one place with no merge machinery. THE TENSION WORTH KNOWING ABOUT: docs/org-scale-vision.md records the opposite destination — \"one graph the whole company plans in\", with the CEO's objectives at the top and everything tracing upward. Federation and one-big-graph cannot both be the end state, and nothing in the design has ever chosen between them. THE DISCRIMINATOR, offered as a finding and not a decision: depth alone does not justify a separate graph. Nesting three levels of graphs costs a coordinate, a roll-up and a freshness check at every seam, and buys nothing that a scope filter would not have delivered — unless something at that level is separately OWNED, separately RELEASED, or separately SHARED. Where those hold, a graph of its own is right. Where they do not, it is ceremony.","name":"OPEN — one graph with levels, or a graph per system composed into a bigger one?","rationale":"Recorded 2026-07-25 because Anthony said plainly he was not convinced by the collaboration design, and an unconvinced author is a finding rather than a disagreement to be argued down. PROMOTED THE SAME DAY on his word (\"let's promote both\"): the brainstorm produced two accepted requirements and stays open on the mechanism, which is the split that keeps both halves honest. req:analyse-at-any-level is the part he needed day to day and is ALREADY DELIVERED by cap:scoped-analysis (option (a), built first because it forecloses nothing). req:design-composes is the federation intent — a system's design as a unit that composes through interfaces — GOVERNED_BY this decision, so nothing gets built toward it until the mechanism is chosen. THIS DECISION THEREFORE STAYS PROPOSED, and that is not hedging: promoting an idea to intent is not the same act as choosing between three architectures, and collapsing this one would assert a shape Anthony has never chosen. Its options and the four hard parts of federation are unchanged above. The discriminator recorded then still stands as the thing to test when it is decided: depth alone does not earn a separate graph — ownership, separate release, or separate sharing does. NOTE FOR WHOEVER COLLAPSES IT: docs/org-scale-vision.md still records the opposite destination (one graph the whole company plans in), and req:design-composes now sits in the graph as accepted intent pointing the other way. That tension is real, on the record, and undecided; it is the strongest reason this decision should be made deliberately rather than discovered.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"🛑 **ANTHONY, 2026-08-14, CHALLENGING THE PREMISE: "we already have an obsolete with discontinued or something like that — are we playing semantics with cancelled?" CHECKED AGAINST THE CODE AND THE GRAPH RATHER THAN ARGUED. HE IS RIGHT FOR THE ABANDONED CASE, AND THE ANSWER WAS ALREADY DECIDED THREE DAYS EARLIER.**

`dec:idea-discontinued-is-a-first-class-state` was **DECIDED on his word 2026-08-11**: a Decision `OBSOLETES` what it withdrew, the decision itself being the source. No enum value, no edge type, no schema stamp move, no upgrade doc.

**IT IS NOT THEORETICAL — IT IS LIVE IN THIS GRAPH.** `dec:the-content-store-is-discontinued` (accepted) obsoletes:
```
cap:content-store       stored status: realized   -> discontinued: true
cap:content-manifest    stored status: realized   -> discontinued: true
cap:session-artifacts   stored status: verified   -> discontinued: true
```
And `is_discontinued` has FOUR readers, which is four more than either retirement edge ever had: `unmotivated_capability`, `unrealized_capability` and `unverified_capability` fall silent, and delivery arithmetic stops counting a discontinued capability as a satisfier (`DeliveryCoverage.satisfied_only_by_discontinued`).

⇒ **ADDING `cancelled` TO `Capability.status` WOULD BE A SECOND WAY TO SAY WHAT THE GRAPH ALREADY COMPUTES — and worse than redundant, because a STORED status can disagree with the COMPUTED one.** The stored status deliberately keeps saying what was BUILT; that is why `get_node` carries `discontinued` separately and warns to read it.

═══ ⚠️ WHAT IS GENUINELY NOT COVERED, AND IT IS MUCH NARROWER THAN ALEX'S FRAMING ═══

The 2026-08-11 decision names its own residual: it *"covers the ABANDONED case; it says nothing about a WISH NOBODY EVER AGREED TO, which has no decision behind it to be the source of an OBSOLETES edge."* **A capability that was only ever an idea has no decision to hang the edge from.** That half belongs to `dec:exploratory-staging`, not to a status enum.

═══ ⭐ SO WHAT ACTUALLY BIT ALEX IS DISCOVERABILITY, NOT A MISSING STATE ═══

His agents typed "DROPPED" into description prose while the mechanism existed and worked. The plausible reason: an agent reads `Capability.status`, sees four values, and **nothing at that point hints that abandonment lives on an edge instead.** `retire-from-design` is the skill that covers it, and measured 2026-08-14 it is among the least-reached-for of the twenty (`fact:skill-use-measured-two-channels-2026-08-14`).

⇒ **THE OPEN QUESTION IS THEREFORE RESHAPED, NOT ANSWERED, AND STAYS ANTHONY'S:** not "does Capability need a cancelled state" (no — measured above) but **"what makes an agent holding an abandoned capability find OBSOLETES instead of typing DROPPED into prose?"** Candidates, none chosen: a hint on `set_capability_status`, a detector that notices abandonment words in description text, or the command coverage now accepted under `dec:idea-does-every-served-skill-get-a-command` putting `retire-from-design` one keystroke away.

════════ THE ORIGINAL REPORT, KEPT ════════

Alex's fleet, 2026-08-09: 'Requirements: deferred / dropped. Capabilities: no equivalent — agents stuff DROPPED into description text.' CONFIRMED AGAINST THE SCHEMA: Requirement.status is [proposed, accepted, deferred, dropped, met]; Capability.status is [planned, in_progress, realized, verified]. WHY IT IS THE WEEK'S OWN DEFECT CLASS AGAIN: a state that cannot be expressed does not disappear — it gets smuggled into prose, exactly as time-bound claims were smuggled into Requirement.statement and an unchosen `enforced` into a default.","name":"OPEN — a Requirement can be deferred or dropped and a Capability cannot, so agents write "DROPPED" into prose the graph cannot compute on","rationale":"Raised by a second consumer project rather than found here, which is the useful part: reflow2's own graph never hit it because this project retires capabilities rather than cancelling them. Kept as a decision point rather than built because it is a schema enum change that would move the stamp and therefore owe an upgrade doc — the first this week that would — and because it touches an already-open question about retirement being modelled in two places. Anthony's to settle.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"UNDECIDED as a vocabulary question, but MUCH SMALLER than it looked, and the skill that tests it is BUILT (2026-07-25, the brainstorm skill). REFRAMED by Anthony the same day, and the reframe was the useful part: what he and his brother were asking for is not a staging GATE, it is a KIND. \"I think I now realize what my brother's idea was trying to say — it is like a brainstorming session where you can work through ideas without committing to anything yet. These would be more like 'ideas' not yet fleshed out and could be held in the graph as just that, 'brainstorming ideas'.\" That dissolves the contradiction this decision was opened over: the git study rejected the index because a gate between every edit and the graph is where intent goes to be forgotten, whereas a brainstorm is the opposite move — the idea DOES enter the graph, immediately, labelled as what it is. Nothing waits outside, so nothing is lost, and the design still never claims a half-formed thought as intent. THE FINDING THAT SHRANK THE QUESTION, from reading the detector while building the skill: the existing vocabulary ALREADY tells a musing from a choice, and a computation already reads the difference. `detect_gaps` raises `undecided_decision_point` only on a proposed Decision holding TWO OR MORE REGISTERED ALTERNATIVES — a fork with a real design export behind each branch (detect.rs: `alts.len() < 2 { continue }`). A proposed Decision whose options live in its prose therefore raises NO gap at all. So brainstormed ideas are silent by construction, and the nudge to choose arrives exactly when the ideas stop being ideas: register_alternative turns an option into a fork, and being asked to decide a fork is correct. Nobody has to remember which is which, and no label was needed to get it. WHAT A `brainstorm` KIND WOULD STILL BUY, and it is now a short list rather than the four-item one recorded yesterday: (a) delivery and certainty counts already exclude Decisions, so nothing is owed there; (b) gap silence is already delivered, per the finding above; (c) what remains is RETIREMENT — an idea nobody has touched in months could be surfaced as a candidate for tidying rather than sitting in the decision list forever, which is a real computation and the only one left standing; and (d) READABILITY — a person scanning 70-odd Decisions cannot tell at a glance which were choices and which were musings, which the skill currently answers with a sentence of prose inside the node rather than with a queryable property. PRIOR FRAMING, KEPT because it was true when written: the ask read as an opt-in \"think first, commit later\" mode; a session making no write calls IS rubber-ducking and the read tools are the ducking aids; and the narrow question was what happens at the END — which the skill now answers as a PROMOTION step, not a commit step.","name":"OPEN — do half-formed ideas get a place in the graph, distinct from things the design asserts?","rationale":"Raised by Anthony and his brother 2026-07-24, reframed by Anthony 2026-07-25, and the skill built the same day on his word (\"go ahead with the brainstorm skill\"). Built as a SKILL and not a schema change deliberately: it tests the practice at the cost of prose, and if the practice sticks the vocabulary question can be answered with evidence instead of taste — whereas a new node type or an enum value would have bought an upgrade doc and a foundation-migration checklist for a noun nobody had used yet. The evidence for the feature is this session itself: Anthony produced four isolation ideas he explicitly did not want to commit to, and the only home for them was a proposed Decision. That worked (dec:concurrent-work-isolation), which is why this is not urgent; it is also a slightly wrong fit, since a Decision node is meant for a choice someone is actually facing, and knowing exactly which part of the fit is wrong is what the finding above now pins down. Left PROPOSED because two of the four original arguments for a kind have dissolved and the remaining two (retirement candidates, at-a-glance readability) are real but small — and whether they are worth a schema change is Anthony's call, not a judgement to be made by the agent that just wrote the skill.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. Anthony asked to think through the mechanics of using git to capture epoch and increment snapshots; these are the options and their costs, not a settlement.

THE TENSION THAT ORGANISES EVERYTHING: git can only store the past. A commit is something that happened. A planned epoch is a claim about a future that has not happened, so there is nothing for git to hold unless someone AUTHORS a speculative design and commits it.

(a) EPOCH BRANCHES — Anthony's original idea, 2026-07-28: "epoch branches: project_x:epoch_1 captures what we expect the graph to look like at epoch_1." A branch is a real place to work: you can draft a future design there, run the detectors on it, and diff it against main with machinery that already exists.
    Costs, recorded beside it rather than against it: a branch is a MOVING POINTER and a plan is a DATED CLAIM — when the plan changes the branch moves, and nothing records that it moved, which is exactly what `req:plans-move-honestly` needs. A speculative full export also restates the entire design to express a delta about a handful of requirements, so it is expensive to author and stale on the next merge to main. And N repos times M epochs is N times M branches, each drifting independently.

(b) PLANS LIVE ONLY IN THE GRAPH. A planned epoch is a node plus scheduled edges — no git object at all, because there is no past to point at. "What does the design look like at epoch 3" becomes a COMPUTED view (today's design plus what is scheduled to be satisfied by then) rather than a stored artifact.
    Cost: you cannot open a future design in an editor or run a detector over it as a whole; you get a projection, not a document.

(c) BOTH, SCOPED DIFFERENTLY — the shape the costs seem to point at. Branches are a fine WORKSPACE for exploring a future architecture and a poor RECORD of a plan. The record lives in the graph as a dated, versioned claim; a branch is somewhere to prototype one when a person wants to see it whole.

WORTH KNOWING BEFORE DECIDING: the forward half of the CAPABILITY view already exists in the vocabulary. `Release.status` is `planned | built | deployed | retired`, so a planned increment is expressible today. The forward half of the TIME view does not: `DesignEpoch.epoch_type` is `baseline | revision | milestone | incident_response | release_cut` with no value meaning "this has not happened yet". That asymmetry is real and is the smallest concrete gap found while thinking this through.","name":"OPEN — does a planned epoch live in git, or only in the graph?","rationale":"Anthony's idea and Anthony's question; recorded so the reasoning survives whichever way it goes. The framing "two paired views of the same architecture" and the epoch-branch mechanism are both his (2026-07-28), as is the request to work out the git mechanics (2026-07-30).

Not argued down: option (a) is recorded with its virtue stated first, because a branch genuinely is the only place you can look at a future design as a whole, and that is not nothing.","status":"proposed"}

{"decision":"RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL.

ANTHONY'S CLARIFICATION, 2026-07-30, and it corrects the framing this node was first written with: what he wants committed is NOT the realized product or a future codebase. It is a SLICE OF THE REFLOW2 GRAPH ITSELF — "this is the planned capabilities of epoch_1, epoch_2 … epoch_n" — so that he can open the repo and see "that is when I get capability X", or "capability Y is not expected until increment_13". His words: "it isn't the realized product/artifact of the project, but snapshot of the project at epoch or increment that I'm looking to capture in git." He is explicitly open to something other than git.

THE FIRST FRAMING HERE WAS WRONG AND IS CORRECTED. This node originally organised everything around "git can only store the past, and a plan is not a past". That is too glib. A plan document is a PRESENT artifact describing a future, and committing one is ordinary — git stores plans perfectly well. The real objection was never to committing plans; it was only ever to using BRANCHES as the record, and that narrower objection stands.

(a) BRANCH PER EPOCH — `epoch_1`, `epoch_2`, each holding a projected design. Matches the mental model directly: check out `epoch_n`, look.
    Costs: checking out a branch normally makes the whole REPO reflect that state, and here there is no future code to reflect, so the branch buys nothing the file would not. A full export is 1.6 MB today, so N epochs is N × 1.6 MB of near-identical JSON, rewritten on every replan. Branches also invite merge semantics that do not apply — nobody merges epoch_2 into main. And the plan's MOVEMENT stays invisible: a branch pointer moves silently, which is exactly what `req:plans-move-honestly` needs to see.

(b) A FILE PER EPOCH ON MAIN — `docs/design/epochs/epoch_3.{md,json}`. Browsing is easier than a checkout, there is one history rather than N, and every replan is an ordinary commit to that file.
    THE PROPERTY THIS BUYS FOR FREE: `git log -p docs/design/epochs/epoch_3.md` IS the plan's revision history. A large part of `req:plans-move-honestly` — "when a planned epoch's content moves, the plan's own change is a dated event on the record" — would be satisfied by git doing what git is good at, rather than by new machinery in reflow2.

(c) RENDER IT, DO NOT AUTHOR IT — and this is what (b) should probably be generated BY. An epoch slice is a VIEWPOINT. `tools/render_views.py` already renders viewpoints as pure projections of the graph, already confesses anything a view needs that the graph cannot supply, and ALREADY RENDERS THE EPOCH CHAIN BACKWARD ("Axis Z as a viewpoint: the epoch chain, and what happened at each"). The forward direction is the same renderer reading scheduled edges instead of recorded ones. Under this option the graph holds the schedule as single source of truth, the renderer emits one small file per epoch, and git holds their history.
    Cost: a generated file can go stale against the graph — which is a drift check reflow2 already knows how to do, and the same one `dataflow.html` staleness already gets in another repo.

WHAT A SLICE ACTUALLY CONTAINS, since "slice" is the word he used and it is much smaller than an export: the epoch and its date, capabilities expected by then, requirements expected satisfied, KPPs required by then, the version combination pinned once it arrives, and the delta against the previous epoch. Kilobytes, not megabytes.

THE OPEN QUESTION IS NARROWER THAN IT WAS: not "git or not git", but WHICH JOB GIT DOES. Git looks right for the HISTORY of the plan document and for pinning arrived epochs; the graph looks right for the schedule itself. The failure mode to avoid is making git the source of truth for the schedule, because then two places disagree about when capability X arrives and neither is wrong.","name":"OPEN — how per-epoch slices of the design become browsable: branches, files, or a rendered viewpoint","rationale":"Anthony's idea, his clarification, and his invitation to suggest something better; recorded so the reasoning survives whichever way it goes.

Kept rather than tidied away: the original framing of this node ("git can only store the past") was mine and was misleading, and the correction is recorded rather than silently overwritten because the prior text is what a reader would otherwise have found and believed. The snapshot at `epoch:wire-planning-cluster` holds the earlier wording.

Not argued down: option (a) is his own original mechanism and is recorded with the mental model it serves stated first. Its costs are listed beside it, not in place of it.","status":"proposed"}

properties.statement:
MEASURED ON THE v0.30.0 CUT, 2026-08-13, and it produced a WRONG COMMITTED RECORD that every other check passed.

THREE BINARY VERSIONS WERE IN PLAY ON ONE MACHINE:

    live MCP server    0.29.0 image   (the session's own tools)
    target/release/    0.28.0, Aug 11 (**what `tools/reflow2_cli.py`'s DEFAULT_BIN resolves to**)
    target/debug/      0.30.0         (built minutes earlier, the only correct one)

The release procedure's replay exists precisely to avoid the live server's old stamp: import into a temp store, export from it with the NEW binary. I ran that replay and passed `C.DEFAULT_BIN`. **The committed export came back stamped `0.28.0` — with PERFECTLY CORRECT LINEAGE**, `prev_content_hash` equal to main's `content_hash`, 2144 nodes, 8447 edges, `graph_id: reflow2`. Every property anyone checks was right except the one that says which reflow2 wrote it. Caught only by reading `stamp.reflow2_version` out of the written file before committing.

⭐⭐ AND THE EXISTING STALENESS CAPABILITY CANNOT SEE THIS, WHICH IS THE FINDING. `cap:the-server-knows-its-own-currency` reports whether **the server's own executable has been REPLACED SINCE IT STARTED** — `ver:the-server-says-when-it-is-stale` demonstrates it by relinking a binary under a running daemon and watching the same server flip to `stale: true`. A server freshly spawned from a THREE-VERSION-OLD build has had nothing replaced under it, so it reads a definite **`stale: false`** and is telling the truth.

⇒ **"MY EXECUTABLE CHANGED UNDER ME" AND "I AM AN OLD BUILD" ARE DIFFERENT FACTS, AND ONLY THE FIRST IS DETECTED.** The second is the one that mis-stamps a release record, and it is undetectable from inside the server: the binary is internally consistent and confident. It is visible only by comparing the stamp against the version the SOURCE claims.

📌 THE NARROW FIX IS FREE AND IS NOW IN [[reflow2-release-cut-procedure]]: name the freshly built binary explicitly in the replay, never `DEFAULT_BIN`, and READ `stamp.reflow2_version` OUT OF THE WRITTEN FILE BEFORE COMMITTING — every cut, every time.

📌 THE WIDER ONE IS NOT TAKEN AND IS NOT OBVIOUS: whether `reflow2_cli.py` should refuse, or at least say, when the binary it is about to drive reports a version older than the workspace's `Cargo.toml`. That is a comparison the CLI can make and currently does not, and it is the same shape as every other finding in this increment — the information existed and did not reach the person.

⚠️ STILL TRUE AT SESSION END: `target/release/reflow2-mcp` on this machine remains **0.28.0**. CI builds its own release artifacts, so the PUBLISHED v0.30.0 binaries are unaffected; anything local defaulting to that path is driving a three-version-old server.

MEASURED 2026-08-12, and self-reported because it produced a false green in this session.

WHAT HAPPENED: `cargo test --workspace 2>&1 | grep -E "^test result:|FAILED" | tail -20` was run as the pre-PR gate. It was reported to the owner as passing. ⚠️ THE EXIT CODE OF A SHELL PIPELINE IS THE EXIT CODE OF ITS LAST COMMAND — `tail` — which is 0 whether cargo passed, failed, or never compiled. The `tail -20` also truncated the evidence to the last 20 result lines, so the absence of a FAILED line in what came back proved nothing about the other 83 suites.

Caught only by noticing the totals looked low: 20 suites / 250 tests against a project that runs 103 suites / 1,138 tests. The re-run with cargo's status captured directly (`cargo test --workspace > log 2>&1; echo $?`) reported exit 0, 103 suites, 1,138 tests, 0 failures — so the answer was right and the METHOD that produced it could not have known.

⇒ THE GENERAL FORM, which is why this is worth a node: PIPING A GATE THROUGH A FILTER CONVERTS ITS VERDICT INTO ITS OUTPUT. Everything the filter drops is unfalsifiable, and the status that survives belongs to the filter. This is the same class as every finding this project already holds about self-report — a green that describes the reporter rather than the thing.

It is also unusually well-camouflaged HERE, because filtering long cargo output is the obviously sensible thing to do, and the filtered output looks like exactly what a passing run looks like.

THE RULE THAT FALLS OUT: redirect a gate to a file and read `$?` from the gate itself; filter the FILE afterwards. `set -o pipefail` also works and is easier to forget. Never take the presence-or-absence of a pattern in filtered output as the verdict.

NOT BUILT INTO ANYTHING. Recorded as a fact rather than a rule because nothing detects it — an agent's shell pipeline is not something reflow2 can see, which is precisely why it needs to be written down where the next session will read it.

AN OPEN PR'S EXPORT GOES STALE WHILE ITS BADGE STAYS GREEN, AND MERGING IT WOULD SUBTRACT DESIGN. Measured on reflow2's own repo, 2026-08-16, on THREE PRs at once — not a hypothetical, and not caused by anything anyone did wrong.

MEASURED, per PR, against `origin/main`:

    #190  export 63 nodes BEHIND main   intended to add 9   — all 9 ALREADY IN MAIN
    #191  export 59 nodes BEHIND main   intended to add 13  — all 13 ALREADY IN MAIN
    #194  export 56 nodes BEHIND main   intended to add 16  — all 16 ALREADY IN MAIN

All three were green on both CI jobs. #194 read `MERGEABLE`.

⭐ THE MECHANISM IS THE SHARED STORE, AND IT CUTS BOTH WAYS. The design graph does not branch with git (`dec:multi-writer-architecture`), so a later session's export from the same store CARRIED EVERY EARLIER BRANCH'S GRAPH WRITES INTO MAIN. Each PR's design content therefore arrived in main WITHOUT that PR being merged. What was left on the branch was a document that could only subtract — `req:stale-seat-knows`'s prediction arriving in practice: a stale export is a COMPLETE document, so it merges cleanly and the missing work simply vanishes.

⚠️ THE HALF THAT MAKES IT DANGEROUS: nothing on the PR says so. The gate runs against the BRANCH's export and its own artifact checksums, so it passes; the branch is internally coherent. The subtraction is only visible by comparing the branch's export against MAIN, which no check does. A reviewer sees green, mergeable, and a diff of one JSON file.

⇒ THE CHECK, cheap and reusable — TWO questions, and the second is the one that decides:

    1. Does this PR's export ADD anything main lacks?
         set(branch nodes) - set(main nodes)          -> 0 means it can only subtract
    2. Are the nodes it INTENDED to add already in main?
         set(branch nodes) - set(merge-base nodes), then test each against main

When (1) is 0 and (2) is all-present, the PR's design half is ALREADY DELIVERED and the export is pure liability. #190 held nothing else, so it was CLOSED rather than merged — refreshing its export would have left an empty PR. #191 and #194 held real code, so each was rebased with `git checkout --ours docs/design/reflow2.json`, its artifact checksums re-accepted against its OWN existing ChangeEvent in main, and re-exported once.

📌 AND THE TRAP INSIDE THE REPAIR: those three PRs were GREEN because their stale exports carried their own artifact checksums. Restoring main's export makes them go RED on DRIFT immediately — which is correct, and must be fixed by re-accepting, never by keeping the stale export that was hiding it.

NOT ESTABLISHED: how long a PR can sit before this becomes true (all three were under 24 hours old), and whether anything could detect it automatically — the comparison needs main, and the gate deliberately only reads the committed export in front of it.

properties.statement:
A SECOND PROJECT HIT `dec:idea-remaining-work-has-no-answer-in-the-graph` AND WORKED AROUND IT THE SAME WAY, WHICH IS THE CORROBORATION THAT NODE DID NOT HAVE. Alex's Grok 4.6 session, 2026-08-14 (Opportunities), in his words: "Remaining-work / increment view: this session used an accepted Decision's PROSE plus Capability `status` as the MVP list. `what_next` ranks open Decisions and does not answer 'what is left to build.'"

WHY IT MATTERS AS EVIDENCE RATHER THAN AS A NEW COMPLAINT: the open question already exists and already names the cause — the artifact layer is modelled at COMPONENT granularity, so it cannot answer a build question asked at capability granularity (see also `fact:the-build-list-is-suppressed-by-realized-via-component`). What was missing was whether anyone outside this project actually needs the answer. They do, and the workaround they reached for independently is identical: read an accepted Decision's PROSE as the plan, and use `Capability.status` as the checklist.

⭐ THE WORKAROUND IS THE FINDING. Both projects fell back to reading a decision's narrative text — unstructured, uncomputable, and exactly the thing a design graph exists to replace. When the graph cannot answer a question people must answer daily, they do not stop asking it; they answer it from prose, and the prose becomes load-bearing without anyone deciding that it should.

HE ALSO NAMES WHAT `what_next` DOES INSTEAD, which is accurate and not a criticism of it: it ranks open Decisions. That is a different question — what needs a human — from what is left to build, and the two are being conflated by callers because only one of them has a tool.

NOT ESTABLISHED: whether an increment view should be derived from Capability status, from a Release manifest, from a plan-increments epoch, or from something new — that choice is the open question's, not this fact's.

properties.statement:
AGENT-GENERATED FEEDBACK from a Grok 4.6 session on one of Alex's projects (2026-08-13, two entries: a remaining-MVP readout and an encouragement capture session), relayed by Anthony 2026-08-14. Produced by telling the agent *"reflow2 is still a development project - please note any issues or gaps or opportunities to improve reflow2 at path/to/feedback.md"*.

⭐⭐⭐ THE REASON THIS NODE EXISTS: **FOUR OF ITS ITEMS WERE INDEPENDENTLY REPRODUCED BY A DIFFERENT AGENT (Claude Opus 5), ON A DIFFERENT GRAPH (reflow2's own), IN A SESSION THAT HAD NOT READ THE FEEDBACK.** One agent reporting friction is an opinion; two agents on different models and different designs hitting the same edges is a defect report.

═══ ✅ CORROBORATED — hit in this session before the file was read ═══

**1. THE NEAR-DUPLICATE GUARD FIRES ON SIBLINGS AND ACROSS NODE TYPES** (their items 1 and 2, second entry). Six refusals in one capture session, every one of them a genuine non-duplicate:
  · a Requirement refused because its OWN governing Decision was "close"
  · a Capability refused because the Requirement it satisfies was "close"
  · a Requirement refused because a Capability created MINUTES EARLIER in the same batch was "close"
  · one Decision refused TWICE, each refusal naming a DIFFERENT batch of near-matches — the declared ones are excluded and the next-nearest surface, so `distinct_from` grows by retry
⇒ **A Requirement, the Decision that governs it and the Capability that satisfies it are the GOLDEN THREAD. They are supposed to share wording.** A guard that reads them as candidate duplicates fires hardest on exactly the capture pattern the skills prescribe. Their words: *"Each refusal named a sibling I had just created, not a true duplicate."*

**2. `add_decision` CANNOT MERGE WITHOUT RESENDING THE BODY** (their item 3, second entry). Schema requires `id` + `name` + `decision`. Confirmed by cost, not just by reading: prepending a DECIDED header to three already-written decisions this session meant resending ~7 KB bodies verbatim each time. Their report adds the sharper risk: **the loop hint on such a merge still reads *"a Decision lands `proposed`"* even when merging an ACCEPTED node** — observed here too, status correctly stayed `accepted`, but the hint invites an agent to "fix" a status that was never wrong.

**3. CAPTURING CORRECTLY INFLATES THE LOOP DEBT** (their item 5, second entry). Their measurement: 62 → 66 never-asked gaps after a capture session, because each new `planned` Capability immediately owes a verification it cannot yet have. **Measured identically here: 74 → 79 gaps across this session's captures.** Their sentence is exact: *"this session created more of them by doing capture correctly."*

**4. `get_node` MISSES SILENTLY** (their item 5, first entry). REPRODUCED ON REFLOW2'S OWN GRAPH: `get_node {node_type: Project, id: "proj:does-not-exist-12345"}` returns `{"node": null}` with no hint — **and this graph holds exactly ONE Project, `proj:reflow2`.** That is precisely the case they describe: *"A miss on a type that has total: 1 should name the existing id."* ⚠️ A NEARBY EDGE, hit here the same day: passing `node_id` instead of `id` is REFUSED loudly and helpfully (*"unknown field `node_id`, expected `node_type` or `id`"*). So a malformed ARGUMENT is diagnosed and a missing NODE is not — the wrong way round, since the second is the commoner mistake.

═══ ⚠️ NOT REPRODUCED HERE — recorded so it is not treated as confirmed ═══

**`get_instructions` TRUNCATION** (their item 6, first entry): they report ~22.6 KB cut mid-sentence, with the standing rules after the cut never arriving — serious, because the repo file is only a pointer. **Called here the same day and the payload arrived COMPLETE**, ending cleanly on its closing line. ⇒ Likely CLIENT-SPECIFIC (an MCP payload budget in their harness) rather than server-side, which makes it a worse defect in one way: it is invisible from this side and the affected agent cannot tell that rules are missing. Their mitigation — serve it in named sections — survives regardless of cause.

═══ 📌 THEIR ITEMS NOT YET ASSESSED HERE ═══

First entry: (1) *"what is left to build?" is not a first-class query* — `what_next` ranks open DECISIONS, and a graph with one open Decision and a large build backlog gets nothing useful; four sources disagreed (Decision prose, Capability `status`, computed delivery, the repo). (2) status-vs-computed-delivery drift. (3) top gaps are hygiene, not product work — wrong default ranking for *"what do we build next?"*. (4) two sources of truth on one increment. (7) orientation tax. (8) *"the loop and the delivery plan share a dashboard and they should not."* (9) **decision-as-checklist is invisible to the temporal axis** — they propose a detector for an accepted Decision whose statement is a running delivery list with no `SCHEDULED_FOR` edges. Second entry: (4) `detect_gaps(scope)` explodes via Project CONTAINS at depth 3 and returns unrelated planned work rather than the seed's own thread.

📌 THEIR OWN PROCESS GAPS, WORTH KEEPING BECAUSE THEY ARE HONEST: they did not run `compare_designs` or `detect_gaps`, guessed a Project id rather than scanning, and did not export after graph writes — the last being the same omission `fact:second-user-first-run-report-2026-08-13` is about.

⚠️ THEIR KIT SIDECAR READ `0.11.0` / `0ec473e` (a 2026-07-25 tarball) WHILE THE LIVE SERVER SERVED A MUCH NEWER SURFACE. **Third independent signal that consumers run stale kits** — with `fact:second-user-notes-2026-08-14-two-items-already-fixed`, which concluded the same about Alex from different evidence. Their suggestion: write the running binary identity where `loop_status` or `graph_report` already expose it (`served_by` exists on `graph_report`).

ALEX'S EARLIER GROK BUILD SESSION NOTES (~2026-08-07/08, binary 0.24.0, a real monorepo, 361 nodes / 621 edges) TRIAGED AGAINST 0.32.1 — a SECOND file, distinct from the 2026-08-14 report already captured as `art:alex-grok-feedback-2026-08-14`. Confirmed distinct by checksum: the 08-14 artifact is `sha256:0318c290…` and this one is `sha256:007e2868…`. It had never been triaged.

⭐ HIS TOP-PRIORITY ASK DID NOT REPRODUCE, AND THAT IS THE HEADLINE. §1.1: `set_decision_status` failing with `Node not found` immediately after a successful `add_decision`, 'especially in a parallel tool batch', which he ranked #1 of six and called 'top pain'. TESTED HERE on 0.32.1 against the shared server, twice: a 2-call batch (create + set status in one message) and a 6-call batch (three creates + three status sets interleaved in one message). ALL EIGHT CALLS SUCCEEDED; every decision came back `proposed` from the create and `accepted` from the set. Scratch nodes deleted afterwards.

⚠️ NOT REPRODUCED IS NOT REFUTED, and three differences could each explain it: he ran 0.24.0 and this is 0.32.1, eight minor versions apart; his harness is Grok Build and this is Claude Code, which may serialise MCP calls within a turn even when they are issued together; and his load was heavier than a six-call batch. ⇒ The honest status is that the reported failure does not occur in THIS configuration, and nobody has yet tested the one where it did.

WHAT IS ALREADY ANSWERED, so it does not need re-asking:
• §2.3 (revising an accepted Requirement by re-calling `add_requirement` erodes intent silently; he asked for a warning) — SHIPPED in v0.32.0 as the constructor `revision` block, which reports the properties overwritten WITH their prior values in full. Exactly his ask, arrived independently from four other reports.
• §4.3 (Capabilities have no `deferred`/`dropped`, so agents write DROPPED into the description) — SETTLED by Anthony as no cancelled state, ever. The ask is declined rather than open.
• §3.1 (large results truncated, `get_instructions` named) — measured during the 08-14 triage and attributed to HIS CLIENT rather than the server.

WHAT SURVIVES AS GENUINELY OPEN, in his own priority order:
① `get_node` BY ID WITHOUT `node_type` (his #3). An agent holds an id from `search_design` and not its type; the lookup then fails. Distinct from the already-fixed 'unknown node_type is refused rather than answered null'.
② SESSION-SCOPED `loop_status` (his #4): 'always dirty on mature graphs — agents ignore or thrash', asking for a 'debt introduced this session' filter. ⭐ CORROBORATED FIRST-HAND AND HARD: across this entire session `loop_status` reported the identical 80 unsurfaced gaps and 16 structural defects from first call to last, and the only way to say anything useful was to compute the delta by hand and report 'unchanged from session start' each time. The per-CONTRIBUTOR scoping that exists is a different axis and does not answer this.
③ IDEMPOTENT LINK HELPERS with a result flag (his #5) — whether re-calling `satisfies`/`allocate`/`contains` is a no-op or an error is undocumented.
④ A HARNESS-AGNOSTIC SESSION-END NUDGE (his #6): on Grok Build `loop_status` reports `nudge: absent` and there is no alternative, so under load agents capture and skip detect-and-ask. He suggests a `session_wrap_up` tool an agent can call. Note this is the SAME failure the loop nudge exists to prevent, arriving on the harness that cannot host it.
⑤ OPTIONAL `status` ON `add_decision` (his #2) — and this is CORROBORATED INDEPENDENTLY by dev_storyflow's dragon Boss the same week ('there is no one-call path to an accepted decision', six times in one session). ⚠️ BUT BOTH RUN INTO ACCEPTED DOCTRINE: `add_decision` deliberately stopped defaulting to `accepted` on 2026-07-25, and `dec:certainty-derived` holds that moving a status is the owner's word. Alex concedes the point himself — 'default proposed is correct for honesty' — and asks only for an optional override. That makes this a question for Anthony rather than a defect.

HIS FRAMING TO KEEP, and it is a priority instruction rather than a finding: 'DO NOT spend meaningful engineering effort on one-time migration' from the early-adopter era (dropping old skill folders, untracking RocksDB layout, rewriting long AGENTS.md). 'Most users will never have to do that upgrade.' Invest instead in keeping future upgrades boring — install.sh replacing binary and kit while never touching graphs, which he names as already the right model.

properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-09 ON THIS GRAPH, ON A REAL MERGE ANTHONY AUTHORISED. `propose_heal` offered to merge the owner's two Contributor nodes and CHOSE THE WRONG SURVIVOR: keep `ctr:anthony` (8 edges, no description), destroy `who:ajs` (161 edges, the full description, and the id form `add_contributor`'s own parameter description gives as its example).

⭐ AND IT SAID SO ITSELF, WHICH IS THE PART WORTH KEEPING. Verbatim from `would_destroy`: "deleting 'who:ajs' keeps only 'ctr:anthony's properties; also replaced: description. THE ALPHABET CHOSE THE VICTIM: both carry the same provenance, so the smaller id survived (BL-29) — nothing about the design decided which of these two lives." The disclosure is exemplary and it is the only reason the merge was not applied as proposed. A tool that names its own arbitrariness is doing the right thing; a tool whose arbitrariness DECIDES is still wrong.

WHY THIS IS EVIDENCE AND NOT AN OPINION: `dec:merge-survivor-provenance` (ACCEPTED) says the survivor is chosen by provenance with id breaking ties. Here both nodes carry the SAME provenance, so the tie-break ran — and the tie-break is alphabetical, which has no relationship to which node the design actually depends on. `fact:defect-merge-survivor-ignores-priority-and-status` already contradicts that decision and the pair has been a standing structural defect (`heal:7456a4d260ca45ce`). THIS IS THE FIRST TIME THE DEFECT HAS BEEN OBSERVED COSTING SOMETHING ON A REAL MERGE rather than argued in the abstract.

A CHEAP SIGNAL THE RULE COULD READ, offered because naming the fix is more useful than naming the fault: EDGE COUNT. 161 against 8 is not a close call, and neither is "has a description" against "has none". Degree is already computable and would have picked correctly here without any new vocabulary. Provenance-then-alphabet is the rule that produced the wrong answer; provenance-then-degree would not have.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY DONE: the merge was performed BY HAND — `record_change` first so the snapshot holds `ctr:anthony` and all 9 of its edges, then the 8 AUTHORED_BY edges re-pointed to `who:ajs` with `role` and `acted_at` preserved and checked for pre-existing overlap (none, so nothing was overwritten), then the node deleted. `detect_defects` went 7 findings to 6 with the duplicate gone.

📝 ONE THING THIS DOES NOT SHOW, stated so the finding is not read wider than it is: `propose_heal --conservative` proposed NOTHING for this duplicate, and only `--aggressive` offered the merge. So the dangerous proposal is not the default. What the default gives instead is silence on a duplicate a human had explicitly asserted, which is its own question.
[BL-105] The degraded surface ignores --http, so the outage it exists to explain is silent again on the new transport — shipped in v0.14.0. FIXED 2026-07-26, same day

So when the graph is already held and --http was asked for, reflow2 serves its one-tool explanation on stdin/stdout while every session that was told to dial http://\u2026:8787/ gets connection-refused. properties.statement: [BL-110] Nothing computes whether the design ever reached git, and git is where the design lives
properties.value: {"evidence": "*Found by me, 2026-07-29, answering Anthony's question \u2014 \"is reflow2 git aware? when an agent calls a reflow2 skill, does it remind the agent to commit and push?\" The honest answer is that reflow2 is git-aware everywhere except the surface that would act on it. Not yet in the graph; belongs in capture-intent when the server is reachable, likely as a requirement rather than a defect.* Where the awareness is real: .reflow2/graph is gitignored, machine-local and single-writer, so the committed export is the only copy anyone else can see; merge.rs ships a driver git itself invokes, taking its ancestor from git merge-base; reflow2_check.py reads git to validate the export hash chain against HEAD~1 ([BL-107]); and sync.rs:91 hands an agent literal recovery steps \u2014 *\"This is not a merge conflict and git will not catch it\u2026 1. git pull --rebase\"* \u2014 on a stale-export refusal. Where it is absent is the loop. report.rs, where loop debt is computed, contains zero occurrences of git or export, so loop_status is structurally incapable of reporting that the graph is ahead of the committed file. The nudge strings never mention committing. The Rust core never invokes git at all \u2014 no Command::new(\"git\") anywhere in crates/. So an agent can design productively for an entire session, never export, never commit, and nothing in the loop notices that the work exists on exactly one machine \u2014 the same failure mode as a stale seat, one layer up, and the one the gitignored-graph architecture makes possible by construction. This is load-bearing for work now in flight: req:graph-indexes-snapshots and dec:epoch-roadmap-storage's (c-refined) shape both divide labour as *git stores the snapshots, the graph owns the index* ([roadmap-and-planned-epochs.md](roadmap-and-planned-epochs.md)) \u2014 a division with nothing verifying that git received its half, before the first planned epoch is ever written. Fix shape, and it is cheap: the graph knows its write generation and the export carries content_hash; comparing the live graph's hash against the committed export's answers *\"is there undeposited work\"* without any new vocabulary, and reflow2_check.py already proves the git side is reachable from the Python tier. Two constraints that must hold. First, git may be absent and its absence is not an error \u2014 the answer is skipped, never guessed, exactly as BL-107's gate already does outside a working tree. Second, VCS neutrality is a deliberate property and must not regress: every integration today is plain git semantics \u2014 driver, refs, pull --rebase, merge-base \u2014 with no forge APIs anywhere, which is why GitLab, Gitea and Bitbucket work unchanged, and why the GitHub MCP server was declined. (tools/install.sh does use gh and GitHub release URLs, but that distributes *reflow2 itself* and ties nobody's *design* to GitHub; the distinction is worth keeping.) Same recurring shape as [BL-107] \u2014 a designed dependency that nothing validates. Size S\u2013M", "origin": "Migrated from docs/backlog.md BL-110 on 2026-08-07 (epoch:backlog-retired). Size estimate carried from the row: S\u2013M."}

properties.statement: [BL-112] The loop nudge counts file edits made outside the project
properties.value: {"evidence": "*Found by me, 2026-07-29, in the same session as [BL-111] and by the same route. Not yet in the graph \u2014 that session had the MCP server bound to the wrong directory, so capture-intent could not run; this row is a staging post and the item should be promoted properly when the graph is reachable.* loop_nudge.py:202 is if tool in EDIT_TOOLS: state[\"edits\"] += 1 \u2014 it matches on the tool name only (EDIT_TOOLS = {\"Edit\", \"Write\", \"MultiEdit\", \"NotebookEdit\"}, so Bash-driven changes are invisible to it), with no check that the edited path lies inside the project. In the session that found it the tally reached 5 while only 4 Edit/Write calls had touched repo files, so at least one edit to a path outside the project was counted; the surplus came from scratch files written under /tmp. A second and probably deeper cause sits underneath: state_dir() at :98 returns a relative Path(\".reflow2\") / \"loop-nudge\", so which project's tally an edit lands in is decided by the hook process's working directory at the moment it runs, not by where the edited file lives \u2014 and write_state does mkdir(parents=True), so a hook that runs anywhere else silently starts a fresh tally in a new directory rather than failing. Both faults point the same way and a path filter alone would not fix the second. The consequence is that the number in the message does not mean what the message says it means: a session that edits four files in an entirely different repository, and this design not at all, trips a nudge asserting that *this* design's as-built record is at risk. That is worse than the noise the threshold exists to bound, because the nudge is not merely frequent but wrong \u2014 and a warning that is wrong in a checkable way is the thing that teaches people to ignore warnings. The fix is a path filter, not relevance detection. The bluntness is deliberate and the comment at loop_nudge.py:226 says so \u2014 *\"the hook cannot know which files are design-relevant, so a count threshold and the once-only rule bound the noise\"* \u2014 and that judgement should stand; scoping the count to the project keeps it exactly as blunt while making it true. Honest subtlety: the tool event's path field differs by tool (Write, Edit, NotebookEdit), and an edit whose path cannot be determined should count rather than be dropped \u2014 silently under-counting would turn a noisy nudge into an absent one, which is the same failure inverted. properties.value: {"evidence": "*Found 2026-07-31 by an adopt pass over a real design-review document in another organisation \u2014 a pre-construction design with no code \u2014 and independently reproduced in reflow2's own graph the same day. A 63-node cluster was likewise reported *\"disconnected from the rest of the design\"* while its parent subsystems carried DEPENDS_ON edges outward and everything shared one Project. In every case the machinery was right and the sentence was wrong. Reproduced here the same day: disconnected_community fired on a Requirement that had just gained an acknowledgement Decision, reporting an island for two nodes sharing the Project \u2014 the [orphan-requirements-hide-from-heal] shape from the other side. This is not a detector bug; it is the class req:schema-prose-is-checked already names \u2014 prose that promises breadth the code does not implement, which is exactly why Project.mode's description was fixed at the source rather than annotated. Same defect, different surface: there it was schema prose, here it is finding prose. Fix shape: every finding states the edge kinds it considered \u2014 *\"no runtime (PROVIDES/CONSUMES/DEPENDS_ON) path; containment edges exist but do not count\"*. Cheap, changes no computation, and it is the difference between a finding a user acts on and one they learn to distrust. The orphan_node half may additionally be a real rule gap: DOCUMENTS arguably *is* ownership for artifact_type of document/spec/diagram, and if so the detector should say so rather than every design document reading as an orphan forever. Decide that separately from the wording. THE CONTROL EXPERIMENT THIS ITEM LACKED, supplied 2026-07-31 by a case study designed end to end through reflow2: propagate_change returned impacted: [] for a change that materially activated a regulatory Constraint sitting three nodes away \u2014 correct given the edges, badly wrong about the world, because the CONSTRAINS edge had never been drawn. Later in the SAME session, same tool, ~16 nodes both times, with edges present, it produced a genuinely valuable answer with correct upstream hop chains that caught two requirements about to be orphaned. Edge density, not graph size, decided whether the tool was useful \u2014 and the output is identical for \"nothing depends on this\" and \"you never drew the edges\", which is the overwhelmingly common case early in a design's life, i.e. exactly when users decide whether to trust the feature. Same disease as this item: the machinery was right and the sentence claimed more than it checked. Fix, one line: when few or no nodes are impacted, report the seeds' connectivity \u2014 *\"0 impacted; note these seeds carry 2 edges total, so this design may be under-linked rather than genuinely isolated\"*. The data already existed: detect_defects had ALREADY flagged that exact node set as a disconnected community in the same session. Two detectors knew and neither told the tool that mattered. INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION OF THIS ITEM'S PROPOSED FIX, arrived at from the other end (2026-07-31, same case study): disconnected_community's SUGGESTION does not know about the detector's own SELECTIVITY. Connectivity is measured over traceability edges; MITIGATES/RISKS/CONTRADICTS do not participate. So a user told to bridge the island draws a TRUE edge of a type that does not count, re-runs, and gets nothing back \u2014 not \"closer\", not \"that edge does not count\", nothing. This is exactly the fix already proposed above, reached independently: *state the edge kinds considered*. Plus a refinement worth taking: if the island already carries non-traceability edges outward, say so \u2014 *\"semantically connected to the design but structurally isolated\"* is a completely different finding from *\"isolated\"*, and in that project it was the true one. properties.statement: [BL-124] acknowledge_defect can never close a disconnected_community, and each attempt writes a junk Decision
properties.value: {"evidence": "*Found 2026-07-31 by a case-study project designed end-to-end through reflow2 (quantum_benchmarking_initiative), confirmed in this codebase and reproduced live in that graph \u2014 the cluster has grown 8 -> 9 -> 10 nodes across attempts.* The two documented behaviours are individually right and jointly fatal. acknowledge_defect (crates/reflow2-core/src/heal.rs:490) creates the review Decision and then draws a GOVERNED_BY edge from *every* affected node to it, deliberately, so \"the review is reachable from the design\". disconnected_community (heal.rs:~734) computes its id by hashing the category with the affected set. For most categories that is fine, because the acknowledgement does not alter what the detector measures. For this one it measures precisely what the acknowledgement modifies: cluster membership. The Decision joins the island it acknowledges, enlarging it by one, minting a new id, resurrecting the defect one node larger \u2014 without limit. So an entire category is permanently unclosable, and the failure is the exact one acknowledge_defect exists to prevent \u2014 its own docs say the point is that \"a list that can never reach zero gets skimmed\". The case study ended three sessions running with loop_status reporting \"1 structural defect outstanding\" for a defect that had been reviewed, understood and accepted, while generate_bridge was correctly *refused* because nothing in the design models the relationship. The honest disposition is the one the bug blocks. Fix shapes, any one sufficient: (1) exclude acknowledgement Decisions from design_network() \u2014 an acknowledgement is a statement *about* the design, not a participant in it, and this also stops them distorting centrality, SPOF and coupling wherever a review has been recorded; (2) compute the defect id from the affected set MINUS acknowledgement nodes; (3) store the affected ids as a property rather than as edges. (1) is the most correct and the widest, and the caller list settles it: design_network() (crates/reflow2-core/src/structure.rs:220) has three callers, not one \u2014 heal.rs:732 (disconnected_community, the reported symptom), propagate.rs:389 (betweenness / centrality) and surprises.rs:88 (surprising_connections). So acknowledgement Decisions are silently perturbing centrality and surprise detection too, in every design where a review has ever been recorded \u2014 unreported distortion in two more places that nobody has looked at. Option (2) would fix the visible symptom at the hash and leave the other two callers still wrong. *Caller list contributed by the case study and verified here.* THE PRACTICAL ARGUMENT FOR PRIORITY, from the same source: that project has now spent FOUR sessions unable to close a defect it correctly understood and correctly judged should be accepted. It tried the acknowledgement route \u2014 blocked by this livelock. It tried the bridge route \u2014 blocked by the selectivity problem folded into [BL-114], which advises an edge whose only correct forms do not count. Both correct routes are shut, so the honest disposition is unreachable by any path, and loop_status reports outstanding debt that is actually a reviewed and settled judgement. That is the skimmed-list failure the acknowledge tools exist to prevent, produced by the tool built to prevent it. Relates to [BL-114] (same detector, message half) and to the review-expiry tension already recorded on req:review-expires-when-what-it-judged-changes: that one expires too *late* on content, this one expires too *eagerly* on membership, and both come from keying a review to a hash of a set. BUILT 2026-08-01 \u2014 fix shape (1), at design_network(). A new is_review_record id rule excludes the decision:ack: prefix that both acknowledgement paths already mint and already strip to recognise their own records, so it is the codebase's existing marker rather than a new convention. ver:acknowledgement-not-structure passing, 5 cases, written before the fix: the two bug cases failed and all three counterweights passed. A review remains recorded, reasoned and reachable \u2014 excluded from the NETWORK, not from the GRAPH \u2014 and still appears in a blast radius, because a review genuinely is affected when what it reviewed changes. BL-86 (shipped in v0.10.1) fixed the *wording* \u2014 it now names both recovery paths instead of wrongly saying \"rebuild\" \u2014 but it did not make the graph openable, and both paths it names have holes: \"export it with the reflow2 that wrote it\" needs the old binary that curl \\ | sh already replaced (req:frictionless-update defeating the migration path), and \"import a committed export\" needs the project to have committed one. The undocumented escape is deleting the sidecar .reflow2/graph.meta.json, which opens the graph as unstamped \u2014 but that silently drops any genuinely-retired-type edges, i.e. it performs exactly the loss the refusal existed to prevent, without naming it. Fix shape: a --migrate path that opens past the stamp check, drops retired types, names what it dropped, and re-stamps \u2014 one step, no old binary, nothing silent. properties.statement: [BL-95] The design cannot see what it was never told about — no detector takes a file on disk as its subject
properties.value: {"evidence": "*Anthony, 2026-07-24, from the storyflow adopt pass: \"it did kind of a superficial job\u2026 my assumption is that the agent should fill in more and more detail as I develop.\"* All 26 gap sources reason about nodes already in the graph (unsatisfied requirement, unrealized capability, unverified capability, \u2026); not one takes an unmodelled file, module or subsystem as its subject. So a graph covering 30% of a codebase reports the same \"0 open gaps\" as one covering 100% \u2014 and the unmodelled fraction is largest exactly where the codebase is largest, i.e. where a design brain is worth most. reflow2 will nag forever about a capability it knows is unverified and say nothing at all about ten subsystems it has never heard of. The only existing counterpart is reconcile_artifacts, which does report files \"present but unknown to the design\" \u2014 but only for paths the agent hands it, so it is discipline, not a detector; nothing fires on its own. Evidence it does not self-correct in practice: merge.rs + alternatives.rs (1,886 lines, *shipped in v0.10.0*) sat unmodelled for two days inside reflow2's own repo and nothing fired (BL-70 session, found only by looking); the whole temporal axis went unused for weeks, equally silent; and BL-74 \u2014 from Anthony's own StoryFlow fleet \u2014 is the same failure at the loop level (skills silently stop under load). The graph deepens where something forces the issue and stays flat everywhere else. Design, and the trap to avoid: the measure must NOT be a file-count ratio \u2014 that would punish exactly the modelling the adopt skill mandates (\"one Artifact per meaningful unit, not per file; a vendored or generated mass = one opaque Component; granularity tracks distinct contracts, not LOC\"). Measure claimed regions, not files: for each directory subtree in an agent-supplied sweep, does *any* node claim it (a location inside it)? Report unclaimed regions ranked by mass, so the biggest silences sort first, and one opaque Component legitimately claims the vendored mass beneath it. Shape: a new op coverage_report(observed_paths, exclusions) \u2014 the sibling of reconcile_artifacts, in drift.rs, same contract (reflow2 performs no file I/O; the agent sweeps and supplies). Reports; never scores, never blocks (dec:report-dont-judge). Exclusions (build output, vendored, generated) are named as excluded, never silently dropped (rule 6). Because detect_gaps takes no arguments and must stay state-derived (dec:loop-status-state-not-history), the sweep optionally records its result as a node the way reconcile records a DriftEvent \u2014 then a gap can be raised from graph state, and the report must say when the sweep was taken so a stale coverage claim is never presented as current (the cap:freshness precedent). Adopt should end with a sweep, so a thin pass is *measured* rather than felt. DONE 2026-07-27 \u2014 coverage_report on the core and the MCP surface, and wired into the adopt skill's Phase 4 so the sweep actually happens rather than being available. Unclaimed paths roll up to the shallowest wholly-unclaimed directory and rank by mass, so a vendored tree arrives as one finding instead of 900 nobody reads. The trap is pinned by its own test: 900 files under one registered directory report ZERO unclaimed, because a file-count ratio would have scored correct coarse modelling as 1-of-901 and called it failure. Exclusions come back named with the rule that excluded them; a registered location the sweep never mentioned is named too, so \"my sweep was narrower than the design\" is distinguishable from \"the file is gone\". 7 cases. Deliberately NOT built, recorded rather than half-done: the sweep is not persisted, so detect_gaps cannot yet raise coverage from graph state \u2014 that needs a node to record a sweep in (a schema change) and a decision on how stale a recorded sweep may be before its claim expires (the cap:freshness precedent). Until then coverage is something a person asks for, and adopt asks", "origin": "Migrated from docs/backlog.md BL-95 on 2026-08-07 (epoch:backlog-retired). properties.statement: CORRECTION TO fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server: THE STRANDED SESSION IS RECOVERABLE WITHOUT AN MCP RECONNECT, AND THE WORKAROUND IS ONE COMMAND. That node states the failure is 'unrecoverable for the life of the session — every later respawn resolves the same dead inode, and only a full MCP reconnect clears it.' The first clause is right and the second is WRONG, proven here on 2026-08-08 by hitting the failure and recovering from it mid-session. WHAT HAPPENED: after the shared daemon's binary was replaced by a `cargo test` relink, the daemon exited and the client's auto-respawn failed with 'could not spawn the shared reflow2 server: No such file or directory (os error 2)' — the documented symptom, including the misleading advice to check a server log that cannot contain the cause. THE RECOVERY, verified by execution: start a replacement daemon BY HAND from the on-disk path, `setsid nohup ./target/debug/reflow2-mcp --graph-path ./.reflow2/graph --serve-shared &`, and the next tool call from the SAME session attached to it and worked normally (claim_report returned, then mint_seat, claim_region, open_questions, and a dozen further calls). No reconnect, no session restart, no context lost. WHY THE ORIGINAL CLAIM WAS WRONG: it reasoned that because the CLIENT resolves the binary through `current_exe()` and that inode is dead, every attempt must fail. True — but only of the client's SPAWN path. Attaching is a separate act: the client looks for a published server for that graph, and a server started by any means satisfies it. The dead inode blocks the client from CREATING a daemon; it does not block it from FINDING one. WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE WORKAROUND: 'unrecoverable, restart the session' is expensive advice for ephemeral seats that are already dying on context exhaustion, and it was written into the graph as measured fact on reasoning alone. The original node's own evidence field says the diagnosis was 'recorded in session handoffs as worth filing and still unfiled' — so the recoverability clause was inherited, never tested. NOTE THE SHAPE, which is the same one this file keeps producing: a claim that was true about one mechanism (spawn) stated as true about the whole situation (the session), with nothing marking which part had been measured.
