AN AGENT-SIDE FIELD REPORT FROM AN UNRELATED PROJECT, 2026-08-11, RECORDED REDACTED ON ANTHONY'S INSTRUCTION — no project name, no design counts, no domain terms. Written by a coding agent that had driven reflow2 through capture, where-am-i readbacks, gap review and acknowledgement, verification recording, and a server upgrade mid-project. Recorded as a fact rather than as proposals because that is what it IS: measured evidence about how reflow2 behaves in someone else's hands, which is the input class dec:idea-field-evidence-is-a-prioritisation-input asks whether to read.

=== SORTED THE WAY ANTHONY ASKED: CONFIRMS-ACCEPTED-INTENT vs NEW PROPOSAL vs ALREADY SATISFIED ===

CONFIRMS ACCEPTED INTENT (the report did not propose these; it independently showed they matter):

1. THE SPAWN ERROR NEVER NAMES THE FILE IT COULD NOT FIND. Confirms fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server (measured here 2026-08-07, fix named in its own evidence field, filed and left unfixed). INDEPENDENT AND SIMULTANEOUS: the same defect blocked a session in this repo on 2026-08-11 for forty minutes. FIXED the same day; their narrower ask — name the path — is in that fix.

2. RE-RUNNING A VERIFICATION IS MORE CEREMONY THAN THE EVENT DESERVES. A recorded check re-ran green twice and last_run_at was left stale, honestly, because updating an unchanged status felt like paperwork. Confirms req:verification-keeps-up (ACCEPTED: "a 'verified' claim says how old the check behind it is"). Their sentence is the sharp part and is not in this graph anywhere: STALE LAST-RUN UNDERMINES ASSURANCE MORE THAN A MISSING VERIFICATION DOES, BECAUSE IT LOOKS CURRENT. An accepted requirement is being defeated by friction rather than by absence.

3. THE QUESTION LEDGER CANNOT SEE THE MOST NATURAL WAY QUESTIONS GET ASKED. The where-am-i skill instructs the agent to put open gaps to the user as prose; doing so leaves open_questions at zero and the loop still reporting the gaps as never asked, because only the gap_to_prompt handshake registers an ask. Confirms the ledger's own purpose (questions outlive sessions, in the wording the user saw, so nobody is re-asked) and reveals a SERVED SKILL BYPASSING IT. Their framing: the debt list nags about work that was done.

4. A SATISFYING CAPABILITY IN ANOTHER GRAPH FORCES A PERMANENT ACKNOWLEDGEMENT. A program deliberately running several graphs found on day one that SATISFIES/REALIZES cannot point across a design boundary, so gaps that are structurally answered stay open forever as acknowledgements. Confirms req:design-composes and req:complementary-pairing (both accepted) and sharpens dec:idea-how-is-a-source-outside-the-repo-registered, recorded here hours earlier from the ARTIFACT side of the identical shape: a reference that cannot leave its own design's boundary.

NEW PROPOSALS (nothing in the graph asks for these):

5. AN ACKNOWLEDGEMENT CANNOT STATE A MACHINE-CHECKABLE RE-REVIEW TRIGGER. Several acknowledgements carried explicit retirement conditions in prose; one had been true for weeks and nothing surfaced it. NARROWER THAN THEY WROTE, and the narrowing matters: expiry machinery EXISTS and recomputes from the affected node set, so this is not "acknowledgements never expire" — it is that they cannot express a CONDITION. Their words: acknowledgements are where gaps go to be forgotten safely, and the safety decays silently.

6. THE LOOP ONLY SEES WHAT AN AGENT HAND-CARRIES IN. Their own synthesis and the strongest thing in the report: the liveliest facts of the month — merged PRs, a review round addressed, a suite re-verified, work scheduled — all landed in commits and PR threads and almost none reached the graph without the agent carrying them. They ask for the loop to SUBSCRIBE to reality rather than be fed it.

7. ARTIFACT CAPTURE IS THE LEAST-REWARDING STEP, SO IT IS THE ONE THAT GETS DEFERRED. Realization sat at zero while many PRs merged — consciously deferred, because modelling Artifacts is the most manual capture in the loop. Anything that makes registration near-free at merge time converts the graph's biggest systematic undercount into signal.

8. THE VERIFICATION DIGEST NAMES COUNTS, NOT SUBJECTS. graph_report gives a per-check count but not WHICH capability, so narrating what a check covers costs extra round trips.

9. TOOL-SURFACE SIZE. ~150 tools is workable behind deferred loading, but a client that eagerly loads schemas pays heavily; they suggest a curated core-subset server mode for small-context agents.

ALREADY SATISFIED — DROPPED PER ANTHONY'S TRIAGE RULE, NO NODE MINTED:

10. CONTRADICTORY SESSION-END MESSAGING (loop_status saying no nudge is installed while a Stop hook fires). ALREADY FOUND AND ALREADY FIXED: filed by a different project on 2026-08-09 and corrected in nudge.rs, which now reports what reflow2 LOOKED AT rather than asserting the world. Their report straddles their own mid-project upgrade. THIS IS THE THIRD PROJECT TO MEET IT, and the first two are why it is fixed.

=== WHAT THE REPORT SAYS REFLOW2 GETS RIGHT, recorded because praise is evidence too and this project keeps only its failures ===

served_by.stale and its derivation rather than version-literal comparison; honest computation over status fields ("computed from the thread, not from a status field", and the requirement-certainty split) which they say stops an agent laundering an assumption into a confirmed fact; refusal to default judgements (maturity_report declining to say where a design SHOULD be; loop_status refusing an unknown contributor id because "nothing is owed to you" is the most dangerous reply to a typo) — they call these the tool's epistemics and say the refusals TEACH them; the where-am-i structure, singling out the never-re-ask-in-different-words rule; acknowledged gaps carrying their full deferral reason, which made a months-long design legible in one call; and error messages that lead with "the design is not lost".

THEIR NET, verbatim and worth keeping intact: "the epistemic core — honest computation, refusal to default judgments, questions as first-class debt — is the product. Most of the friction above is the same shape: reality moves outside the graph, and the loop only sees what the agent hand-carries in. Cheapening that carry (asks, re-runs, artifacts, cross-graph facts) is where the remaining leverage is."

HONEST BOUND ON THIS NODE: one report, one agent, one project, and it is the agent's perspective rather than the human user's. Items 1 and 10 are independently corroborated by this repo's own measurements; items 2 through 9 are single-source, and recording them here is not evidence that anyone else needs them.

WHERE FEEDBACK TRIAGE ACTUALLY STANDS ACROSS THE THREE SOURCES, so the next session does not redo it or assume it is finished. Written because the previous standing note claimed things were uncaptured that had in fact shipped, which is what happens when a to-do list about feedback lives outside the graph it is about.

⭐ THE HEADLINE IS HOW MUCH WAS ALREADY DONE. Of everything checked today, the large majority was already captured, already shipped, or already settled. FOUR new facts came out of roughly forty items examined. That ratio is the useful number: the log is now mostly a record of things reflow2 has answered.

The ~2026-08-07/08 one on binary 0.24.0 had NEVER been triaged and now is, as `fact:alex-grok-0240-feedback-triaged-2026-08-16` — his top-priority ask did not reproduce on 0.32.1, and five of his six asks are either shipped, settled, or now recorded. ⚠️ HIS SEVEN 'OPPORTUNITIES' WERE NOT UNCAPTURED, contrary to the standing note: five had shipped or been recorded, and the near-duplicate guard caught the remaining two as existing nodes when this session tried to create them. properties.statement:
MEASURED 2026-08-10 by reading which edge constants each analysis module actually spans (structure.rs, flow.rs, budget.rs, hierarchy.rs, heal.rs, surprises.rs, allocate.rs, propagate.rs) and joining that against edge counts in the live export.

    populated edge types                               35   (of 61 declared — 26 are never used at all)
    types reached by ANY graph analysis                12
    types reached by NONE                              23   = 2,293 of 7,446 edges, 31%

THE GOLDEN THREAD IS IN THE UNANALYSED SET. GOVERNED_BY (867), REALIZES (199), SATISFIES (175), VERIFIES (139) — the core traceability of the whole design — have never been cycle-checked, never had centrality run on them, never been community-detected. Nor has PRECEDES (47), which IS the delivery plan. Meanwhile DEPENDS_ON (173 edges) carries FOUR separate analyses (structure, budget, hierarchy, allocate).

THE CAUSE IS WIRING, NOT CAPABILITY. Every algorithm needed is already imported from dynograph and already runs: betweenness_centrality, leiden, cut_structure, connected_components, find_cycle, strongly_connected_components. Each is nailed to one purpose-specific edge subset at its call site. Graph algorithms are edge-type agnostic; the wiring is not. Anthony's own earlier tool (/home/ajs7/reflow/tools/system_of_systems_graph.py) took the opposite shape — ONE graph built from all edges, then nx.simple_cycles and degree analysis over it — and he ran it as a routine sanity check on nearly every graph.

WHAT THE MISSING ANALYSES ACTUALLY FOUND WHEN RUN BY HAND, so the gap is not reported as hypothetical:

    GOLDEN THREAD  SATISFIES+REALIZES+VERIFIES+ALLOCATED_TO   677 edges   0 cycles
    REASONING      GOVERNED_BY+OBSOLETES+CAUSES+ANTICIPATES   893 edges   1 cycle
    THE PLAN       PRECEDES+SCHEDULED_FOR                      70 edges   0 cycles
    TIME/HISTORY   HAS_SNAPSHOT+AT_EPOCH+VALID_FROM+VALID_TO  646 edges   0 cycles
    RISK           RISKS+BLOCKS+CONTRADICTS+VIOLATES+MASKS     35 edges   0 cycles

The single cycle is dec:an-unplanned-cut-slips-every-later-increment-by-one CAUSES dec:idea-a-planned-increment-is-named-by-content-not-by-number, which OBSOLETES it back — a TIME SEQUENCE rendered as a loop by a projection with no clock, not faulty reasoning. SO THE DESIGN IS STRUCTURALLY CLEAN EVERYWHERE NOBODY WAS LOOKING, which is a result worth having and could not previously be obtained.

AND A SECOND READING THE DESIGN ALREADY ASKED FOR. dec:orientation-is-computed-not-written names the genuinely missing thing as "WHICH FEW DECISIONS SHAPE EVERYTHING ELSE — neither what-next nor where-am-i answers it today, and it is what a newcomer actually needs". Centrality over GOVERNED_BY is that computation and had never been run. Run: the top governors are rule:no-foreclosure, the owner's-word authority rule, a-graph-per-ownership-boundary, systems-are-functional-not-the-file-tree, and the-LLM-speaks-the-graph-remembers-the-human-decides. THE SHAPE MATTERS MORE THAN THE LIST: influence is FLAT, not concentrated — max reach 13, the top five carry 16% of the edges, and 66 of 120 governed nodes are governed by exactly one thing. There is no small set of load-bearing roots. That is evidence against the design being a deep decision tree: a tree has a trunk and this does not.

THE EXCLUSIONS ARE LOAD-BEARING AND THAT WAS PROVEN THE EXPENSIVE WAY. The first centrality run returned garbage — the ten most influential "decisions" were all decision:ack: review records, which structure.rs already excludes from the design network (ver:acknowledgement-not-structure). Excluding them took GOVERNED_BY from 867 edges to 255: TWO THIRDS OF THAT EDGE TYPE IS BOOKKEEPING. A naive run-everything-on-everything gives a confident wrong answer on the first attempt, so any general surface must carry the exclusion list as part of each projection's definition rather than as a caveat.

MEASURED 2026-08-13 by experiment on a scratch graph, because the answer could not be read off the schema and reading `get_node`'s signature only hints at it.

THE QUESTION Anthony asked: does each node within a graph have a unique id? THE ANSWER: no — the unique key is (node_type, node_id), not node_id alone.

WHAT WAS RUN. Created `thing:same` as a Capability and again as a Requirement in one graph: BOTH PERSISTED and both read back independently, with their own names. Then created `thing:same` as a Capability a second time: it MERGED with no error — the property passed overwrote, the `name` omitted survived, and `scan_nodes` reported one Capability. The storage key is `{graph_id}\x00{type}\x00{id}`, which is why `get_node` demands a type as well as an id.

⭐ THREE LEVELS, AND ONLY THE MIDDLE ONE IS ENFORCED:
  · `graph_id` ACROSS STORES — NOT unique, nothing checks it (see fact:two-adopted-stores-share-one-graph-id-2026-08-13)
  · (type, id) WITHIN a graph — unique BY CONSTRUCTION, it is the storage key
  · `id` ALONE within a graph — NOT unique; only the `cap:` / `req:` / `dec:` prefix convention keeps it clean

THE CONVENTION HOLDS IN PRACTICE AND IS NOT ENFORCED: across all 2,113 nodes of reflow2's own design, ZERO ids appear under more than one node type. Three types legitimately carry two prefixes each and none is a collision — Component `cmp:` (48) plus `sys:` (8, the functional systems from dec:bl83a-functional-decomposition); Decision `dec:` (222) plus `decision:` (126, the generated review-acknowledgement records); Contributor `who:` (5) plus ONE lingering `ctr:`, the residue of the Contributor fork.

🛑 WHY IT MATTERS FOR FEDERATION, and this is the asymmetry worth keeping: reflow2 is careful about id collisions ONE LEVEL DOWN and has nothing one level up. `mirror_surface` REFUSES a colliding node id and leaves the local node untouched, on the stated ground that "two designs using one id for different things is a naming conversation between their owners." The same hazard between two DESIGNS is a silent overwrite in a BTreeMap. Node collisions are a conversation; graph collisions are data loss.

AN INSTANCE OF THE RISK BL-185 RECORDS, WITH A MEASURED COST — and it is the agent's own working order, not somebody else's.

BL-185 has carried Anthony's words since 2026-08-03: "Developing tests as you design is extremely important. It shapes system architecture, forces clear thinking about edge cases early... Confirmation bias: Testing code you already wrote proves what it does, not necessarily what it should do." He raised the same question again on 2026-08-11 — the TENTH time in one session that a fresh thought landed on something the graph already held, and the only one where the prior record is his own verbatim reasoning on an OPEN fork nobody has chosen.

WHAT WAS ACTUALLY DONE, TWICE, ON 2026-08-11:
  PR #149 (spawn_daemon)      implementation first, then tests, then mutation-checking
  PR #151 (search-first)      implementation first, then tests, then mutation-checking
Neither was test-first. Both were mutation-checked, which is this repo's real rigour and is a DIFFERENT property: mutation-checking proves a test can fail, it does not prove the test asks the right question.

⭐ THE COST WAS MEASURABLE AND IS THE POINT. PR #151's check refused two requirements whose statements were three words long ("Session A wrote this." / "Session B wrote this.") — a plainly wrong result, found by CI on an unrelated suite, not by any test written for the feature. The cause was an absent signal rather than a bad threshold: near-empty documents share most of their tokens by construction. THAT IS A BOUNDARY CONDITION, and "what are the boundary values" is precisely the question test-first forces before an author is attached to an implementation. It is also the GENESIS case — a young design is all short statements — so the miss was not exotic.

Under the old stdio/exclusive-RocksDB behaviour a second session was SILENTLY BLINDED, and their PROTOCOL literally instructed workers NOT to run reflow2. Seven sessions read AND wrote concurrently with nobody blocked, queued or blinded — and the `REFLOW2-HOLD`/`RELEASE` ritual they used to run on the boss channel is simply GONE. A whole coordination protocol deleted, not merely eased. (2) SERVER-SIDE BEHAVIOUR REACHES EVERY ATTACHED SESSION WITH NO RESTART. When the server rolled to 0.24.0 the fixed detectors reached all attached seats MID-SESSION — one seat watched defects 42 -> 6 happen live in its own tool output. Only the TOOL LIST is negotiated at connect, so a session needs restarting ONLY if it needs a genuinely new tool. Measured consequence: they restarted 1 session instead of 6 and five kept their context. The reporter calls this major, non-obvious, and asks that it be kept and documented loudly. (3) `claim_region` BEING ADVISORY RATHER THAN A LOCK IS THE RIGHT CALL and they explicitly defend it: it makes overlap visible without inventing a blocking primitive; nobody deadlocked, nobody waited on a peer, and no claim ever had to be force-released after a session died. A lock would have recreated the exact problem `--shared` just solved. (4) `mint_seat` + `add_contributor` AS SEPARATE CONCEPTS held up once the roles were clear — seat = this session for claim_region, contributor = durable authorship. (5) CONCURRENT READS OF THE SAME NODES WERE COMPLETELY UNEVENTFUL, including reading nodes while workers wrote elsewhere — no staleness, no error, no surprise. (6) WORKERS RUNNING THE DESIGN BRAIN CHANGED THE QUALITY OF THEIR REPORTS: findings came back as graph evidence with node ids the boss could re-resolve, instead of prose that had to be taken on trust. THEIR EXPLICIT 'WHAT NOT TO CHANGE' LIST: advisory-not-lock claims; the refusal to accept an artifact checksum silently (design_holds vs design_updated vs baseline_established called a genuinely good forced question); per-property merge; skills served rather than installed, so they never go stale in a repo; and `--shared` itself.

properties.statement:
**ANTHONY, 2026-08-14: "always trying to improve the probability that an agent uses a reflow2 skill or tool — we can probably look at the stats." MEASURED ACROSS EVERY RETAINED TRANSCRIPT. TWO FINDINGS: THE TREND IS ALREADY STEEPLY UP, AND THE INSTRUMENT THAT WOULD TELL HIM SO UNDERCOUNTS BY A THIRD.**

═══ ⭐⭐ THE TREND, BY WEEK (get_skill channel, sessions with ≥1 reflow2 call) ═══
```
week         sessions   with-skill   rate
2026-07-13       4          0         0%
2026-07-20      16          1         6%
2026-07-27      22         14        64%
2026-08-03      15         15       100%
2026-08-10       6          5        83%   <- 5 of 6; the one miss is THIS session
```
**The headline aggregate (35 of 63 = 56%) is an artefact of averaging over the era before the fix.** On current behaviour the rate is 83–100%. ⚠️ The last two buckets are small (15 and 6 sessions) and the trend is not proof of causation — nothing here isolates WHICH change moved it.

═══ 🛑 THE INSTRUMENT MEASURES ONE OF TWO CHANNELS ═══

`surface_usage.py` counts skill use as **`get_skill` calls**. In the reflow2 checkout a skill is far more often invoked as a **slash command** — Claude Code loads `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` as `/<name>`, and that path never touches `get_skill`. Counting only invocation markers (`<command-name>`, the Skill tool's base-directory line), never mere mentions of a path:
```
sessions with >=1 reflow2 call         63
  get_skill  (what the instrument sees) 35   56%
  slash-command / Skill invocation      55   87%
  EITHER                                60   95%
  invoked a skill, counted as ZERO      25
```
⇒ **25 sessions used a skill and register as total failures.** `where-am-i` is the clearest case: **37 local invocations against 4 `get_skill` calls**, because `/where` is one of the shipped commands.

⚠️ A FIRST ATTEMPT AT THIS MEASUREMENT WAS WRONG AND IS RECORDED AS SUCH: matching `skills/<name>/SKILL.md` anywhere in a transcript reported 90%, because it also matched `ls` output, greps of the skill tree, and the SessionStart hook's own catalogue. **Mentions are not invocations.** The numbers above use invocation markers only.

═══ ⭐⭐ WHY THE BIAS IS THE SAME BLIND SPOT FOUND TWICE ALREADY TODAY ═══

The local channel **exists only where the skill files do** — the reflow2 checkout, which holds all twenty as the compile sources. A CONSUMER INSTALL HAS NEITHER THE SOURCES NOR MOST COMMANDS, so `get_skill` really is their only channel and the instrument is correct for them. **It is wrong precisely and only for the maintainer's own sessions**, which are the ones he reads.

This is the third instance in one day of one structural fault: `fact:the-commands-cover-nine-of-twenty-skills-and-the-checkout-cannot-feel-it` (the checkout resolves all 20 as commands, a consumer resolves 9) and `fact:updating-reflow2-does-not-update-a-project-already-set-up` (the developer's kit is a SYMLINK, a consumer's is a frozen tarball). **`req:the-tool-finds-its-own-blind-spots` keeps arriving in the ENVIRONMENT rather than in a detector.**

→ AND IT CUTS BOTH WAYS ON `dec:idea-does-every-served-skill-get-a-command`: a skill WITH a command is invoked locally and vanishes from `get_skill`; a skill WITHOUT one can arrive by no other route. **The eleven uncovered skills are the only ones the instrument can see honestly.**

═══ 🛑 TWO SKILLS HAVE NEVER BEEN INVOKED BY EITHER CHANNEL, IN ANY RETAINED SESSION ═══

**`ingest-corpus` and `link-projects`** — zero `get_skill`, zero invocations. link-projects was WRITTEN 2026-08-13 (PR #169) to make the linking process reusable, and the process has not been run through it since. A skill nobody reaches for is not evidence it is unneeded, but it is the sharpest case `dec:bl-155` describes: reflow2 cannot tell UNUSED from UNREACHABLE.

═══ THE SESSION THAT PRODUCED THIS MEASUREMENT IS THE ONE MISS ═══

🛑 Session `809c87ed`, 2026-08-14: 43 reflow2 calls, **zero `get_skill`**. It invoked `/capture-session` locally — so the instrument's verdict is wrong in MECHANISM — **and it is right in SUBSTANCE anyway: building the decomposition detector, `impact-check` was never opened before changing an existing design, and the Stop hook had to point out that `propagate_change` had been skipped.** Recorded rather than argued away: the honest reading is that one skill was used where two or three applied.

═══ SEPARATE SIGNAL WORTH KEEPING: THE SURFACE IS MISSING BULK FORMS ═══

45.3% of tool-to-tool transitions are the SAME tool called again (3474/7671). Worst: `release_includes` 989 self-loops over 1010 calls in 8 sessions (~126 per session) — and `release_includes_all` already exists, so this is a DISCOVERABILITY failure, not a missing feature. Then `set_artifact_checksum` (288/522, 40 sessions), `create_node` (150/393). **Nobody calls one tool 126 times because they want to.**

⇒ 118 of 149 served tools were called at least once; 35 never were. Absence stays WEAK evidence — only retained transcripts are visible, and a tool used before the window looks identical to one never used.

"WHAT IS LEFT TO BUILD?" HAS NO ANSWER IN REFLOW2, AND THE REASON IS NARROWER AND WORSE THAN THE REPORT THAT PROMPTED THE CHECK.

ORIGIN: item 1 of the Grok 4.6 agent feedback of 2026-08-13 (`fact:agent-feedback-corroborated-2026-08-14`) — *"'What is left to build?' is not a first-class query. `what_next` ranks open Decisions."* Verified on reflow2's own committed export at `c18a4a1`, 2026-08-14, per `req:agent-authored-feedback-is-reproducible-and-never-leaves-unasked`.

═══ ✅ THEIR CLAIM CONFIRMED ═══

`what_next` (no args) on reflow2's graph returned **12 items: 3 marked + 4 ranked + 1 unexplored + 4 shaping — every one a Decision.** `open_total: 118`, `unranked_pool: 87`. Zero Requirements, zero Capabilities. Its own description says so honestly (*"which decisions to settle next"*), so this is a scope fact rather than a bug. `arrival_delta` requires a DesignEpoch or Release `target_id`, so it cannot answer for a design whose remaining work is not scheduled onto one.

THE HONEST ANSWER, computed directly from the export:
```
Requirements 164   accepted 115  proposed 36  dropped 9  deferred 4
Capabilities 161   verified 77  realized 41  planned 40  in_progress 3
accepted + live + NOT delivered ............ 9
live planned/in_progress capabilities ..... 43
```
**None of those 43 appears in any tool's answer to "what next".**

═══ 🛑🛑 THE MECHANISM, AND IT IS THE REAL FINDING ═══

`unrealized_capability` LOOKS like the build list — *"Nothing builds capability X"* — but fires only 3 times against 43 planned capabilities. `detect.rs` suppresses it three ways, and the decisive one is **`realized_via_component`**:

```rust
fn realized_via_component(&self, cap_id) -> bool {
    for alloc in outgoing(cap_id, ALLOCATED_TO) {
        if !incoming(alloc.to_id, REALIZES).is_empty() { return true }
    }
    false
}
```

⭐ **IT ASKS WHETHER THE COMPONENT HAS ANY ARTIFACT — NOT WHETHER THE CAPABILITY DOES.** Measured over the 39 live planned capabilities holding no artifact of their own:
```
suppressed by realized_via_component ....... 34   <-- the guard
suppressed by owner_claims_built ...........  2
would actually raise the gap ...............  5
```
⇒ **IN A MATURE PROJECT EVERY COMPONENT ALREADY HAS CODE, SO EVERY NEW PLANNED CAPABILITY IS BORN PRE-SUPPRESSED.** The four captured earlier the same day prove it: `cap:init-asks-which-harness` → `cmp:packaging` (1 artifact), `cap:nudge-absence-says-why` → `cmp:packaging` + `cmp:service` (6), `cap:decomposition-coverage-is-asked` → `cmp:detect` (1), `cap:the-design-interview-precedes-the-capture` → `cmp:skills` (2). All four are `planned`, none has an artifact, **and reflow2 will never ask what gets built for any of them.**

⚠️ THE SUPPRESSION IS DELIBERATE AND WELL-ARGUED, WHICH IS WHY THIS IS A DESIGN QUESTION RATHER THAN A BUG. The BL-42 comment in `detect.rs` records the reasoning: a storyflow adopt trial produced *"13 of 51 gaps, every one produced by following the adopt skill's own instruction to model artifacts coarsely over a system that is entirely built"*, and its stated bargain is *"the question is dropped and the number is kept (`realization` in `graph_report`)"*. **The guard solves the brownfield-adopt noise problem and creates the greenfield-increment blindness problem, and nothing recorded the second half.**

═══ ⚠️ A WRONG FIRST DIAGNOSIS, KEPT ON THE RECORD ═══

This session first blamed `owner_claims_built` — the guard that skips a capability whose owning Component is marked `realized`. **Measurement refuted it: only 2 of 39, and the four components involved are all `planned`, not `realized`.** The correct guard was found only by reading `realized_via_component` and counting. Recorded because the same failure — asserting a mechanism from a plausible description instead of measuring it — is the one `dec:idea-intent-crosses-designs` already documents twice about this project.

═══ 📌 WHAT WAS NOT CHECKED ═══

The computation predicts **5** capabilities would raise the gap; the gate reported **3** *"Nothing builds capability"* notes. The 2-item discrepancy was NOT run down — likely `is_discontinued` handling or scope filtering differing from the approximation used here (OBSOLETES targets). **The direction and magnitude of the finding do not depend on it, but the exact figure should not be quoted as though it were reconciled.** Also unchecked: whether `graph_report`'s `realization` number — the half of BL-42's bargain that was kept — is actually reachable by an agent asking what to build next.

MEASURED 2026-08-10 while starting req:what-changed-since-i-looked-and-by-whom (accepted; dev_storyflow api-boss fleet ask #3): THE CHANGE LEDGER RECORDS WHAT MOVED AND NEVER WHO MOVED IT.

    ChangeEvents in this design                     360
    ChangeEvents carrying AUTHORED_BY                 0
    changed subjects carrying AUTHORED_BY       79 of 378  (21%)
    edge types carrying a `seat` property          NONE except CLAIMS

THE REQUIREMENT ASKS FOR SOMETHING THE GRAPH CANNOT ANSWER. Its words are 'what changed since time T, AND BY WHOM - writes by OTHER SEATS over an interval'. Neither half of the who is recorded: ChangeEvents have no author at all, and seat identity (<machine>:<pid>:<mint>) lives only on CLAIMS edges, which are advisory, session-scoped and released at checkout. So even perfect authorship on ChangeEvents would answer 'which contributor', never 'which seat' - and on a shared server, which is where api-boss asked the question from, those are different questions.

WHAT EXISTS AND HOW FAR IT GETS. `changelog_view` already answers the WHAT half well: it compares two moments (Release or DesignEpoch ids), buckets the difference by rules the graph records, and returns `unmapped` rather than guessing. Its entries carry bucket, evidence, rule and subject_id - and no author. So the missing piece is exactly the who, not the what.

⚠️ WHY BUILDING THE QUERY FIRST WOULD BE WRONG. A `by` column derived from what exists would be populated for 21% of subjects and empty for the rest, and an empty cell would read as 'nobody' rather than 'not recorded' - the CANNOT-TELL-NONE-FROM-CANNOT-SAY failure this project has now met five times and names in `req:the-loop-says-what-is-owed-to-a-person`. It would look like the requirement was satisfied.

⇒ THE SUBSTRATE COMES FIRST: a ChangeEvent should carry who made it. That is a small change at every creation site and one open question - reflow2 has no notion of a CURRENT contributor, so the author must be supplied by the caller, and an optional parameter that is usually omitted reproduces the hole it was added to close. Whether attribution should be REQUIRED on a write, defaulted from a seat, or left optional is a real decision and it is the user's: making it required breaks every existing caller, and making it optional makes it decorative.

NOT A BLOCKER FOR THE WHAT HALF: `changelog_view` could be wired to this requirement as PARTIAL coverage today, honestly labelled, so the accepted intent stops reading as untouched while the who half is decided.

**ANTHONY, 2026-08-14, ON HIS WORK COMPUTER, JUST AFTER UPDATING: `● Unknown command: /capture-session`. THE SKILL EXISTS, IS SERVED, AND HAS NO COMMAND — AND THE ONE PLACE THAT CANNOT REPRODUCE THIS IS THE REPO WHERE THE DECISION WAS MADE.**

═══ MEASURED, 2026-08-14 ═══
```
getting-started/skills/     20 skills served
getting-started/commands/   11 command files
```
The eleven: `/adopt /brainstorm /debt /decisions /gaps /genesis /health /kpp /req /rules /where`.

Two of them front a TOOL, not a skill — `debt.md` calls `loop_status`, `decisions.md` queries. So **nine commands front a skill, and ELEVEN OF THE TWENTY SKILLS ARE FRONTED BY NOTHING**: capture-session, ci-gate, impact-check, ingest-corpus, link-artifacts, link-projects, parallel-work, plan-increments, report-friction, retire-from-design, revise-design.

⇒ On a consumer install those eleven are reachable only if the agent thinks to call `get_skill`. **`capture-session` is one of them, and it is the skill whose own text says the user should not have to be the trigger.**

═══ ⭐⭐ WHY NOBODY HERE COULD SEE IT ═══

Anthony, correcting this session: *"seems to work here fine, as well as /capture-intent."* **He is right, and the reason is the finding.**
```
.claude/skills/   20 directories   <- the SOURCE the binary compiles in
```
Claude Code loads a project's `.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md` as `/<name>`. This checkout holds all twenty **as sources**, so in reflow2's own repo every skill resolves as a slash command — including the eleven that ship with none. `/capture-intent` resolves here for that reason and cannot resolve on a consumer install, where nothing is copied (`dec:skills-served`).

**The decision's own question (`question:5aa0248a4e730d34`) asked whether commands should ship "so a consumer project gets the same ergonomics reflow2's own repo has". The repo's ergonomics come from the SKILL SOURCES, not from the commands — so the eleven were never sized against the twenty they were meant to match.** This is `req:the-tool-finds-its-own-blind-spots` arriving in the environment again, the same shape as the symlinked kit in `fact:updating-reflow2-does-not-update-a-project-already-set-up` and found the same day.

═══ 🛑 THE GUARD IS ASYMMETRIC, AND THAT IS WHY IT STAYED QUIET ═══

`dec:commands-are-the-exception` names ONE rot direction and closes it: *"a command could name a skill that no longer exists. `skill_lint` fails on exactly that."* **The opposite direction — a skill that no command names — is checked by nothing.** Grepped `tools/test_init.py` and `tools/skill_lint.py`: no assertion pins the command count or compares the two sets, so every skill added since has shipped uncovered in silence. Nine of the eleven uncovered skills postdate the decision.

═══ 🛑 AND THE RECORD SAYS EIGHT ═══

`dec:commands-are-the-exception`, `chg:commands-ship` and `ver:install-reaches-the-agent` all say **eight** slash commands and enumerate them. **Eleven ship** — `/adopt`, `/genesis` and `/rules` were added without the record moving. Nothing pins the number, so nothing noticed.

═══ ✅ THE OPEN QUESTION IS ANSWERED, AND THE ANSWER IS SHARPER THAN EITHER HYPOTHESIS ═══

This node previously left open WHY he expected `/capture-session` there, naming two readings: he reached for a skill he knew existed, or the project predates `dec:skills-served` and carried copied skills the update pruned.

**ANTHONY, 2026-08-14: "I believe the project pre-dates the capture-session skill."** MEASURED: capture-session shipped in `4a9f4e7` (PR #163) on **2026-08-12**, released in v0.29.0 the same day.

⇒ **THE PRUNED-COPY READING IS RULED OUT FOR THIS SKILL. A project set up before 2026-08-12 never held a capture-session copy to prune — the skill did not exist when its kit was written.** So the command was never there, was never removed, and could not have resolved at any point in that project's life.

⭐⭐ **WHICH LEAVES THE FIRST READING, AND IT IS A CLEANER DEMONSTRATION OF THE BLIND SPOT THAN THE MEASUREMENT ABOVE.** He knew the skill's NAME — and the place he could have learned it is the reflow2 checkout, where `.claude/skills/capture-session/` makes it a working slash command. **The maintainer learned a skill's name in the one environment where typing it works, then typed it where it never could.** The blind spot is not only that the repo cannot reproduce the defect; it is that the repo actively TEACHES the wrong affordance.

📌 SECOND-ORDER, AND IT COMPOUNDS: a project set up before 2026-08-12 also carries a KIT from before then, so whatever commands it does have are that generation's. `fact:updating-reflow2-does-not-update-a-project-already-set-up` — the binary updates, the per-project kit does not — applies to this machine directly. `reflow2 init . --harness=claude` is what refreshes it; `ls .claude/commands` says whether `init` was ever run there at all.

A CONSUMER'S NUMBER-ONE ASK IS MISDIAGNOSED, AND BUILDING IT WOULD CHANGE NOTHING. Alex's fleet (Grok Build harness, binary 0.24.0) filed a report on 2026-08-09 whose top-priority item is 'read-after-write for the creating session', from a real and repeatable symptom: immediately after a successful `add_decision`, a `set_decision_status` on the same id fails with `Node not found`, and a sequential retry succeeds. THE SYMPTOM IS REAL. THE CAUSE IS NOT WHAT THEY THINK. Read-after-write ALREADY HOLDS and cannot be the problem: `add_decision` takes an exclusive `write_lock()` (capture.rs:620), performs the write, and the guard drops before the response is returned, so any later lock acquisition sees the node. There is no visibility window to close. WHAT IS ACTUALLY HAPPENING is in their own environment notes: 'heavy parallel tool calls in a single agent turn'. Fire `add_decision` and `set_decision_status` concurrently and NOTHING ORDERS THEM. The RwLock serialises ACCESS, not INTENT — so `set_decision_status` can legitimately win the lock first, at which instant the node genuinely does not exist and `Node not found` is the correct answer. 'Retrying sequentially usually succeeds' is consistent with both readings, which is why the misdiagnosis is easy; the tell is that it reproduces ONLY in parallel batches. WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN THE BUG: their asks #1 and #2 are the same problem, and only #2 works. #1 (read-after-write) would be engineering effort spent making true something that is already true. #2 (optional `status` on `add_decision`) FIXES IT COMPLETELY, by collapsing two order-dependent calls into one that cannot be misordered. So the correct response to their highest-priority ask is to DROP IT and build their second. THE GENERAL FIX IS A DESCRIPTION, NOT A FEATURE: no tool description says that parallel batches carry no ordering, or that a create-then-modify pair must be sequenced. That is their section 1.2 ('parallel multi-write batches are fragile') and it is the honest root of both items. SAME SHAPE AS THIS WEEK'S OTHER FINDINGS: a caller cannot distinguish 'the write is not visible yet' from 'the write has not happened yet', and the surface never told them which world they are in — the same family as a value that cannot tell a choice from a default. NOT VERIFIED BY EXECUTION HERE: the mechanism was read from the code rather than reproduced with a concurrent client, so this is an analysis-grade finding. A reproduction would be two overlapping tool calls against one server asserting the failure disappears when they are sequenced.

MEASURED 2026-08-12, twice in one session. `cap:degraded-surface` is VERIFIED and this does NOT falsify it — the capability did exactly what it promises. What this records is that its diagnosis CANNOT REACH a whole class of caller.

WHAT WAS OBSERVED: `tools/reflow2_cli.py` began answering `error: set_artifact_checksum: tool not found` for a tool that plainly exists and had worked minutes earlier. The natural reading is that the tool was renamed or removed. Both readings are wrong.

THE MECHANISM, traced rather than guessed. A `--serve-shared` daemon (pid 728580) held the store's write lock — confirmed with `fuser .reflow2/graph/LOCK`. A second server could not open the store, so it correctly served the DEGRADED SURFACE: a handshake plus exactly one tool, `reflow2_unavailable`, whose name is the diagnosis, with the translated reason in the server instructions, the remedies in the tool payload, and an explicit do-not-conclude-reflow2-is-missing. All of that was built, and all of it was present.

⇒ AND NONE OF IT WAS SEEN, because the caller never asked for it. The CLI goes straight to `tools/call` by NAME. rmcp's tool router then answers `invalid_params("tool not found")` — rmcp-2.2.0 `handler/server/router/tool.rs:567`, a generic string with no context, not reflow2's text at all. The CLI printed it faithfully. THE DIAGNOSIS LIVES IN THE HANDSHAKE AND THE TOOL LIST, AND A BY-NAME CALLER READS NEITHER.

So the careful part — "do not conclude reflow2 is missing" — was rendered as, precisely, "this tool does not exist". The capability's own stated purpose is that the server explains its own absence instead of vanishing; against a direct caller it vanishes.

WHY IT MATTERS BEYOND THE CLI: any client that caches a tool list, or that calls by name from a script, is in this class. The degraded surface is reachable only by a client that re-reads the surface after failing — which is the client least likely to be a script.

FIX DIRECTION, NOT DECIDED: the refusal for an unknown tool name is rmcp's, so reflow2 cannot reword it in place. Either the CLI re-reads `tools/list` on any `tool not found` and surfaces `reflow2_unavailable` if that is all there is, or the degraded server declines the call in a way that carries its own text. The first is cheap, local, and needs no upstream change.

NOTE ON THE LOCK ITSELF: this is NOT `fact:defect-rebuild-strands-the-shared-server`, which is a deleted-inode spawn failure. Different cause, and that one is fixed. This is ordinary single-writer contention behaving as designed, reported unrecognisably.

MEASURED 2026-08-09 by READING dev_storyflow's committed export (1,373 nodes, 2,570 edges, stamp 0.26.1) at Anthony's direction. READ ONLY — nothing was written to storyflow, and `describe_designs` was used first precisely because it reads the sidecar without opening the store.

ANTHONY PREDICTED IT BEFORE THE MEASUREMENT: "I can almost already tell you that reflow2 does not interface with dynograph-foundation the same way that storyflow interfaces with dynograph-foundation." **CONFIRMED, AND THE SHAPE IS MORE USEFUL THAN THE PREDICTION.**

=== THE TWO CONSUMERS USE DIFFERENT SURFACES THROUGH DIFFERENT TRANSPORTS ===

reflow2 (projectB) consumes dynograph as a **RUST LIBRARY API**, five `required` interfaces:
  ifc:req-dyno-core-api        Core model types (Schema, Value, DynoError)
  ifc:req-dyno-graph-api       Graph algorithms API
  ifc:req-dyno-storage-api     StorageEngine Rust API
  ifc:req-dyno-resolution-api  EntityResolver API
  ifc:req-dyno-vector-api      Vector, HNSW and statistics API

storyflow (projectD) consumes it as a **REST API OVER HTTP**:
  ifc:dynograph_api                      DynoGraph (dag_plus) REST API
  ifc:dynograph_temporal_api             temporal endpoints
  ifc:dynograph_inferences               generic inference-edge endpoint
  ifc:dynograph_relationships_catalog    relationships catalog endpoint
  ifc:dynograph_apply_fixes              apply-fixes proposal-batch contract
  ifc:foundation_api                     Foundation engine API

⭐⭐ SO THE DIAMOND DOES NOT MEET AT AN INTERFACE. IT MEETS AT DYNOGRAPH'S INTERNALS. Two consumers, two DISJOINT surfaces, one shared implementation beneath both. That reframes the risk rather than dissolving it: a change confined to the Rust crate API cannot touch storyflow's REST endpoints, and a change to the engine BENEATH both touches everything — and **neither consumer's graph can see that layer at all**, because each declares only the surface it personally uses.

⇒ THE CHECK THAT WOULD ACTUALLY HAVE ANSWERED THE 2026 INCIDENT is therefore NOT "do B and D require the same interface" — they do not, and a naive diamond detector would have reported all-clear. It is "**did the change reach below both published surfaces into shared implementation**", which is a question about A's OWN internal structure and is answerable only inside A's graph.

=== ⚠️ THE PREREQUISITE IS UNDONE ON D'S SIDE ===

**storyflow declares ZERO `required` interfaces.** 53 Interfaces: 44 `internal`, 9 `unset`, 0 `required`, 0 `published`. That is EXACTLY the state reflow2 was in on 2026-08-06, before PR #130 — and `dec:linked-repos-poc` named it then: "the linking works, the labelling does not exist." **The labelling now exists on B's side and not on D's, so the seam is still one-ended and nothing pairs.** Declaring dynograph's endpoints `required` in storyflow is the cheapest possible next step and it is entirely inside a graph Anthony owns.

THE LOCAL LINEAGE GATE'S VERDICT DEPENDS ON WHEN YOU RUN IT RELATIVE TO COMMITTING — NOT ONLY ON WHAT THE FILE SAYS. Measured 2026-08-14 while amending PR #175 to cover captures made after its first export.

SEQUENCE, REPRODUCIBLE:
```
1. git checkout origin/main -- docs/design/reflow2.json    (restore baseline f9a65a)
2. export_graph --overwrite                                 (writes 4b93b0, prev=f9a65a)
3. reflow2_check --export docs/design/reflow2.json          -> FAIL, exit 1
     "records sha256:f9a65a… where sha256:5c393f… is expected"
4. git commit --amend                                       (HEAD now carries 4b93b0)
5. reflow2_check --export docs/design/reflow2.json          -> OK, exit 0, 80 notes
```
**THE FILE WAS BYTE-IDENTICAL AT STEPS 3 AND 5.** Only the git HEAD moved. The gate reads the export committed at HEAD to decide what the new file should chain FROM; before the amend that was the branch's earlier export (`5c393f`), after it that was main (`f9a65a`), and only the second comparison is the one CI makes.

⇒ **THE OPERATIONAL RULE: RUN `reflow2_check` AFTER COMMITTING OR AMENDING, NEVER BEFORE.** Run beforehand it answers a question nobody asked — whether the working file chains from a commit that is about to stop existing.

⭐ THE PAIR THIS COMPLETES, AND IT IS WHY THIS IS WORTH RECORDING SEPARATELY. `fact:the-local-lineage-gate-cannot-see-a-stacked-export` records the OPPOSITE error: the local gate PASSING on a commit CI rejected, because CI checks out the PR MERGE commit where `HEAD~1` is MAIN. Together they say the same thing from both sides — **the gate is always reasoning about a PAIR of commits, and both failure modes come from that pair differing between local and CI.** Neither is a bug in the gate; both are a bug in when it is trusted.
  · stacked branch → local PASSES, CI FAILS (that fact)
  · pre-amend → local FAILS, CI would have PASSED (this fact)

📌 THE STEP THAT MADE THE AMEND CORRECT, worth keeping because skipping it is the silent failure: **restore the export from `origin/main` BEFORE re-exporting.** Exporting on top of the branch's own committed export would have chained `5c393f → new`, giving TWO hops against the merge base and the CI failure `dec:export-once-per-pr` exists to prevent. The restore is what keeps it one hop.

⚠️ NOT ESTABLISHED: whether the gate could tell these apart itself — e.g. by naming which commit it compared against, so a reader can see it is answering about `HEAD` rather than about the merge base. That would make both failure modes self-explaining rather than needing two recorded facts to interpret. Not attempted here.

**ONE ROCKSDB STORE SERVES EVERY GIT BRANCH, SO THE LIVE GRAPH DOES NOT BRANCH — AND THE PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCE IS A WORKFLOW RULE NOTHING STATES: YOU CANNOT HAVE TWO OPEN PULL REQUESTS THAT BOTH MAKE GRAPH WRITES.**

OBSERVED 2026-08-14 while holding PR #182 open (design-record writes) and being asked to build the command coverage accepted in it. `.reflow2/graph` is a single store shared by whatever branch is checked out; `git checkout <branch>` does not switch it. So any export taken on a second branch carries **the first branch's uncommitted graph writes too**, and both PRs then contain each other's nodes.

⇒ **THE CALL MADE, AND WHY:** the command-coverage build was FOLDED INTO #182 rather than opened as a third PR. **One PR at a time while graph writes are outstanding.** The alternative — branching from main and exporting — would have produced an export containing #182's nodes with a `prev_content_hash` pointing at main, i.e. a document silently claiming work that another open PR also claims. `rule:the-export-is-written-once-per-branch` and `dec:export-once-per-pr` constrain the export WITHIN a branch and say nothing about two branches sharing one store.

⚠️ **NOT MEASURED HERE:** the collision was avoided rather than reproduced. What is established is the mechanism (one store, no per-branch isolation) and the decision taken because of it — not an observed corrupted export. A deliberate reproduction would be cheap and has not been done.

MEASURED 2026-08-13, by running the gate on both sides of the same commit.

WHAT HAPPENED: a branch was based on another unmerged branch that had already exported. `reflow2_check` was reasoned to be safe because the chain was sound commit to commit — main `029fd47f` → `6e7f7717` → `bfcc8350`, each export recording its predecessor's content hash. CI FAILED the LINEAGE clause anyway, reporting that it found `6e7f7717` where `029fd47f` was expected.

⭐ THE MEASUREMENT, taken afterwards on the exact commit CI rejected:

    git checkout <the stacked commit>
    python3 tools/reflow2_check.py --export docs/design/reflow2.json
    → reflow2 check: OK — design and build agree (75 note(s))

**THE LOCAL GATE PASSES ON THE COMMIT CI FAILS, AND BOTH ARE CORRECT.** `_export_pair` compares HEAD against HEAD~1. Locally HEAD~1 is the branch's own parent — the other unmerged branch — so the chain checks out. In CI, GitHub Actions checks out the PULL REQUEST'S MERGE COMMIT, whose first parent is MAIN. Against that base the branch holds TWO exporting commits, which is two hops, which is the violation.

⇒ THE GENERAL FORM: **the local lineage check cannot detect a stacked-export violation by construction, because the thing that makes it a violation is the merge base, and locally there is no merge base.** A green local gate on a branch stacked on another unmerged branch is not weak evidence — it is no evidence, and it will read as reassurance.

This is not a defect in the gate. `dec:export-once-per-pr` is stated per PULL REQUEST, and the tool's own failure message already names this as its third cause — "THIS PR ALREADY HAS AN EARLIER EXPORTING COMMIT, and your chain is sound… FOLD the exporting commits into a single last commit instead" — added by `chg:lineage-message-names-its-decision` precisely because the earlier wording misled. The message was right and was reached only after CI had already spent the round trip.

⇒ WHAT WOULD HAVE CAUGHT IT EARLIER, and it is one command rather than a build — **COUNT THE COMMITS, NOT THE PATHS**:

    git log --format=%h origin/main..HEAD -- docs/design/reflow2.json | wc -l

More than 1 means the PR violates the rule whatever the hashes say. Measured on this branch: **1** after the fix, **2** on the version CI rejected.

⚠️ THE OBVIOUS-LOOKING FORM OF THIS COMMAND IS BROKEN, and it was written into this node's first version before being caught: `git log --format= --name-only … | sort -u | wc -l` counts distinct PATHS, and since the path is pinned by the pathspec it prints 1 forever — including on the two-commit branch CI had already rejected. It is the same shape as `fact:a-piped-gate-reports-the-pipes-exit-code-not-the-gates`: a check whose output looks exactly like a pass no matter what is true.

📌 AND THE REASON A STACKED BRANCH LOOKED RIGHT IN THE FIRST PLACE, recorded because the next person will have the same reason: the requirement being satisfied existed only in the other branch's export, so basing on main appeared to risk a SATISFIES edge pointing at a node main does not hold.
